Ergo non apud Deum justificatus est ex operibus. Valet argumentatio, Quia gloriatio in nobisipsis, non tollitur per legem operum, sed per legem fidei, Rom. 3. 27. Nam in quæstione apud homines, an Abraham sit justus, proferre potest Abraham opera sua, & gloriari, dicens, Ego ostendam tibi opera mea, & ita apud homines justificabitur, seu pro justo reputabitur ex operibus: At in quæstione, an sit justus coram Deo, renunciare oportet eum suis operibus, & confugere ad promissionem benedictionis in Christo, ipsius semine venturo, ut justificetur ex fide in Christum solâ.
units.tr: He confirms this thesis about Abraham with five arguments. The first argument: If Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast of, but not before God; that is, he has something to boast of. Therefore he was not justified before God by works. The inference holds, because boasting in ourselves is excluded not by the law of works but by the law of faith, Romans 3:27. For in the question among men whether Abraham is righteous, Abraham can bring forward his works and boast, saying, "I will show you my works," and so among men he will be justified, or will be reckoned righteous, by works. But in the question whether he is righteous before God, he must renounce his works and flee to the promise of blessing in Christ, his seed who was to come, so that he may be justified by faith in Christ alone.

units.la: Verf. 3. Quid enim Scriptura dicit? Credidit autem Abraham Deo, & imputatum est ei ad justitiam.
units.tr: Verse 3. For what does Scripture say? "Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness."

units.la: Ratio 2. Scriptura testatur, Genes. 15. 6. Abrahamum justificatum esse ex fide, seu ex fide imputatam fuisse ei justitiam. Ergo non ex operibus, sed ex fide justificatus est.
units.tr: Argument 2. Scripture testifies, Genesis 15:6, that Abraham was justified by faith, or that righteousness was reckoned to him through faith. Therefore he was justified not by works but by faith.

units.la: Verf. 4. Atqui ei qui operatur, merces non imputatur ex gratia, sed ex debito.
units.tr: Verse 4. Now to one who works, the wage is not reckoned as grace but as debt.

units.la: Ratio 3. Mercenario operanti, seu justitiam ex operibus quærenti, merces non potest esse gratuita, sed ex debito, seu ex merito tribuenda est: Assumere licet, At Abrahamo merces imputata erat ex gratia. Ergo Abraham non erat mercenarius, seu qui justificationem ex operibus quærebat.
units.tr: Argument 3. To a hireling who works, that is, who seeks righteousness by works, the wage cannot be given freely, but must be paid as something owed, or as something merited. It may be assumed: but to Abraham the wage was reckoned as grace. Therefore Abraham was not a hireling, or one who sought justification by works.

units.la: Verf. 5. Ei vero qui non operatur, sed credit in eum qui justificat impium, imputatur fides sua ad justitiam.
units.tr: Verse 5. But to one who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned for righteousness.

units.la: Ratio quarta, in hunc sensum, Ei qui non est mercenarius, sed renuncians justitiæ propriæ, credit in Deum, qui impium, ad Christum fugientem scilicet, justificat gratis, fides sua imputatur ad justitiam. Assumere licet, At talis erat Abrahami. Ergo Abraham non est justificatus ex operibus coram Deo, sed fides ei imputata est in justitiam; seu, Benedictio promissa in Christo venturo, fide recepta per Abrahamum, ei imputata est in justitiam.
units.tr: Argument 4, to this effect: To one who is not a hireling, but who renounces his own righteousness, believes in God who justifies the ungodly freely, namely one who flees to Christ, his faith is reckoned for righteousness. It may be assumed: but such was Abraham. Therefore Abraham was not justified before God by works, but his faith was reckoned to him for righteousness; or, the blessing promised in the Christ who was to come, received by faith by Abraham, was reckoned to him for righteousness.

units.la: Verf. 6 Sicut etiam David declarat beatum eum hominem, cui Deus imputat justitiam absque operibus: dicens,
units.tr: Verse 6. Just as David also declares the blessedness of the man to whom God reckons righteousness apart from works, saying,

units.la: Verf. 7. Beati quibus remissæ sunt legis transgressiones, & quorum tecta sunt peccata,
units.tr: Verse 7. Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven, and whose sins are covered.

units.la: Verf. 8. Beatus vir cui non imputarit Dominus peccatum.
units.tr: Verse 8. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not reckon sin.

units.la: Ratio 5. David testatur in Psal. 32. 12. felicitatem dari ei cui justitia imputatur absque operibus, & cujus justitia consistit, non in bonis operibus, sed in remissione peccatorum, seu malorum operum. Ergo talis fuit justificatio Abrahami necessario: consistens scilicet, non in operum ejus perfectione, sed in remissione ipsius peccatorum. Idem intellige de justificatione omnium, quod jam ostendit Apostolus.
units.tr: Argument 5. David testifies in Psalm 32:1–2 that happiness is given to him to whom righteousness is reckoned apart from works, and whose righteousness consists not in good works but in the forgiveness of sins, or of evil works. Therefore the justification of Abraham was necessarily of this kind: consisting, namely, not in the perfection of his works but in the forgiveness of his sins. Understand the same concerning the justification of all, which the Apostle has now shown.

units.la: Verf. 9 Ista igitur beatitatis declaratio in circumcisionem solum an & in praeputium cadit? Dicimus enim imputatam fuisse Abrahae fidem ad justitiam.
units.tr: Verse 9. Does this declaration of blessedness, then, fall upon the circumcision only, or upon the uncircumcision also? For we say that faith was reckoned to Abraham for righteousness.

units.la: Secunda Pars.
units.tr: Second Part.

units.la: Secunda pars Capitis, in qua probat hanc justificationis Abrahami, & vitae aeternae, seu beatitudinis obtinendae rationem, per fidem scilicet, communem esse praeputio, seu Gentibus, & circumcisioni seu Judaeis. Proponitur quaestio hoc versu: cujus responsio sequitur reliquis versibus dum probat communem esse Gentibus & Judaeis.
units.tr: The second part of the chapter, in which he proves that this manner of Abraham's justification, and of obtaining eternal life, or blessedness, namely through faith, is common to the uncircumcision, or the Gentiles, and to the circumcision, or the Jews. The question is put in this verse, and its answer follows in the remaining verses, while he proves it common to Gentiles and Jews.

units.la: Verf. 10. Quomodo ergo imputata est? quum esset in circumcisione, an quum esset in praeputio? non in circumcisione, sed in praeputio.
units.tr: Verse 10. How then was it reckoned? When he was in circumcision, or when he was in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision.

units.la: Probat hanc justificandi, & beatitudinis obtinendae rationem, communem esse praeputiatis, seu Gentibus, non minus quam circumcisis Judaeis, septem argumentis. Primum argumentum, a statu incircumcisionis in quo erat Abraham, cum justus pronunciatus est, ut patet ex historia Genes. 15. 6. Imputata est Abrahamo justitia per fidem, cum adhuc esset incircumcisus: Ergo haec justificationis ratio communis est, etiam incircumcisis credentibus.
units.tr: He proves with seven arguments that this manner of justifying and of obtaining blessedness is common to the uncircumcised, or the Gentiles, no less than to the circumcised Jews. The first argument is from the state of uncircumcision in which Abraham was when he was pronounced righteous, as is clear from the history in Genesis 15:6. Righteousness was reckoned to Abraham through faith while he was still uncircumcised. Therefore this manner of justification is common also to believers who are uncircumcised.

units.la: Verf. 11. Et signum accepit circumcisionis quod esset sigillum justitiae fidei receptae in praeputio: ut esset pater omnium credentium in praeputio, imputata etiam ipsis justitia:
units.tr: Verse 11. And he received the sign of circumcision, as a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had while uncircumcised, so that he might be the father of all who believe while uncircumcised, that righteousness might be reckoned to them also.

units.la: Verf. 12. Et pater circumcisionis, iis videlicet qui non solum sunt ex circumcisione, sed qui etiam incedunt vestigiis fidei patris nostri Abrahami, quae fuit in praeputio.
units.tr: Verse 12. And the father of circumcision, namely to those who are not only of the circumcision, but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith of our father Abraham, which he had while uncircumcised.

units.la: Abraham à Deo signum accepit circumcisionis, ad obsignandum fœdus gratiæ, seu justitiam fidei, quam habebat incircumcisus, in eum finem, ut pater esset Fidelium incircumcisorum, pariter & Circumciforum, qui nempe & sunt filij carnis, & filij fidei Abrahæ. Ergo justitia fidei communis est circumcisis & incircumcisis fidelibus, seu sequentibus vestigia fidei Abrahami nondum circumcili. Dicitur autem Abraham pater Credentium, eo quod sit primum eminens exemplum fidei, & justitiæ per fidem imputatæ, & exemplo suo autor omnibus ut credant.
units.tr: Abraham received from God the sign of circumcision, to seal the covenant of grace, or the righteousness of faith, which he had while uncircumcised, to this end, that he might be the father of uncircumcised believers, and likewise of the circumcised, who are indeed both children of the flesh and children of the faith of Abraham. Therefore the righteousness of faith is common to circumcised and uncircumcised believers, or to those who follow the footsteps of the faith of Abraham while not yet circumcised. Abraham is called the father of believers because he is the first and most eminent example of faith and of righteousness reckoned through faith, and by his example he is the author to all that they should believe.

units.la: Verf. 13. Non enim per Legem promissio cessit Abrahamo aut semini ejus, ut hæres esset mundi, sed per justitiam fidei.
units.tr: Verse 13. For the promise did not come to Abraham or to his seed through the Law, that he should be heir of the world, but through the righteousness of faith.

units.la: Probat Abrahamum patrem esse non nisi fidelium tantum, incircumciforum, pariter & circumcisorum, & simul addit argumentum tertium, Promissio facta Abrahæ & semini ejus, quod hæres futurus fuerit terræ Canaan in typo, & mundi & cœli in veritate, restitutus ad jus in Adamo deperditum, non obtigit ei per legem, seu ex conditione operum, sed obtigit ei per absolutam promissionem justificato jam per fidem, & fidei justitiam habenti. Ergo ejus filij non sunt ij qui sunt ex lege, quærentes scilicet justitiam ex operibus, sed ij soli qui sunt ex fide, quærrentes justitiam ex fide, id est, omnes & soli credentes, circumcisi pariter & incircumcisi, quibus ex æquo communis est justitia fidei, & hæreditas promissa. Valet argumentum, nam si pater Abraham non est hæres mundi, nec habet justitiam nisi per fidem. Certè nulli sunt ejus filij præter fideles, qui ex fide habent justitiam, & ex justitia hæreditatem.
units.tr: He proves that Abraham is the father not of the circumcised but only of believers, both uncircumcised and circumcised, and at the same time adds a third argument: The promise made to Abraham and to his seed, that he would be heir of the land of Canaan in type, and of the world and heaven in truth, restored to the right lost in Adam, did not come to him through the law, or by the condition of works, but came to him by an absolute promise, he being already justified by faith and possessing the righteousness of faith. Therefore his sons are not those who are of the law, that is, who seek righteousness by works, but those alone who are of faith, who seek righteousness from faith; that is, all and only believers, circumcised and uncircumcised alike, to whom the righteousness of faith and the promised inheritance are equally common. The argument holds, for if Abraham the father is not the heir of the world, he has no righteousness except through faith. Certainly there are no sons of his except the faithful, who have righteousness from faith and inheritance from righteousness.

units.la: Verf. 14. Etenim si ii qui ex Lege sunt, hæredes sunt, inanis facta est fides, & cassa reddita est illa promissio:
units.tr: Verse 14. For if they which are of the law be heirs, faith is made void, and the promise made of none effect.

units.la: confirmans etiam superius, Si qui ex Lege sunt, seu qui quærunt justitiam ex operibus, filij essent Abrahæ, & hæredes vitæ, & participes justitiæ, tum fides inanis redderetur, & promissio vana: At hoc absurdum. Ergo qui ex lege sunt, hæredes non sunt, sed soli credentes filii sunt Abrahami, & hæredes vitæ & justitiæ. Valet argumentum, quia si ex fide & promissione datur justitia & hæreditas, dantur etiam gratuito. Si autem ex operibus & lege dantur, tum ex debito & ex merito, non autem ex gratia. Meritum enim seu debitum tollit gratiam, & per consequens fidem & promissionem irritas reddit.
units.tr: Confirming what was said above: if those who are of the law, that is, those who seek righteousness by works, were the sons of Abraham and heirs of life and partakers of righteousness, then faith would be made void and the promise empty. But this is absurd. Therefore those who are of the law are not heirs; only the believers are the sons of Abraham and heirs of life and righteousness. The argument holds, because if righteousness and inheritance are given by faith and promise, they are also given freely. But if they are given by works and law, then they are given by debt and merit, and not by grace. For merit or debt abolishes grace, and consequently renders faith and promise void.

units.la: Verf. 15.
units.tr: Verse 15.

units.la: Verf. 15. Nam Lex iram efficit : ubi enim non est Lex , ibi nec transgressio est.
units.tr: Verse 15. For the law worketh wrath: for where no law is, there is no transgression.

units.la: Arg. 5. Confirmans superius, Lex iram affert quaerentibus justitiam ex operibus scilicet, id est in peccati reos, condemnationem & mortem pronunciat propter transgressiones, quae nullae effent fi lex non eflet. Ergo qui ex lege sunt, justitiae & vitae non sunt haeredes, sed foli & omnes qui ex fide sunt, incircumcisi pariter & circumcisi haeredes justitiae & vitae sunt.
units.tr: Argument 5. Confirming what was said above: the law brings wrath upon those who seek righteousness by works, that is, it pronounces condemnation and death upon those guilty of sin because of transgressions, which would not exist if there were no law. Therefore those who are of the law are not heirs of righteousness and life; only those who are of faith, the uncircumcised as well as the circumcised, are heirs of righteousness and life.

units.la: Verf. 16. Propterea ex fide est haereditas, ut fit per gratiam ut firma fit promissio toti femini: id est, non solum ei quod est ex Lege, verumetiam ei quod est ex fide Abrahami, qui est pater omnium nostrum,
units.tr: Verse 16. Therefore it is of faith, that it might be by grace, to the end that the promise might be sure to all the seed: that is, not only to that which is of the law, but also to that which is of the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all.

units.la: Arg. 6. Eo ipso consilio, Deus constituit ut haereditas eflet ex fide, ut appareat esse ex gratia, seu per gratiam. Ergo foli & omnes fideles incircumcisi, pariter & circumcisi sunt haeredes. Valet argumentum, quia fides & gratia commeant, mutuo fe ponunt & tollunt, fides sola gratia nititur, solam gratiam amplectitur, gratia tantum credenti promittitur & datur ; Posito ergo quod haereditas fit per gratiam, ponitur etiam quod fit per fidem, & posito quod fit per fidem, ponitur etiam quod fit per gratiam, & quod fideles foli sint ex gratia haeredes.
units.tr: Argument 6. By this very counsel God ordained that the inheritance should be of faith, so that it might appear to be of grace, or by grace. Therefore the believers alone, uncircumcised as well as circumcised, are heirs. The argument holds, because faith and grace go together, and they mutually posit and remove one another: faith rests on grace alone, embraces grace alone, and grace is promised and given only to the believer. Therefore, given that the inheritance is by grace, it is also posited that it is by faith; and given that it is by faith, it is also posited that it is by grace, and that the believers alone are heirs by grace.

units.la: Ut firma ] Arg. 7. Haereditas est ex fide, & per gratiam, ex Deo consilio, ut promissio firma fit toti femini, non solum ei quod est femen Abrahae ex lege naturae, & simul fidem habet, hoc est circumcisis Judaeis fidelibus, sed etiam ei femini quod non est ex lege naturae seu carne, sed tantum ex fide Abrahae, id est incircumcisis fidelibus inter Gentes : Ergo nisi promissionem justitiae, & haereditatis, ex conditione legis perficiendae suspendentes, infirmam & incertam reddere vellemus, totum femen Abrahae, seu omnes & foli credentes circumcisi & incircumcisi, sunt ex fide haeredes cum patre Abrahamo, qui secundum fidem pater est omnium nostrum credentium ex Judaeis & Gentibus. Res patet, quia lex seu conditio operum promissionem haereditatis redderet infirmam, & prorsus incertam : siquidem quod a nobis & nostris operibus pendet firmum esse non potest, tum quia nos mutabiles sumus, tum quia conditio operum jam propter infirmitatem nostram est impossibilis. Sed quod ex gratia est,
units.tr: That the promise may be sure ] Argument 7. The inheritance is of faith and by grace, by the counsel of God, so that the promise may be sure to the whole seed: not only to that which is the seed of Abraham by the law of nature and at the same time has faith (that is, the circumcised Jewish believers), but also to that seed which is not of the law of nature or of the flesh, but only of the faith of Abraham (that is, the uncircumcised believers among the Gentiles). Therefore, unless we wished to make the promise of righteousness and inheritance weak and uncertain by making it depend on the condition of fulfilling the law, the whole seed of Abraham, that is, all and only the believers, circumcised and uncircumcised, are heirs of faith together with the father Abraham, who according to faith is the father of us all who believe, both of the Jews and of the Gentiles. This is plain, because a law or condition of works would render the promise of inheritance weak and wholly uncertain: for what depends on us and our works cannot be firm, both because we are changeable and because the condition of works is now impossible on account of our weakness. But what is of grace,

units.la: Quod per fidem est, Quod in Christo est, firmum est necessario. Quia nititur Dei immutabili benevolentia, & Christi merito.
units.tr: What is by faith and what is in Christ is necessarily firm, because it rests on the unchanging goodwill of God and on the merit of Christ.

units.la: Verf. 17. Sicut scriptum est, patrem multorum gentium constitui te ) coram eo cui credidit, Deo videlicet, vivificante mortuos: et vocante quae non sunt, tanquam sint.
units.tr: Verse 17. As it is written, I have made thee a father of many nations, before him whom he believed, even God, who quickeneth the dead, and calleth those things which be not as though they were.

units.la: Tertia Pars.
units.tr: The Third Part.

units.la: TErtia pars Capitis, In qua commendatur fides Abrahami, in usum omnium fidelium, ut discant ejus exemplo magis magisque credere. Elogii seu commendationis fidei Abrahami rationes sunt sex.
units.tr: The third part of the chapter, in which the faith of Abraham is commended, for the use of all believers, so that they may learn by his example to believe more and more. There are six reasons for the praise or commendation of Abraham's faith.

units.la: Prima ratio, Quia Abraham (ob fidem suam scilicet) Dei oraculo & speciali sententia, declaratus est pater multarum nationum, & proinde pater omnium nostrum credentium, secundum fidem: Siquidem sicut vi divinae promissionis, Abraham genuit Isacum, & non vi naturae; sic vi divinae promissionis pollicentis fore, ut esset pater multarum nationum, Abraham amplexus est in filios fideles omnes, in ipsius semen inserendos; atque ita in virtute promissionis quasi genuit, vel concepit fideles sibi ut filios promissos, id quod ostendit clarius, vocando Abrahamum patrem fidelium, καὶ ἐναντι τῷ Θεῷ, non tantum coram Deo, seu in conspectu Dei, id est, spirituali modo, & in Dei aestimatione patrem, sed etiam ad similitudinem Dei, e regione, per aliquam similitudinem, respondentem Deo cui credidit; siquidem in actu fidei Abraham in luce faciei omnipotentis Dei ipsum alloquentis, constitutus, credebat quod Deus promittebat; quos Deus filios promittebat, ille per fidem praesentes statuebat, atque ita pater aliquo modo eorum evadebat, ad similitudinem Dei.
units.tr: First reason. Because Abraham, on account of his faith, was declared by God's oracle and special sentence to be the father of many nations, and therefore the father of all of us who believe, according to faith. For just as Abraham begot Isaac by the power of the divine promise and not by the power of nature, so by the power of the divine promise, which pledged that he would be the father of many nations, Abraham embraced all faithful persons as sons to be grafted into his seed. Thus, by the force of the promise, he as it were begot or conceived the faithful as his promised sons. This is shown more clearly by calling Abraham the father of believers [καὶ ἐναντι τῷ Θεῷ], not only before God, or in the sight of God, that is, in a spiritual manner and as father in God's estimation, but also in the likeness of God, opposite, by a certain resemblance, answering to the God in whom he believed. For in the act of faith Abraham, placed in the light of the face of almighty God who spoke to him, believed what God promised. Those whom God promised as sons, he by faith set before himself as present, and so became in some way their father, in the likeness of God.

units.la: Vivificante ] Ratio 2. Quia Abraham per fidem defixit oculos in Dei omnipotentiam & veritatem, efficaciter producentem vitam ex morte, & entia ex nihilo, & cum effectu vocantem nondum entia, ut sint seu ut entitatem habeant: cui omnipotenti veritati cum Abraham credidit, fides ipsius induit quandam similitudinem veritatis Dei omnipotentis, & efficiacis.
units.tr: Who quickens. Reason 2. Because Abraham by faith fixed his eyes on the omnipotence and truth of God, who effectually brings life out of death and things out of nothing, and who with effect calls the things that are not as though they were, that is, so that they have being. When Abraham believed this almighty and effectual truth, his faith took on a certain likeness to the truth of almighty and effective God.

units.la: Verf. 18. Qui Abrahamus contra spem sub spe credidit fore ut ipse sierit pater multarum gentium; secundum id quo ei dictum fuerat, Ita erit semen tuum.
units.tr: Verse 18. Who against hope believed in hope that he would become the father of many nations, according to what had been said to him: So shall your seed be.

units.la: Ratio 3. Quia Abraham credidit sub spe spirituali, hoc est, firmam & invictam concepit in corde fiduciam, cum spe eventus promissi firma & vivaci; contra ipsem, scilicet carnis, rationis & totius naturæ, quæ nihil nisi impossibilitatem objectabant, & quasi affirmabant fieri non potuisse ejus semen, sicut Deus dixerat.
units.tr: Reason 3. Because Abraham believed in spiritual hope, that is, he conceived in his heart a firm and unconquered trust, together with a firm and lively hope of the promised outcome, against the flesh itself, reason, and all of nature, which objected nothing but impossibility, and as it were affirmed that his seed could not come about, as God had said.

units.la: Verf. 19. Ac minime infirmus fide non consideravit suum ipsius corpus jam emortuum, quum centum circiter natus esset annos, nec emortuum uterum Sarae.
units.tr: Verse 19. And, not being weak in faith, he did not consider his own body, already dead, since he was about a hundred years old, nor the dead womb of Sarah.

units.la: Ratio 4. Quia non fuit imbecillis fide, nec insipiens: non consideravit, seu non æstimavit impedimenta fidei suæ objecta, à se & uxore sua, quasi jam mortuus, respectu prolificationis, sed potius potentiam & veritatem Dei promittentis magnificabat.
units.tr: Reason 4. Because he was not weak in faith, nor foolish. He did not consider, or did not reckon, the obstacles to his faith, namely that he and his wife were as good as dead as far as bearing children went, but rather he magnified the power and truth of God who promised.

units.la: Verf. 20. Ad hanc promissionem autem Dei non addubitavit incredulitate: sed corroboratus fuit fide: tributa gloria Deo:
units.tr: Verse 20. He did not waver in unbelief at the promise of God, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God.

units.la: Ratio 5. Quia non disputavit adversus promissionem, nec cessit objectionibus, quas infidelitas suggesserat, sed fortiter defendit Dei verbum, & tentationibus se oppositi; gloriam veritatis & omnipotentiæ Deo tribuens.
units.tr: Reason 5. Because he did not dispute against the promise, nor yield to the objections which unbelief suggested, but stoutly defended the word of God against the temptations set against him, giving glory to the truth and omnipotence of God.

units.la: Verf. 21. Ac plene certioratus est, eum quod promiserat, posse etiam efficere.
units.tr: Verse 21. And, being fully assured, he was persuaded that what he had promised he was also able to do.

units.la: Ratio 6. Quia gloriam veritatis tribuit Deo loquenti, explena persuasione potentiæ ipsius ad præstandum promissa: Nam data promissione, nulla quæstio est de voluntate faciendi: sed quæ superest quæstio, quærit de potentia promittentis; Qua quæstione missa, Abraham acquievit in promissione illius, quem omnipotentem sciebat.
units.tr: Reason 6. Because he ascribed glory to God's truth in speaking, through a full persuasion of his power to perform what was promised. For once the promise is given, there is no question about the will to do it; the only remaining question concerns the power of the one who promises. When that question was set aside, Abraham rested in the promise of him whom he knew to be almighty.

units.la: Verf. 22. Quapropter etiam hoc imputatum est ei ad justitiam.
units.tr: Verse 22. Therefore it was also reckoned to him for righteousness.

units.la: Ratio 7. commendationis fidei Abrahami, Quod ipsius fides (hoc actu ostendens se veram esse, eam scilicet quæ hominem in Dei conspectu humiliatum, & exinanitum, Deo promittenti agglutinat) in justitiam imputata sit; Quia nempe benedictionem in semine suo venturo, id est Christo promissam, pro justitia sua amplectebatur.
units.tr: Reason 7 of the commendation of Abraham's faith: that his faith (showing by this act that it is true faith, that is, the faith which joins a man, humbled and emptied before the sight of God, to the God who promises) was imputed for righteousness, because he embraced for his righteousness the blessing promised in his future seed, that is, in Christ.

units.la: Verf. 23, Non scriptum est autem propter eum solum, quòd hoc imputatum fuerit ei:
units.tr: Verse 23. Now it was not written for his sake alone, that it was reckoned to him;

units.la: Verf. 24. Sed etiam propter nos, quibus futurum est ut imputetur, iù nimirum qui credunt in eum qui suscitavit Iesum Dominum nostrum ex mortuis.
units.tr: Verse 24. But also for our sake, to whom it shall be reckoned, if we believe on him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead.

units.la: Jam exemplum fidei Abrahæ, accommodat Apostolus in usum communem fidelium, quasi pignore dato hoc exemplo, promittens fore, ut fides nostra in IESUM CHRISTUM, in justitiam similiter nobis imputanda sit. Utque nos invitet ad credendum, comparat primò Euangelium, nobis DEI nomine per ministros prædicatum, de CHRISTI morte & resurrectione pro nobis, promissioni factæ Abrahamo: Deinde, exigit fidem in DEUM, qui hanc nobis factam gratiam, per prædicationem Euangelii offert, ut credamus cum Abrahamo. Et denique pronunciat fidem nostram in DEUM, qui ultro sibi satisfecit in morte CHRISTI, & resuscitavit à mortuis CHRISTUM, (ut nobis, jam morte ipsius partam justitiam, imputaret, & applicaret) non minus certo in justitiam nostram imputandam esse, quam certum est Abrahami fidem, ipsi esse imputatam ad justitiam; & quam certum est hoc scriptum esse, non propter eum solùm, sed etiam propter nos, quibus futurum est, ut fides hæc imputetur similiter in justitiam.
units.tr: Now the Apostle applies the example of Abraham's faith to the common use of believers, as if this example were given as a pledge, promising that our faith in Jesus Christ shall likewise be reckoned to us for righteousness. And to invite us to believe, he first compares the gospel, which is preached to us in God's name through ministers, concerning Christ's death and resurrection for us, with the promise made to Abraham. Then he requires faith in God, who offers to us through the preaching of the gospel the grace granted to us, that we may believe with Abraham. And finally he declares that our faith in God, who of his own accord was satisfied in the death of Christ and raised Christ from the dead (so that he might reckon and apply to us the righteousness already obtained by his death), shall be reckoned to us for righteousness no less surely than Abraham's faith was reckoned to him for righteousness, and as surely as it is written that this was not for his sake alone, but also for ours, to whom this faith shall likewise be reckoned for righteousness.

units.la: Verf. 25. Qui traditus fuit morti propter offensas nostras, & suscitatus ad nostri justificationem.
units.tr: Verse 25. Who was delivered up to death for our offences, and was raised again for our justification.

units.la: Hujus certitudinis fundamentum collocat in duplici actu judiciali DEI erga CHRISTUM. Primus actus est, Traditio CHRISTI sponsoris in mortem propter offensas nostras: Alter est resuscitatio CHRISTI ad nostri justificationem; Quorum primò testatur DEUS ex pacto translata esse peccata redemptorum in CHRISTUM: Altero verò, sibi abundè pro peccatis ipsorum esse satisfactum, & redemptos in persona sponsoris esse justificatos. Unde sequitur, redemptis, cum per fidem consentiunt in fœdus hoc in Euangelio revelatum, fidem imputari ad justitiam; seu justitiam à CHRISTO partam ipsis adjudicari, ut sicut in persona sponsoris justificati sunt, sic etiam in seipsis justificentur.
units.tr: He lays the foundation of this certainty in the twofold judicial act of God toward Christ. The first act is the delivering up of Christ the surety to death for our offences. The second is the raising of Christ for our justification. By the first, God testifies that by covenant the sins of the redeemed were transferred to Christ; by the second, that full satisfaction has been made to him for their sins, and that the redeemed have been justified in the person of their surety. Hence it follows that when the redeemed consent by faith to this covenant revealed in the gospel, their faith is reckoned to them for righteousness; that is, the righteousness obtained by Christ is adjudged to them, so that as they were justified in the person of their surety, so they may also be justified in themselves.

units.la: Caput quintum.
units.tr: Chapter 5.

units.la: Vit prima confirmatio hujus divinæ rationis justificandi peccatores, per fidem in Christum: sequitur secunda confirmatio, à solida consolatione, quam hæc justificandi ratio præstat, adversus iram & peccatum.
units.tr: The first confirmation of this divine manner of justifying sinners through faith in Christ; the second confirmation follows, from the solid consolation that this manner of justification affords against wrath and sin.

units.la: Capitis partes sunt duæ: In priori proponitur consolatio in fructuum justitiæ per fidem in Christum, enumeratione, ad versum sextum: In altera ostenditur consolationis soliditas, ad finem.
units.tr: The parts of the chapter are two: In the first, consolation is set forth from the fruits of justice through faith in Christ, by enumeration, to verse six: In the second, the solidity of the consolation is shown, to the end.

units.la: Verf. 1. Justificati igitur ex Fide, pacem habemus apud Deum per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum.
units.tr: Verse 1. Being justified therefore by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: Prima pars Capitis, In qua, ad ostendendam consolationem, quam suppeditat justificatio per fidem in CHRISTUM, enumerat novem ipsius fructus, quorum alij ex aliis dependent.
units.tr: In the first part of the chapter, to show the consolation that justification through faith in Christ supplies, he enumerates nine of its fruits, some of which depend on others.

units.la: Primus fructus est Pax, seu reconciliatio erga DEUM, jam placatum per Mediatorem, seu Pacificatorem CHRISTUM.
units.tr: The first fruit is peace, or reconciliation with God, now appeased through the Mediator, or Peacemaker, Christ.

units.la: Verf. 2. Per quem etiam fide addusti fuimus in hanc gratiam per quam stamus, & gloriamur sub spe gloriæ Dei.
units.tr: Verse 2. Through whom also we have been brought by faith into this grace in which we stand, and we glory in hope of the glory of God.

units.la: Secundus fructus, est quotidiana quasi manuductio nostri, per CHRISTUM fide apprehensum, ad favorem & gratiam DEI, ut ea magis magisque utamur, fruamur, & in eam quasi penitius ingrediamur.
units.tr: The second fruit is a daily, as it were, leading of us, apprehended in Christ by faith, into the favour and grace of God, so that we may use it more and more, enjoy it, and enter into it, as it were, ever more deeply.

units.la: Stamus Tertius fructus, est confirmatio nostri in hoc statu gratiæ, ne excidamus, sed stemus constanter.
units.tr: We stand. The third fruit is the confirmation of us in this state of grace, so that we do not fall away but stand firm.

units.la: Gloriamur Quartus fructus est gloriatio de certissima spe cœlestis gloriæ, olim apud DEUM fruendæ.
units.tr: We glory. The fourth fruit is the glorying in the most certain hope of heavenly glory, to be enjoyed one day with God.

units.la: Verf. 3. Neque id solum, sed etiam gloriamur de afflictionibus, scientes quod afflictio tolerantiam efficiat:
units.tr: Verse 3. And not only this, but we also glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation works patience:

units.la: Verf. 4. Tolerantia vero experientiam, experientia autem spem:
units.tr: Verse 4. And patience, experience; and experience, hope:

units.la: Quintus fructus, est gloriatio adversus omnes afflictiones, eaque in mediis rebus adversis, quibus obnoxii sumus post justificationem in hac vita.
units.tr: The fifth fruit is glorying against all tribulations, even in the midst of adversities to which we are subject after justification in this life.

units.la: Scientes Sextus fructus, gloriandi ansam præbens in afflictionibus, est certa cognitio, seu persuasio proficiendi in sanctitate per crucem, seu afflictiones; Quia per afflictiones Deus patientiam nos docet, per patientiam nova subinde suæ in nobis, & erga nos, gratiæ documenta præbens, nobis experientiam donat; per experientiam auget, & confirmat fidem nostram, & spem de subinde nova, & tandem plena liberatione futura.
units.tr: Knowing. The sixth fruit, which gives occasion for glorying in afflictions, is the certain knowledge, or persuasion, of making progress in holiness through the cross, that is, through afflictions. For through afflictions God teaches us patience; through patience, from time to time, he gives us fresh proofs of his favour in us and toward us; he gives us experience; through experience he increases and confirms our faith and our hope of a deliverance that is to come, at first new, and at last full.

units.la: Verf. 5. Porrò spes non pudefacit, eo quòd charitas Dei effusa est in cordibus nostris per Spiritum sanctum qui datus est nobis.
units.tr: Verse 5. Now hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

units.la: Septimus fructus, est Certitudo de boni sperati possessione, seu immunitas à pudefactione, quam efficit spei conceptæ frustratio: siquidem spes ex fide justificante orta, & ad hunc modum excitata, & aucta, sperantem non fallit, non pudefacit.
units.tr: Seventh. The seventh fruit is the certainty of possessing the good hoped for, or immunity from the disappointment that the frustration of a conceived hope brings; for hope arising from justifying faith, and so stirred up and increased, does not deceive the one who hopes, does not disappoint.

units.la: Effusa ] Octavus fructus confirmans priorem, Est sensus divinæ erga nos dilectionis, corda nostra subinde perfundens, & replens: qui sensus ut arrha quædam spem de futuris bonis confirmat.
units.tr: Poured out ] The eighth fruit, confirming the former, is the sense of God's love toward us, which from time to time floods and fills our hearts; and this sense, as a kind of pledge, confirms hope of future good things.

units.la: Spiritum ] Nonus fructus, est Spiritus sanctus, in uberiori mensura donatus nobis qui in Christum credimus; qui Spiritus operatur hunc sensum divinæ erga nos dilectionis, & unà testatur cum spiritibus nostris, quod nos simus filij Dei, reliquaque sua in nobis omnia opera ad regenerationem, consolationem & salutem spectantia, efficit. Ad hos omnes fructus, & privilegia, jus habent omnes justificati per fidem: Quod si aliqui, vel Infantes in Christo & Rudes, vel Impediti tentatione aliqua, justificatos se non sciant, vel non agnoscant, vel Spiritum consolatorem, nequitia aliqua sua contristentur, non mirum etiamsi ex his fructibus consolationem non percipiant.
units.tr: Spirit ] The ninth fruit is the Holy Spirit, bestowed in a more abundant measure on us who believe in Christ; this Spirit works this sense of God's love toward us, and together with our spirits bears witness that we are the children of God, and effects all his other works in us that concern regeneration, comfort and salvation. All who are justified through faith have a right to all these fruits and privileges. But if some, either infants and untaught in Christ, or hindered by some temptation, do not know or acknowledge that they are justified, or are saddened by some wickedness of their own, grieving the Comforter, it is no wonder if they do not receive consolation from these fruits.

units.la: Verf. 6. Christus enim, quum nullis adhuc viribus essemus, præstituto tempore pro impiis mortuus est.
units.tr: Verse 6. For Christ, when we were still without strength, died at the appointed time for the ungodly.

units.la: Verf. 7. Enimverò vix pro justo quisquam moriatur: nam pro bono viro forsitan aliquis etiam mori sustineat.
units.tr: Verse 7. Indeed scarcely would anyone die for a righteous man: for the good man perhaps someone would even dare to die.

units.la: Verf. 8. Commendat autem suam erga nos charitatem Deus, eo quòd quum adhuc essemus peccatores, Christus pro nobis mortuus sit.
units.tr: Verse 8. But God commends his love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.

units.la: Verf. 9. Justificati igitur nunc ejus sanguine, servabimur multò magis per eum ab ira illa.
units.tr: Verse 9. Being justified therefore now by his blood, we shall be saved much more through him from that wrath.

units.la: Secunda Pars.
units.tr: Second Part.

units.la: SEcunda pars Capitis, in qua consolationis soliditatem, adversus iram & peccatum ostendit comparatione duplici, quarum prima est Christi cum Christo, ad versum 12. Altera est Christi (qui fecundus est Adam) cum Adamo primo nostro parente, ad finem.
units.tr: The second part of the chapter, in which he shows the firmness of the comfort against wrath and sin by means of a double comparison. The first is of Christ with Christ, up to verse 12. The second is of Christ (who is the second Adam) with Adam, our first parent, to the end. (first)

units.la: Comparationis Christi cum Christo tria sunt membra, in quibus probatur justificatos ab ira fervandos, tribus argumentis: Primum membrum comparationis est efficaciæ Christi dilectionis erga nos, ante justificationem, cum efficacia dilectionis ejus erga nos, post juftificationem nostram; In hunc sensum, Cum nos in peccato & miseria, deftituti viribus ad nosmet liberandum jacebamus, Christus in plenitudine temporis, pro nobis impiis, est mortuus, versu 6. Quanta dilectio inter homines, erga justum, vix reperitur, nisi forte pro probo, & sibi utili, audeat alquis mori, versu 7. Unde commendatur charitas Christi, seu Dei, erga nos, ex eo, quod cum adhuc effemus peccatores, nondum justificati, Christus pro nobis mortuus fit, ut scilicet ab ira servaremur, versu 8. Ergo multò major erit dilectionis ejus efficacia erga nos jam justificatos ejus sanguine, ut servemur per eum ab ira; v. 9. Valet argumentum quia dilectionis Christi efficacia erga nos justificatos, non potest esse minor quam erga nos in peccatis jacentes: hoc primum est argument.
units.tr: The comparison of Christ with Christ has three parts, by which it is proved, with three arguments, that the justified are to be kept from wrath. The first part of the comparison is between the efficacy of Christ's love towards us before justification and the efficacy of his love towards us after our justification. To this effect: when we lay in sin and misery, destitute of strength to free ourselves, Christ in the fullness of time died for us, the ungodly (verse 6). Scarcely anyone is found who would die for a righteous man; perhaps for a good man, and one useful to himself, someone might dare to die (verse 7). Whence the love of Christ, or of God, towards us is commended, in that while we were still sinners, not yet justified, Christ died for us, so that we might be saved from wrath (verse 8). Therefore his love will be much more efficacious towards us, now justified by his blood, so that we are saved by him from wrath (verse 9). The argument holds, because the efficacy of Christ's love towards us, once justified, cannot be less than towards us lying in sins. This is the first argument.

units.la: Verf. 10.
units.tr: Verse 10.

units.la: Nam si quum inimici essemus, reconciliati fuimus Deo per mortem Filij ejus, multo magis reconciliati servabimur per vitam ipsius.
units.tr: For if, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, being reconciled, we shall be saved by his life.

units.la: Secundum membrum comparationis, est efficaciæ Christi mortis ante justificationem, & Christi vitæ post justificationem, in hunc sensum; Si cum inimici essemus, efficax fuit Christi mors, ad reconciliationem nostri erga Deum, procurandam, multo magis vita Christi efficax erit, ad servandum ab ira nos jam justificatos & reconciliatos: Quia absurdum est statuere, Christum à mortuis suscitatum, & viventem in Cœlo, non servaturum ab ira nos, pro quibus ut servaremur ab ira, & mortuus, & resuscitatus à mortuis est: & hoc est secundum argumentum.
units.tr: The second part of the comparison is between the efficacy of Christ's death before justification and the efficacy of Christ's life after justification, to this effect: if, when we were enemies, the death of Christ was efficacious to procure our reconciliation with God, much more will the life of Christ be efficacious to save us, now justified and reconciled, from wrath. For it is absurd to maintain that Christ, raised from the dead and living in heaven, will not save from wrath us for whose salvation from wrath he both died and was raised from the dead. This is the second argument.

units.la: Verf. 11.
units.tr: Verse 11.

units.la: Neque id solùm, verum etiam gloriamur in Deo per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, per quem nunc reconciliationem recepimus. Tertium membrum comparationis, est efficaciæ, seu virtutis CHRISTI, ad procurandum & efficiendum, ut DEUS ipse noster fit, quasi res nostra propria, quod majus est, cum efficacia seu virtute CHRISTI ad servandum nos ab ira, quod minus est, in hunc sensum: Non id solùm, scilicet habemus per CHRISTUM, ut servemur ab ira, sed etiam quod omnium maximum est, gloriamur in DEO, tanquam in nostro peculio, per Dominum nostrum IESUM CHRISTUM, qui non solùm reconciliationem nobis impetravit, sed nunc justificatis per fidem applicavit, & DEUM reconciliatum nostrum quasi proprium reddidit. Ergo certi sumus nos ab ira servandos, atque hoc est tertium argumentum, In quibus omnibus soliditas consolationis eorum qui fide justificantur, ostenditur.
units.tr: And not only so, but we also rejoice in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received the reconciliation. The third part of the comparison is between the efficacy, or power, of Christ to bring about and effect that God himself becomes ours, as if it were our own possession, which is greater, and the efficacy or power of Christ to save us from wrath, which is less. To this effect: not only do we have through Christ that we are saved from wrath, but also, which is the greatest of all, we rejoice in God as in our own property, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who not only obtained reconciliation for us but has now applied it to us who are justified through faith, and has made the reconciled God, as it were, our own. Therefore we are certain that we shall be saved from wrath. This is the third argument. In all of these the firmness of the comfort of those who are justified by faith is shown.

units.la: Verf. 12.
units.tr: Verse 12.

units.la: Propterea sicut per unum hominem peccatum in mundum introiit, ac per peccatum mors: & ita in omnes homines mors pervasit, in quo homine omnes peccarunt.
units.tr: Therefore, as through one man sin entered into the world, and death through sin; and so death passed upon all men, in whom all have sinned.

units.la: Altera comparatio est CHRISTI & Adami, tendens ad ostendendum, CHRISTI justitiam non minus efficacem esse, ad servandum justificatos per fidem, quam Adami peccatum efficax est, ad perdendum non justificatos. Comparationis autem membra sunt sex: Primum membrum, Sicut per unum hominem, Adamum scilicet, peccatum introiit in mundum, & per peccatum mors: & ita in omnes homines, qui filii sunt Adami per naturam, mors transiit, quatenus quidem in eo, ut in communi parente omnes peccarunt: Ita per unum hominem CHRISTUM, secundum Adamum, justitia introiit in mundum, & per justitiam vita, & ita in omnes homines, qui filii sunt CHRISTI per gratiam, (quales sunt fide justificati omnes) vita transit, quatenus quidem in eo, ut in communi parente sponsore & patrono, omnes justificantur. Hæc antithesis colligenda nobis reliinquitur ex sequentibus, & potissimum ex fine versus 14. ubi Christus Adami antitypus statuitur, quia porta nimirum est, & fons justitiæ, & vitæ, sicut Adamus fuit porta, & fons peccati, & mortis.
units.tr: The other comparison is between Christ and Adam, aiming to show that the righteousness of Christ is no less efficacious to save the justified through faith than the sin of Adam is efficacious to destroy the unjustified. The comparison has six parts. The first part: as through one man, Adam, sin entered the world, and death through sin, and so death passed to all men who are sons of Adam by nature, in so far as in him, as their common parent, all sinned; so through one man, Christ, the second Adam, righteousness entered the world, and through righteousness life, and so life passes to all men who are sons of Christ by grace (all those justified by faith), in so far as in him, as their common parent, surety and patron, all are justified. This antithesis is left for us to gather from what follows, and chiefly from the end of verse 14, where Christ is set as the antitype of Adam, because he is the door and the fountain of righteousness and life, just as Adam was the door and the fountain of sin and death.

units.la: Verf. 13.
units.tr: Verse 13.

units.la: Nam usque ad Legem peccatum erat in mundo: peccatum vero esse non putatur non existente Lege.
units.tr: For until the Law sin was in the world; but sin is not reckoned to exist where there is no Law.

units.la: Verf. 14.
units.tr: Verse 14.

units.la: Regnavit autem mors ab Adam usque ad Mosen, in eos etiam qui non peccaverant adsimilitudinem transgressionis Adam, qui est typus illius qui erat futurus.
units.tr: Yet death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who had not sinned after the likeness of the transgression of Adam, who is a type of the one who was to come.

units.la: Probat peccatum introiisse in mundum, per unum hominem Adamum, & propagatum esse in Adami posteros, quia ab Adamo, usque ad scriptam legem a Mose, peccatum & erat in mundo, imputabatur; & quod fieri non potuisset, nisi fuisset aliqua lex, saltem non scripta seu innata, nam si lex nulla fuisset, neque scripta neque innata, non potuisset peccatum imputari verf. 13. At imputatum est, quia supplicium inflictum est; si quidem stipendium peccati mors, regnavit ab Adam usque in Mosen, non tantum in adultos, sed etiam in infantes, qui originaliter peccarunt quidem in eo, (cum omnes in Adamo unus quasi homo fuerint,) licet non actualiter, seu ad similitudinem actualis peccati Adami. verf. 14. Summa est, Mors fuit, ergo stipendium peccati fuit, ergo peccatum fuit, ergo lex fuit, & peccatum per unum in omnes propagatum est. Vocat autem Adamum typum futuri, nempe secundi Adami Christi, ut intelligamus, respondere oportuisse Christum, in salutaribus suis effectis, Adamo in suis exitialibus effectis, idque ex Dei instituto, qui in perdito humani generis fonte, repraesentari voluit futurum hominum salvatorem Christum, ut Christus agnoscatur non minus fons, caput & radix justitiae, & vitae derivandae in suos, quam Adam fuit fons, caput & radix, derivandi peccati & mortis in suos.
units.tr: He proves that sin entered the world through one man, Adam, and was passed on to Adam's posterity, because from Adam until the written law given by Moses, sin both existed in the world and was imputed. This could not have happened unless there was some law, at least an unwritten or innate one; for if there had been no law at all, neither written nor innate, sin could not have been imputed (verse 13). But it was imputed, because punishment was inflicted. For the wages of sin is death, and death reigned from Adam until Moses, not only over adults but also over infants, who sinned originally in Adam (since all were, as it were, one man in Adam), though not actually, but after the likeness of Adam's actual sin (verse 14). The sum is this: there was death, therefore there was the wages of sin, therefore there was sin, therefore there was law, and sin was passed through one man to all. He calls Adam a type of the one to come, namely Christ, the second Adam, so that we understand that Christ had to correspond, in his saving effects, to Adam in his destructive effects. This was by God's appointment, who wished that the future Saviour of mankind be represented in the ruined source of the human race, so that Christ is acknowledged to be the source, head and root of righteousness and life to be derived to his own, no less than Adam was the source, head and root from which sin and death are derived to his own.

units.la: Verf. 15. At non ut offensa ita etiam est quod Deus gratificatur, nam si unius illius offensa multi mortui sunt, multo magis gratia Dei & donatio per gratiam quae est unius illius hominis Iesu Christi, in multos exundavit.
units.tr: Verse 15. But the free gift is not like the offence. For if through the offence of the one many died, much more the grace of God and the gift by grace, which is of the one man Jesus Christ, has abounded unto many.

units.la: Secundum membrum comparationis in dissimilitudine, quae primum, breviter proponitur, deinde fusius explicatur. Offensa hominis non est par gratuito dono Dei, nam bonum quod est a Deo, efficaciae & virtutis est divinae, adeoque in immensum superat malum quod est ab homine. Quare si unius hominis, id est Adami offensa, multis ab eo naturaliter prognatis, potuit afferre mortem, multo magis Gratia Dei infinita, & donum gratuitum unius hominis Iesu Christi, qui etiam Deus est, abundanter afferet vitam illis, qui spiritualiter prognati sunt a Christo. Summa est, scire nos vult, Potentiorem esse Christi gratiam ad salvandum, quam est offensa Adami ad perdendum, & dona quae per Dei gratiam data sunt, excellentiora esse quam quae amisit Adam.
units.tr: The second member of the comparison, the dissimilarity, which was first stated briefly, is now explained more fully. The offence of man is not equal to the free gift of God, for the good that comes from God is of divine efficacy and power, and so it exceeds the evil that comes from man beyond measure. Therefore, if the offence of one man, that is Adam, could bring death to the many naturally descended from him, much more will the infinite grace of God, and the free gift of the one man Jesus Christ, who is also God, abundantly bring life to those who are spiritually born of Christ. The sum is that he wants us to know that Christ's grace is more powerful to save than Adam's offence is to destroy, and that the gifts given by God's grace are more excellent than those Adam lost.

units.la: Verf. 16. Neque ut illud quod introiit per unum qui peccavit, ita est quod donatur. nam reatus quidem est ex una offensa ad condemnationem: quod autem gratificatur Deus est ex multis offensis ad justificationem.
units.tr: Verse 16. Nor is the gift like the one who sinned: for the judgment came from one offence to condemnation, but the free gift of God comes from many offences to justification.

units.la: Tertium membrum comparationis, ostendens dissimilitudinem esse, inter malum quod per unum peccantem Adamum introiit, & donum, quod est per IESUM CHRISTUM, Quia justum Dei judicium ex uno peccato Adami, processit ad justam condemnationem ipsius, & omnium in ejus lumbis naturae lege comprehensorum: Gratia vero seu gratuitum Dei donum, non tantum liberat ab illo uno & a peccato originali, sed etiam a multitudine peccatorum actualium, quae quisque superaddit, ad plenam usque justificationem suorum, ab omni peccato. Summa est, Condemnatio est ab una offensa, donum gratiae vero est absolutio ab omnibus offensis.
units.tr: Third, the member of the comparison showing the dissimilarity between the evil that entered through the one sinning Adam and the gift that is through Jesus Christ. For God's just judgment proceeded from the one sin of Adam to the just condemnation of him and of all who in his loins were included by the law of nature. But grace, or God's free gift, frees not only from that one sin and from original sin, but also from the multitude of actual sins that each person adds, right up to full justification of his people from every sin. The sum is that condemnation comes from one offence, but the gift of grace is absolution from all offences.

units.la: Verf. 17. Etenim si per unam illam offensam mors regnavit per illum unum, multo magis ii qui exundantiam illam gratiae & doni justitiae recipiunt, in vita regnabunt per unum Iesum Christum.
units.tr: Verse 17. For if by that one offence death reigned through that one man, much more those who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness will reign in life through the one Jesus Christ.

units.la: Quartum membrum comparationis, cum confirmatione superioris, in hunc sensum: Si per unum, unius Adami peccatum, mors introiens, tanquam rex subjugavit sibi humanum genus, multo magis justificati per fidem, qui redundantem Dei gratiam, & donum justitiae, accipiunt, ex gratia regnabunt in vita, per unum IESUM CHRISTUM. Quanto igitur excellentius est regnum vitae, (quod subditos suos reges facit, & vitae aeternae consortes cum CHRISTO,) regno mortis, (quod perdit omnes sibi subditos) tanto superat donum CHRISTI, delictum Adami, respectu efficaciae.
units.tr: Fourth, the member of the comparison, with confirmation of the previous one, to this effect: If through the one sin of the one Adam death entered, and like a king subjected the human race to itself, much more those justified by faith, who receive the overflowing grace of God and the gift of righteousness, will reign in life by grace through the one Jesus Christ. Therefore, as the kingdom of life (which makes its subjects kings and partakers of eternal life with Christ) is more excellent than the kingdom of death (which destroys all its subjects), so the gift of Christ surpasses the trespass of Adam in its efficacy.

units.la: Verf. 18. Nempe igitur sicut per unam offensam reatus venit, in omnes homines ad condemnationem: ita per unam justificationem beneficium redundavit in omnes homines ad justificationem vitae.
units.tr: Verse 18. Therefore, as through one offence the judgment came upon all men to condemnation, so through one righteous act the benefit has overflowed upon all men to justification of life.

units.la: Quintum membrum comparationis; Sicut per unius Adami lapsum, reatus venit in omnes homines, naturali propagatione ab Adamo oriundos, ad eos condemnandos, sic per obedientiam unius CHRISTI, qui obediens fuit patri usque ad mortem, expiatio venit, ad justificationem salvificam, omnium hominum, qui spirituali regeneratione a CHRISTO oriundi sunt.
units.tr: Fifth, the member of the comparison: As through the fall of the one Adam the judgment came upon all men, descended from Adam by natural propagation, to condemn them, so through the obedience of the one Christ, who was obedient to the Father even unto death, atonement came for the saving justification of all men who are born again spiritually from Christ.

units.la: Verf. 19. Sicut enim per illam inobedientiam unius illius hominis, peccatores constituti sunt illi multi: ita per unius obedientiam, justi constituentur multi.
units.tr: Verse 19. For as by the disobedience of that one man many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one many will be made righteous.

units.la: Sextum membrum comparationis, ad illustrationem & confirmationem prioris, In hunc sensum; Sicut per inobedientiam unius Adami, factum est,ut multi tanquam peccatores,in DEI judicio,habiti & tractati sint,propterea scilicet quod ex ipso secundum carnem prognati essent, ita vicissim per obedientiam unius CHRISTI, multi constituentur justi, id est, tanquam justi habebuntur & tractabuntur, nempe omnes illi qui fide in CHRISTUM insiti, ex ipso secundum spiritum propogati sunt: Æquum enim est ut non altius penetret virus peccati, seu inobedentiæ Adami in ejus sobolem, quam penetrat virtus obedientiæ CHRISTI, in CHRISTI sobolem: Et consentaneum est, ut sicut unum unius Adami peccatum imputatum est ejus liberis, ad condemnationem & mortem, sic unius CHRISTI obedientia integra, à vitæ initio, ad mortem usque constanter fluens, imputetur CHRISTI filiis, ad justificationem & vitam æternam obtinendam.
units.tr: Sixth, the member of the comparison, serving to illustrate and confirm the former, to this effect: As through the disobedience of the one Adam many were made to be regarded and treated as sinners in God's judgment, because they were descended from him according to the flesh, so in turn through the obedience of the one Christ many are made righteous, that is, they will be regarded and treated as righteous, namely all those who are grafted into Christ by faith and born from him according to the Spirit. For it is fitting that the poison of sin, or Adam's disobedience, should not penetrate his offspring more deeply than the power of Christ's obedience penetrates the offspring of Christ. And it is consistent that, just as the one sin of the one Adam was imputed to his children for condemnation and death, so the entire obedience of the one Christ, flowing constantly from the beginning of his life to his death, should be imputed to Christ's sons for obtaining justification and eternal life.

units.la: Verf. 20. Lex verò praeterea intrroiit ut redundaret offensa illa: sed ubi redundavit peccatum, ibi superabundavit gratia illa.
units.tr: Verse 20. Moreover the law entered in, that the offence might abound; but where sin abounded, grace did much more abound.

units.la: Verf. 21. Ut quemadmodum regnaverat illud peccatum ad mortem: ita etiam gratia illa regnaret per justitiam ad vitam aeternam, per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum.
units.tr: Verse 21. So that as sin had reigned unto death, so also grace might reign through righteousness unto eternal life, through Jesus Christ our Lord.

units.la: Totam hanc comparationem illustrat, & claudit, ostendendo abundantiam quantamcunque peccatorum in justificando, nihil aliud efficere posse,quam ut Gratia CHRISTI erga justificatum ex fide,illustrior evadat, idque facit solutione objectionis de fine, & usu Legis promulgatæ.
units.tr: He illustrates and concludes this whole comparison by showing that however great the abundance of sins may be, in justifying it can accomplish nothing other than to make the grace of Christ toward the one justified by faith more conspicuous. He does this by answering the objection about the purpose and use of the promulgated law.

units.la: Quæri posset, si mors regnabat, per legem naturæ, seu non scriptam ante Mosen, quid opus erat lege scriptâ? Et cum ex Lege non fit justitia, ut supra dictum est, quorsum data est Lex? Respondet ostendendo triplicem Legis latæ finem: Primus, Lex subintroiit, ut augeretur offensa, hoc est, Lex prohibens peccatum, & imperans justitiam, medio tempore inter Adam & CHRISTUM subingressa est, ut peccata, quæ quotidie admitebantur, & tamen præ ignorantia non agnoscebantur, cognoscerentur peccata esse, utque conspicua foret naturalis hominum pravitas, quæ facit ut quanto magis tò magis requirit Lex justitiam, tantò magis concupiscentia inardescat contra Legem; utque sic latens in hominibus peccatum, in apertum produceretur, & abundare agnoscceretur.
units.tr: One might ask: if death reigned through the law of nature, or the unwritten law before Moses, why was a written law needed? And since, as was said above, righteousness does not come from the law, why was the law given? He answers by showing the threefold purpose of the law that was given. The first: the law entered in, that the offence might abound. That is, the law forbidding sin and commanding righteousness came in between Adam and Christ, so that the sins which were committed daily, yet were not recognised because of ignorance, might be known as sins, and so that the natural wickedness of men might be made plain, which causes the more the law demands righteousness, the more concupiscence rages against the law; and so that sin, lying hidden in men, might be brought into the open and be recognised as abounding.

units.la: Sed ubi ] Secundus finis, ut ex abundantia peccati in justificandis, appareret superabundantia gratiæ Christi erga justificatos, siquidem ubi auctum est peccatum in convictione hominum justificandorum, ibi superabundare comperitur gratia Christi justificantis, erga justificatos.
units.tr: But where [Sed ubi]: the second purpose: that from the abundance of sin in the justifying, the superabundance of Christ's grace toward the justified might appear. For where sin has increased in the conviction of those to be justified, there the grace of Christ, which justifies, is found to superabound toward the justified.

units.la: Quemadmodum ] Tertius finis, ut clarius manifestata, per legem latam, vi peccati tanquam regis, ad mortem condemnatis inferendam potestatem suam exercentis, illustrius in Euangelio manifestaretur vis justitiæ Christi, tanquam superioris regis, prævalentis, non solùm ad regnum peccati abolendum, sed etiam ad vitam æternam justificatis conferendam. Quantò igitur vis peccati dominantis in homines non justificatos, eosque in mortis æternæ barathrum ducentis, trahentis, protrudentis, clarius apparet; tantò virtus, potentia, excellentia Gratiæ Christi, PECCATUM debellantis, profligatis, abolentis, subjectos servosque ejus creptos, justificantis, sanctificantis, & ad vitam æternam potenter evehentis, manifestius declaratur.
units.tr: Just as [Quemadmodum]: the third purpose: that, since by the law given, sin, acting as a king and exercising its power to inflict death on the condemned, was made clearer, the power of Christ's righteousness might be more illustriously manifested in the Gospel, as that of a superior king, prevailing not only to abolish the kingdom of sin but also to confer eternal life on the justified. Therefore, the more clearly the power of sin, ruling over men who are not justified and dragging, thrusting and pushing them into the abyss of eternal death appears, the more manifestly is the virtue, power and excellence of Christ's grace declared, which conquers sin, overthrows and abolishes it, justifies, sanctifies and powerfully raises up to eternal life those subjects and slaves of sin who have been snatched away.

units.la: Caput sextum.
units.tr: Chapter 6.

units.la: Tertia Confirmatio Doctrinæ de justificatione gratuita per fidem in Christum, Quod ad promovendam sanctitatem magnopere conducat.
units.tr: The third confirmation of the doctrine of justification freely by faith in Christ, that it greatly helps to promote holiness.

units.la: Capitis duæ sunt partes: In prima ostendit per fidem in Christum, seu doctrinam de gratuita hac justificationis ratione, variis modis promoveri studium sanctitatis, ad versum 12. In altera hortatur fide justificatos ut sanctitati studeant, ad finem. Verf. 1. Quid igitur dicemus? permanebimus in peccato, ut gratia auctior fiat? Verf. 2. Absit: qui mortui sumus peccato, quomodo adhuc vivemus in eo?
units.tr: The chapter has two parts. In the first, he shows that by faith in Christ, or by this doctrine of free justification, the pursuit of holiness is advanced in various ways, to verse 12. In the second, he exhorts those justified by faith to devote themselves to holiness, to the end of the chapter. Verse 1: What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? Verse 2: God forbid. How shall we, who are dead to sin, live any longer in it?

units.la: Objectionem solvendo, quæ ex hac doctrina oriri videtur, proponit Thesin confirmandam, quod scilicet hæc doctrina de gratia, seu gratuita tuita justificatione, ad sanctitatem promovendam faciat. Dicat aliquis, an perseverabimus in peccatis nostris, nos qui per fidem justificati sumus, ut gratia Dei abundantior appareat, sicut haec doctrina de gratuita justificatione per imputationem justitiae Christi innuere videtur? Respondet negando, & aversando: Absit, inquit, a nobis haec cogitatio; Quasi diceret, Justificati per fidem non debent indulgere peccato, sed sanctitati studere, & hanc propositionem confirmat decem argumentis.
units.tr: By answering an objection that seems to arise from this doctrine, he sets forth the thesis to be confirmed: that this doctrine of grace, namely free justification, promotes holiness. Someone might say: shall we persist in our sins, we who are justified through faith, so that the grace of God may appear more abundant, as this doctrine of free justification through the imputation of Christ's righteousness seems to suggest? He answers by denying and rejecting the idea: "God forbid," he says; that is, those justified by faith ought not to indulge in sin but to devote themselves to holiness. He confirms this proposition with ten arguments.

units.la: Primum argumentum, Peccato mortui sumus, quatenus, cum Christo nomen dedimus, ut justificaremur & sanctificaremur per eum, peccato renunciavimus, ne plus cum peccato haberemus commercii, quam mortuis solet esse cum viventibus. Ergo nos justificati non debemus, nec jure possumus, amplius vivere in peccato, seu peccato indulgere.
units.tr: The first argument: we are dead to sin, inasmuch as, when we gave our name to Christ, that we might be justified and sanctified through him, we renounced sin, so that we should have no more dealings with sin than the dead usually have with the living. Therefore we who are justified ought not, and by right cannot, live any longer in sin, or indulge it.

units.la: Verf. 3. An ignoratis, nos quotquot baptizati sumus in Christum Iesum, in mortem ejus esse baptizatos?
units.tr: Verse 3: Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?

units.la: Arg. 2. Nos (ut scitis) qui gratis justificati sumus per fidem in Christum, cum per baptismum insiti sumus in Christum, etiam insiti sumus in societatem mortis ejus, per baptismum; per quod sacramentum & obstrinximus nos Christo, ad moriendum peccato, & Christus se obstrinxit nobis, ad vim mortis suae communicandam nobis, ut reipsa moreremur peccato. Ergo non debemus peccato indulgere, sed sanctitati studere.
units.tr: Argument 2: We (as you know) who have been justified freely through faith in Christ, when by baptism we were engrafted into Christ, were also engrafted through baptism into the fellowship of his death; and by this sacrament we bound ourselves to Christ to die to sin, and Christ bound himself to us to communicate to us the power of his death, so that we should in fact die to sin. Therefore we ought not to indulge sin, but to devote ourselves to holiness.

units.la: Verf. 4. Consepulti sumus igitur ei per baptismum in mortem: ut sicuti suscitatus est Christus ex mortuis in gloriam patris, ita & nos nova vita ambulemus.
units.tr: Verse 4: We are buried therefore with him by baptism into death, so that as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, so we also should walk in newness of life.

units.la: Arg. 3. Communio nostra cum Christo sepulto, per baptismum nobis obsignata est, in abolitionem veteris hominis, & peccati, id est, non tantum ut nos obligaremur, ad studendum abolitioni veteris hominis, sed etiam ut certi redderemur de mortificatione & abolitione peccati, per virtutem sepulturae Christi. Ergo non debemus peccato indulgere, sed ejus abolitioni studere.
units.tr: Argument 3: Our communion with the buried Christ is sealed to us in baptism, for the abolition of the old man and of sin; that is, not only are we obliged to strive for the abolition of the old man, but we are also made certain of the mortification and abolition of sin through the power of Christ's burial. Therefore we ought not to indulge sin, but to strive for its abolition.

units.la: Arg. 4. Sicut sepulturae, sic etiam resurrectionis Christi societas, seu communio, nobis in baptismo obsignatur; ut quemadmodum excitatus est Christus a mortuis, ad beatam & immortalem vitam, in gloriam Patris, ipsum potenter excitantis, ita nos operam daremus, & per fidem, CHRISTI virtutem applicaremus, ad emergendum ex peccatis, & ambulandum in novitate vitæ, ad gloriam DEI nos potenter renovantis. Ergo non debemus peccato indulgere, sed sanctitati studere.
units.tr: Argument 4: Just as the fellowship, or communion, of Christ's burial is sealed to us in baptism, so also that of his resurrection; so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead to a blessed and immortal life, to the glory of the Father who raised him up by his power, so we should labour and, through faith, apply the power of Christ, to rise out of sins and walk in newness of life, to the glory of God who renews us by his power. Therefore we ought not to indulge sin, but to devote ourselves to holiness.

units.la: Verf. 5. Nam si cum eo plantati coaluimus assimilatione mortis ejus, nimirum etiam resurrectionis assimilatione coalescemus:
units.tr: Verse 5: For if we have grown together with him by the likeness of his death, we shall certainly also grow together by the likeness of his resurrection.

units.la: Arg. 5. ductum ab unione spirituali arctissima nostri cum CHRISTO per fidem, quæ unio causa est communicatæ nobis virtutis, ex CHRISTI morte & resurrectione profluentis: Per fidem enim inserimur in CHRISTUM, ut palmites in vitem, & hæc insitio superinducit nobis, eam conformitatem cum CHRISTI morte, & resurrectione, ut in nobis peccato morientibus, Christus moriens, & in nobis vitæ novitati studentibus, Christus resurgens, in similitudine quadam sui, & in effectu virtutis suæ conspici possit. Hinc argumentum confirmans superius; Quando CHRISTO complantamur per fidem, adeo arctè unimur cum eo, ut conformitas in nobis sequatur necessario cum ipso moriente, in mortificatione peccati, & cum ipso resurgente, in novitate vitæ. Ergo nisi unionem cum ipso, & insitionem in ipsum, nullam factam esse profiteri vellemus, peccatis renunciandum, & sanctitati studendum est nobis.
units.tr: Argument 5: drawn from the most close spiritual union of us with Christ through faith, which union is the cause of the virtue communicated to us, flowing from Christ's death and resurrection. For through faith we are grafted into Christ, as branches into the vine, and this grafting brings upon us such conformity to Christ's death and resurrection that in us, dying to sin, Christ dying may be seen, and in us, striving after newness of life, Christ rising, in a certain likeness of himself and in the effect of his power. Hence the argument confirming the above: when we are planted together with Christ through faith, we are so closely united with him that conformity necessarily follows in us, with him dying in the mortification of sin, and with him rising in newness of life. Therefore, unless we wish to profess that there is no union with him and no grafting into him, we must renounce sins and devote ourselves to holiness.

units.la: Verf. 6. Illud scientes, veterem illum nostrum hominem cum eo crucifixum esse, ut cassum reddatur corpus peccati, ne nos amplius serviamus peccato.
units.tr: Verse 6: Knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be made void, that we should no longer serve sin.

units.la: Arg. 6. A judiciali unione quam habemus cum CHRISTO crucifixo: Cujus argumenti vis ut perspiciatur, quatuor tenenda sunt: 1. Quod CHRISTUS in cruce pendens ut sponsor pro nobis personam nostram coram DEI tribunali gesserit: 2. Quod supplicium luerit debitum corruptæ nostræ naturæ, seu veteri nostro homini sic dicto, quia naturæ pravitas in regenitis senescit, & interitui appropinquat. 3. Quod in se receperit fore ut vetus noster homo in nobis necaretur. 4. Quod nos quos repræsentabat ipso facto obligaverit ad operam dandam mortificationi peccati per ejus spiritum, ne post justificationem amplius peccato serviremus. Hinc argumentum, Scimus, seu credimus veterem nostrum hominem judicialiter crucifixum esse cum CHRISTO eo fine, ut in nobis per fidem justificatis enervetur corpus peccati, (sic vocatur habitualis peccati compacta colluvies in unum quasi monstrosum corpus suis membris jam paratum ad actu peccandum) ne amplius post justificationem serviamus peccato. Ergo nobis studendum est mortificationi peccati, nisi fidem unionis nostrae judicialis cum Christo in cruce pendente, abjicere vellemus.
units.tr: Argument 6: from the judicial union we have with the crucified Christ. To see the force of this argument, four things must be held: (1) that Christ, hanging on the cross, acted as surety for us, bearing our person before the tribunal of God; (2) that he paid the penalty owed by our corrupted nature, or our so-called old man, because the depravity of nature grows old in the regenerate and draws near to its destruction; (3) that he undertook that our old man would be put to death in us; (4) that by his Spirit he bound us, whom he represented, by the very fact, to labour at the mortification of sin, so that after justification we should no longer serve sin. Hence the argument: We know, or believe, that our old man was judicially crucified with Christ to this end, that in us who are justified by faith the body of sin (so is called the habitual heap of sin, compacted into one monstrous body, its members already prepared to sin in act) might be weakened, so that after justification we should no longer serve sin. Therefore we must strive for the mortification of sin, unless we wish to cast away the faith of our judicial union with Christ hanging on the cross.

units.la: Verf. 7. Etenim qui mortuus est, liberatus est à peccato.
units.tr: Verse 7: For he who has died is freed from sin.

units.la: Arg. 7. A fructu hujus unionis cum Christo in cruce moriente: Quicunque mortuus est veteri suo domino peccato, justificatur, & liberatur à jugo & dominio peccati, ne amplius ei serviat, nec mandatis peccati obtemperet: Assumere licet, At nos justificati fide, in Christo moriente in cruce pro peccato, mortui sumus veteri nostro domino peccato. Ergo justificamur, & liberamur à jugo & dominio peccati, ne amplius ei serviamus, vel mandatis ejus obtemperemus. Quid enim servitii amplius peccatum exigat à nobis, quos in cruce & morte Christi capitis nostri, quasi decollavit?
units.tr: Argument 7: from the fruit of this union with Christ dying on the cross. Whoever has died to his old master, sin, is justified and freed from the yoke and dominion of sin, so that he no longer serves it nor obeys its commands. Let this be assumed: but we, justified by faith, have died to our old master, sin, in Christ dying on the cross for sin. Therefore we are justified and freed from the yoke and dominion of sin, so that we no longer serve it or obey its commands. For what further service could sin demand from us, whom Christ our head has, as it were, beheaded on the cross and in his death?

units.la: Verf. 8. Quod si mortui sumus cum Christo, credimus fore ut etiam ei convivamus.
units.tr: Verse 8: Now if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him.

units.la: Arg. 8. Si cum Christo morimur, id est, morienti Christo adhaeremus, in ejus virtute, mortificationi peccati studentes, dubitare non licet, quin vitam etiam spiritualem, novam & coelestem, una cum eo victuri simus. Ergo peccati mortificationi studendum est.
units.tr: Argument 8: If we die with Christ, that is, if we cleave to Christ dying, labouring in his power at the mortification of sin, there is no room for doubt that we shall also live with him a spiritual life, new and heavenly. Therefore we must strive for the mortification of sin.

units.la: Verf. 9. Ut qui sciamus Christum suscitatum ex mortuis, non amplius mori: mortem inquam, ei non amplius dominari.
units.tr: Verse 9: Knowing that Christ, being raised from the dead, dies no more; death, I say, no longer has dominion over him.

units.la: Arg. 9. confirmans superius, Credimus Christum resurrexisse, ad vitam immortalem, nec amplius morti unquam futurum obnoxium, sed semper viventem velle, & posse novam vitam in nobis perpetuare, ne mors in peccatis nobis amplius dominetur. Ergo sicut non frustra credimus, ipsius virtute nos vitam novam, & aeternam, cum eo victuros, sic etiam studere debemus, ut perpetuetur vita illa nova, ad quam cum Christo resurreximus, nec permittere ut mors in peccatis unquam adversus nos amplius praevaleat, seu dominetur.
units.tr: Argument 9, confirming the above: we believe that Christ rose to an immortal life, and will never again be subject to death, but always lives and is able to perpetuate the new life in us, so that death in sins no longer has dominion over us.
