Therefore, just as we do not believe in vain that by his power we shall live with him a new and eternal life, so we ought to strive that that new life, into which we have risen with Christ, may be perpetuated, and not allow death ever again to prevail or have dominion over us in sins.

units.la: Verf. 10 Nam quod mortuus est, peccato mortuus est semel: quod autem vivit, vivit Deo.
units.tr: Verse 10: For in that he died, he died to sin once; but in that he lives, he lives to God.

units.la: Verf. 11.
units.tr: Verse 11.

units.la: Vers. 11 Ita etiam vos colligite, vos tum mortuos esse peccato, tum vero vivere Deo per Christum Iesum Dominum nostrum.
units.tr: Verse 11: So also you, consider yourselves dead to sin, but alive to God through Christ Jesus our Lord.

units.la: Sicut Christus ad abluendum, & abolendum peccatum, per mortem suam, semel tantum mortuus est, resurgens vero a mortuis, perpetuo vivit in Dei gloriam, sic etiam vos qui justificati estis, fidei ratiocinio colligite, & statuite vos in Christi morte unica, semel esse mortuos peccato expiando, nec ultra ad moriendum pro peccato teneri; semel esse mortuos peccato exautorando, nec ultra ad serviendum peccato teneri: semel esse mortuos peccato destruendo, nec ad mortificandum peccatum, virtute Christi posse destitui: sed in ejus resurrectione ad vitam immortalem, vivendam Deo, sive in Dei gloriam, perpetuo teneri, & ut vivere possitis Deo, in aeternum, satis vos habere virium, & auxilii per Christum Iesum Dominum nostrum. Tantum igitur abest, ut per doctrinam justificationis gratuitae, aperiatur via ad perseverandum in peccatis, ut contra nihil ea sit ad sanctitatem conducibilius, vel efficacius.
units.tr: Just as Christ, to wash away and abolish sin, died once only through his death, but rising from the dead lives forever to the glory of God, so also you who are justified should reckon by the reasoning of faith, and establish that you are dead to sin once for all, in the one death of Christ: dead to sin in expiating it, so that you are no longer bound to die for sin; dead to sin in discharging it, so that you are no longer bound to serve sin; dead to sin in destroying it, so that by the power of Christ you cannot be deprived of the means of mortifying sin. Rather, in his resurrection you are bound forever to live the immortal life, to live to God, that is, to the glory of God; and that you may live to God forever, you have enough strength and help through Christ Jesus our Lord. So far is it from the case that the doctrine of free justification opens a way to persevering in sins; on the contrary, nothing is more conducive or effective to holiness than it.

units.la: Secunda Pars.
units.tr: Second Part.

units.la: Vers. 12. Ne regnato igitur peccatum in mortali vestro corpore, ut auscultetis ei in cupiditatibus corporis.
units.tr: Verse 12. Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, so that you should obey it in the lusts of the body.

units.la: Sequitur secunda pars Capitis, in qua, ex praecedentibus hortationem infert Apostolus, ad omnes fide justificatos, ut sanctitati studeant. Thesis probanda eadem est, quae superior, nempe tenentur justificati, non permanere in peccato, sed sanctitati studere: argumenta affert tredecim, quorum tria priora hortatione sequenti includuntur.
units.tr: The second part of the chapter follows, in which the Apostle, drawing on what has gone before, exhorts all who are justified by faith to strive after holiness. The thesis to be proved is the same as before, namely that the justified are bound not to remain in sin but to strive after holiness. He brings thirteen arguments, of which the first three are contained in the following exhortation.

units.la: Hortationis autem membra tria sunt, & argumenta totidem, ad confirmandam thesin hortatione involutam. Primum membrum hortationis est, ne obediant peccato cupiditatibus corporis pravis indulgendo.
units.tr: The exhortation has three parts, and there are as many arguments, to confirm the thesis enfolded within the exhortation. The first part of the exhortation is that they should not obey sin by indulging the wicked lusts of the body.

units.la: Est hoc; Morem gerere pravis cupiditatibus corporis, est regnum peccati, seu diaboli unde liberati estis, denuo admittere in mortali corpore vestro; quod justificatis horrorem debet incutere. Ergo jam justificati non debetis peccato indulgere, sed sanctitati studere.
units.tr: The argument is this: to give way to the wicked lusts of the body is to readmit into your mortal body the reign of sin, or of the devil, from which you have been freed; and this ought to strike horror into the justified. Therefore, since you are already justified, you must not indulge sin, but strive after holiness.

units.la: Vers. 13 Neque sistite membra vestra arma injustitiae peccato: sed sistite vos Deo ut ex mortuis vivos, & membra vestra arma justitiae Deo. Secundum membrum hortationis, ne militent huic tyranno, peccato scilicet, adhibentes facultates animæ, vel corporis, ut satellites, ad pugnandum pro peccato, in quo habetur Arg. 2. Peccato servire, est facultates animæ, & membra corporis, exhibere ut arma iniquitatis, ad pugnandum pro peccato & diabolo, contra Deum & propriam salutem, quod justificatis abominandum esse debet. Ergo justificati non debent peccato servire.
units.tr: Verse 13. Neither yield your members as weapons of unrighteousness to sin, but yield yourselves to God, as those who are alive from the dead, and your members as weapons of righteousness to God. The second part of the exhortation: they should not fight for this tyrant, sin, by lending the faculties of soul or body as its soldiers to fight for it. The argument is: to serve sin is to offer the faculties of the soul and the members of the body as weapons of iniquity, to fight for sin and the devil against God and one's own salvation. This ought to be abhorrent to the justified. Therefore the justified must not serve sin.

units.la: Sistite ] Tertium membrum hortationis, Ut sistant se milites, & servos Deo liberatori ex mortuis, in quo est Arg.3 Deus vos a morte in peccatis, & perditione æterna, revocavit in vitam ut serviatis justitiæ, & pro Deo adversus ejus hostes, decertetis. Ergo sanctitati studere debetis.
units.tr: Yield] The third part of the exhortation: that they should yield themselves as soldiers and servants to God, their deliverer from the dead. The argument is: God has called you back from death in sins and from eternal perdition to life, so that you should serve righteousness and fight for God against his enemies. Therefore you ought to strive after holiness.

units.la: Verf. 14. Peccatum enim vobis non dominabitur, non enim estis sub Lege, sed sub gratia.
units.tr: Verse 14. For sin shall not have dominion over you, for you are not under the law, but under grace.

units.la: Arg. 4. Si contendatis, & pugnetis adversus Peccatum, Tyrannus ille non recuperabit in vobis regnum, quod amisit, nec dominabitur vobis peccatum, sed vos victores per Christum evadetis: Ergo sanctitati studere debetis.
units.tr: Fourth argument: if you contend and fight against sin, that tyrant will not recover in you the kingdom he has lost, nor will sin have dominion over you; rather, through Christ you will emerge as victors. Therefore you ought to strive after holiness.

units.la: Non enim ] Arg. 5. confirmans superius, Non estis sub lege, seu fœdere operum, in quo mandatum distrietam exigit obedientiam, sed vires non confert ad obediendum, sed estis sub gratia, seu fœdere gratiæ, in quo gratia Dei, cum mandato, fidelibus confert vitam, & vires ad obtemperandum. Ergo certi de victoria adversus peccatum, sanctitati studere debetis.
units.tr: For] Fifth argument, confirming what was said above: you are not under the law, that is, the covenant of works, in which the commandment demands strict obedience but does not supply the strength to obey. You are under grace, that is, the covenant of grace, in which the grace of God, together with the commandment, gives believers life and strength to obey. Therefore, being certain of victory over sin, you ought to strive after holiness.

units.la: Verf. 15. Quid igitur peccabimus, quod non sumus sub Lege, sed sub gratia? Absit.
units.tr: Verse 15. What then? Shall we sin because we are not under the law but under grace? God forbid.

units.la: Repetit & rejicit absurdam objectionem libertinorum, qui gratiam Dei, trahunt in licentiam peccandi, quum contra sequatur ex dictis scilicet, Quia sumus sub gratia: Ideo non indulgendum peccato.
units.tr: He repeats and rejects the absurd objection of the libertines, who turn the grace of God into a licence to sin, whereas what follows from what has been said is the opposite: because we are under grace, sin must not be indulged.

units.la: Verf. 16. An nescitis quod cui sistitis vos servos ad auscultandum, ejus servi estis cui auscultatis, sive peccati ad mortem, sive obedientiæ ad justitiam?
units.tr: Verse 16. Do you not know that to whom you yield yourselves as servants to obey, his servants you are whom you obey, whether of sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness?

units.la: Arg. 6. Confutandæ objectioni obiter inserviens; Quum servos vos esse ejus cui obeditis, & mercedem reportare, servitio congenerem, necesse sit, sive obediatis peccato, sive divinis præceptis obediatis, nisi velletis peccati servi haberi, & æternæ mortis mercedem reportare, cavendum ne peccato indulgeatis, & si velletis servi Dei haberi, ut justi & vitæ hæredes pronunciemini, sanctitati vobis studendum est necessario.
units.tr: Sixth argument, serving incidentally to refute the objection: since it is necessary that you are the servants of the one you obey and receive a wage akin to servitude, whether you obey sin or obey the divine precepts, you must take care not to indulge sin, unless you wish to be held servants of sin and to receive the wage of eternal death. And if you wish to be held servants of God, to be pronounced righteous and heirs of life, you must necessarily strive after holiness.

units.la: Verf. 17. Gratia autem sit Deo quòd fuistis quidem servi peccati, sed ex corde auscultastis ei formæ doctrinæ in quam estis traditi:
units.tr: Verse 17. But thanks be to God that you were servants of sin, but you have obeyed from the heart that form of doctrine into which you were delivered.

units.la: Arg. 7. Per Dei gratiam, transiit tempus servitii, quod præstabatis peccato, ante regenerationem, & jam conversi, sincere doctrinæ Euangelii obedire incepistis, cui tanquam typo traditi estis, & cujus impressionem jam recepistis: Ergo redire ad servitium peccati, vel recedere ab obedientia sanæ doctrinæ indignum est, sed in obedientia doctrinæ cui traditi estis, pergere oportet.
units.tr: Seventh argument: by the grace of God the time of servitude that you rendered to sin before regeneration has passed. Now that you are converted, you have begun to obey sincerely the doctrine of the Gospel, to which you were delivered as into a mould, and whose impression you have now received. Therefore to return to the servitude of sin, or to withdraw from obedience to sound doctrine, is unworthy; one must persevere in obedience to the doctrine to which you were delivered.

units.la: Verf. 18. Et liberati à peccato, mancipati estis justitiæ
units.tr: Verse 18. And being made free from sin, you were made servants of righteousness.

units.la: Arg. 8. A peccato jam liberati, per omnipotentis Dei brachium, mancipati estis justitiæ & sanctitati; Ergo mancipationis jure, ut servi justitiæ, servire sanctitati tenemini.
units.tr: Eighth argument: now freed from sin by the arm of almighty God, you have been made servants of righteousness and holiness. Therefore, by the right of this enslavement, you are bound to serve holiness as servants of righteousness.

units.la: Verf. 19. Hominum more loquor, propter infirmitatem carnis vestræ. Nempe sicut stituistis membra vestra serva impuritati & legis transgressioni, ad patrandam legis transgressionem: ita nunc sistite membra vestra serva justitiæ ad sanctimoniam.
units.tr: Verse 19. I speak after the manner of men, because of the infirmity of your flesh. For as you have yielded your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity, unto iniquity, so now yield your members to serve righteousness unto sanctification.

units.la: Post excusatam terrenæ similitudinis crassitiem, quæ in multis, non respondet rebus his spiritualibus, quam tamen adhibere, visum est Spiritui Sancto, propter infirmitatem Romanorum, ex parte carnalium, qui sublimiorem, seu magis spiritualem loquendi modum, tam facile capere non poterant, repetit hortationem & addit arg. 9. Membra vestra aliquando præbuistis immunditiæ, & in universum injustitiæ serva, ad opera injustitiæ patranda, Ergo nunc æquum est, ut pari saltem studio, præbeatis membra vestra serva justitiæ, ad sanctificationem vestram, & non minus segnes esse, ad recte agendum quam olim strenui eratis ad peccandum.
units.tr: After excusing the crudeness of an earthly comparison, which in many respects does not match these spiritual things, but which the Holy Spirit thought fit to use because of the weakness of the Romans, who were partly carnal and could not so easily grasp a more elevated or more spiritual mode of speech, he repeats the exhortation and adds the ninth argument: you once yielded your members as servants to uncleanness and to iniquity in general, to commit works of iniquity. Therefore it is only fair now that you yield your members, with at least equal zeal, as servants of righteousness, for your sanctification. You should be no less slow to act rightly than you once were eager to sin.

units.la: Verf. 20. Quum enim servi eratis peccati, liberi eratis justitiæ.
units.tr: Verse 20. For when you were servants of sin, you were free from righteousness.

units.la: Arg. 10. Confirmans superius, Quum essetis mancipia peccati, ut liberos à justitia vos gessistis, nam non omnino obtemperastis justitiæ in illa re.
units.tr: Tenth argument, confirming what was said above: when you were slaves of sin, you conducted yourselves as free from righteousness, for in that matter you were not wholly obedient to righteousness.

units.la: [Remark: the last lines are printed in the bottom margin area; catchword "illa re".] ulla re, Ergo æquum est jam cum mancipia estis justitiæ, ut liberos vo<bl>ß-</bl> geratis à peccato, nec ei obtempe retis omnino.
units.tr: Therefore it is only fair now, since you are slaves of righteousness, that you be free from sin and not obey it at all.

units.la: Verf. 21. Quem igitur fructum habebatis tunc ex iis de quibus nunc erubescitis ; nam finis illorum mors est.
units.tr: Verse 21. What fruit then did you have from those things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death.

units.la: Nullum alium fructum, ex anteacta vita in peccatis percepistis, præter pudorem, qui nunc vobis incutitur, nec expectare poteratis alium fructum tandem, præter mortem æternam, quæ finis est peccati. Ergo cavendum vobis, ne amplius serviatis peccato.
units.tr: You had no fruit from your former life in sins except the shame that now besets you, nor could you expect any other fruit in the end but eternal death, which is the end of sin. Therefore you must take care not to serve sin any longer.

units.la: Verf. 22. Nunc vero liberati à peccato, servi autem facti Deo, habetis fructum vestrum in sanctimoniam: finem autem vitam æternam.
units.tr: Verse 22. But now being made free from sin, and become servants to God, you have your fruit unto holiness, and the end everlasting life.

units.la: Postquam vindicati in libertatem, à peccati servitute, mancipati fuistis Deo, sanctimoniæ vestræ fructum habetis, iplam indies augescentem sanctimoniam, & tandem habituri estis in fine, vitam æternam. Ergo studendum diligenter sanctitati.
units.tr: Having been set free from the servitude of sin and made servants of God, you have the fruit of your holiness, which grows daily, and in the end you are to have everlasting life. Therefore holiness must be diligently pursued.

units.la: Verf. 23. Nam stipendia peccati mors: donum autem Dei est vita æterna, in Christo Iesu Domino nostro.
units.tr: Verse 23. For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

units.la: Confirmans superiora, in hunc sensum; firma sunt omnia, quæ hactenus dicta sunt in hoc argumento, nam statutum est ex Dei sententia, stipendium peccati peccatoribus, secundum meritum reddere mortem æternam; vitam vero æternam, cum justificatione & sanctitate, quæ cum vita æterna connectuntur, non ex debito, sed ex gratia dare, ut donum gratuitum; idque non nisi in Domino nostro Iesu Christo. Ergo non indulgendum peccato ne pereamus, sed cum fide in Christum conjungendum studium sanctitatis, quam sanctitatem cum vita æterna gratis donaturum esse Deum, credentibus in Christum & sanctitati studentibus, ex superioribus probatum est.
units.tr: Confirming what precedes, in this sense: everything said so far in this argument is firm. For it is decreed by God's sentence that the wages of sin are paid to sinners, according to their merit, as eternal death; but eternal life, together with justification and holiness, which are joined to eternal life, he gives not as a debt but out of grace, as a free gift, and this only in our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore we must not indulge sin lest we perish, but the pursuit of holiness must be joined with faith in Christ. It has been proved from what precedes that God will freely bestow holiness together with eternal life on those who believe in Christ and strive after holiness.

units.la: Caput
units.tr: Chapter

units.la: Ortatus est superiori Capite justificatos per fidem, ad sanctimoniam : Quia autem ii qui maximè student sanctitati, maximè sentiunt, & lugent vim peccati inhabitantis, nondum extincti : Ideo in horum gratiam sequitur, Quarta confirmatio gratuitæ justificationis per fidem in Christum, quod consolationem præbeat Sanctorum conscientiis afflictis, propter imperfectam obedientiam Legis, & peccati inhabitantis in se reliquias.
units.tr: Having urged, in the preceding chapter, that the justified by faith should press on to holiness, the Apostle now recognises that those who most earnestly pursue holiness are also the ones who most feel and lament the power of the sin that dwells in them, which is not yet extinguished. For their sake, therefore, there follows a fourth confirmation of free justification by faith in Christ, which offers consolation to the consciences of the saints distressed by the imperfect obedience of the Law and by the remnants of indwelling sin within them.

units.la: Capitis tres sunt partes: In prima, ut consolationem capiant justificati, adversus imperfectam obedientiam Legis, agit de justificatorum liberatione à fœdere legali, & novo nexu ipsorum in fœdere gratiæ, qui primus est locus consolationis, ad verf. 7. Secunda continet apologiam, pro legis sanctitate; solutis duabus contra legem objectionibus, ad verf. 14. Intertia, habetur secundus locus consolationis, in quo, luctam suam, adversus reliquias peccati in se, & victoriam reportatam, ex doctrina justificationis per fidem in Christum, proponit Apostolus, ut in suo exemplo, & experientia, consolationem caperent, conscientia luctantes.
units.tr: The chapter has three parts. In the first, so that the justified may take comfort against the imperfect obedience of the Law, the Apostle deals with the liberation of the justified from the legal covenant and their new bond in the covenant of grace, which is the first ground of consolation, down to verse 7. The second contains a defence of the holiness of the law, after two objections against the law have been answered, down to verse 14. In the third, which is the second ground of consolation, the Apostle sets out, from the doctrine of justification by faith in Christ, his own struggle against the remnants of sin within him and the victory he has won, so that those struggling in conscience might take comfort from his example and experience.

units.la: Prima Pars.
units.tr: First Part

units.la: Verf. 1. AN ignoratis fratres (peritos enim Legis alloquor) legem tantispep dominari cuiquam quanto tempore ipse vivit?
units.tr: Verse 1. Do you not know, brothers (for I am speaking to men who know the Law), that the law rules over a man only for as long as he lives?

units.la: Verf. 2. Nam viro addicta mulier, viventi viro devincta est per legem: quòd si mortuus fuerit vir, liberata est à lege viri.
units.tr: Verse 2. For a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives; but if the husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband.

units.la: Verf. 3 Proinde vivente viro mœcha vocabitur si fiat alterius viri: sin autem mortuus fuerit vir ejus, libera est à lege illa; ut non sit mœcha, si fiat alterius viri.
units.tr: Verse 3. So then, while her husband lives, she will be called an adulteress if she marries another man; but if her husband dies, she is free from that law, so that she is not an adulteress if she marries another man.

units.la: Quod ad primam partem attinet, comparatione à matrimonio sumpta, ostendit justificatos liberari à conjugali fœdere legis, ut desponsati per novum fœdus gratiæ, novo marito Christo, fructus justitiæ feramus, in nova legis obedientia, in gloriam novi mariti nostri Christi.
units.tr: As for the first part, by an comparison drawn from marriage, the Apostle shows that the justified are released from the marriage bond of the law, so that, betrothed to a new husband through the new covenant of grace, Christ, we may bear the fruits of righteousness in a new obedience to the law, to the glory of our new husband, Christ.

units.la: Protasin comparationis proponit, tribus primis versibus, in hunc sensum: Quemadmodum nulla lex dominatur mortuis, (ut scitis) sed viventibus tantùm, verf. 1. Et nominatim, lex conjugii, seu fœdus matrimoniale dissolvitur, altero conjuge mortuo, ita ut uxor, mortuo marito, sine adulterio, nubere possit alteri, verf. 2, & 3. sic vos, &c. ut mox patebit.
units.tr: He sets out the first half of the comparison in the first three verses, to this effect: just as no law rules over the dead (as you know), but only over the living, vers. 1; and specifically, the law of marriage, or the matrimonial covenant, is dissolved when one spouse dies, so that a wife, once her husband is dead, may marry another without adultery, vers. 2 and 3; so you also, as will soon become clear.

units.la: Verf. 4. Itaque fratres mei, vos quoque mortificati estis Legi in corpore Christi: ut effetis alterius, ejus videlicet qui ex mortuis suscitatus est, ut fructum feramus Deo.
units.tr: Verse 4. Therefore, my brothers, you too have been put to death to the Law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, namely to him who was raised from the dead, that we may bear fruit to God.

units.la: Sequitur apodosis comparationis, in hunc sensum; Sic vos, qui olim desponsati quasi eratis legi per foedus operum conjugale, mortuo CHRISTO pro vobis, ut Legi, & Justitiae, & Foederi Operum satisfieret vestro nomine, judicialiter mortui estis legi, seu foederi legali, in corpore CHRISTI: (nam lex, seu foedus legale interfecit CHRISTUM, & vos in eo) & per consequens liberati estis a conjugio Legis, seu conjugali foedere legis; ita ut sine justitiae violatione novum matrimoniale foedus Gratiae feriatis cum CHRISTO ex mortis suscitato. In hunc finem ostendit, dirempti matrimonii, inter foedus operum seu legis, & nos, finem esse, non ut viveremus pro libitu nostro, sed ut excitati a statu, seu conditione mortis, per resurrectionem CHRISTI, essemus alterius, seu desponsaremur alteri marito, illi videlicet, qui excitatus est a mortuis, id est, CHRISTO qui resurrexit a mortuis, & nos in vitam novam secum excitavit, sibique secundum foedus gratiae desponsavit, ut CHRISTO, seu foederi gratiae desponsati, fructum feramus novae obedientiae in Dei gloriam.
units.tr: There follows the second half of the comparison, to this effect: so you, who were once, as it were, bound to the Law by the marital covenant of works, Christ having died for you so that the Law, righteousness and the covenant of works might be satisfied on your behalf, have been judicially put to death to the Law, or to the legal covenant, in the body of Christ (for the law, or the legal covenant, killed Christ, and you in him). Consequently you have been released from the marriage of the Law, or from the marital covenant of the law, so that, without any violation of righteousness, you may enter a new matrimonial covenant of grace with Christ, raised from the dead. To this end he shows that the purpose of the dissolved marriage between the covenant of works or of the law and us is not that we should live as we please, but that, roused from the state or condition of death through the resurrection of Christ, we should belong to another, or be betrothed to another husband, namely to him who was raised from the dead, that is, to Christ who rose from the dead, and who has raised us with him into a new life and betrothed us to himself according to the covenant of grace, so that, betrothed to Christ, or to the covenant of grace, we may bear the fruit of new obedience to the glory of God.

units.la: Consolationis justificatorum, imperfectionem obedientiae suae deflentium, argumenta sunt quinque.
units.tr: There are five arguments of consolation for the justified who lament the imperfection of their obedience.

units.la: Mortificati Primum argumentum; Liberati estis, a foedere operum legali, quod nullam admittit obedientiam, praeter perfectam, & omnibus numeris absolutam: Ergo consolationem habetis, vos omnes justificati, qui defletis imperfectionem novae vestrae obedientiae.
units.tr: Mortified: the first argument. You have been released from the legal covenant of works, which admits no obedience except a perfect obedience, absolute in every respect. Therefore you all who are justified, who lament the imperfection of your new obedience, have consolation.

units.la: Alterius Arg. 2. Desponsati jam estis, alteri marito CHRISTO scilicet, qui excitatus est ex mortuis, qui quum obedientiae vestrae imperfectiones praestare poterit, & secundum foedus gratiae, & inchoatam obedientiam vestram, gratam Deo reddere, in se receperit, consolationem habetis vos, qui imperfectionem obedientiae vestrae defletis.
units.tr: Another's: argument 2. You are now betrothed to another husband, namely Christ, who was raised from the dead. Since he is able to make up for the imperfections of your obedience, and has taken it upon himself, according to the covenant of grace, to make your begun obedience acceptable to God, you have consolation, you who lament the imperfection of your obedience.

units.la: Fructum Arg. 3. Desponsati estis CHRISTO, a mortuis excitato ut non maneatis steriles, sed fructus feratis, in gloriam Dei: Ergo consolationem habetis vos, qui imperfectionem obedientiae vestrae lugetis.
units.tr: Fruit: argument 3. You are betrothed to Christ, raised from the dead, so that you may not remain barren but bear fruit to the glory of God. Therefore you who mourn the imperfection of your obedience have consolation.

units.la: Verf. 5. Quum enim essemus in carne, effectus peccatorum per Legem exsistentes agebant in membris nostris, ad fructum ferendum morti:
units.tr: Verse 5. For when we were in the flesh, the sinful passions, which operate through the Law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death.

units.la: Argument.
units.tr: Argument.

units.la: Confirmans superius, à conditionis nostræ mutatione, cum essemus in carne irregeniti, (& per consequens, sub fœdere legali) affectus peccatorum, seu prava desideria, per sanctam Dei Legem excitabantur, & se potenter exercebant, in membris seu facultatibus nostris omnibus, & animæ & corporis, usque ad peccati actualis, mortiferum fructum proserendum: Ergo à pari sequetur, cum jam sumus regeniti, & per consequens sub fœdere gratiæ, sancta desideria, per fœdus novum, & mandatum novum excitata, potenter etiam se exerent, in membris nostris, ad fructum bonorum operum ferendum Deo, ne maneamus steriles. Quæ consolatio non est exigua; Nam si nos per fidem, fœdus gratiæ apprehenderemus, animasque nostras per ipsius promissiones nobis applicatas, excitaremus, non dubium est, quin uberiores fructus bonorum operum profereremus. Id enim ipsum est, quod Christus dicit, Iohan. 15. 5. Ego sum vitis, vos palmites: is qui manet in me, & in quo ego maneo, hic fert fructum multum: nam seorsim me nihil potestis facere.
units.tr: Confirming what was said above, from the change in our condition: when we were in the flesh, unregenerate (and consequently under the legal covenant), the sinful passions, or depraved desires, were stirred up by the holy law of God and exercised their power in all our members or faculties, both of soul and body, until they brought forth the deadly fruit of actual sin. Therefore, by parity, it follows that now that we are regenerate, and consequently under the covenant of grace, holy desires, stirred up by the new covenant and the new commandment, will likewise exercise their power in our members, so that we may bear the fruit of good works for God and not remain barren. This consolation is no small one. For if we laid hold of the covenant of grace by faith, and stirred up our souls by its promises applied to us, there is no doubt that we would bring forth more abundant fruits of good works. This is exactly what Christ says, John 15:5. I am the vine, you are the branches; he who abides in me, and in whom I abide, bears much fruit; for apart from me you can do nothing.

units.la: Vers. 6. Nunc autem liberati sumus à Lege, mortuo eo in quo detinebamur: ut serviamus in novitate spiritus, ac non in vetustate literæ.
units.tr: Verse 6. But now we have been released from the Law, dead to that in which we were held, so that we serve in the newness of the Spirit and not in the oldness of the letter.

units.la: Explicans & confirmans superius, à fine mutatæ conditionis nostræ, Nunc post justificationem scilicet, per Gratiam Christi liberati sumus à fœdere legis, (mortuo illo fœdere in quo detinebamur, vel mortuis nobis in Christo, in quo judicialiter continebamur) eo ipso fine ut serviamus Deo, vi Spiritus sancti novas vires conferentis, novos & spirituales fructus ferendo, & non superficiales, seu hypocriticos fructus, quales litera veteris fœderis legalis jam aboliti ad summum proferebat. Ergo sine suo non excidet Deus, sed justificatos, dolentes de imperfecta obedientia sua, feraces reddet bonorum operum, in Spiritus novitate; fructus enim qui proveniunt vi fœderis gratuiti, verè novi sunt, & à Spiritu regenerante, & novas vires ad bene agendum subinde suppeditante oriuntur; fructus verò, qui vi fœderis operum proferntur, vel sunt naturæ corruptæ aperta rebellio adversus Dei Legem, vel simulata in externo opere tantùm obedientia, quales sunt Pharifæorum fructus, qui in litera, id est, externa specie, & titulo tenus Legi obediebant, sine omni cordis renovatione.
units.tr: Explaining and confirming what was said above, from the purpose of our changed condition: now, that is, after justification, through the grace of Christ we have been released from the covenant of the law (that covenant in which we were held having died, or we having died to it in Christ, in whom we were judicially included), with exactly this end: that we should serve God, by the power of the Holy Spirit conferring new strength, bearing new and spiritual fruits, and not superficial or hypocritical fruits, such as the letter of the old, now abolished, legal covenant at most produced. Therefore God will not, without his own fault, fail the justified who lament the imperfection of their obedience; he will make them fruitful in good works, in the newness of the Spirit. For the fruits that come through the force of the gratuitous covenant are truly new, and arise from the regenerating Spirit, who from time to time supplies new strength for doing well; whereas the fruits produced by the force of the covenant of works are either the open rebellion of corrupt nature against God's Law, or an obedience feigned in outward work alone, such as the fruits of the Pharisees, who obeyed the Law in the letter, that is, in outward appearance and title only, without any renewal of the heart.

units.la: Secunda Pars.
units.tr: Second Part.

units.la: Verf. 7. Quid ergo dicemus? Lex peccatum est? Absit. Sed peccatum non cognovi nisi per Legem, nam ipsam quoque cupiditatem non nossem, nisi Lex dixisset, Non concupisces.
units.tr: Verse 7. What shall we say then? Is the law sin? God forbid. But I had not known sin except through the law; for I would not have known covetousness unless the law had said, You shall not covet.

units.la: Secunda pars Capitis, apologiam continens, pro legis sanctitate insolutione duarum objectionum, ex supra dictis ortarum: Prima objectio: Cum affectus peccatorum, seu pravi, & vitiosi motus, excitentur a lege, ut dictum est, videtur lex esse peccatum, seu causa peccati.
units.tr: The second part of the chapter, containing a defence of the holiness of the law, resolves two objections arising from what has been said above. First objection: since the affections of sin, that is, the depraved and vicious motions, are stirred up by the law, as has been said, it seems that the law is sin, or the cause of sin.

units.la: Respondet negando; Absit, ut ea apud nos cogitatio obtineat. Rationes negationis suae reddit tres, in quibus est apologia pro lege, experientia sua illustratas: Prima ratio, quia lex monstrat peccatum, & detegit ipsius malitiam, quod sua experientia confirmat, qui latentem in corde concupiscentiam ipse non agnovisset esse peccatum, nisi eam lege prohibitam perspexisset: Ergo lex sancta est.
units.tr: He answers by denying this: "God forbid that such a thought should prevail among us." He gives three reasons for his denial, which contain a defence of the law, illustrated by his own experience. The first reason: the law shows sin and reveals its malice, as his own experience confirms. He who had not recognised the concupiscence lying hidden in his heart as sin would not have known it, unless he had seen it forbidden by the law. Therefore the law is holy.

units.la: Verf. 8. Sed peccatum occasione per illud praeceptum sumpta, effecit in me totam cupiditatem: Nam absque Lege peccatum quidem erat mortuum.
units.tr: Verse 8. But sin, taking occasion by that commandment, produced in me all manner of covetousness; for apart from the law sin lay dead.

units.la: Ratio 2. Quia peccatum inhabitans, seu naturae habitualis pravitas, est causa actualium peccatorum; lex vero non est causa, sed occasio, eaque non oblata, sed arrepta tantum ad peccandum, ut ipse compertum habebat: Nam peccatum inhabitans (inquit) seu naturae pravitas, arrepta occasione ex prohibitione Concupiscentiae in lege, tanto magis inflammata est; & nitens in vetitum, genuit in me omnis generis cupiditates, & pravos motus contra legem.
units.tr: Second reason: the indwelling sin, that is, the habitual depravity of nature, is the cause of actual sins; but the law is not the cause, only the occasion, and not an occasion offered but merely seized upon for sinning, as he himself had found. For indwelling sin (he says), or the depravity of nature, seizing the occasion from the prohibition of covetousness in the law, was all the more inflamed; and striving toward what was forbidden, it begot in me every kind of covetousness and depraved motion against the law.

units.la: Nam absque Id confirmat a figuo, quia lege non cognita, peccatum latet, torpet, & quasi mortuum jacet, ubi vero accedit lex, excitatur & se prodit; sicut sordes absente sole latent, adveniente vero excitantur, se produnt & fatent, non solis, sed suo vitio. Ergo sancta est lex.
units.tr: For apart from He confirms this by a comparison: when the law is not known, sin lies hidden, lies dormant, and lies as if dead; but when the law arrives, sin is roused and reveals itself. Just as filth lies hidden while the sun is absent, but when the sun comes it is stirred up, shows itself and is exposed, not by the sun's fault but by its own vice. Therefore the law is holy.

units.la: Verf. 9. Ego vero vivus eram absque Lege quondam: praecepti autem illius adventu peccatum quidem revixit, Ego vero mortuus sum.
units.tr: Verse 9. I was indeed alive without the law once; but when the commandment came, sin revived, and I died.

units.la: Experientia sua amplius hoc explicat, offendens se olim, cum Pharisaeus esset & irregenitus, opinione sua vivum fuisse, id est, admodum justum, & minime reum mortis æternæ: sed cum apertis ipsius oculis, per DEI gratiam verus legis sensus ipsi apertus est, tum se comperisse vim peccati, & se reum mortis æternæ, manifeste perspexisse.
units.tr: He explains this further from his own experience, confessing that formerly, while he was a Pharisee and unregenerate, he was alive in his own opinion, that is, quite righteous and by no means liable to eternal death. But when, by the grace of God, the true sense of the law was opened to him with his eyes open, then he clearly perceived the power of sin and that he was liable to eternal death.

units.la: Verf. 10. Et inventum est illud mandatum quod erat ad vitam, mihi cedere ad mortem.
units.tr: Verse 10. And the commandment, which was ordained to life, was found by me to be unto death.

units.la: Ex hac experientia duo se didicisse ait; Primum, finem mandati, & effectum per se, esse bonum, quia mandatum DEI bonum est, & ordinatum per se ad vitam, si homines ei obtemperassent. Alterum, Effectum legis per accidens esse mortem, quatenus mortem interminatur peccatori, & eum qui peccavit, reum peragit mortis, urgetque ex justitia, ut morti tradatur.
units.tr: From this experience he says he learned two things. First, that the end and effect of the commandment, in itself, is good, because God's commandment is good and ordained in itself to life, if men had obeyed it. Second, that the effect of the law by accident is death, insofar as it threatens death to the sinner, and as the law pronounces the one who has sinned liable to death, and by justice demands that he be delivered to death.

units.la: Verf. 11. Nam peccatum occasione per illud praeceptum sumpta, seduxit me, & per illud occidit.
units.tr: Verse 11. For sin, taking occasion by that commandment, deceived me, and by it slew me.

units.la: Verf. 12. Itaque Lex ipsa quidem sancta, & Praeceptum illud sanctum, ac justum & bonum est.
units.tr: Verse 12. Therefore the law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy, just, and good.

units.la: Tertia ratio, pro legis apologia; Peccatum inhabitans, est causa seduc-tionis, & mortis, arreptā tantum occasione ex lege, seu mandato, sicut ipse experientia didicerat; Nam cogitantem de vetitis in lege, Peccatum invitavit, & allexit ad vetita, & polluit, atque ita per mandatum mortis magis magisque obnoxium ipsum reddidit. Ergo lex tota sancta est, & nominatim mandatum illud vetans concupiscentiam, sanctum, justum, & bonum est, nempe quia à sancto DEO, secundum æquitatem, & ad nostram utilitatem, datur.
units.tr: Third reason, in defence of the law: indwelling sin is the cause of seduction and death, seizing only the occasion from the law or commandment, as his own experience had taught him. For sin, enticing and drawing him who thought about what was forbidden in the law, led him to the forbidden things and defiled him, and so by the commandment made him more and more liable to death. Therefore the whole law is holy, and especially that commandment forbidding covetousness is holy, just, and good, namely because it is given by the holy God, in accordance with equity and for our benefit.

units.la: Verf. 13. Ergo quod bonum est, mihi factum est mors? Absit: sed peccatum mihi factum est mors, ut appareret esse peccatum mihi per id quod bonum est efficiens mortem, id est, ut peccatum fieret admodum peccans per illud praeceptum.
units.tr: Verse 13. Was then that which is good made death unto me? God forbid. But sin, that it might appear to be sin, working death in me by that which is good, so that sin through the commandment might become exceedingly sinful.

units.la: Secundi objectio; diceret aliquis, Ergo ne quod bonum est, mihi cessit in causam mortis; Respondet aversando calumniam: siquidem discernenda est occasio à causa, & usus rei, ab abusu. Absolvit igitur legem, & in peccatum inhabitans, culpam omnem conjicit. Immo, inquit, non lex sed peccatum inhabitans mihi est causa mortis, & prodit se esse peccatum, quatenus per bonam DEI legem irritatum & accensum in me, vitiosos motus & legi DEI rebelles, excitavit, mortemque hac ratione mihi tanto magis accersivit; ut ita peccatum innatum, maxime peccans in me per illud mandatum manifestaretur. Quod opportune dictum est, ad obturandum omnibus os, qui concupiscentiam illam innatam, & nunc omnibus naturalem, alioqui negarent peccatum esse nisi ea & actualium peccatorum & mortis causa, esse comperiretur: atque haec est pro lege apologia.
units.tr: Second objection: someone might say, "Then has what is good become a cause of death to me?" He answers by rejecting the calumny, since the occasion must be distinguished from the cause, and the use of a thing from its abuse. He therefore acquits the law and lays all the blame upon indwelling sin. "No," he says, "it is not the law but indwelling sin that is the cause of my death, and it shows itself to be sin, in that, provoked and kindled by God's good law, it stirred up in me vicious motions rebellious to God's law, and in this way brought death upon me all the more; so that the innate sin, being exceedingly sinful in me, might be made manifest through that commandment." This was rightly said, to stop the mouths of all those who would deny that innate concupiscence, which is now natural to all, is sin, unless it were found to be the cause of actual sins and of death. And this is the defence of the law.

units.la: Tertia Pars.
units.tr: Third Part.

units.la: Verf. 14. Scimus enim Legem esse spiritualem: at ego carnalis sum, venditus ut subjicerer peccato,
units.tr: Verse 14. For we know that the Law is spiritual; but I am carnal, sold so that I should be subject to sin.

units.la: Tertia pars Capitis, in qua habetur secundus locus consolationis eorum, qui defient suae obedientiae Legi praestitae imperfectionem, ab exemplo Apostoli, luctantis cum eodem malo, & victoriam reportantis, beneficio gratuitae justificationis, ut apparet ex versu ultimo. Vis argumenti haec est, Ipse ego deflens in me vim peccati luctor adversuseam, consolationem capiens, ex justificatione per fidem in CHRISTUM: Ergo & vos sancti athletae in luctu vestro consolationem accipite.
units.tr: The third part of the chapter, in which we have the second ground of comfort for those who lament the imperfection of their obedience to the Law. It is drawn from the example of the Apostle, who struggles with the same evil and wins the victory by the benefit of free justification, as appears from the last verse. The force of the argument is this: I myself, lamenting the power of sin in me, struggle against it and take comfort from justification by faith in Christ. Therefore you too, holy athletes, receive comfort in your mourning.

units.la: In Apostoli lucta, triplex paroxysmus proponitur, & triplex victoria in recessu, ubi febris jam refrixit: In quibus omnibus immiscentur consolationis argumenta aliqua, ducta ab Apostoli experientia: Primus paroxysmus oritur ex triplici dissidio; Tertium dissidium est legis & suiipsius. Ego, inquit, cum reliquis fidelibus agnosco legem spiritualem, quae tota sapiat sanctitatem Spiritus Dei, & ad spiritualem vivendi rationem, referatur tota. Sed meipsum cum respicio, & cum Legis spiritualitate confero meam obedientiae imperfectionem, cogor meipsum (respectu veteris in me hominis nondum mortificati) carnalem agnoscere, & tanquam mancipium venditum ut subjicerer peccato, e cujus vinculis expedire me nequeo, quin saepe abripiar quo nollem.
units.tr: In the Apostle's struggle three paroxysms are set forth, and three victories in the remission, when the fever has already cooled. In all of them some arguments of comfort, drawn from the Apostle's experience, are mingled in. The first paroxysm arises from a threefold dissent; the third dissent is between the Law and himself. "I," he says, "together with the other faithful, acknowledge the Law to be spiritual, which wholly savours of the holiness of the Spirit of God and is wholly directed to a spiritual way of living. But when I look at myself, and compare my imperfection in obedience with the spirituality of the Law, I am forced to acknowledge myself (with respect to the old man in me, not yet mortified) as carnal, and as a slave sold to be subject to sin, from whose bonds I cannot free myself, so that I am often carried away to what I would not."

units.la: Verf. 15. Quod enim perpetro, non agnosco: non enim quod volo hoc ago, sed quod odi, hoc facio.
units.tr: Verse 15. For what I do, I do not acknowledge: for I do not what I would, but what I hate, that I do.

units.la: Probat quod dixit, & secundum dissidium ostendit inter actiones suas, & judicium suum renovatum: Quod perpetro, inquit, non agnosco, non approbo; nempe cum actiones meas examino ad perfectam normam legis, cogor multa in actionibus meis, non approbare, sed condemnare. Tertium dissidium ostendit, inter actiones suas, & volantatem suam renovatam, non ago, quod volo bonum (inquit) impeditus scilicet, à corpore peccati in me; & quod odi malum hoc facio, à regula deficiens ubi nolem: vellem enim Legi Dei obedientiam perfectam praestare, sed minimè praesto, & in multis pecco.
units.tr: He proves what he has said, and shows the second dissent, between his actions and his renewed judgment: "What I do," he says, "I do not acknowledge, I do not approve." That is, when I examine my actions by the perfect rule of the Law, I am forced not to approve many of my actions but to condemn them. He shows the third dissent, between his actions and his renewed will: "I do not do the good that I would," he says, being hindered, of course, by the body of sin in me; and "what I hate, that I do," failing the rule where I would not. For I would wish to render perfect obedience to the Law of God, but I by no means render it, and I sin in many things.

units.la: Verf. 16. Quod si id facio quod nolo, consentio Legi quod bona sit.
units.tr: Verse 16. If then I do that which I would not, I consent to the Law that it is good.

units.la: Fuit primus paroxysmus, sequitur victoria in recessu, & consolationis argumenta tria, quibus Apostolus se & reliquos athletas consolatur. Primum argumentum, Ego ipse Apostolus, in numero sum eorum, qui deflent suae sanctitatis imperfectionem, & eandem luctam, cum iis & molestiam in me percipio, ex mea obedientiae imperfectione. Ergo consolationem habent, deflentes suae sanctitatis imperfectionem, cum nihil alienum à sanctis reliquis, imo ne Apostolis quidem, patiantur.
units.tr: There was the first paroxysm; there follows the victory in the remission, and three arguments of comfort by which the Apostle comforts himself and the other athletes. The first argument: I, the Apostle, am among those who lament the imperfection of their holiness, and I perceive the same struggle with them and the same distress in myself, arising from the imperfection of my obedience. Therefore those who lament the imperfection of their holiness have comfort, since they suffer nothing foreign to the other saints, indeed not even to the Apostles.

units.la: Consentio ] consolationis est, Quod ex hac luctu emergat indicium sanctificationis inchoatae in luctante, & consensus in Dei legem, ut bonam & sanctam: nam si quod nolo hoc facio, tum consentio Legi quod bona sit: Et idem indicium suae sanctificationis habent omnes deflentes suae obedientiae imperfectionem.
units.tr: I consent belongs to comfort: from this struggle there emerges a sign of sanctification begun in the one who struggles, and a consent to the Law of God as good and holy. For if I do what I do not will, then I consent to the Law that it is good. And all who lament the imperfection of their obedience have the same sign of their sanctification.

units.la: Verf. 17. Nunc itaque non amplius ego id perpetro, sed peccatum quod in me habitat, id perpetrat.
units.tr: Verse 17. Now then it is no more I that do it, but sin that dwelleth in me.

units.la: Consolationis est, Quod lugenti sibi imperfectionem suam improbanti, & condemnanti eam, non imputetur illud malum, (quod etiam intelligendum est de reliquis sanctis athletis,) sed peccato in se habitanti: quia Deus, deflentes naturae suae pravitatem, aestimat à meliori ipsorum parte, renovata scilicet, quae praevalet, & praevalitura est, cum peccati inhabitantis mortificatione, & abilitione, à qua renovata parte denominatur Christianus athleta; Non amplius, inquit, ego id perpetro.
units.tr: It belongs to comfort that the evil (which must also be understood of the other holy athletes) is not imputed to one who mourns his imperfection, disapproves of it and condemns it, but to the sin that dwells in him. For God, when they lament the depravity of their nature, esteems them by their better part, namely the renewed part, which prevails and will prevail with the mortification and abolition of the indwelling sin; and from this renewed part the Christian athlete is named. "It is no more I," he says, "that do it."

units.la: Verf. 18. Novi enim non habitare in me (id est in carne mea) bonum: nam velle adest mihi, sed ut quod bonum est perficiam, non assequor.
units.tr: Verse 18. For I know that in me (that is, in my flesh) dwelleth no good thing: for to will is present with me; but how to perform that which is good I find not.

units.la: Alter paroxysmus, consistens etiam in dissidio triplici; Primum est inter ipsum veterem hominem; seu qua parte nondum erat renovatus, & ipsum novum hominem, seu qua parte renovatus erat, & hic ipse renovatus, condemnat seipsum non renovatum, ut vacuum omni bono, & receptaculum idoneum cuivis malo; Novi, inquit, non habitare in me, id est, in carne mea, (seu corrupta, & nondum purgata natura, quam ex carnali generatione traho) ullum bonum spirituale, per quod Deo placeam.
units.tr: The second paroxysm, also consisting of a threefold dissent. The first is between the old man himself, or the part of him not yet renewed, and the new man, or the part renewed; and the renewed man condemns the unrenewed self as empty of all good and a fit receptacle for any evil. "I know," he says, "that in me, that is, in my flesh" (that is, in my corrupt nature, not yet cleansed, which I derive from carnal generation) "there dwells no spiritual good by which I might please God."

units.la: Probat quod dixit, & secundum dissidium proponit, inter voluntatem suam renovatam, & impotentem carnem, seu naturam perversam, impedientem, ne motus sancti, a spiritu excitati, executioni mandentur.
units.tr: He proves what he has said, and sets forth the second dissent, between his renewed will and the powerless flesh, or perverse nature, which hinders holy motions, stirred up by the Spirit, from being carried into execution.

units.la: Vers. 19 Non enim facio bonum quod volo; sed malum quod nolo, hoc ago.
units.tr: Verse 19. For the good that I would, I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do.

units.la: Tertium dissidium, inter voluntatem renovatam, & carnem, seu veterem hominem, non tantum impedientem, renovatae voluntatis executionem, sed etiam contraria voluntati renovatae effecta mala producentem. Miretur hic aliquis, quid sibi velit, cum de mali perpetratione loquitur; cum sciamus omnes ex Scripturis, quam sancte, & immaculate, se gesserit in omnibus Apostolus noster, post conversionem suam. Sed mirandum non erit, cum perpendimus, eum pro sanctitatis eximia mensura, qua donatus erat, non potuisse naturae suae rebelles motus intueri, quin se reum perageret, & boni omissi, & mali perpetrati: Observabat enim motus illos, vel impedientes, ne omnes officii sui partes, erga Deum & homines, quam exactissime praestaret, vel polluentes aliquo modo, in Dei conspectu, actiones suas omnes, legi Dei contrarias esse. Quid mirum ergo, si hunc in modum, se tanquam eximium peccatorem pingat?
units.tr: The third dissent is between the renewed will and the flesh, or the old man, which not only hinders the execution of the renewed will but also produces evils contrary to the renewed will. Someone may wonder here what he means when he speaks of committing evil, since we all know from the Scriptures how holily and blamelessly our Apostle conducted himself in everything after his conversion. But it will not be surprising if we consider that, given the extraordinary measure of holiness with which he was endowed, he could not look upon the rebellious motions of his nature without judging himself guilty both of the good omitted and of the evil committed. For he observed those motions, either hindering him from rendering as exactly as possible every part of his duty towards God and men, or in some way polluting all his actions in the sight of God, so that they were contrary to the Law of God. What wonder, then, if in this way he portrays himself as an extraordinary sinner?

units.la: Vers. 20. Quod si id facio ego quod ego nolo, non amplius ego id perpetro, sed peccatum quod in me habitat, id perpetrat.
units.tr: Verse 20. Now if I do that which I would not, it is no more I that do it, but sin that dwelleth in me.

units.la: Sequitur victoria, post hunc paroxysmum, & repetita consolatio sui ipsius, & reliquorum Sanctorum, Quod deflenti sibi, hanc suam impersectionem, non fit imputandum admissum peccatum, sed corruptioni suae naturae, seu habituali peccato inhabitanti, perditioni & abolitioni destinato: & quod obluctetur peccato, idcirco denominetur ipse a meliori, & renovata sui parte, ut supra vers. 17. non vero a parte deteriori.
units.tr: After this paroxysm follows the victory, and a renewed comfort for himself and the other saints: that the sin committed is not to be imputed to one who laments this imperfection of his, but to the corruption of his nature, or to the habitual sin dwelling in him, destined for destruction and abolition; and that, because he struggles against sin, he is named from his better and renewed part, as above in verse 17, and not from the worse part.

units.la: Vers. 21. Invenio igitur volenti mihi facere bonum, hanc legem impositam esse, quod mihi malum adjaceat. Tertius paroxysmus, constans triplici dissidio; Primum est inter se renovatum, sanctitati studentem: & pravam inclinationem, ei adhærentem, ipsumque ex necessitate quadam, tanquam lege aliqua ad malum incitantem, & impellentem.
units.tr: Verse 21. I find then a law, that, when I would do good, evil is present with me. The third paroxysm, consisting of a threefold dissent. The first is between the renewed self, striving after holiness, and the depraved inclination that clings to it, and which, by a certain necessity, as by some law, urges and impels him to evil.

units.la: Verf. 22. Delector enim Lege Dei quòd ad interiorem hominem.
units.tr: Verse 22. For I delight in the Law of God after the inward man.

units.la: Verf. 23. Sed video aliam legem in membris meis belligerantem adversus Legem mentis meæ, & captivum reddentem me legi peccati, quæ est in membris meis.
units.tr: Verse 23. But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity to the law of sin which is in my members.

units.la: Secundum dissidium, est inter hominem interiorem spiritualem, seu renovatum, cum suis affectibus renovatis, & Dei lege, ex altera parte; & hominem exteriorem, animalem, seu veterem non renovatum, instructum membris suis, & facultatibus, cum suis motibus rebellibus, ex altera parte; adversus legem Dei, & legem, seu inclinationem mentis renovatæ, pugnantem, & prævalentem aliquando; & captivum se reddentem pravæ suæ naturæ inclinationi. Hæc pugna est, de qua Galat. 5. 17. Caro concupiscit adversus spiritum, & spiritus adversus carnem: hæc autem inter se opposita sunt, ut non quæcunque volueritis eadem faciatis: Quam luctam soli intelligunt, qui eam intra se sentiunt, & vim peccati, etiam sanctissimas actiones suas, aliquo modo polluentis, & vitæ suæ telam totam, longè latèque pervadentis experiuntur.
units.tr: The second dissent is between the inward, spiritual man, or the renewed man with his renewed affections, and the Law of God, on the one hand; and the outward, animal man, or the old unrenewed man, furnished with his members and faculties and their rebellious motions, on the other hand; warring against the Law of God and against the law, or inclination, of the renewed mind, and sometimes prevailing, and bringing him into captivity to the inclination of his depraved nature. This is the struggle of which Gal. 5. 17 speaks: The flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; and these are contrary the one to the other, so that ye cannot do the things that ye would. Only those understand this struggle who feel it within themselves, and experience the power of sin, which in some way pollutes even their most holy actions and spreads far and wide through the whole web of their life.

units.la: Verf. 24. Ærumnosus ego homo: quis me eripiet ex isto corpore mortis?
units.tr: Verse 24. Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?

units.la: Tertium dissidium, est inter Concupiscentiam pravam, & sanctum Dei servum, prostratum, jacentem, & sub oppressione victricis perversitatis naturæ, seu corporis hujus mortiferi, gementem, lamentantem, & ad Deum liberatorem exclamantem.
units.tr: The third conflict is between the perverse concupiscence and the holy servant of God, who is prostrate and lying down, groaning under the oppression of the victorious perversity of nature, or of this deadly body, lamenting and crying out to God the deliverer.

units.la: Verf. 25. — Gratias ago Deo per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum.
units.tr: Verse 25. I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

units.la: Post paroxysmum, sequitur victoria, & consolatio per fidem in justificantem Christum, unà cum gratiarum actione, ad Deum liberatorem, qui consolationem paravit in Christo, non iis qui peccato indulgent, sed iis qui peccata deflent. Verf. 25. Nempe igitur ipse ego mente quidem servio Legi Dei, carne vero legi peccati.
units.tr: After the paroxysm follows victory and consolation through faith in Christ the justifier, together with thanksgiving to God the deliverer, who has prepared consolation in Christ not for those who indulge in sin but for those who mourn their sins. Verse 25. So then I myself, with the mind, indeed serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin.

units.la: Tandem sedatâ mente, post affectum, & doloris ob peccatum inhabitans; & gaudii, propter speratam liberationem per Christum, Apostolus proponit seipsum denuo, commilitonem, cum reliquis sanctis, in hoc sacro bello, adversus reliquias peccati; In hunc sensum: Nempe igitur, ipse ego Apostolus, (ut in consolationem eorum qui peccata sua deflent summatim recolligam, quae de me ipse dixi) profiteor, me non aequutum esse, eam mensuram sanctitatis, ad quam aspiro: Sed una cum reliquis Sanctis, lugens, & luctans, sub spe liberationis, pergo: Et quasi divisus à meipso, luctantibus inter se, spiritu & carne in me, mente quidem, seu parte mei spirituali, & renovata, cum delectatione, servio Legi Dei: Carne vero, seu parte mei non renovatâ, ipse inquam, tanquam captivus legi peccati, seu corruptae naturae inclinationi praevalenti, subjugatus servio.
units.tr: At last, with the mind calmed after the emotion and pain caused by the sin dwelling in him, and after the joy at the liberation hoped for through Christ, the Apostle once more sets himself forth, as a fellow soldier with the other saints, in this holy war against the remnants of sin. To this sense: So then I myself, the Apostle (to gather up briefly, for the consolation of those who mourn their sins, what I have said of myself), profess that I have not attained that measure of holiness to which I aspire; but together with the other saints, mourning and struggling, I press on in hope of deliverance. And as if divided from myself, with spirit and flesh struggling against each other within me, I serve the law of God with the mind, that is, with my spiritual and renewed part, with delight; but with the flesh, that is, my unrenewed part, I myself, I say, as a captive to the law of sin, that is, to the inclination of corrupt nature prevailing over me, serve in subjection.

units.la: Caput octavum.
units.tr: Chapter 8.

units.la: Quinta Confirmatio, Justificationis per fidem est, quod haec justificandi ratio, solidam consolationem praebeat, non solum adversus omne malum, post hanc vitam metuendum, sed etiam adversus omnes molestias, & afflictiones, quibus obnoxii sunt Dei filij in hac vita.
units.tr: The fifth confirmation of justification by faith is that this way of being justified gives solid comfort, not only against every evil to be feared after this life, but also against all the troubles and afflictions to which the children of God are liable in this life.

units.la: Capitis tres sunt partes, Prima est consolatio Justificatorum, adversus condemnationis metum, qui vexare posset, lugentes suae sanctificationis imperfectionem, & peccati in se reliquias; Quam consolationem propriam facit justificatorum studentium sanctitati, seclusis irregenitis, peccato indulgentibus, ad verf. 9. eamque applicat Romanis, ad verf. 12. Et applicatam, in usum trahit, ad verf 17 Secunda pars continet consolationes Justorum, adversus huius vitae calamitates, quibus Fideles obnoxii sunt, ad verf. 31. Tertia pars continet Justificatorum Triumphum de omnibus hostibus, ad finem.
units.tr: The chapter has three parts. The first is the comfort of the justified against the fear of condemnation, which could trouble those who mourn the imperfection of their sanctification and the remnants of sin in themselves. The author makes this comfort the proper possession of those justified who strive after holiness, excluding the unregenerate who indulge in sin, and he addresses it to the Romans at verse 9, and applies it to them at verse 12. Having applied it, he draws it into use at verse 17. The second part contains the comfort of the righteous against the calamities of this life, to which the faithful are liable, up to verse 31. The third part contains the triumph of the justified over all their enemies, to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Verf. 1. Nulla igitur nunc est condemnatio iis qui sunt in Christo Iesu, qui non secundum carnem ambulant, sed secundum spiritum. Ex superioribus, infert consolationem Justificatorum, adversus condemnationis metum, quem incutere posset, peccati in se habitantis, conscientia: Nulla (inquit) est condemnatio iis, qui verâ fide insiti sunt CHRISTO: Et quia multi profitentur fidem, quam non habent, describit verè fideles, & justificatos, ab hac proprietate, quod non indulgeant peccato, nec ultrò sequantur, carnis, & corruptæ naturæ suæ ductum, sed secundum DEI mandata ambulent, & motus Spiritus sancti, intus suadentis, ut vitæ suæ cursum, secundum verbi DEI regulam, dirigant, lubentes sequantur.
units.tr: Verse 1. "There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit." From what has gone before, he draws the comfort of the justified against the fear of condemnation which the consciousness of the sin dwelling in them could stir up. There is no condemnation (he says) for those who are truly grafted into Christ by true faith. And because many profess a faith they do not have, he describes the truly faithful and justified by this mark: they do not indulge in sin or willingly follow the lead of the flesh and their corrupt nature, but walk according to God's commands, and gladly follow the movements of the Holy Spirit, who urges them inwardly to direct the course of their life according to the rule of God's Word.

units.la: Verf. 2. Nam Lex Spiritus vitæ qui est in Christo Iesu, liberavit me à lege peccati & mortis.
units.tr: Verse 2. "For the law of the Spirit of life, which is in Christ Jesus, has made me free from the law of sin and death."

units.la: Hanc consolationem, deberi verè justificatis, sanctitatis studiosis, probat tribus argumentis.
units.tr: He proves that this comfort is owed to those truly justified and eager for holiness by three arguments.

units.la: Argumentum primum, Lex fidei, vitæ, & Spiritus in CHRISTO, seu fœdus Gratiæ, liberavit unumquemque fidelem, & me nominatim, à lege mortis & peccati, seu à fœdere Operum: Ergo Justificatis, verè cum CHRISTO unitis, nulla est condemnatio. Per legem enim spiritus vitalis in CHRISTO, intelligit legem Fidei, seu fœdus Gratiæ, quia per fidem, seu fœdus gratiæ, accipitur Spiritus, & vitæ CHRISTI communio. Per legem verò mortis & peccati, intelligit legem operum, ut Rom. 3 27. seu fœdus operum, per quam legem, seu fœdus, fit convictio de peccato, & condemnatio reorum ad mortem.
units.tr: The first argument: the law of faith, life and the Spirit in Christ, that is, the covenant of grace, has set free every believer, and me by name, from the law of death and sin, that is, from the covenant of works. Therefore there is no condemnation for the justified, who are truly united with Christ. By "the law of the vital Spirit in Christ" he means the law of faith, or the covenant of grace, because through faith, or the covenant of grace, the Spirit and the communion of Christ's life are received. By "the law of sin and death" he means the law of works, as in Romans 3:27, or the covenant of works, through which law, or covenant, sin is convicted and the guilty are condemned to death.

units.la: Verf. 3. Nam quæ Legis erat impotentia quum viribus esset destituta in carne, Deus suo ipsius Filio misso in forma consimili carni peccato obnoxia, idque pro peccato, condemnavit peccatum in carne.
units.tr: Verse 3. "For what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh."

units.la: Arg. 2. Cum lex impotens comperta est, ad justificationem procurandam, propter carnis, seu humanæ naturæ, jam corruptæ, impotentiam, ad perfectam obedientiam ei præstandam. DEUS misso Filio in carnem, ejusdem naturæ cum nostra, similemque in omnibus (excepto peccato) in Filii sui carne crucifixa, condemnavit peccatum nostrum, ut expiatione facta pro nobis, prorsus aboleretur e nobis. Ergo peccatum non poterit nobis justificatis, qui in CHRISTO sumus, esse causa condemnationis, & sic nulla nobis est condemnatio.
units.tr: Argument 2. Since the law was found powerless to procure justification, because of the weakness of the flesh, that is, of human nature now corrupted, in rendering it perfect obedience, God, by sending his Son in the flesh, of the same nature as ours and in all things like us (apart from sin), condemned our sin in the crucified flesh of his Son, so that, once expiation had been made for us, it might be utterly abolished from us. Therefore sin cannot be a cause of condemnation for us who are justified and in Christ, and so there is no condemnation for us.

units.la: Verf. 4. Ut jus illud Legis compleatur in nobis, qui non secundum carnem ambulamus, sed secundum Spiritum.
units.tr: Verse 4. "That the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit."

units.la: Eo ipso fine, condemnatum est peccatum, in condemnato & mortuo CHRISTO, pro nobis, ut nobis in CHRISTO semel condemnatis, & mortuis, Legi satisfactum esse in nobis comperiretur; in nobis, inquam, qui non carnis desideria sequimur, sed ductum Spiritus sancti; Ergo nulla jam nobis restat condemnatio.
units.tr: For this very end, sin was condemned in Christ, who was condemned and died for us, so that, since we have been condemned and died with Christ, it might be found that the law has been satisfied in us. In us, I say, who do not follow the desires of the flesh but the lead of the Holy Spirit. Therefore no condemnation remains for us.

units.la: Verf. 5. Nam qui secundum carnem sunt, quae carnis sunt sapiunt: qui vero sunt secundum Spiritum, quae Spiritus sunt.
units.tr: Verse 5. "For those who are according to the flesh mind the things of the flesh, but those who are according to the Spirit mind the things of the Spirit."

units.la: Cur hanc consolationem, propriam fecerit sanctitati studentium, seclusis omnibus irregenitis, seu peccato indulgentibus, rationes reddit quatuor. Prima ratio, Carnales, & irregeniti, sola carnalia, & vitiosa sapiunt & affectant: regeniti vero sapiunt, & affectant spiritualia: Ergo non mirum, quod soli sanctitatis studiosi, ad immunitatis à condemnatione consolationem, admittantur, carnales vero excludantur.
units.tr: Why he made this comfort the proper possession of those who strive after holiness, excluding all the unregenerate, or those who indulge in sin, he gives four reasons. First reason: the carnal and unregenerate savour and aim only at carnal and vicious things, but the regenerate savour and aim at spiritual things. Therefore it is not surprising that only those eager for holiness are admitted to the comfort of immunity from condemnation, and the carnal are excluded.

units.la: Verf. 6. Nam quod sapit caro, mors est: quod autem sapit Spiritus, vita & pax.
units.tr: Verse 6. "For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace."

units.la: Ratio 2. Ipsa prudentia carnalium hominum moderatrix consiliorum & actionum ipsorum, fertur tantum ad ea, quae carni placent, sine respectu ad DEUM, & vitam aeternam, & sic ad mortem tantum fertur: Prudentia vero spiritus, seu habitus dirigens actiones renatorum, fertur ad ea, quae ad vitam & pacem spiritualem spectant; Ergo non mirum, si soli eximantur regeniti, & spirituales, à condemnatione, non vero carnales.
units.tr: Reason 2. The very prudence of carnal men, which governs their counsels and actions, is directed only to what pleases the flesh, without regard to God and eternal life, and so is directed only to death. But the prudence of the Spirit, that is, the disposition directing the actions of the reborn, is directed to what concerns spiritual life and peace. Therefore it is not surprising if only the regenerate and spiritual are exempted from condemnation, and not the carnal.

units.la: Verf. 7. Quoniam quod sapit caro inimicitia est adversus Deum. Legi enim Dei non subjicitur: nam ne potest quidem.
units.tr: Verse 7. "Because the mind of the flesh is enmity against God; for it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be."

units.la: Ratio. 3. Confirmans priorem; Carnis prudentia ipsa, politicorum ingeniorum praecipua virtus, DEO inimica est, siquidem sua tantum quaerit, & curat, DEO semper posthabito, & rejecto, nec enim legi DEI, vel subjicitur, vel subjicii quidem potest: nam finibus suis carnalibus, non potest non subjicere animam, Caelum, DEUM, & omnia; de iisque agere, prout carni, & finibus carnalibus, conducibile existimat: Non mirum ergo carnales non eximi à condemnatione.
units.tr: Reason 3, confirming the former. The very prudence of the flesh, the chief virtue of worldly wits, is hostile to God, since it seeks and cares only for its own things, always setting God aside and rejecting him. Nor is it subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be made subject; for with its carnal ends it cannot but subject the soul, heaven, God and all things to itself, and deal with them as it judges useful to the flesh and carnal ends. It is not surprising, then, that the carnal are not exempted from condemnation.

units.la: Verf. 8. Ergo qui in carne sunt, Deo placere non possunt.
units.tr: Verse 8. "So those who are in the flesh cannot please God."

units.la: <bl>Ratio</bl> 4. Quicunque irregeniti sunt, in statu carnis, seu corruptæ naturæ, Deo placere non possunt, quia non possunt non studere illis rebus, quæ sibi placent. Non ergo mirum, quod non eximantur è condemnatione.
units.tr: Reason 4. Whoever are unregenerate, in the state of the flesh or corrupt nature, cannot please God, because they cannot but be devoted to those things which please themselves. It is not surprising, therefore, that they are not exempted from condemnation.

units.la: Verf. 9. Vos autem non estis in carne, sed in Spiritu: siquidem Spiritus Dei habitat in vobis, quòd siquis Spiritum Christi non habet, is non est ejus.
units.tr: Verse 9. "But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, since the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his."

units.la: Applicando proprietatem Justificatorum Romanis, applicat etiam consolationem de immunitate à condemnatione iisdem Romanis, ad quos scribit, de iis judicans ex charitate: prudenter interim ipsos alloquitur, ne hypocrisin in quovis foveret. Rationes autem applicationis dat quatuor.
units.tr: In applying the property of the justified to the Romans, he also applies to the same Romans the comfort of immunity from condemnation, judging of them out of charity; meanwhile, he wisely addresses them so that he does not foster hypocrisy in anyone. He gives four reasons for the application.

units.la: Prima ratio. Vos non estis obnoxij imperio carnis, non estis irregeniti, sed in statu spirituali, spiritus ductum sequentes. Ergo nulla vobis condemnatio, seu, quod idem est, ad vos pertinet prædicta consolatio.
units.tr: First reason. You are not subject to the dominion of the flesh; you are not unregenerate, but in a spiritual state, following the lead of the Spirit. Therefore the aforesaid comfort is yours, or, which is the same thing, there is no condemnation for you.

units.la: <bl>Ratio</bl> 2. confirmans superiorem, Spiritus Christi, corda vestra, & vitam vestram formans ad sanctitatem, habitat in vobis; nam nisi sic de vobis judicarem, vos etiam ad Christum non pertinere existimarem; nam qui Christi Spiritum sanctificantem non habet, nondum Christi vivum membrum est. Ergo nulla vobis est condemnatio.
units.tr: Reason 2, confirming the former. The Spirit of Christ, forming your hearts and your lives to holiness, dwells in you. For unless I judged so of you, I would think you did not belong to Christ either; for whoever does not have the sanctifying Spirit of Christ is not yet a living member of Christ. Therefore there is no condemnation for you.

units.la: Verf. 10. Porrò si Christus in vobis est, corpus quidem mortuum est propter peccatum: spiritus autem, vita est propter justitiam.
units.tr: Verse 10. "But if Christ is in you, the body is indeed dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness."

units.la: <bl>Ratio</bl> 3. Cum Christus sit in vobis, licet corpus quidem vestrum ratione reliquiarum peccati, non nisi in morte abolendarum, morti sit destinatum, & certò moriturum: Spiritus tamen regenerationis datus vobis, est ipsa vita æterna in vobis, seu animabus vestris inchoata, propter justitiam Christi imputatam. Ergo nulla vobis est condemnatio.
units.tr: Reason 3. Since Christ is in you, although your body, by reason of the remnants of sin, which can be abolished only in death, is destined for death and will certainly die, nevertheless the Spirit of regeneration given to you is eternal life itself within you, begun in your souls, on account of the righteousness of Christ imputed to you. Therefore there is no condemnation for you.

units.la: Verf. 11. Sed si Spiritus ejus qui suscitavit Iesum ex mortuis, habitat in vobis, is qui excitavit Christum ex mortuis, vivificabit etiam mortalia corpora vestra per inhabitantem ipsius spiritum in vobis.
units.tr: Verse 11. "But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you."

units.la: Ratio 4. Spiritus Christi inhabitans in vobis, domicilium suum non est unquam omnino defuturus, sed vos gloriosum, & dignum se hospitium immortale, sibi redditurus; In quem finem, Deus, non minus certo, & potenter vestra etiam corpora mortalia, ad vitam immortalem vivificabit, quam Christi corpus, a mortuis excitavit: Ergo nulla vobis est condemnatio.
units.tr: Fourth reason: The Spirit of Christ dwells in you; he will never wholly leave his dwelling, but will restore you as a glorious and worthy immortal dwelling-place for himself. To that end God will, no less surely and powerfully, quicken your mortal bodies to immortal life, just as he raised up Christ's body from the dead. Therefore there is no condemnation for you.

units.la: Verf. 12. Nempe igitur fratres, debitores sumus non carni, ut secundum carnem vivamus, sed Spiritui.
units.tr: Verse 12. Therefore, brothers, we are debtors not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh, but to the Spirit.

units.la: Applicatam Romanis consolationem, de immunitate a condemnatione, trahit jam in usum, hortando eos, ut sanctitati studeant, & ita sibi firmam consolationem reddant. Hortationis argumenta sunt sex.
units.tr: Having applied to the Romans the comfort of immunity from condemnation, he now turns it to use by exhorting them to devote themselves to holiness, so that they may secure this firm comfort for themselves. There are six arguments of exhortation.

units.la: Argumentum primum. Devincti sumus omnibus modis, ad serviendum Spiritui sancto, nos de officio nostro, intus, & ex verbo suo, quotidie commonenti; non vero debemus carni, seu naturae pravitati servire, vel ejus desideriis obsequi, quippe cui nihil debemus, praeter odium, & mortificationis media, persolvere. Ergo sanctitati studendum.
units.tr: First argument. We are bound in every way to serve the Holy Spirit, who daily reminds us of our duty, inwardly and through his word. We ought not to serve the flesh, that is, the corruption of nature, or obey its desires, since we owe it nothing except hatred and the putting to death of its works. Therefore we must devote ourselves to holiness.

units.la: Verf. 13. Nam si secundum carnem vixeritis, futurum est ut moriamini; sed si Spiritu actiones corporis mortificetis, vivetis.
units.tr: Verse 13. For if you live according to the flesh, you are going to die; but if by the Spirit you mortify the deeds of the body, you will live.

units.la: Arg. 2. Si carnis, seu corruptae naturae desideria, vobis pro regula statuatis, ut secundum ea, vitam instituatis vestram, morte aeterna moriemini: Ergo nisi perire vultis, sanctitati studendum.
units.tr: Second argument. If you set the desires of the flesh, that is, of corrupted nature, as your rule, so that you order your life according to them, you will die an eternal death. Therefore, unless you want to perish, you must devote yourselves to holiness.

units.la: Arg. 3. Si Spiritui Dei obtemperaveritis, solis mediis ab ipso praescriptis utentes, & virtutem ipsius, quam vobis in Christum credentibus suppeditabit, adhibentes, ad motus pravos & actiones corporis carnalis pravas mortificandum; haud dubie vitam aeternam ex Dei gratia consequemini. Ergo sanctitati studendum.
units.tr: Third argument. If you obey the Spirit of God, using only the means prescribed by him and applying the power which he supplies to you who believe in Christ, to mortify wicked motions and the wicked deeds of the carnal body, you will without doubt obtain eternal life by the grace of God. Therefore we must devote ourselves to holiness.

units.la: Verf. 14. Quotquot enim Spiritu Dei aguntur ij sunt filii Dei.
