units.la: Præceptum 13. Ut pacem sectemur cum omnibus; Cui additur limitatio, si fieri potest, & quantum per nos fieri potest, ut media pacis omnia tentemus, & si turbulentum quid acciderit, aliorum sit reatus, non nostER.
units.tr: Precept 13: that we pursue peace with all. To this is added the qualification if it be possible, and as far as it can be done by us: that we try all the means of peace, and if some disturbance arises, the guilt belongs to others, not to us.

units.la: Verf. 19. Non ipsi vosmetipsos ulcisentes dilecti, sed date locum iræ; scriptum est enim, Mihi est ultio: ego rependam, dicit Dominus:
units.tr: Verse 19. Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.

units.la: Præceptum 14. Prohibens specialiter magis quam supra, talionem; quia proclivio res sumus ad vindictam: Idcirco amicè vetat vindictam privatam, & Jubet, ut sinamus iram & nostram, & adversariorum defervescere, neque hanc, neque illam dictis factisve foventes, vel irritantes, addito gravi argumento, quia De i partes sunt, vel Immediatè, vel per magistratum, Injurias nobis illatas vindicare. In casu inculpatæ tutelæ, quid faciendum, ex locis communibus petendum.
units.tr: Precept 14: forbidding retaliation more specifically than above, since we are prone to vengeance. Therefore he kindly forbids private vengeance and commands that we let both our anger and that of our adversaries cool, fostering or provoking neither by word nor deed. He adds a weighty argument: there are two ways to avenge injuries done to us, either immediately or through the magistrate. What is to be done in the case of blameless self-defence is to be sought from the commonplaces.

units.la: Verf. 20. Itaque si esurit inimicus tuus, ciba cum: si sitit, da ei potum: hoc enim si feceris, carbones ignis coacervabis in caput ejus.
units.tr: Verse 20. Therefore if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head.

units.la: Præceptum 15. De benefaciendo inimicis nostris, cum occasio, & ipsorum necessitas requirit; hæc autem ratio additur, quia hac probatione, quasi carbones coacervamus in eos ut vel mollescant, sicut metallum liquescit igne, si in illis aliquid sit bonæ indolis: vel conviction, & damnatio ipsorum, reddatur tanta gravior, idque non nostrâ, sed ipsorum culpâ.
units.tr: Precept 15: concerning doing good to our enemies when the occasion and their need require it. The reason is added: by this kindness we heap coals upon them, so that they may either soften, as metal melts in fire, if there is some good disposition in them, or their conviction and condemnation be rendered all the heavier, and that through their own fault, not ours.

units.la: Verf. 21. Ne vincitor à malo: sed vince bono malum.
units.tr: Verse 21. Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good.

units.la: Præceptum 16. Eodem tendens, sed generalius est, ut in certanda cum inimicis, recte de victoria judicemus; quæ non est, cum malum malo rependere studemus, aut malum malo superare certamus: vincimur enim tum potius à malo, quam vincimus; sed victoria hæc unica est, cum rectè: recte agendo, superamus malum, & ad hanc victoriam quaerendam hic hortatur.
units.tr: Precept 16: tending to the same end but more general: that in contending with enemies we judge rightly about victory. It is not victory when we strive to repay evil with evil, or contend to overcome evil with evil; for then we are rather overcome by evil than overcome it. This victory alone is true, when by acting rightly we overcome evil, and he exhorts us to seek this victory.

units.la: Caput Decimumtertium.
units.tr: Chapter Thirteen.

units.la: DErgit hortari, ut fructus ferant professione dignos; erga Magistratus, & cujusvis ordinis homines. Capitis dux sunt partes: Prima, de subjectione civili, ad versum octavum: Altera de dilectione, quatenus secundam Legis tabulam respicit.
units.tr: Ergo it urges that they bear fruit worthy of their profession, toward the magistrates and men of every rank. The chapter has two parts. The first, concerning civil subjection, runs to verse 8. The second, concerning love, insofar as it relates to the second table of the Law.

units.la: Omnis anima potestatibus supereminentibus subjecta esto. Non enim est potestas nisi a Deo: & quae sunt potestates, sunt a Deo ordinatae.
units.tr: Let every soul be subject to the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: and the powers that be are ordained of God.

units.la: Hortatio proponitur primis verbis, Ut omnis anima, seu omnis homo subjiciatur, seu subordinetur potestatibus supereminentibus, id est, civili Magistratui: Argumenta hortationis sunt decem.
units.tr: The exhortation is set out in the first words: that every soul, or every man, be subject or subordinated to the higher powers, that is, to the civil magistrate. There are ten arguments for the exhortation.

units.la: ris, vel ordinis, est à DEI institutione, & ordinatione.
units.tr: ...of rank or order, is from the institution and ordinance of God.

units.la: Verf. 2. Itaque quisquis se opponit potestati, Dei ordinationi resistit: qui autem resistunt, ipsi sibi condemnationem auferent.
units.tr: Verse 2. Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God: and they that resist shall receive to themselves damnation.

units.la: poenam, cum à DEO, tum à Magistratu.
units.tr: ...punishment, both from God and from the magistrate.

units.la: Verf. 3. Nam magistratus non sunt terrori bonis operibus, sed malis. Vis autem non terreri potestate? quod bonum est facito, & laudem ab ipsa obtinebis.
units.tr: Verse 3. For rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil. Wilt thou then not be afraid of the power? Do that which is good, and thou shalt have praise of the same.

units.la: Arg. 4. Quia Magistratus officium à DEO ordinatur, ut cohibeat malos, & mala opera puniat, non verò bona: Ergo ei subjici debemus.
units.tr: Argument 4. Because the office of the magistrate is ordained by God to restrain the wicked and to punish evil works, and not good ones; therefore we ought to be subject to him.

units.la: Verf. 4. Dei enim minister est tuo bono. Quod si feceris quod malum est, metue: non enim frustra gladium gestat, Nam Dei minister est, ultor ad iram ei qui quod malum est fecerit.
units.tr: Verse 4. For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.

units.la: Arg. 6. Quia Magistratus est minister Dei in nostrum bonum, nam per Magistratum, Deus honesta & utilia nobis praecipit & procurat, & malos tollit, quod nobis est conducibile.
units.tr: Argument 6. Because the magistrate is God's minister for our good. For through the magistrate God prescribes and provides what is honourable and useful for us, and removes the wicked, which is profitable for us.

units.la: Non enim ] Arg. 7. Quia gladio armatur, ad puniendum malos, authoritate ad hoc divinitus ei tributa. Idcirco metuere, & subjici oportet maleficii reos, etiam in capitis periculo jam constitutos.
units.tr: For he] Argument 7. Because he is armed with the sword to punish the wicked, with authority divinely given to him for this purpose. Therefore those guilty of wrongdoing ought to fear and submit, even when they are already placed in peril of their life.

units.la: Verf. 5. Quapropter necesse est subjici, non solum propter iram, sed etiam propter conscientiam.
units.tr: Verse 5. Wherefore ye must needs be subject, not only for wrath, but also for conscience sake.

units.la: Arg. 8. Quia est necessarium subjici, non solum ad vitandam iram principis, & poenas civiles, sed etiam ad retinendam bonam conscientiam, respectu praecepti Divini, subjectionem praecipientis.
units.tr: Argument 8. Because it is necessary to be subject, not only to avoid the anger of the prince and civil penalties, but also to keep a good conscience, out of respect for the divine command that enjoins subjection.

units.la: Verf. 6. Propter hoc enim etiam tributa solvitis: siquidem ministri Dei sunt in hoc ipsum incumbentes.
units.tr: Verse 6. For for this cause pay ye tribute also: for they are God's ministers, attending continually upon this very thing.

units.la: Arg. 9. Quia etiam tributa debemus Magistratibus, ut Dei ministris, defensioni politicae incumbentibus, & huic soli negotio vacantibus: Idcirco iis subjici debemus.
units.tr: Argument 9. Because we also owe tributes to the magistrates, as ministers of God, who are engaged in the defence of the commonwealth and devoted to this task alone. Therefore we ought to be subject to them.

units.la: Verf. 7. Reddite igitur omnibus quod debetis: cui tributum debetur, tributum: cui vectigal, vectigal: cui timor, timorem: cui honor, honorem.
units.tr: Verse 7. Render therefore to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom; fear to whom fear; honour to whom honour.

units.la: Arg. 10 Per modum conclusionis illatum; Quia sicut Justum est, unicuique suum tribuere, sic etiam magistratui tributum, vectigal, timorem, honorem, persolvere; pro ut omnia aut aliqua ex his, magistratui superiori, aut inferiori, & ipsorum ministris debentur.
units.tr: Argument 10, drawn as a conclusion: because just as it is right to give each his own, so too it is right to pay the magistrate tribute, customs, fear and honour; as all or some of these are owed to the magistrate, whether superior or inferior, and to their ministers.

units.la: Secunda Pars.
units.tr: Second Part.

units.la: Verf. 8. Nemini quicquam debete, nisi hoc, ut alii alios diligatis, nam qui diligit alterum, Legem implevit.
units.tr: Verse 8. Owe no one anything, except that you love one another; for he who loves another has fulfilled the Law.

units.la: Secunda pars Capitis, in qua sanctitatem vitae, & dilectionem praecipit, quatenus secundam tabulam respicit: Hortationis argumenta sunt sex.
units.tr: The second part of the chapter, in which he enjoins holiness of life and love, insofar as it regards the second table. The arguments for this exhortation are six.

units.la: Nisi ] Argumentum primum. Quia dilectio perpetuo debetur; Ergo persolvenda perpetuo.
units.tr: Except] First argument. Because love is always owed; therefore it is always to be paid.

units.la: Implevit ] Arg. 2. Quia dilectio proximi, est legis impletio: Ergo dilectioni studendum.
units.tr: Has fulfilled] Second argument. Because love of neighbour is the fulfilling of the Law; therefore we ought to strive after love.

units.la: Verf. 9. Siquidem illud, Non moechaberis, Non occides, Non furaberis, Non falsum testimonium dices, Non concupisces, & si quod aliud est mandatum, in hoc sermone summatim comprehenditur a nempe, Diliges proximum tuum sicut teipsum.
units.tr: Verse 9. For this, "You shall not commit adultery, You shall not kill, You shall not steal, You shall not bear false witness, You shall not covet," and whatever other commandment there is, is summed up in this saying, namely, "You shall love your neighbour as yourself."

units.la: Hoc argumentum confirmat, duabus rationibus, prima est ab enumeratione praeceptorum secundae tabulae, quae ad dilectionis praeceptum, referuntur omnia.
units.tr: This argument is confirmed by two reasons. The first is from the enumeration of the precepts of the second table, all of which are referred to the precept of love.

units.la: Verf. 10. Charitas proximum non afficit malo. Itaque charitas est completio Legis.
units.tr: Verse 10. Love does no wrong to a neighbour. Therefore love is the fulfilling of the Law.

units.la: est; Quia dilectio, nullo malo, quod per legem prohibetur, proximum afficit: idcirco dilectio, est impletio legis, eique idcirco studendum est.
units.tr: Because love does no evil to a neighbour, which the law forbids; therefore love is the fulfilling of the law, and therefore it is to be pursued.

units.la: Verf. 11. Idque, perspecta opportunitate, quod videlicet tempus jam sit nos a somno expergisci. Nunc enim propius nos est salus quam quum credidimus:
units.tr: Verse 11. And this, knowing the opportune time, namely that it is now the hour for us to wake from sleep. For now our salvation is nearer than when we first believed.

units.la: Quo urget fructus fidei, ex dilectione sancta nostri, & proximorum, Quia haec fructificatio satis diu neglecta est, cum in somno peccati jacebamus per naturam, & jam tempus est, ut experrectos nos demonstremus ex hoc somno peccati, regenerationis fructus ferendo.
units.tr: Here the fruit of faith urges us, from our holy love of ourselves and of our neighbours; for this fruitfulness has been neglected long enough, while by nature we lay in the sleep of sin; and now it is time that we show ourselves awakened from this sleep of sin, by bearing the fruit of regeneration.

units.la: Arg. 4. Quia propinquior est salus nostra, quam cum primum conversi fuimus ad fidem. Studendum ergo eo magis, ut fructus fidei, & spei de salute adventante, uberiores feramus ex dilectione.
units.tr: Fourth argument. Because our salvation is nearer than when we first were converted to the faith. Therefore we ought all the more to strive to bear more abundant fruit of love from the faith and hope of the approaching salvation.

units.la: Verf. 12. Nox processit, dies autem propinquat. Abjiciamus igitur opera tenebrarum, & induamur habitu qui luci conveniat.
units.tr: Verse 12. The night is far spent, the day is at hand. Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness, and put on the armour of light.

units.la: Hujus seculi & nostrae etiam ignorantiae, & caecitatis nox processit, & consumpta est maxima ex parte, quantum attinet ad conditionem naturae corruptae,id est,instat finis corrupti hujus mundi & abolitio corruptionis naturae nostrae: Ergo facessant opera noctis, tenebrarum, ignorantiae, & peccati.
units.tr: The night of this age, and of our own ignorance and blindness, has advanced and is for the most part spent, so far as concerns the condition of corrupt nature; that is, the end of this corrupt world and the abolition of the corruption of our nature is at hand. Therefore let the works of night, of darkness, of ignorance and of sin depart.

units.la: Arg. 6. Dies, seu status illuminationis, & regenerationis plenae in gloria futura, appropinquavit, & in jam inchoata nostra regeneratione illucescere coepit, quasi diluculo: Ergo arma induamus, ut certemus contra Diabolum, peccatum, & mundum, semper quod bonum est agentes.
units.tr: Sixth argument. The day, or the state of illumination and of full regeneration in future glory, has drawn near, and in our regeneration, already begun, it has begun to dawn, as at daybreak. Therefore let us put on arms, that we may fight against the devil, sin and the world, always doing what is good.

units.la: Verf. 13. Ut interdiu, composite incedamus: non in comessationibus & ebrietatibus, non cubilibus ac proterviis, non lite & invidia. Hinc deducit quasi conclusionem hortatoriam quadruplicem:
units.tr: Verse 13. Let us walk properly, as in the day: not in revelling and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envy. From this he deduces, as it were, a fourfold hortatory conclusion:

units.la: Ambulemus ] Prima hortatio est, ut decenter incedamus, sicut decet filios lucis, per Euangelii gratiam regenitos.
units.tr: Let us walk] The first exhortation is that we walk becomingly, as befits the children of light, born again through the grace of the Gospel.

units.la: Comessationibus ] Secunda hortatio est, ut ab intemperantia, & foeditate omni abstineamus, nominatim ut comessationes, ebrietates, & scortationes, & turpem lasciviam, (quâ in cubilibus, & cubiculis, se polluere solent profani) & litem, & invidiam, caveamus & abhominemur.
units.tr: Revelling] The second exhortation is that we abstain from intemperance and every foulness, namely that we guard against and abhor revellings, drunkenness and fornication, and base lasciviousness (in which the profane are accustomed to defile themselves in beds and bedchambers), and strife and envy.

units.la: Verf. 14. Sed induimini Domino Iesu Christo, & carnis curam ne habete, ad explendas cupiditates.
units.tr: Verse 14. But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to fulfil its lusts.

units.la: Tertia hortatio est, ut induamus CHRISTUM, quod dixit, potius quam induamus temperantiam, & virtutes alias, praedictis vitiis contrarias, quia nisi CHRISTUM, ipsiusque Justitiam, nobis imputatam per fidem, primo loco, arctissime amplectamur, & retineamus, ut ex hoc fonte virtutem, ad recte agendum hauriamus, Justitia nostra, non superabit Philosophorum aut Pharisaeorum Justitiam. Nam etiam tum, cum virtute Spiritus CHRISTI, aliquid praestitimus in sanctitate, superinduere rursum oportet CHRISTUM, ut nuditatem nostram, & operum nostrorum imperfectionem, & pollutionem tegat CHRISTI Justitia.
units.tr: The third exhortation is that we put on CHRIST, which he says rather than that we put on temperance and other virtues contrary to the aforementioned vices; because unless we first most closely embrace and retain CHRIST and his righteousness imputed to us through faith, we shall not draw from this fountain the virtue to act rightly; our righteousness will not surpass the righteousness of the Philosophers or the Pharisees. For even when, by the power of the Spirit of CHRIST, we have achieved something in holiness, it is necessary to put CHRIST on again, so that the righteousness of CHRIST may cover our nakedness, and the imperfection and pollution of our works.

units.la: Carnis ] Quarta hortatio; Ut necessario, & legitimo creaturarum usu, ad corporis valetudinem contenti, non curemus, ut satisfaciamus carnis appetitui immoderato, nec indulgeamus voluptatibus carnis, nam qui corporis nimiam curam habet, animam negligit.
units.tr: Flesh] The fourth exhortation is that, being content with the necessary and lawful use of created things for the health of the body, we should not take care to satisfy the immoderate appetite of the flesh, nor indulge the pleasures of the flesh; for he who has excessive care of the body neglects the soul.

units.la: Caput Decimumquartum.
units.tr: Chapter 14.

units.la: Equuntur praecepta, de officiis fidelium mutuis, in usu Christianae libertatis: Fidelium alii, ut conversi Gentiles, persuasi erant de libertate sua Christiana, seu liberatione à jugo Moysis, nec ferias legales, nec delectum ciborum observabant; alii erant, ut Judaei aliqui, in hoc articulo infirmiores, non satis confirmati de libertate sua, qui reverentia legis Divinae, cibis à Mose vetitis abstinebant: Jejunia, dies festos, Sabbatha, Calendas observabant: Inter hos, ortum dissidium opus Euangelii interturbabat, & impediebat. Utrisque junctim praecepta dat Apostolus, ad verf. 13. confirmatis vero in fide, seu in persuasione suae libertatis seorsim, reliquo capite.
units.tr: The precepts follow concerning the mutual duties of believers in the use of Christian liberty. Some of the believers, such as converted Gentiles, were persuaded of their Christian liberty, or deliverance from the yoke of Moses, and did not observe the legal festivals or the distinction of foods. Others, like some Jews, were weaker on this point and not sufficiently confirmed in their liberty. Out of reverence for the divine law, they abstained from the foods forbidden by Moses and observed fasts, feast days, Sabbaths and new moons. Because of these differences, a dispute arose between them that disturbed and hindered the work of the Gospel. The Apostle gives precepts to both groups together, up to verse 13, and then to the confirmed in faith, or those persuaded of their liberty, separately in the rest of the chapter.

units.la: Verf. 1. Eum vero qui fide est infirmus assumite, non tamen ad certamina disceptationum.
units.tr: Verse 1. Receive the one who is weak in faith, but not for disputes over opinions.

units.la: Suadet Apostolus, ut sese mutuo conjungant, cum ii quibus erat persuasum de abrogatione Legis Ceremonialis, tum infirmi in hac persuasione seu fide, & ut abstineant à contentiosis disputationibus, hac de re, hortatur utrosque, initio facto à confirmatis in fide.
units.tr: The Apostle urges that those who were persuaded that the ceremonial law had been abrogated should join with those who were weak in this persuasion or faith, and that both should refrain from contentious disputes on this matter. He begins by addressing those who are confirmed in faith.

units.la: Verf. 2. Alius quidem credit vesci licere quibusvis: alius autem fide infirmus, edit olera.
units.tr: Verse 2. One believes that he may eat anything, but the one who is weak in faith eats only vegetables.

units.la: Occasionem dissidii & disputationis ostendit in exemplo ciborum, dum alii carne quavis vescuntur, sine metu ceremonialis interdicti: alii non persuasi, à carnibus illis vetitis abstinent, oleribus, seu quovis alio cibo contenti.
units.tr: He shows the occasion of the dispute and argument by the example of foods: some eat any kind of meat without fear of the ceremonial prohibition, while others, not persuaded of this, abstain from those forbidden meats and are content with vegetables or some other food.

units.la: Verf. 3. Qui edit, non edentem ne pro nihilo habeto: & qui non edit, edentem ne condemnato Deus enim eum assumpsit.
units.tr: Verse 3. Let not him who eats despise him who does not eat, and let not him who does not eat judge him who eats, for God has received him.

units.la: Rixas, inter has, & mutuam condemnationem in tali casu vetat Apostolus: Argumenta adhibens novem.
units.tr: The Apostle forbids quarrels between these groups and their mutual condemnation in such a case, and he gives nine arguments.

units.la: Argumentum primum. Quia Deus utrumque assumpsit in societatem gratiae filii sui; indignum igitur alterum ex his, in tali casu alterum contemnere, vel condemnare: Iniquum enim erat à confirmatioribus contemni infirmos tanquam superstitiosos novitios: similiter ab infirmis condemnari confirmatos in fide tanquam profanos.
units.tr: The first argument: because God has received both into the fellowship of his Son's grace, it is unworthy to despise or condemn the one or the other in such a case. It would be unjust for the more confirmed to despise the weak as superstitious novices, and likewise for the weak to condemn the confirmed in faith as profane.

units.la: Verf. 4. Tu quis es qui condemnas alienum famulum? proprio Domino perstat aut cadit, stabilietur autem: potest enim Deus eum stabilire.
units.tr: Verse 4. Who are you to judge another's servant? To his own master he stands or falls; but he will be made to stand, for God is able to make him stand.

units.la: Iniquum est alienum servum sine vocatione à Deo judicare, quia Domini interest, non alieni, sive pereat, sive servetur servus ipsius: Ergo, alius alium condemnare non debet, hac in re.
units.tr: It is unjust to judge another's servant without a call from God, because it concerns the Lord, not another person, whether his servant perishes or is preserved. Therefore one person should not condemn another in this matter.

units.la: Quia qui servus est Christi stabilietur à Christo, qui & potest & vult eum servare: Ergo Judicium, Christi Judicio contrarium, seu mutua condemnatio peccatum est.
units.tr: Because the one who is Christ's servant will be made to stand by Christ, who both can and wills to preserve him, a judgment contrary to Christ's judgment, that is, mutual condemnation, is a sin.

units.la: Verf. 5. Alius quidem aestimat diem prae die, alius autem pariter aestimat quemvis diem. Unusquisque in animo suo plene certioratus esto.
units.tr: Verse 5. One person esteems one day above another, another esteems all days alike. Let each be fully convinced in his own mind.

units.la: O
units.tr: O

units.la: Proponit aliud exemplum occasionis dissidii, in dierum à Moyse præscriptorum observatione, quos dies alii, Judæi nempe conversi quidam, ex conscientia legis, dicebant observandos esse præ aliis: alii vero, Gentiles scilicet, ex conscientia libertatis per Christum partæ, peræque æstimabant hos dies, & alios lege ceremoniali non præscriptos. Hic etiam dilludium, & mutuam condemnationem vetat Apostolus, & regulam recte se gerendi, in tali casu præscribit: Scilicet ut studeat unusquisque, in his de lege ceremoniali controversiis, solidas ad fulciendam fidem suam rationes habere, sive facti, sive omissionis suæ; atque ita addit argumentum quartum, Ne mutuo se condemnent: Quia in prædicto casu, cum persuasione solidè fundata, poterat aliquis facere, & alius cum persuasione solidè fundata, abstinere. Ergo iniquum erat ut in hoc casu, alter alterum condemnaret. Apostoli enim, in Concilio Hierosolymitano, liberaverant Gentes, à Jugo Moysis, quia illis lex ceremonialis nunquam erat posita; à Judæis vero, Apostoli, necessitatem ceremoniarum tollentes, liberum usum interim relinquebant illis aliquantisper, donec post tempus aliquod, clarius illucescente Euangelio, sepeliendam esse Synagogam perspicue videre possent; Quare, plena persuasione, poterant Gentes Ceremonias missas facere, & Judæi eas observare, saltem quamdiu Dei indulgentia stare passa est templum Hierosolymitanum, cui alligatæ erant præcipuæ ceremoniæ.
units.tr: He sets out another example of the occasion of dispute, concerning the observance of the days prescribed by Moses. Some, namely converted Jews, said from conscience of the law that these days were to be observed above others; others, namely Gentiles, from conscience of the liberty obtained through Christ, valued these days equally with the others, which the ceremonial law had not prescribed. Here too the Apostle forbids the quarrel and mutual condemnation, and he prescribes the right rule of conduct in such a case: that each one should take care, in these controversies about the ceremonial law, to have solid reasons to support his faith, whether for doing or for omitting something. And so he adds a fourth argument, that they should not condemn one another. In the case described, one person could act with a well-founded persuasion, and another could abstain with a well-founded persuasion. Therefore it was unjust in this case for one to condemn the other. For the Apostles, in the Council of Jerusalem, had freed the Gentiles from the yoke of Moses, because the ceremonial law had never been laid upon them. As for the Jews, the Apostles, by removing the necessity of the ceremonies, left them free use of them for a time, until, after some period, with the Gospel shining more clearly, they could plainly see that the synagogue was to be buried. Hence the Gentiles could, with full persuasion, set aside the ceremonies, and the Jews could observe them, at least as long as God's indulgence allowed the temple at Jerusalem to stand, to which the principal ceremonies were tied.

units.la: Verf. 6 Qui curat diem, Domino curat: & qui non curat diem, Domino non curat. Qui edit, Domino edit: gratias enim agit Deo: & qui non edit, Domino non edit, & gratias agit Deo.
units.tr: Verse 6. He who observes the day, observes it to the Lord; and he who does not observe the day, does not observe it to the Lord. He who eats, eats to the Lord, for he gives thanks to God; and he who does not eat, does not eat to the Lord, and gives thanks to God.

units.la: Arg. 5. Quia Judæus, observans diem, lege Moysis præscriptum, & à cibo vetito abstinens, & similiter Gentilis, legem Moysis non observans, in Dei gloriam, cum gratiarum actione agebat uterque; Judæus, quia cibi satis non vetiti habebat; Gentilis, quia quovis cibo vesci licebat, gratias agebat: neuter ergo ab altero condemnandus.
units.tr: Fifth argument: because the Jew, observing the day prescribed by the law of Moses and abstaining from forbidden food, and likewise the Gentile, not observing the law of Moses, both acted to the glory of God with thanksgiving. The Jew gave thanks because he had food that was not forbidden; the Gentile gave thanks because he might eat any food. Neither, then, is to be condemned by the other.

units.la: Verf. 7. Nullus enim nostrum sibi ipsi vivit, & nullus sibi ipsi moritur.
units.tr: Verse 7. For none of us lives to himself, and none of us dies to himself.

units.la: Verf. 8. Nam sive vivimus, Domino vivimus; sive morimur Domino morimur. Sive igitur vivamus, sive moriamur, Domini sumus.
units.tr: Verse 8. For whether we live, we live to the Lord; or whether we die, we die to the Lord. Whether we live or die, we are the Lord's.

units.la: Verf. 9. Ad hoc enim Christus & mortuus est & resurrexit, & revixit: ut et mortuis & viventibus dominetur.
units.tr: Verse 9. For to this end Christ died and rose and lived again, that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living.

units.la: Confirmat finem propositum observanti, & non observanti ceremonias, & simul addit argumentum sextum; Quorum nullus est juris sui, sed alieni, nec sibi vivit, nec moritur, sed Christo tantum, illi tenentur actiones suas, & omissiones ad Christi gloriam dirigere, simul etiam non condemnare conservos suos: At nostrum, seu Fidelium, nullus sibi vivit, vel moritur, nullus est juris sui, versu 7. sed Christo vivimus, & morimur, in Ejus honorem & usum, ad quem cura nostri, in vita & morte pertinet, verf. 8. Quod probat; Quia Christus, in eum finem, mortuus est, & resurrexit, ut Dominium in Redemptos, viventes & morientes acquireret, & exerceret: sequitur ergo, fideles non debere se mutuo condemnare, vel contemnere.
units.tr: He confirms the purpose stated, for the one who observes the ceremonies and the one who does not, and at the same time adds a sixth argument. Neither of them has a right over himself but belongs to another. Neither lives to himself nor dies to himself, but both are bound to direct their actions and omissions to the glory of Christ, and at the same time not to condemn their fellow servants. Now none of us, that is, of the faithful, lives or dies to himself, and none has a right over himself, verse 7; but we live and die to Christ, for his honour and use, to which our care in life and death belongs, verse 8. This is proved because Christ died and rose for this end, that he might acquire and exercise lordship over the redeemed, both living and dying. It follows, then, that the faithful ought not to condemn or despise one another.

units.la: Verf. 10. Tu vero cur condemnas fratrem tuum? aut etiam tu cur pro nihilo habes fratrem tuum? Omnes enim sistemur apud tribunal Christi.
units.tr: Verse 10. But you, why do you judge your brother? Or you again, why do you despise your brother? For we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ.

units.la: Arg. 7. Fideles, fratres sunt, sive Judæi, sive Gentiles sint: Non ergo debent se invicem judicare, vel contemnere.
units.tr: Seventh argument: believers are brothers, whether they are Jews or Gentiles. Therefore they ought not to judge or despise one another.

units.la: Sistemur] Arg. 8. Omnes judicandi sunt, ad tribunal Christi: Ergo cavere debent omnes, ne se mutuo, temere judicent.
units.tr: We shall stand: eighth argument. All are to be judged before the judgment seat of Christ. Therefore all ought to take care not to judge one another rashly.

units.la: Verf. 11. Scriptum est enim, Vivo ego, dicit Dominus, Certè mihi flectet omne genu, & omnis lingua palam agnoscet Deum.
units.tr: Verse 11. For it is written, As I live, saith the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall openly confess God.

units.la: Id confirmat, testimonio Isaiæ, prædicentis cap. 45. 23. Christum futurum omnium Judicem, & omnes subjectionem suam, ipsi, ut Deo confessuros.
units.tr: He confirms this by the testimony of Isaiah, who foretold, in chapter 45, verse 23, that Christ would be the future judge of all, and that all would confess their subjection to him as to God.

units.la: Verf. 12. Nempe ergo unusquisque nostrum de seipso rationem reddet Deo.
units.tr: Verse 12. So then each of us shall give account of himself to God.

units.la: Verf. 13.— Ne amplius igitur alij alios judicemus:
units.tr: Verse 13. Let us therefore no longer judge one another.

units.la: Arg. 9 Ex superiori deductum, Unusquisque redditurus est rationem Christo, de seipso, versu 12. Ergo seipsum debet quisque ad judicium Dei parare, non proximum judicare.
units.tr: Ninth argument: from what was said above, that each of us will render account to Christ for himself (verse 12). Therefore each ought to prepare himself for the judgment of God, not to judge his neighbour.

units.la: Secunda Pars.
units.tr: The Second Part.

units.la: Verf.— 13. Sed hic potius adhibete judicium, ut ne fratri proponatis quidpiam, ad quod impingat vel offendat.
units.tr: Verse 13. But rather judge this, that no one put a stumbling block or an offence before a brother.

units.la: Altera pars Capitis, in qua post generalis hortationis conclusionem, orditur specialem, ad firmos propriè spectantem, ne abutantur libertate suâ, cum infirmorum offendiculo, verf. 13.
units.tr: This is the second part of the chapter, in which, after the conclusion of the general exhortation, he begins a special one, properly directed to the strong, that they not abuse their liberty to the stumbling of the weak, verse 13.

units.la: Verf 14. Novi, & persuasum habeo per Dominum Iesum, nihil esse impurum per se: sed ei qui reputat aliquid esse impurum, id ei impurum esse.
units.tr: Verse 14. I know, and am persuaded through the Lord Jesus, that nothing is unclean in itself; but to him who reckons anything to be unclean, it is unclean.

units.la: Praeoccupat objectionem: Diceret aliquis, persuasum habeo, per Christi gratiam, nullum cibum, sub Euangelio, impurum, aut vetitum esse. Ergo quovis cibo, licet vesci indifferenter: Respondet, negando consequentiam: quia purus cibus, edenti redditur impurus, duobus modis; primo, si cum illicitum opinatus fuerit edens.
units.tr: He anticipates an objection: someone might say, "I am persuaded, through the grace of Christ, that no food is unclean or forbidden under the Gospel; therefore one may eat any food indifferently." He answers by denying the consequence: food that is pure is made unclean for the eater in two ways. First, if the eater supposes it to be unlawful.

units.la: Verf. 15. Verum si propter escam frater tuus tristitia afficitur, non jam secundum charitatem ambulas. Ne esca tua illum perdito pro quo Christus mortuus est.
units.tr: Verse 15. But if because of food your brother is grieved, you no longer walk according to love. Do not destroy with your food him for whom Christ died.

units.la: Secundo, cibus est impurus, Si quis persuasus de libertate sua, edat cum fratris offensione, seu tristitia: In quo casu, probat non edendum cum scandalo, vel cavendum esse, ne abutantur libertate, idque undecim argumentis.
units.tr: Second, food is unclean if anyone, persuaded of his liberty, eats it with offence or grief to his brother. In this case he proves that one must not eat with scandal, or must take care not to abuse liberty, and he does so with eleven arguments.

units.la: Argumentum primum, Pugnat cum charitate, agere in indifferentibus, cum infirmorum offensione. Ergo non abutendum libertate.
units.tr: The first argument: it is contrary to love to act in matters of indifference with the offence of the weak. Therefore liberty must not be abused.

units.la: Arg. 2. Scandalum ponere infirmo, ex natura operis, tendit in perditionem fratris, pro quo mortuus est Christus, & qui offendiculum ponit fratri, in sensu judiciali perdidit fratrem: quia quantum in ipso est, perditionis accersendae ei causa est. Ergo non abutendum libertate.
units.tr: Argument 2. To put a stumbling block before the weak, by the nature of the deed, tends to the destruction of a brother for whom Christ died; and whoever places a stumbling block before a brother, in the judicial sense destroys the brother, since so far as lies in him he is the cause of bringing destruction upon him. Therefore liberty must not be abused.

units.la: Arg. 3. Comedens cum scandalo, facto se opponit Christi morientis merito, & intentioni: ille enim mortuus est, ut infirmus servaretur; edens vero, cum offendiculo, facit quod in ipso est, ut infirmus perdatur. Ergo non abutendum libertate.
units.tr: Argument 3. By eating with scandal, one by the deed opposes the merit and intention of the dying Christ; for he died that the weak might be saved, whereas one who eats with offence does what lies in him, that the weak might perish. Therefore liberty must not be abused.

units.la: Verf. 16. Ne vestrum igitur bonum blasphemator.
units.tr: Verse 16. Let not then your good be evil spoken of.

units.la: Arg. 4. Edens cum scandalo, facit ut blasphemetur, & in contemptum veniat fides Christiana; & ut libertas Christiana, apud infirmos, & extraneos, male audiat. Ergo non abutendum libertate.
units.tr: Argument 4. By eating with scandal, one causes Christian faith to be blasphemed and brought into contempt, and Christian liberty to be ill spoken of among the weak and outsiders. Therefore liberty must not be abused.

units.la: Verf. 17. Non enim est regnum Dei esca & potus, sed justitia, & pax & gaudium per Spiritum sanctum.
units.tr: Verse 17. For the kingdom of God is not eating and drinking, but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Arg. 5. Quia (ut est 1 Cor. cap. 8. verf 8.) cibus & potus, non promovent Christi regnum spirituale, sed Justitia, Pax, & Gaudium, reliquique fructus Spiritus. Ergo abstinere tenemur a cibis, seu rebus adiaphoris, cum periculum est, ne intempestivo usu libertatis turbemus regnum CHRISTI.
units.tr: Argument 5. Because (as is said in 1 Cor. chap. 8, verse 8) food and drink do not advance the spiritual kingdom of Christ, but righteousness, peace, and joy, and the other fruits of the Spirit. Therefore we are bound to abstain from foods, or things indifferent, when there is danger that by an untimely use of liberty we disturb the kingdom of Christ.

units.la: Vers. 18 Nam qui per hæc servit Christo, gratus est Deo, & probatur hominibus.
units.tr: Verse 18. For he who serves Christ in these things is acceptable to God and approved by men.

units.la: Arg. 6. Qui his, id est, cibo, potu, aliisque similibus rebus indifferentibus, prudenter utuntur ad CHRISTI servitium, (sumentes scilicet, cum per ejus veniam licet, & abstinentes, prout CHRISTI negotium inde promoveri poterit) grati sunt DEO, & hominibus accepti. Ergo recte utendum libertate.
units.tr: Argument 6. Those who use these things, that is, food, drink, and other similar matters of indifference, prudently for the service of Christ (taking them, namely, when by his permission it is lawful, and abstaining when the business of Christ can be promoted thereby) are pleasing to God and acceptable to men. Therefore liberty is rightly to be used.

units.la: Vers. 19. Nempe igitur quæ ad pacem faciunt, sectemur, & quæ ad mutuam ædificationem.
units.tr: Verse 19. Therefore let us pursue the things which make for peace, and the things by which one may build up another.

units.la: Arg. 7. Per consectarium, ex superiori argumento, hortationis modo deductum. Sic utendum libertate, ut per pacem, & ædificationem, promoveatur CHRISTI regnum: Ergo non debemus uti libertate Christiana, nisi prout paci, & ædificationi, inservire poterit maximè.
units.tr: Argument 7. As a corollary, drawn in the manner of an exhortation from the previous argument: liberty is to be so used that the kingdom of Christ is advanced through peace and edification. Therefore we ought not to use Christian liberty except insofar as it can most of all serve peace and edification.

units.la: Vers. 20. Ne cibi causa destrue opus Dei. Omnia quidem munda: sed malum est homini qui edens offendit.
units.tr: Verse 20. Do not destroy the work of God for the sake of food. All things indeed are clean; but it is evil for the man who eats with offence.

units.la: Arg. 8. Propter rei leviculæ commoditatem, (qualis est certi cibi, certo tempore usus) non debet opus DEI destrui, aut fratris salus periclitari. Ergo non edendum cum scandalo.
units.tr: Argument 8. For the convenience of a trifling thing (such as the use of a certain food at a certain time) the work of God must not be destroyed, nor the salvation of a brother endangered. Therefore one must not eat with scandal.

units.la: Omnia ] Occurrit objectioni; Diceret aliquis omnia, id est, ea de quibus nunc agimus esculenta, licita sunt. Respondet, verum esse de rebus per se consideratis, sed illicita esse (in casu scandali) edenti cum offensione infirmorum.
units.tr: All things] He meets an objection: someone might say that "all things," that is, the foods of which we now speak, are lawful. He answers that this is true of things considered in themselves, but that they are unlawful (in the case of scandal) for one who eats with the offence of the weak.

units.la: Vers. 21. Bonum est non edere carnes, neque bibere vinum, neque quicquam facere in quo frater tuus impingit vel offenditur, vel infirmus est.
units.tr: Verse 21. It is good not to eat flesh, nor to drink wine, nor to do anything by which your brother stumbles, or is offended, or is weak.

units.la: Arg. 9. Bonum est abstinere, à quovis cibo vel potu, quando periculum est, ne frater, aliquo modo deterior, in negotio religionis reddatur, per cibi, potusve nostri sumptionem: Ergo abstinendum in tali casu.
units.tr: Argument 9. It is good to abstain from any food or drink whenever there is danger that a brother, in some way made worse, may be harmed in the matter of religion through our eating or drinking. Therefore one must abstain in such a case.

units.la: Vers. 22. Tu fidem habes: apud temetipsum habe in conspectu Dei. Beatus qui non condemnat seipsum in eo quod approbat.
units.tr: Verse 22. Have faith? Have it to yourself before God. Blessed is he who does not condemn himself in what he approves.

units.la: Occurrit objectioni, Fidem habeo de libertate meâ, eamque ut profitear necesse est. Respondet, negando necessariam esse confes‐ sionem, per modum facti, in casu scandali, quia consistit libertas, cum abstinentia non minùs quam cum usu rei; quare jubet ut obji‐ciens contentus sit, in tali casu, fidei suæ de libertate, interna as‐sertione apud Deum.
units.tr: He meets the objection: "I have faith about my liberty, and it is necessary that I profess it." He answers by denying that confession in the form of an outward act is necessary in the case of scandal, since liberty consists in abstinence no less than in the use of a thing; therefore he bids the objector be content, in such a case, with his faith in his liberty, asserted inwardly before God.

units.la: Confirmat responsionem aphorismo, quo continetur: Qui in eo, quod certò novit esse sibi licitum, ut eo vel utatur, vel ab eo abstineat, ita utitur libertate sua, ut libertatis suæ ad scandalum abusu, se non reddat condemnationis reum, est beatus. Ergo abstinen‐dum in tali casu.
units.tr: He confirms the answer by an aphorism, which contains this: whoever uses or abstains from that which he knows for certain to be lawful for him, so uses his liberty that he does not make himself guilty of condemnation by abusing it to scandal, is blessed. Therefore one must abstain in such a case.

units.la: Qui verò dubitat, si ederit, condemnatus est, quoniam non edit ex fide: quicquid verò ex fide non est, peccatum est.
units.tr: But whoever doubts, if he eats, is condemned, because he does not eat from faith; and whatever is not from faith is sin.

units.la: Periculum est ne infirmus fluctuans, inducatur mero intem‐pestivo edentis exemplo, ut dubitante conscientia edat, & sic peccet, & in damnationis reatum incurrat. Ergo in tali casu abstinendum.
units.tr: There is danger that the wavering weak one may be led, by the untimely example of the eater, to eat with a doubting conscience, and so sin and incur the guilt of condemnation. Therefore in such a case one must abstain.

units.la: Hoc argumento, & deterret infirmum, ne cujusvis exemplo, dubitante conscientia edat, & pariter firmum deterret ab esu intempestivo, ne causa sit alieni peccati, & reatus.
units.tr: By this argument he both deters the weak from eating, with a doubting conscience, by the example of anyone at all, and likewise deters the strong from untimely eating, lest he be the cause of another's sin and guilt.

units.la: Probat peccare edentem dubitante conscientiâ, quia non edit ex fide, seu ex persuasione, quod factum licitum sit: Quicquid autem fit non ex fide, quod opus licitum sit, peccatum esse pronunciat.
units.tr: He proves that one who eats with a doubting conscience sins, because he does not eat from faith, that is, from the persuasion that the deed is lawful; and he pronounces that whatever is done not from faith that the deed is lawful, is sin.

units.la: Caput Decimumquintum.
units.tr: Chapter 15.

units.la: DUÆ sunt Capitis partes, in prima pergit Apostolus in hortatione ad firmiores in fide de libertate Christiana, ut re‐ ctè se gerant erga infirmiores, ad vers. 13. In altera est Epi‐ stolæ quasi peroratio, ad finem.
units.tr: The chapter has two parts. In the first, the Apostle continues with an exhortation to the stronger in faith, concerning Christian liberty, that they should conduct themselves rightly toward the weaker, as far as verse 13. The second is, as it were, the peroration of the Epistle, to its end.

units.la: Vers. 1, DEbemus autem nos qui firmi sumus, infirmitates imbecillorum portare, ac, non indulgere nobisipsis.
units.tr: Verse 1. We then who are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves.

units.la: Quod ad primam attinet, quia in dislidio, de usu rerum indifferenti‐um, nulla concordia absque peccato, probabiliter expectari potest, nisi firmiores in libertatis suæ usu, attemperent se infirmioribus; Idcirco hortatur, ut id faciant, & portent infirmitates infirmorum, tolerantes, & sublevantes eos patientiâ, & consilio prudenti, tanquam ægris in causa, illis condonantes. Argumenta hortationis sunt septem.
units.tr: As for the first part: since, in a dispute about the use of indifferent things, harmony without sin can scarcely be expected unless the stronger, in their use of liberty, accommodate themselves to the weaker, he therefore exhorts them to do so, and to bear the infirmities of the infirm, tolerating them and supporting them with patience and prudent counsel, as physicians do with the sick, granting them indulgence. There are seven arguments of the exhortation.

units.la: Argumentum primum, Robustiorum partes sunt, & jure naturæ, & Jure divino, onera infirmorum portare. Ergo firmi in fide infirmorum infirmitatem in rebus his mediis tolerare debent.
units.tr: The first argument: it is the duty of the stronger, both by the law of nature and by divine law, to bear the burdens of the weak. Therefore those who are strong in faith ought to tolerate the infirmity of the weak in these matters that are indifferent.

units.la: Arg. 2. Robustiores, qui hoc officium erga infirmiores præstare recusant, comperientur rei φιλαυτιας suis affectibus, & commodis privatis, tantùm studentes. Ergo infirmi tolerandi sunt.
units.tr: Argument 2. Those stronger ones who refuse to render this duty to the weaker will be found guilty of self-love [φιλαυτίας], caring only for their own affections and private advantages. Therefore the weak are to be borne with.

units.la: Verf. 2. Itaque unusquisque nostrùm proximo placeat, ipsius bono, id est, ad ejus ædificationem.
units.tr: Verse 2. Thus let each of us please his neighbour for his good, that is, for his edification.

units.la: Arg. 3. Quia omnes tenemur proximo placere, cum ad ipsius ædificationem, & bonum fieri potest: Addit in ædificationem, ne in cujusvis gratiam, malum admittamus.
units.tr: Argument 3. Because we are all bound to please our neighbour, when this can be done for his edification and good. He adds for edification, lest we admit evil to gratify anyone at all.

units.la: Verf. 3 Etenim Christus non placuit sibiipsi, sed sicut scriptum est, Convitia eorum qui convitiantur tibi, inciderunt in me.
units.tr: Verse 3. For Christ did not please himself, but as it is written, The reproaches of those who reproach you have fallen upon me.

units.la: Arg. 4. Quo etiam confirmatur superius, à Christi exemplo: Christus non utilitatis suæ, sed infirmitatis, & salutis nostræ rationem habens, non sibi placuit, sed nobis; quod probat, quia peccata nostra, quæ naturâ sua sunt Dei opprobria, portavit Christus, ut nos liberaret à pœnis meritis, & oneri nostro suppositu t tergum suum: Ergo cedendum nobis est, saltem in rebus indifferentibus, de jure nostro, in gratiam infirmorum, ut salventur.
units.tr: Argument 4. By which the above is also confirmed, from the example of Christ: Christ, having regard not to his own advantage but to our infirmity and salvation, did not please himself but us. This is proved by the fact that Christ bore our sins, which by their nature are reproaches against God, and took upon his back the burden laid on us, so that he might free us from the punishments we deserved. Therefore we ought to yield, at least in indifferent matters, some of our right, for the sake of the weak, that they may be saved.

units.la: Verf. 4. Nam quæ ante scripta sunt, ad nos docendos ante scripta sunt: ut per tolerantiam & consolationem Scripturarum, spem retineamus.
units.tr: Verse 4. For whatever was written before was written for our instruction, that through patience and the comfort of the Scriptures we might have hope.

units.la: Hoc exemplum, in imitationem trahendum probat, ex generali fine totius Scripturæ, qui est ædificatio nostri, (in fide, & obedientia,) per promissiones, præcepta, & exempla: ut nos per omnia adversa, Dei voluntati patienter morem gerentes, consolationem, & spem ex Scripturis habeamus.
units.tr: He proves that this example is to be followed from the general end of all Scripture, which is our edification (in faith and obedience) through promises, precepts and examples, so that we, in all adversities, patiently submitting to the will of God, may have comfort and hope from the Scriptures.

units.la: Verf. 5. Deus autem auror tolerantiæ & consolationis, det vobis ut idem alij in alios affecti sitis, secundum Christum Iesum.
units.tr: Verse 5. Now may the God of patience and comfort grant you to be of the same mind toward one another, according to Christ Jesus.

units.la: Argumentum claudit precatione, ut Deus, qui patientiæ, & consolationis fons est, & dator, det illis eundem inter se affectum, secundum Christi exemplar, id est, ut idem sentiant, juxta Christi doctrinam, & se mutuò diligant, nam si dilectio fuerit in rebus mediis, concordia erit.
units.tr: He concludes the argument with a prayer: that God, who is the source and giver of patience and comfort, would grant them the same disposition toward one another, according to the pattern of Christ, that is, that they may think alike, following the teaching of Christ, and love one another mutually; for if there is love in things indifferent, there will be harmony.

units.la: Verf. 6. Ut concorditer uno ore glorificetis Deum ac Patrem Domini nostri Iesu Christi.
units.tr: Verse 6. That with one mouth you may together glorify God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: Precationis finis est, ut discordia, & dissensione omni remota, uno corde & ore, concorditer glorificent Deum, ac patrem Christi qui nos in filios adoptavit, & fraternitatis vinculo, cum Christo, & inter nos mutuò, sociavit.
units.tr: The aim of the prayer is that, with all discord and dissension removed, they may with one heart and one mouth glorify God together, and the Father of Christ, who has adopted us as sons and joined us to Christ and to one another by the bond of brotherhood.

units.la: Verf. 7. Propterea alios assumite alij, sicut & Christus assumpsit nos in gloriam Dei.
units.tr: Verse 7. Therefore receive one another, as Christ also received us, to the glory of God.

units.la: Arg. 5. Itidem ab exemplo Christi, illatum ex superioribus, hortationis modo; Christus misertus nostri, assumpsit nos infirmos, & indignos, in societatem gloriae Dei, condonatis peccatis nostris: Ergo debemus nos, infirmiores, & ut videntur forsan, indigniores, condonatis infirmitatibus, assumere in societatem dilectionis, pacis, & concordiae nostrae.
units.tr: Argument 5. Likewise, from the example of Christ, inferred from what precedes, in the manner of an exhortation: Christ, having mercy on us, received us when we were weak and unworthy, into the fellowship of the glory of God, our sins having been forgiven. Therefore we, who are stronger and perhaps seem more worthy, ought, our infirmities being forgiven, to receive the weak into the fellowship of our love, peace and harmony.

units.la: Verf. 8. Illud autem dico, Iesum Christum ministrum fuisse circumcisionis, pro Dei veritate, ut confirmaret promissiones Patrum.
units.tr: Verse 8. Now I say that Jesus Christ was a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers.

units.la: Arg. 6. Etiam ab exemplo Christi; Servivit Christus circumcisioni, seu Judaeis, inter ipsos praedicans, & ministri munia omnia exequens propter foedus cum ipsorum patribus ictum: Ergo omnes Christianos decet, erga Judaeos infirmiores in fide eodem cum Christo animo esse, etiam propter foedus cum ipsorum patribus ictum.
units.tr: Argument 6. Also from the example of Christ: Christ served the circumcision, that is, the Jews, preaching among them and performing all the duties of a minister, on account of the covenant made with their fathers. Therefore it becomes all Christians to have toward the weaker Jews in faith the same mind as Christ, even on account of the covenant made with their fathers.

units.la: Verf. 9. Et ut Gentes pro misericordia glorificent Deum: sicut scriptum est, Propterea celebrabo te inter Gentes, & nomini tuo psallam.
units.tr: Verse 9. And that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy; as it is written, For this reason I will praise you among the Gentiles, and sing to your name.

units.la: Arg. 7. Ab exemplo etiam Christi: qui inter Judaeos praedicavit, non tantum ut veritatis Dei, & promissionum Patriarchis factarum, complementum promoveret; sed etiam eo fine ut Gentes, per Judaeos, & cum Judaeis conversae, Deum una glorificarent: indignissimum ergo, si Judaei & Gentes se mutuò contemnerent de rebus indifferentibus.
units.tr: Argument 7. Also from the example of Christ, who preached among the Jews not only to advance the fulfilment of God's truth and of the promises made to the patriarchs, but also with the purpose that the Gentiles, converted through the Jews and together with the Jews, might glorify God with one voice. It is most unworthy, therefore, if Jews and Gentiles despise one another over indifferent matters.

units.la: Propterea Quod attinet ad Gentes, probat ex Scriptura, intendisse Christum, eas in societatem Judaeorum vocare, quadruplici oraculo; primum est, ex Psal. 18. verf. 50. In quo, Christus sub typo Davidis, promittit, se praedicaturum Dei nomen, inter Gentes. Verf. 10. Et rursum dicit, Gaudete Gentes cum populo ejus.
units.tr: Therefore. As to the Gentiles, he proves from Scripture that Christ intended to call them into fellowship with the Jews, by four oracles. The first is from Psalm 18, verse 50, in which Christ, under the type of David, promises that he will proclaim the name of God among the Gentiles. Verse 10. And again he says, Rejoice, O Gentiles, with his people.

units.la: Oraculum secundum, ex Deut. 32. verf. 43. in quo, Gentes jubentur lætari, cum Judæis, ut populo Dei: Ergo, isti populo, associabuntur Gentes.
units.tr: The second oracle is from Deuteronomy 32, verse 43, in which the Gentiles are bidden to rejoice with the Jews as the people of God. Therefore the Gentiles will be joined to that people.

units.la: Verf. 11. Et rursum, Laudate Dominum omnes Gentes, & collaudate eum omnes populi.
units.tr: Verse 11. And again, Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and let all the peoples praise him.

units.la: Oraculum tertium ex Psal. 117. verf. 1. Gentes jubentur laudare Deum; Ergo misericordiam consequentur.
units.tr: The third oracle, from Psalm 117, verse 1: the Gentiles are bidden to praise God; therefore they will obtain mercy.

units.la: Verf 12. Et rursum Esaias dicit, Erit radix Jesse, & qui exurgat ad imperandum Gentibus: in ipso Gentes sperabunt.
units.tr: Verse 12. And again Isaiah says, There shall be a root of Jesse, and he who rises to rule the Gentiles; in him the Gentiles shall hope.

units.la: Oraculum quartum, ex Isaiæ 11. verf. 10. CHRISTUS regnabit, ut imperator Gentium, & Gentes credent in eum: Ergo convertentur.
units.tr: The fourth oracle, from Isaiah 11, verse 10: Christ will reign as the ruler of the Gentiles, and the Gentiles will believe in him; therefore they will be converted.

units.la: Verf. 13. Utinam verò Deus spei impleat vos omni gaudio, & pace credendo, ut sspe abundetis per virtutem Spiritus sancti.
units.tr: Verse 13. May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that you may abound in hope through the power of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Claudit totam hanc hortationem, de abstinentia ab intempestivo usu libertatis, in esculentis, in casu scandali, voto ardentissimo: ut Deus Christianam hanc abstinentiam à cibo, compenset abundantia spiritualium donorum, quæ repletio majorem lætitiam ipsis crearet, ex dulcedine fidei, & pacis à Spiritu sancto, quam alioqui, ex omnibus deliciis ciborum, capere potuissent.
units.tr: He concludes this whole exhortation, concerning abstinence from the untimely use of liberty in foods, where scandal would arise, with a most fervent wish: that God would compensate this Christian abstinence from food with an abundance of spiritual gifts, which fullness would create greater joy in them, from the sweetness of faith and of peace given by the Holy Spirit, which they could otherwise have derived from all the delights of food.

units.la: Verf. 14. Persuasum autem habeo, & ipse ego de vobis, fratres mei, quod ipsi per vos plenì sitis bonitate, impleti omni cognitione, & qui possitis etiam vos mutuò admonere.
units.tr: Verse 14. I am persuaded, my brothers, and I myself am persuaded about you, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge, and able also to admonish one another.

units.la: Verf. 15. Audacius verò scripsi vobis, fratres, aliquatenus veluti commonefaciens vos, propter gratiam quæ data est mihi à Deo,
units.tr: Verse 15. But I have written to you rather boldly, brothers, in some measure as reminding you, because of the grace given me by God,

units.la: Verf. 16. Ad hoc ut sim minister Iesu Christi apud Gentes, operans Euangelio Dei, ut oblatio Gentium fiat accepta, sanctificata per Spiritum sanctum.
units.tr: Verse 16. That I should be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles, serving the gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Altera pars capitis, continens epistolæ quasi perorationem, In qua primum ostendit scribendi, simul & ad eos nondum veniendi causam, quod etiamsi persuasum haberet, Romanos abundare gratiâ, & cognitione, qua valeant se mutuò hortari, & docere, in omnibus supradictis;
units.tr: The second part of the chapter, which contains the peroration of the Epistle. In it he first shows the reason for writing, and at the same time for not yet coming to them: although he was persuaded that the Romans abounded in grace and knowledge, so that they were able to exhort and teach one another in all the things mentioned above,

units.la: Liberius tamen, & fusius se ad ipsos scripsisse; primum, quia commonefactio de cognitis erat ipsis utilis; deinde, quia authoritate Apostolica ex gratia sibi à Deo data, ministerium suum inter Gentes, (& per consequens inter Romanos) ita curare oportuit ut Gentes conversæ & quasi mactatæ, quo ad veterem hominem per ejus Euangelium, offerrentur Deo, tanquam victima sanctificata per Spiritum sanctum, & Deo accepta propter Christum.
units.tr: Nevertheless he had written to them more freely and at greater length; first, because a reminder of what they already knew was useful to them; then, because by the apostolic authority given him by the grace of God, he had to attend to his ministry among the Gentiles (and consequently among the Romans) in such a way that the Gentiles, converted and as it were slaughtered as to the old man through his gospel, might be offered to God as a victim sanctified by the Holy Spirit and acceptable to God through Christ.

units.la: Verf. 17. Habeo igitur quod glorier per Christum Iesum, in iis quæ ad Deum pertinent.
units.tr: Verse 17. I have therefore whereof I may glory through Christ Jesus, in those things which pertain to God.

units.la: Ut superiori doctrinæ sua constet authoritas, hunc suum Apostolatum commendat sextuplici nomine; primò à spiritualibus effectis, per Christi virtutem productis, quæ apud Deum saltem, sunt in magno pretio, ut ut homines ea parvi æstim£nt.
units.tr: To make his authority agree with the foregoing doctrine, he commends his apostleship under six heads. First, from the spiritual effects produced by the power of Christ, which are held in high esteem, at least before God, although men value them little.

units.la: Verf. 18. Non enim sustinuerim quicquam loqui quod non effecerit Christus per me, adducendis ad obedientiam Gentibus verbis & factis.
units.tr: Verse 18. For I dare not speak of anything which Christ has not wrought through me, to bring the Gentiles to obedience, by word and deed.

units.la: Secundo à conversione Gentium, de qua neque audet plus dicere quam verum est, neque potest dicere, vel quantum fecerit, vel quid omiserit Christus ad conversionem Gentium, per ipsius ministerium.
units.tr: Second, from the conversion of the Gentiles. He dares say no more than is true, and he cannot say either how much Christ has done, or what He has left undone, for the conversion of the Gentiles through his ministry.

units.la: Verf. 19. Virtute signorum ac prodigiorum, virtute Spiritus Dei: adeo ut ab Hierosolymis & circumjacentibus regionibus, usque ad Illyricum, impleverim prædicandi Euangelij Christi munus.
units.tr: Verse 19. Through mighty signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit of God; so that from Jerusalem and the surrounding regions, as far as Illyricum, I have fully discharged the office of preaching the gospel of Christ.

units.la: Tertiò, A signis Apostolatus sui, scilicet virtutibus, miraculis, & potentia Spiritus sancti, qui per miracula convincebat Gentes, de certitudine doctrinæ Euangelicæ.
units.tr: Third, from the signs of his apostleship, namely the powers, miracles and might of the Holy Spirit, who by miracles convinced the Gentiles of the certainty of the evangelical doctrine.

units.la: Adeo ut ] Quartò à multitudine triumphatarum Gentium, per ipsius ministerium, inter quas erant illæ omnes, quæ inter Hierosolymam, & Dalmatiam interjacent, ad tractum circiter mille quadringentorum milliarium, ut æstimatur, præter provincias circumjacentes in circuitu.
units.tr: So that Fourth, from the multitude of Gentiles won over through his ministry, among whom were all those lying between Jerusalem and Dalmatia, over a distance of about fourteen hundred miles, as is reckoned, besides the provinces round about on every side.

units.la: Verf. 20 Ita porro contendens euangelizare, non ubi nominatum esset Christus, ut ne super alienum fundamentum ædificarem:
units.tr: Verse 20. Yet so I strove to preach the gospel, not where Christ was already named, lest I should build upon another man's foundation:

units.la: Quintò, Ab erectione Ecclesiarum Dei, in illis locis, quarum collectio sicut erat solius Christi Authoris, sic erat solus ministerii Pauli, non ullius alius ex Apostolis.
units.tr: Fifth, from the founding of the churches of God in those places. The gathering of them was the work of Christ alone as its author, and of Paul's ministry alone, and of no other apostle.

units.la: Verf. 21. Sed sicut scriptum est, Quibus non est annunciatum de eo, videbunt: & qui non audierunt, intelligent.
units.tr: Verse 21. But as it is written, To whom he was not spoken of, they shall see: and they that have not heard shall understand.

units.la: Sexto, Quia, in ipsius ministerio implebatur oraculum Prophetæ evidentissimè.
units.tr: Sixth, because in his ministry the oracle of the prophet was most clearly fulfilled.

units.la: Verf. 22. Quapropter etiam sæpe inhibitus sum venire ad vos.
units.tr: Verse 22. For which cause also I have been much hindered from coming to you.

units.la: Verf. 23. Nunc vero quum non amplius habeam locum in his regionibus, summum autem desiderium habeam veniendi ad vos à multis annis:
units.tr: Verse 23. But now, having no more place in these regions, and having had a great desire these many years to come to you;

units.la: Verf. 24. Quando proficiscar in Hispaniam, veniam ad vos: Spero enim fore, ut iltac præteriens, conspiciam vos, & à vobis deducar illuc: si tamen vestra consuetudine prius ex parte expletus fuero.
units.tr: Verse 24. Whenever I journey into Spain, I will come to you: for I hope to see you in passing, and to be brought on my way there by you, if first I may be somewhat filled with your company.

units.la: Posito in superioribus fundamento excusationis, quod hactenus ad Romanos non venisset, versu 22. & 23. spem facit adventus sui, & commorationis aliquantisper inter eos in itinere suo, quod versus Hispaniam meditabatur, postquam ipsorum consuetudine tanquam aromatum odore perfusus fuerit.
units.tr: Having laid down in what precedes the foundation of his excuse, that he had not hitherto come to the Romans, in verses 22 and 23 he holds out hope of his coming and of a brief stay among them on his journey, which he was planning towards Spain, once he had been refreshed by their company as by the fragrance of spices.

units.la: Verf. 25. Nunc autem proficiscor Hierosolymam, ministrans sanctis.
units.tr: Verse 25. But now I go to Jerusalem, to minister to the saints.

units.la: Verf. 26. Libuit enim Macedonia & Achaia conferre aliquid in pauperes sanctos qui sunt Hierosolymis.
units.tr: Verse 26. For it has pleased Macedonia and Achaia to make some contribution for the poor saints who are at Jerusalem.

units.la: Tempus adventus exprimit, postquam scilicet profectus fuisset Hierosolymam, & eleemosynas Græcarum Ecclesiarum, sanctis in Judæa pauperibus refocillandis obtulisset.
units.tr: He states the time of his arrival: namely, after he had gone to Jerusalem and presented the alms of the Greek churches to refresh the poor saints in Judea.

units.la: Verf. 27. Libuit enim eis inquam, & debitores eorum sunt, nam si spiritualia ipsorum bona Gentibus communicata sunt, debent etiam ipsæ in carnalibus eis ministerio suo adesse.
units.tr: Verse 27. For it has pleased them, I say, and they are their debtors; for if the Gentiles have been made partakers of their spiritual things, they ought also to minister to them in carnal things.

units.la: Eleemosynam hanc deberi Judæis probat, quia Euangelium à Judæis ad Gentes pervenerat.
units.tr: He proves that this alms is owed to the Jews, because the gospel had come to the Gentiles from the Jews.

units.la: Verf. 28. Hoc igitur ubi perfecero, & eis consignavero hunc fructum, abibo istac in Hispaniam.
units.tr: Verse 28. When therefore I have performed this, and have sealed to them this fruit, I will go by way of you into Spain.

units.la: Verf. 29. Scio vero me, quum veniam ad vos cum plena benedictione Euangelij Christi venturum. Post traditam collectam, quasi obsignatam, sine diminutione, promittit se venturum ad eos. Interim spem facit benedictionis spiritualis, per ipsius ministerium, in Romanos conferendæ, cum adveniret. Quod dicit, ut gratior veniret, & ut ardentius expeteretur, simul, & expectaretur, à Romanis.
units.tr: Verse 29. And I know that when I come to you, I shall come in the fullness of the blessing of the gospel of Christ. After the collection has been handed over, as if sealed, without loss, he promises that he will come to them. Meanwhile he holds out hope of a spiritual blessing to be conferred upon the Romans through his ministry when he arrives. He says this so that he may come the more welcome, and so that he may be the more eagerly desired and awaited by the Romans.

units.la: Vers. 30. Precor autem vos, fratres, per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, & per charitatem Spiritus, ut concertetis mihi vestris pro me apud Deum orationibus.
units.tr: Verse 30. Now I beseech you, brethren, by our Lord Jesus Christ, and by the love of the Spirit, that you strive together with me in your prayers to God for me;

units.la: Denique obtestatur enixè, ut precibus apud Deum, pro ipso contendant, in tribus petitionibus.
units.tr: Finally, he earnestly entreats them to contend on his behalf in prayer to God, in three requests.

units.la: Vers. 31. Ut liberer ab iis qui non obediunt sermoni in Judæa: utque ministerium hoc meum erga Hierosolymam acceptum sit sanctis;
units.tr: Verse 31. That I may be delivered from them that do not obey the word in Judea; and that my ministry which I have for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints;

units.la: Prima est, ut liberetur ab insidiis infidelium in Judæa, qui sanguinem ejus maximè sitiebant.
units.tr: The first is that he may be delivered from the snares of the unbelievers in Judea, who were especially thirsting for his blood.

units.la: Ministerium] Petitio 2. Ut eleemosynæ, quas portaturus erat Hierosolymam, forent fratribus Judæis acceptæ.
units.tr: Ministry The second request is that the alms which he was to carry to Jerusalem might be acceptable to the Jewish brethren.

units.la: Vers. 32. Ut cum gaudio veniam ad vos, per voluntatem Dei, unàque vobiscum refocillèr.
units.tr: Verse 32. That I may come to you with joy by the will of God, and together with you be refreshed.

units.la: Petitio 3. Ut cum gaudio Romam veniret, & cum ipsis congaudēret.
units.tr: The third request is that he might come to Rome with joy and rejoice together with them.

units.la: Vers. 33. Deus autem pacis sit cum omnibus vobis. Amen.
units.tr: Verse 33. Now the God of peace be with you all. Amen.

units.la: Interim orans, ut Deus ipsos in pace custodiret, ne contentionibus suis, opus Euangelii, inter se impedirent.
units.tr: Meanwhile he prays that God would keep them in peace, so that they would not, by their contentions, hinder the work of the gospel among themselves.

units.la: Caput Decimumsextum.
units.tr: Chapter Sixteen.

units.la: DUÆ sunt Capitis partes præcipuæ: In prima post commendationem Phœbes, quæ Epistolam hanc, ut appareret, ad Romanos perferebat, honorificè salutat, spectatæ fidei, aliquot Sanctos, ad vers. 17. In secunda parte, post orationem, ut caveant sibi à schismaticis, salutationes Sanctorum aliquot nomine, qui apud se erant, dum Epistolam hanc mitteret, suis salutationibus adjungit, votisque ardentissimis Epistolam claudit.
units.tr: There are two main parts to this chapter. In the first, after commending Phoebe, who was carrying this Epistle to the Romans, he greets with honour several saints of proven faith, down to verse 17. In the second part, after a prayer that they would guard themselves against schismatics, he adds his own greetings, in the name of several saints who were with him when he sent this letter, and he closes the Epistle with the most heartfelt wishes.

units.la: Commendo autem vobis Thaeben sororem nostram, quae est ministra Ecclesiae Cenchreensis:
units.tr: I commend to you Phoebe our sister, who is a servant of the Church at Cenchreae:

units.la: Vers. 2. Ut eam excipiatis in Domino covenienter sanctis, & adsitis ei quacunque in re ipsi usus fuerit vobis: nam haec tum multis hospitium praebuit, tum mihi etiam ipsi.
units.tr: Verse 2. That you receive her in the Lord, as becomes saints, and assist her in whatever business she may need you for; for she has been a helper of many, and of me also.

units.la: Cenchreae, portus fuit, Corintho vicinus; In hoc oppidulo, Ecclesia collecta fuit; sumptus, quos ferre non poterat haec Ecclesia, sustinuisse videtur Phaebe, domicilium suum, quasi commune diversorium, advenis Christianis, liberaliter patefaciens; ideoque ministra Ecclesiae nominata est: Nam fuisse ex collegio pauperculārum viduarum, quas Ecclesia alebat publico stipendio, (1. ad Tim. 5.) non videtur, sed officium ipsarum suppleviisse, & sumptibus suis sustinuisse est verisimile, quia ipsi Apostolo, & multis etiam aliis, hospitium liberale praebuerat: & profectionem tam longam, ex Graecia Romam usque suscipere, negotia saecularia habere Romae curanda, quae Ecclesiae totius notitia, & auxilio, & in eum finem, Apostolica intercessione digna essent, signa sunt non pauperioris, sed opulentae, & notabilis foeminae, quam idcirco vult a Romanis recipi in Domino, id est, Christiano affectu & Domini causa, & tractari digne sanctis, id est, ut decebat & Romanorum, & Phaebes conditionem externam, sanctitate ornatam.
units.tr: Cenchreae was a harbour near Corinth. A congregation was gathered in this little town. Since this congregation could not bear its expenses, Phoebe seems to have supported it, freely opening her home, as a kind of common lodging, to Christian travellers. That is why she is named a servant of the Church. It does not appear that she belonged to the company of poor widows whom the Church supported at public expense (1 Tim. 5.), but it is likely that she performed their duties and maintained them at her own cost, since she had offered generous hospitality to the Apostle himself and to many others as well. To undertake so long a journey from Greece to Rome, and to have secular business to attend to at Rome, business which deserved the knowledge and help of the whole Church, and the Apostle's intercession for that purpose, are signs of a woman who was not poor but wealthy and distinguished. For this reason he wants her to be received by the Romans in the Lord, that is, with Christian affection and for the Lord's sake, and to be treated as becomes saints, that is, as was fitting both for the Romans and for Phoebe, whose outward condition was adorned with holiness.

units.la: Vers. 3. Salutate Priscillam & Aquilam, adjutores meos in Christo Iesu:
units.tr: Verse 3. Greet Priscilla and Aquila, my helpers in Christ Jesus:

units.la: Vers. 4. Qui pro anima mea suam ipsorum cervicem supposuerunt: quibus non ego solus gratias ago, sed etiam omnes Ecclesiae Gentium: )
units.tr: Verse 4. Who have laid down their own necks for my life, to whom not only I give thanks, but also all the churches of the Gentiles.

units.la: Salutationes, Sanctorum nominibus, & encomiis, satis distinguuntur, ut analysi hic non opus sit, sufficient ad institutum nostrum, notae aliquot.
units.tr: The greetings, with the names and commendations of the saints, are sufficiently clear that no detailed analysis is needed here. A few notes will suffice for our purpose.

units.la: Quomodo adjutores Apostoli, fuerint Priscilla & Aquila; patet ex Act. 18. quo loco, licet privati fuerint, quantum tamen privatim fieri potuit ab ipsis in vocatione sua se continentibus, studiose in doctrina Christi propaganda laborabant, pro peritia sua & zelo singulari; In quo negotio, ut nominatur uxor ante maritum, sic primas tenuisse videtur.
units.tr: How Priscilla and Aquila were the Apostle's helpers is clear from Acts 18. There, although they were private persons, and although they kept within their calling as far as a private person could, they laboured diligently to spread the teaching of Christ, with their skill and singular zeal. In this work, since the wife is named before the husband, she seems to have held the first place.

units.la: Cervicem ] In periculo persecutionis aliquo, vel tumultu, apparet Priscillam, & Aquilam, fortiter egisse causam Apostoli, ejusque vitam cum vitae suae periculo eripuisse, quo nomine, omnes Ecclesiae, quae curabant Apostoli salutem, gratias illis debebant.
units.tr: Necks. In some danger of persecution or tumult, it appears that Priscilla and Aquila boldly defended the Apostle's cause and rescued his life at risk to their own. For this, all the churches that cared for the Apostle's safety owed them thanks.

units.la: Verf. 5. Item Ecclesiam quæ in domo eorum est. Salutate Epænetum mihi dilectum, primitias Achaiæ in Christo.
units.tr: Verse 5. Likewise greet the church that is in their house. Greet Epaenetus, my beloved, the firstfruits of Achaia in Christ.

units.la: Per Ecclesiam, videtur intelligere solum familiam ipsorum, pie instituztam, & quotidie vacantem rebus sacris, inter labores manuarios, propter quandam Ecclesiæ similitudinem; quia non dicit, Ecclesiam quæ convenit in ædibus eorum, sed quæ est, seu habitat in domo eorum, nisi existimemus, simul etiam Ecclesiæ toti præbuisse hospitium, sicut Gaius, de quo verf. 23.
units.tr: By "the church," he seems to mean only their household, piously instructed and daily occupied with sacred things amid their manual labours, and called a church by a certain likeness to the Church. He does not say "the church which meets in their house," but "which is, or dwells, in their house." Unless we suppose that they also offered hospitality to the whole Church, as Gaius did (see verse 23).

units.la: Epænetus dicitur primitiæ Achaiæ; quia inter primos, ad fidem conversus est, sicut & 1 Cor. 16. 15. Stephanæ familia, eodem nomine, inter præcipuæ notæ, & in fide spectatos Christianos, laudatur.
units.tr: Epaenetus is called the firstfruits of Achaia because he was among the first converted to the faith, as also in 1 Cor. 16:15, where the household of Stephanas, of the same name, is praised among the chief Christians of note and proven in the faith.

units.la: Verf. 6. Salutate Mariam, quæ multum laboravit erga nos.
units.tr: Verse 6. Greet Mary, who has laboured much for us.

units.la: Mariæ studium erga fideles, & Apostolos, cognosci, & agnosci vult ab Ecclesia, ut simile studium foveret, vel excitaret in aliis.
units.tr: He wants the diligence of Mary towards the faithful and the Apostles to be known and acknowledged by the Church, so that it might foster or stir up a similar diligence in others.

units.la: Verf. 7. Salutate Andronicum & Juniam, cognatos meos, & concaptivos meos, qui sunt insignes inter Apostolos qui etiam ante me fuerunt in Christo.
units.tr: Verse 7. Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen and my fellow prisoners, who are of note among the Apostles, and who were also in Christ before me.

units.la: Andronicus & Junia, consanguinei Apostoli, vocantur insignes inter Apostolos, quia Apostolis omnibus noti, & approbati, & in pretio ab iis habiti sunt, qui etiam ante Apostolum Paulum converti erant ad fidem, & cum Apostolo passionum pro Evangelio, in Carcere & vinculis, consortes erant.
units.tr: Andronicus and Junia, kinsmen of the Apostle, are called notable among the Apostles, because they were known and approved by all the Apostles and held in esteem by them. They had been converted to the faith even before the Apostle Paul, and they shared with the Apostle in sufferings for the Gospel, in prison and in chains.

units.la: Verf. 8. Salutate Ampliam dilectum mihi in Domino
units.tr: Verse 8. Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord.

units.la: Amplias dilectione dignus in Domino dicitur, propter fidem, & pietatem scilicet, à Domino ei datam.
units.tr: Ampliatus is called beloved in the Lord, namely on account of the faith and piety bestowed on him by the Lord.
