units.la: Vers. 16. An ignoratis cum qui agglutinatur scorto, unum esse corpus cum scorto? Erunt enim, inquit, qui duo erant, caro una.
units.tr: Verse 16. Know ye not that he which is joined to an harlot is one body? For two, saith he, shall be one flesh.

units.la: Ut hoc argumentum confirmet, probat primò ex analogia matrimonii, concubitum cum scorto, unam carnem facere scortantes; & per consequens scortantem, fieri partem seu membrum scorti: Ergo scortatio minimè licita.
units.tr: To confirm this argument, he first proves from the analogy of marriage that those who fornicate make one flesh with the harlot by intercourse; and consequently that the fornicator becomes a part or member of the harlot. Therefore fornication is by no means lawful.

units.la: Vers. 17. Qui verò agglutinatur Domino, unus cum eo spiritus est.
units.tr: Verse 17. But he that is joined unto the Lord is one spirit.

units.la: Deinde probat fideles esse membra Christi, Quia fide juncti, seu agglutinati, sunt unum corpus mysticum cum Christo, unum spirituale corpus, seu unus spiritus.
units.tr: Next he proves that believers are members of Christ, because, joined or cemented to him by faith, they are one mystical body with Christ, one spiritual body, or one spirit.

units.la: Vers. 18. Fugite scortationem, omne peccatum quod fecerit homo, extra corpus est: sed qui scortatur, in proprium corpus peccat.
units.tr: Verse 18. Flee fornication. Every sin that a man commits is outside the body; but he who commits fornication sins against his own body.

units.la: Thesin convertit in dehortationem, & addit Arg. 4. ex comparatione aliorum peccatorum: Alia peccata abutuntur objecto extra posito, primò & principaliter, scortatio verò ipso corpore primò abutitur, dehonestatque corpus plusquam ullum aliud peccatum; Ergo scortatio illicita.
units.tr: He turns the thesis into a dehortation and adds a fourth argument from the comparison with other sins: other sins misuse an object lying outside the person, first and principally; but fornication misuses the body itself first, and dishonours the body more than any other sin does. Therefore fornication is unlawful.

units.la: Vers. 19. An ignoratis corpus vestrum esse templum Spiritus sancti, qui est in vobis, quem habetis à Deo, neque vos esse vestri juris?
units.tr: Verse 19. Do you not know that your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own?

units.la: Vers. 20. Nam empti estis pretio: glorificate igitur Deum in corpore vestro, & in spiritu vestro, quae sunt Dei.
units.tr: Verse 20. For you were bought with a price. Glorify God therefore in your body and in your spirit, which are God's.

units.la: Arg. 5. Corpora nostra sunt Templum Spiritus sancti, qui est in nobis, ncbis, à Deo nobis donatus: Ergo non sunt polluenda fornicatione. Neque vos ] Arg. 6. Fideles non sunt sui juris, sed pretio sanguinis Christi empti: Ergo non tantum cavere debent, ne se fornicatione polluant, sed etiam studere, ut sancta corporis & animæ conversatione Deum redemptorem, cujus sunt peculium, glorificent.
units.tr: Fifth argument: our bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in us, given to us by God; therefore they must not be polluted by fornication. "And you are not your own": sixth argument: believers are not their own, but were bought with the blood of Christ; therefore they must not only take care not to defile themselves with fornication, but also strive to glorify God the Redeemer, whose possession they are, by a holy way of life in body and soul.

units.la: Caput septimum.
units.tr: Chapter 7.

units.la: Articulus Epistolæ quintus de casibus Matrimonialibus.
units.tr: Fifth article of the Epistle, on matrimonial cases.

units.la: Postolus de casibus Matrimonialibus consultus à Corinthiis, hoc Capite respondet, ad quinque ipsorum quæsita.
units.tr: The Apostle, consulted by the Corinthians about matrimonial cases, in this chapter answers five of their questions.

units.la: Verf. 1. Cæterum de quibus mihi scripsistis, bonum fuerit viro mulierem non attingere.
units.tr: Verse 1. Now concerning the things whereof ye wrote unto me: It is good for a man not to touch a woman.

units.la: Verf. 2. Sed propter fornicationes, suam quisque uxorem habeto, & proprium quæque virum habeto.
units.tr: Verse 2. Nevertheless, to avoid fornication, let every man have his own wife, and let every woman have her own husband.

units.la: Primum quæsitum, de viris qui in cælibatu aut viduitate degebant, an expediret ipsis uxorem ducere: rationes quærendi erant duæ, metus molestiarum, & metus pollutionis in matrimonio. Quod ad primam rationem attinet, meminerimus Corinthios jam in persecutionis periculo constitutos fuisse, licet jam prospere agentes, plerique nihil metuerint; Respondet Apostolus, in tali casu constitutis, si nulla matrimonium contrahendi incumbat necessitas, bonum seu commodum esse non ducere uxorem: Sed ubi periculum peccandi ex incontinentia adesset, prospiciendum esse adversus fornicationis, & peccati, potius quam molestiarum periculum; & matrimonium contrahendum.
units.tr: The first question concerned men who lived in celibacy or widowhood, whether it was expedient for them to take a wife. There were two grounds for asking: fear of troubles, and fear of pollution in marriage. As to the first ground, we should remember that the Corinthians were placed in danger of persecution; although they were now prospering, many of them feared nothing. The Apostle answers that for those in such a case, if no necessity of contracting marriage lies upon them, it is good and advantageous not to take a wife. But where there is danger of sinning through incontinence, one must provide against the danger of fornication and sin rather than against the danger of troubles, and marriage must be contracted.

units.la: Verf. 3. Uxori vir debitam benevolentiam reddito: similiter autem & uxor viro.
units.tr: Verse 3. Let the husband render unto the wife due benevolence: and likewise also the wife unto the husband.

units.la: Quod ad scrupulum attinet, ne commercio matrimoniali inquinari conscientiam putaret quisquam, pronunciat non solum torum conjugalem immaculatum esse, sed etiam jus tori petenti conjugi concedi debere, additis quatuor rationibus. Prima ratio; Quia illa benevolentia debita est ex lege matrimonii.
units.tr: As to the scruple, lest anyone think his conscience would be defiled by marital intercourse, he declares that the marriage bed is not only undefiled, but that the right of the bed must also be granted to a spouse who asks for it. He gives four reasons. The first reason: because that benevolence is owed by the law of marriage.

units.la: \ Cif. 4 Uxor proprium corpus non habet in potestate, sed virsimiliter autem & vir proprium corpus non habet in potestate, sed uxor.
units.tr: Verse 4. The wife hath not power of her own body, but the husband: and likewise also the husband hath not power of his own body, but the wife.

units.la: Ratio 2. Quia ex pacto conjugali potestas & jus est marito, in corpus uxoris: & uxori in corpus mariti, ad vitandam scortationem praecipuè.
units.tr: Reason 2. Because by the marriage covenant the husband has power and right over the wife's body, and the wife over the husband's body, chiefly in order to avoid fornication.

units.la: \ Verl. 5. Ne fraudate alter alterum, nisi forte ex consensu ad tempus, ut vacetis jejunio & precibus, & rursum simul convenite, ne tentet vos Satanas propter incontinentiam vestram.
units.tr: Verse 5. Defraud ye not one the other, except it be with consent for a time, that ye may give yourselves to fasting and prayer; and come together again, that Satan tempt you not for your incontinency.

units.la: Ratio 3. Quia alioqui sequeretur injusta fraudatio alterius partis, si commercium denegetur, absque ratione.
units.tr: Reason 3. Because otherwise there would follow an unjust defrauding of the other party, if intercourse were refused without reason.

units.la: Hoc dictum limitat exceptione speciali, nisi cum ex consensu utriusque partis constitutum fuerit, ut ad tempus, jejunio & precibus vacarent.
units.tr: This statement is qualified by a special exception: unless it has been agreed by the consent of both parties that they should devote themselves to fasting and prayer for a time.

units.la: Ratio 4. Quia post tempus dictum, si negetur postulata benevolentia, periculum est, ne tentet Satanas ad adulterium partem fraudatam, propter ipsius incontinentiam.
units.tr: Reason 4. Because after the time agreed, if the requested benevolence is refused, there is a danger that Satan will tempt the defrauded party to adultery, on account of the other's incontinence.

units.la: Verf. 6. Hoc autem dico ex concessione, non ex imperio.
units.tr: Verse 6. But I speak this by permission, and not of commandment.

units.la: Verf. 7. Nam velim omnes homines esse ut & ipse sum: sed unusquisque proprium donum habet ex Deo, alius quidem ita, alius autem ita.
units.tr: Verse 7. For I would that all men were even as I myself am. But every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that.

units.la: Exponit hanc sententiam suam, de matrimonio contrahendo & conjugali commercio utendo, non esse praeceptum universale, quasi juberet omnes matrimonium contrahere, sed concessionem seu permissionem tantum universalem esse in casu incontinentiae: simpliciter enim, si per DEI voluntatem fieri posset, Apostolus optaret Corinthiis qui quaestionem movebant, & continentiam & commoda caelibatus, quae Deus, sibi largitus erat; sed quia unicuique non est datum continentiae donum: concessisse se dicit, quae concessit.
units.tr: He explains that this statement of his, about contracting marriage and using conjugal intercourse, is not a universal command, as though he ordered everyone to marry. It is only a general concession or permission in the case of incontinence. For simply, if it could happen by the will of God, the Apostle would wish for the Corinthians who raised the question both continence and the advantages of celibacy, which God had bestowed on him. But since the gift of continence is not given to everyone, he says that he has conceded what he has conceded.

units.la: Verf. 8. Dico autem caelibibus & viduis bonum esse eis, si sic manserint, ut & ego maneo.
units.tr: Verse 8. I say therefore to the unmarried and widows: It is good for them if they abide even as I.

units.la: Verf. 9. Quod si se non continent, matrimonium contrahant: nam melius est matrimonium contahere quàm uri. Hinc summam dictorum colligit, ut plane respondeat iis qui in coe-libatu aut viduitate degebant, commodum esse & expedire, ut in eo statu maneant, si continere poterint; sin minus, ut matrimonium contrahant.
units.tr: Verse 9. But if they cannot contain, let them marry. For it is better to marry than to burn. From this he draws the sum of what has been said, so that he plainly answers those who lived in celibacy or widowhood: it is advantageous and expedient for them to remain in that state if they can contain; but if not, that they should marry.

units.la: Rationem reddit, quia cavendum ipsis erat potius à libidinum ardoribus, qui peccato polluunt conscientias, quam à matrimonii molestiis etiam illis molestiis, quae persecutionis tempore matrimonium sequuntur.
units.tr: He gives the reason: they ought rather to guard against the burnings of lust, which defile the conscience with sin, than against the troubles of marriage, even those troubles which follow marriage in a time of persecution.

units.la: Verf. 10. Iis autem qui matrimonio juncti sunt denuntio, non ego, sed Dominus, Uxor à viro ne sese ipsa separato.
units.tr: Verse 10. And unto the married I command, yet not I but the Lord: Let not the wife depart from her husband.

units.la: Secundum quaesitum est de divortiis; ejus partes duae sunt: prima est, de utroque conjuge fideli, an divortium facere Christianis conjugatis sit licitum, extra casum adulterii scilicet? Respondet nefas esse. Ut responsionem confirmet, negat se quicquam novi, seu ex revelatione speciali praecipere, sed praeceptum vetus authoritate Domini repetere, qui in matrimonii institutione sanxit, ut conjugati una caro essent, & proinde illicitam esse separationem, aut divortium.
units.tr: The second question concerns divorces. It has two parts. The first is: between two believing spouses, is it lawful for Christians who are married to divorce, that is, outside the case of adultery? He answers that it is wrong. To confirm his answer, he says that he is not teaching anything new, or prescribing by special revelation, but repeating an old precept on the authority of the Lord, who in instituting marriage ordained that the married should be one flesh, and that therefore separation or divorce is unlawful.

units.la: Verf. 11. Quod si sese separarit, maneat caelebs, aut viro reconciliator: & vir uxorem ne dimittito.
units.tr: Verse 11. But and if she depart, let her remain unmarried, or be reconciled to her husband: and let not the husband put away his wife.

units.la: Quod si vero uxor, (necessarias causas discedendi, ut periculum vitae, vel simile quid praetendens) discesserit, jubet eam vel reconciliari marito, vel à matrimonio novo abstinere, & per consequens multo magis à fornicatione sibi cavere: Idque praecipit, & in protervia vel impatientiae poenam, & in sinceritatis probationem; ne haec libertas in licentiam trahatur; Interim viro praecipit, ne vel dimittat uxorem, vel discedendi causam ei praebeat.
units.tr: But if the wife departs, pretending necessary causes for leaving, such as danger to life or something similar, he orders her either to be reconciled to her husband or to abstain from a new marriage, and consequently, much more, to guard herself against fornication. He commands this both as a punishment for perversity or impatience, and as a test of sincerity, so that this freedom may not turn into licence. Meanwhile he commands the husband neither to put away his wife nor to give her a reason for leaving.

units.la: Verf. 12. Reliquis autem ego dico, non Dominus, Si quis frater uxorem habet infidelem, quae libens consentiat ad habitandum cum eo, ne eam dimittito:
units.tr: Verse 12. But to the rest speak I, not the Lord: If any brother hath a wife that believeth not, and she be pleased to dwell with him, let him not put her away.

units.la: Verf. 13. Et uxor quae habet virum infidelem, qui libens consentiat ad habitandum cum ea, ne eam dimittito.
units.tr: Verse 13. And the woman which hath an husband that believeth not, and if he be pleased to dwell with her, let her not leave him.

units.la: Altera pars quaesiti, qua quaeritur de conjugatis, quorum alter infidelis est, an divortium sit licitum? Ad hanc partem responsurum se dicit, ex speciali revelationis authoritate, Quia in lege à Deo non determinatum erat, quid Christianis in illo casu faciendum sit, hoc est, quod dicit, non Dominus, videlicet in lege veteri determinavit, sed ego, nempe à DOMINO ex speciali revelatione determinabo; primâ responsionis parte, vetat ne dimittatur pars infidelis, si ea manere cupit.
units.tr: The second part of the question, which asks about spouses of whom one is unbelieving, whether divorce is lawful, is what he now says he will answer, not in the Lord's name but on his own, but I, namely determining it by special revelation from the Lord. In the first part of his answer he forbids the unbelieving party to be put away, if that party wishes to remain.

units.la: Verf. 14. Maritus enim infidelis sanctificatus est in uxore; & uxor infidelis sanctificata est in viro: alioqui certè liberi vestri impuri essent: nunc autem sancti sunt.
units.tr: Verse 14. For the unbelieving husband is sanctified by the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified by the husband: else were your children unclean; but now are they holy.

units.la: Rationes reddit quinque: Ratio prima; Quia infidelis persona sanctificatur, licet non in se, tamen in usum fidelis; conjugis licet non simpliciter, eousque tamen ut conjugium parti fideli, & liberis; procreatis sanctum fit. Ergo ne dimittatur conjunx infidelis manere cupiens.
units.tr: He gives five reasons. The first reason: because the unbelieving person is sanctified, not indeed in himself, but for the use of the believing spouse; not simply, but to such an extent that the marriage becomes holy for the believing party and for the children born. Therefore the unbelieving spouse who wishes to remain must not be put away.

units.la: Alioqui Ratio 2. Confirmans priorem ab absurdo; Quia alioqui Christianorum liberi, in tali casu, non essent nati sub fœdere; non essent nati Christiani, & CHRISTO sanctitate consecrationis dicati; Cujus contrarium verum est: Ergo ne dimittatur conjunx infidelis manere cupiens.
units.tr: Else Reason 2. Confirming the former by an argument from absurdity: because otherwise the children of Christians, in such a case, would not be born under the covenant; they would not be born Christians, and dedicated to Christ by the holiness of consecration. The opposite is true. Therefore the unbelieving spouse who wishes to remain must not be put away.

units.la: Verf. 15. At si infidelis se separet, separatus esto, non est servituti subjectus, frater aut soror in hujusmodi rebus: sed ad pacem vocavit nos Deus.
units.tr: Verse 15. But if the unbelieving depart, let him depart. A brother or a sister is not under bondage in such cases: but God hath called us to peace.

units.la: Priusquam reliquas rationes addat, alteram responsionis partem proponit; si pars infidelis cohabitare noluerit,& abierit; in hoc casu, pronunciat matrimonium solutum esse, & partem fidelem liberam esse.
units.tr: Before he adds the remaining reasons, he sets out the other part of the answer: if the unbelieving party is unwilling to live together and departs, in this case he declares that the marriage is dissolved and the believing party is free.

units.la: Ad pacem Ratio 3. Probans non dimittendam partem infidelem cohibitare volentem: Quia fideles vocantur ad pacem, cum omnibus colendam. Ergo si pars infidelis æquas pacis conditiones admittit, non dimittenda est.
units.tr: But God hath called us to peace Reason 3. Proving that the unbelieving party who wishes to live together must not be put away: because believers are called to peace, which is to be cultivated with all. Therefore, if the unbelieving party accepts fair conditions of peace, he must not be put away.

units.la: Verf. 16. Ecquid enim nosti uxor an sis virum servatura? aut ecquid nosti vir, an sis uxorem servaturus.
units.tr: Verse 16. For what knowest thou, O wife, whether thou shalt save thy husband? or how knowest thou, O man, whether thou shalt save thy wife?

units.la: Ratio 4. Quia per cohabitationem, infidelis potest lucrifieri.
units.tr: Reason 4. Because through cohabitation the unbelieving party may be gained.

units.la: Verf. 17. Sed ut unicuique donum partitus est Deus, ut unumquemque vocavit Dominus, ita incedat: & ita in Ecclesiis omnibus constituo.
units.tr: Verse 17. But as God hath distributed to every one, as the Lord hath called every one, so let him walk: and so ordain I in all churches.

units.la: Ratio 5. Quia singuli in qualibet conditione, vocatione honesta seu licita, in qua Deus ipsos providentia sua constituit, manere debent: sicut in omnibus Ecclesiis docebat Apostolus: Ergo etiam in conjugio manendum cum infidelí cohabitare volente: Nam cum matrimonium in Ethnicismo contractum fuisset, vocationem alterius ad gratiam Iesu CHRISTI, noluit Deus fraudi esse parti nondum conversæ. Eadem opera legem ponit Apostolus fidelibus servis, ne jugum excutiant infidelis heri, qui conversum ad fidem servum non cupiebat dimittere.
units.tr: Fifth reason: each person ought to remain in whatever condition, honest or lawful calling, in which God by his providence has placed him, as the Apostle taught in all the Churches. Therefore, also in marriage, one should remain with an unbelieving spouse who is willing to live together. For when a marriage had been contracted in heathenism, God did not wish the calling of the one party to grace in Jesus Christ to be a disadvantage to the party not yet converted. By the same token the Apostle lays down the rule for believing slaves, that they should not throw off the yoke of an unbelieving master, who did not want to dismiss a slave who had come to faith.

units.la: Verf. 18. Circumcisus aliquis vocatus est? ne attrahat præputium, in præputio aliquis vocatus est? ne circumcidatur.
units.tr: Verse 18. Was anyone called while circumcised? Let him not become uncircumcised. Was anyone called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised.

units.la: Verf. 19. Circumcisio nihil est, & præputium nihil est, sed observatio mandatorum Dei.
units.tr: Verse 19. Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of God's commandments.

units.la: Antecedens illustrat & confirmat inductione, primò, circumcisionis & Incircumcisionis, quarum neutra Christiano curanda erat, sed hoc unicuique spectandum erat tantùm ut in utroque statu, Dei præcepta moralia observarentur.
units.tr: He illustrates and confirms the preceding point by induction: first, from circumcision and uncircumcision, neither of which a Christian ought to be concerned about; each person should look only to this, that in either state he observes God's moral precepts.

units.la: Verf. 20. Unusquisque in qua vocatione vocatus fuit, in ea maneat.
units.tr: Verse 20. Let each one remain in the calling in which he was called.

units.la: Hinc, quia in uno exemplo inductionis plenitudo facilè apprehendi potuerat, infert generalem thesin, de manendo in eo vitæ statu, in quo Deus unumquemque vocaverat.
units.tr: Hence, since the fullness of the induction could easily be grasped from the one example, he draws the general thesis that one should remain in the state of life in which God has called each person.

units.la: Verf. 21. Servus vocatus es? ne sit tibi cura: sed si potes etiam liber fieri, potius eo utere.
units.tr: Verse 21. Were you called as a slave? Let it not trouble you; but if you can also become free, rather use it.

units.la: Deinde addit aliud membrum inductionis, de servitute, In qua manendum monet, nisi Deus ad libertatem ostium aperiret.
units.tr: Then he adds another member of the induction, concerning slavery, in which he advises us to remain unless God opens a door to freedom.

units.la: Verf. 22. Etenim qui in Domino vocatus est servus, libertus Domini est: similiter & qui liber vocatus est, servus est Christi.
units.tr: Verse 22. For he who was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord's freedman; likewise he who was called free is Christ's slave.

units.la: Rationem reddit: Quia servitus corporalis non diminuit de spirituali Christianorum libertate, a peccati reatu, & ira, nec corporalis libertas eximit à servitio Christi.
units.tr: He gives the reason: bodily servitude does not diminish the spiritual liberty of Christians, from the guilt of sin and wrath; nor does bodily liberty exempt anyone from the service of Christ.

units.la: Verf. 23, Pretio empti estis, ne efficiamini servi hominum.
units.tr: Verse 23. You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men.

units.la: Obiter admonet, ut sive liberi sive servi sint corpore; caveant ne ex præcepto, seu voluntate hominum faciant quæ in se illicita sunt, quia illud esset, hominibus servire contra Christum, qui ipsos pretio emerat ut in omnibus, non hominum, sed redemptoris voluntatem facerent.
units.tr: He admonishes in passing that, whether they are free or slaves in body, they should take care not to do, by the command or will of men, things that are unlawful in themselves; for that would be to serve men against Christ, who bought them with a price so that in everything they might do, not the will of men, but the will of their Redeemer.

units.la: Verf. 24. Unusquisque in quo vocatus fuit fratres, in hoc maneat apud Deum.
units.tr: Verse 24. Brothers, each one in the condition in which he was called, in that let him remain with God.

units.la: Unde ne quis temere à vocatione discederet, denuò inculcat generale præceptum de manendo in præsenti vitæ statu & conditione apud Deum, id est, in obedientia Dei, donec ipsi visum esset ipsorum conditionem mutare.
units.tr: Therefore, lest anyone rashly depart from his calling, he again impresses the general precept of remaining, before God, in the present state and condition of life, that is, in obedience to God, until he sees fit to change their condition.

units.la: Vers. 25. De virginibus autem imperium Domini non habeo; sententiam verò meam hac in re dico, ut cui Dominus per misericordiam dederit fidum esse.
units.tr: Verse 25. Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord; but I give my opinion in this matter, as one who by the Lord's mercy is faithful.

units.la: Tertium quæsitum; de virginibus maribus & fœminis, matrimonium ne contraherent, an non? Ad quod respondsurus præfatur nullum se habere præceptum speciale scilicet, quo vel præcipiatur, vel prohibeatur virginitatis status, sed fideliter datum se consilium, & sententiam de commodo, ut decebat eum cui Dominus pro sua misericordia fidelem esse concesserat.
units.tr: The third question: whether men and women who are virgins should contract marriage or not. To this he replies by saying beforehand that he has no special command, either commanding or forbidding the state of virginity, but gives faithful counsel and an opinion about what is advantageous, as was fitting for one whom the Lord, in his mercy, had granted to be faithful.

units.la: Vers. 26. Existimo igitur hoc bonum esse propter instantem necessitatem, bonum hoc inquam esse homini ita esse.
units.tr: Verse 26. I think therefore that this is good because of the present distress; that it is good for a man to remain so.

units.la: Vers. 27. Alligatus es uxori? ne quære dissolutionem, solutus es ab uxore? ne quære uxorem.
units.tr: Verse 27. Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek a divorce. Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife.

units.la: Responsionis partes sunt tres: Prima, In præsenti necessitate, seu persecutionis periculo, licut conjugatos vetat, ne dimittant uxores suas, ita commodius esse dicit, si cœlibes vitam continuarent in cœlibatu, nempe si donum, ut supra dictum est, continentiæ habuerint.
units.tr: The answer has three parts. First, in the present distress, or danger of persecution, just as he forbids married people to dismiss their wives, so he says it is more convenient if the unmarried continue in celibacy, namely if they have the gift of continence, as was said above.

units.la: Vers. 28. Quod si etiam duxeris uxorem, non peccasti: & si nupserit virgo, non peccavit: sed afflictionem in carne habituri sunt qui sunt hujusmodi. ego verò vobis parco.
units.tr: Verse 28. But even if you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned; yet those who are of this kind will have affliction in the flesh. But I spare you.

units.la: Altera pars responsionis in qua docet, matrimonii contractionem non esse peccatum, sed molestiis obnoxiam; de quibus molestiis non vult dissere amplius, ne dissuadere videatur à matrimonio plus quam tutum esset.
units.tr: The second part of the answer, in which he teaches that contracting marriage is not a sin, but is liable to troubles; he does not wish to discuss these troubles further, lest he seem to dissuade from marriage more than is safe.

units.la: Vers. 29. Hoc autem aio, fratres, quoniam opportunum tempus est angustum in posterum: ut & qui habent uxores, sint ut non habentes.
units.tr: Verse 29. But this I say, brothers: the appointed time is short from now on; so that those who have wives should be as though they had none.

units.la: Vers. 30. Et qui flent, ut non flentes: & qui gaudent, ut non gaudentes: & qui emunt, ut non obtinentes.
units.tr: Verse 30. And those who weep, as though they did not weep; and those who rejoice, as though they did not rejoice; and those who buy, as though they did not possess.

units.la: Tertia responsionis pars, in qua præcipit ut sive matrimonium contraxerint, sive non, caveant sibi ne hujus vitæ brevis commodis vel incommodis, voluptatibus vel molestiis multùm moveantur, sed moderatè res prosperas, & adversas ferentes, se ad futuram vitam comparent, parati semper tristiora ferre, & lætiora relinquere, pro Dei voluntate, hoc enim est idem quasi uxorem non habeant, non fleant, &c. Cum conjugio prudenter utentes, non impediuntur in cursu suo, ad regnum Cœlorum, sed expediti pergunt, per fletum & gaudium, per vitæ hujus commoda & incommoda, negotia omnia, & mutationes omnes.
units.tr: The third part of the answer, in which he commands that, whether they have contracted marriage or not, they take care not to be greatly moved by the brief advantages or disadvantages, pleasures or troubles of this short life; but, bearing prosperity and adversity with moderation, they should prepare themselves for the future life, always ready to bear sadder things and to give up happier ones, according to God's will. For this is the same as if they had no wives, did not weep, and so on. Those who use marriage wisely are not hindered in their course to the kingdom of heaven, but go on unencumbered, through weeping and rejoicing, through the advantages and disadvantages of this life, through all its affairs and all its changes.

units.la: Verf. 31. Et qui utuntur hoc mundo, ut non abutentes: praeterit enim species hujus mundi.
units.tr: Verse 31. And those who use this world, as not abusing it; for the form of this world passes away.

units.la: Hujus ratio redditur; Quia ut umbra evanida citò praetereunt & bona & mala hujus vitæ: Idcirco debemus rebus hujus vitæ uti, tanquam in transcursu; ita ut nos in cursu non retardent.
units.tr: The reason for this is given: just as a fleeting shadow, both the good and the evil of this life quickly pass away; therefore we ought to use the things of this life as though in passing, so that they do not hold us back in our course.

units.la: Verf. 32. Velim autem vos absque sollicitudine esse. Qui caelebs est, sollicitus est de iis quæ sunt Domini, quomodo placiturus sit Domino:
units.tr: Verse 32. But I would have you be without anxiety. He who is unmarried is anxious about the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord.

units.la: Verf. 33. At qui duxit uxorem, sollicitus est de iis quæ sunt mundi, quomodo placiturus sit uxori.
units.tr: Verse 33. But he who has married is anxious about the things of the world, how he may please his wife.

units.la: Consilii de virginitate servanda duas dat rationes; Prima ratio, ut eximantur à sollicitudine, quam metus persecutionis, & necessitatis praesentis, poslet injicere conjugatis: Ratio 2. Quia cælebs vir commodius vacare possit rebus divinis, seu exercitiis religionis atendere, & Deo immeditatè placere; Conjugatus verò tenetur, & cogitur ex vocatione, rebus terrenis, & curis œconomicis tempus impendere: & sic uxori in licitis placere; quæ cura licet obedientia esse possit, ubi in Dei timore praestatur, non tamen tam immediata est obedientia, & Deo propinqua, quam illa quæ in exercitiis religionis posita est.
units.tr: He gives two reasons for the counsel to keep virginity. The first reason: that they may be freed from the anxiety which fear of persecution and the present necessity could bring upon married people. The second reason: because an unmarried man can more conveniently be free to attend to divine things, or the exercises of religion, and to please God immediately; but a married man is bound and compelled by his calling to spend time on earthly things and domestic cares, and so to please his wife in lawful matters. This care, though it can be obedience when it is rendered in the fear of God, is not so immediate an obedience, nor so near to God, as that which consists in the exercises of religion.

units.la: Verf. 34. Discreta sunt, ea quæ est uxor, & ea quæ est virgo: quæ est cælebs, sollicita est de iis quæ sunt Domini, ut sit sancta cum corpore, tum spiritu: quæ verò nupta est, sollicita est de iis quæ sunt mundi, quomodo placitura sit viro,
units.tr: Verse 34. There is a difference between the wife and the virgin. She who is unmarried is anxious about the things of the Lord, that she may be holy both in body and in spirit; but she who is married is anxious about the things of the world, how she may please her husband.

units.la: Idem discrimen esse indicat, inter statum virginum & nuptarum; Quod virgo possit cum paucioribus avocamentis, & minori difficultate, sacris exercitiis, corpore & animo, quasi sanctior vacare, quia non habet familiam pro qua sollicita sit: Haec sanctitas dicitur non ut opponitur peccato, sed ut opponitur civili seu communi; quomodo ministerium Euangelii sanctius vocari potest, aliquà vocatione civili: uxor verò, cum œconomicis, & studio placendi marito suo, distrahi solet, nec tam liberè sacris exercitiis vacare potest.
units.tr: He indicates the same distinction between the state of virgins and of married women: a virgin, with fewer distractions and less difficulty, can devote herself to sacred exercises, in body and mind, as one who is more holy, because she has no household for which she must be anxious. This holiness is not called holiness as opposed to sin, but as opposed to what is civil or common; just as the ministry of the Gospel can be called more holy by a certain civil calling. A wife, however, is usually distracted by domestic affairs and by the effort to please her husband, and cannot devote herself to sacred exercises as freely.

units.la: Verf. 35. Hæc autem dico vestro commodo : non ut laqueum vobis injiciam, sed ut decenter & apte adhærescatis Domino, absque ulla distractione.
units.tr: Verse 35. I say this for your own advantage: not to throw a noose upon you, but so that you may attend to the Lord fittingly and suitably, without any distraction.

units.la: Totum hoc consilium exponit Apostolus, quod tendat horsum tantum, ut convenientius & commodius, decenter & apte compositi, sine distractione attendant Deum in exercitiis religionis, si donum continentiæ habuerint, non ut laqueum injiciat necessitatis, abstinendi à matrimonio, si donum continentiæ non habuerint.
units.tr: The Apostle sets out this whole counsel, which aims only at this: that those who have the gift of continence, being more suitably and conveniently disposed, may attend to God in the exercises of religion, fittingly and suitably, without distraction; not that he might throw on them the noose of a necessity to abstain from marriage if they did not have the gift of continence.

units.la: Verf. 36. Cæterum si quis sese existimat aliquid indecorum in virginem suam committere, si flòrem ætatis excedat, & ita debet fieri: quod vult faciat, non peccat: jungantur matrimonio.
units.tr: Verse 36. But if anyone thinks he is behaving unseemly toward his virgin daughter, if she is past the flower of her age, and it ought so to be done: let him do what he wills; he does not sin; let them marry.

units.la: Quartum quæsitum; de parentum officio, in quorum potestate sunt filiæ nubiles, utrum consultum sit, filias suas virgines nuptum dare an non? Responsionis duæ sunt partes, Prima ex suppositione triplici:
units.tr: Fourth question: concerning the duty of parents, in whose power marriageable daughters are, whether it is advisable to give their daughters in marriage as virgins or not. The answer has two parts. The first rests on a threefold supposition:

units.la: 1. Si quis filiam suam, supra quam expediret, à nubendo se detinuisse suspicetur: 2. Si filia florem ætatis excesserit, id est, annum vicesimum attigerit, & ὑπέραχμ quasi dicas superadulta esse inceperit. 3. Si videat, ad nuptias, animum virginis inclinantem, sequatur voluntatem virginis & suam: jungantur matrimonio filia & gener, quem pater delegerit, non peccat parens in eo.
units.tr: (1) If a man suspects that he has kept his daughter from marriage longer than is fitting; (2) if the daughter has passed the flower of her age, that is, has reached her twentieth year, and has begun to be, as it were, superadult [ὑπέρακμος]; (3) if he sees the maiden's inclination tending toward marriage, and he follows both her wish and his own: let the daughter and the son-in-law whom the father has chosen be joined in marriage. The parent does not sin in this.

units.la: Verf. 37. Qui verò perstat firmus in corde, nec adigitur necessi-tate, sed in potestate habet propriam voluntatem, & hoc decrevit in corde suo, ut servet suam virginem, benè facit.
units.tr: Verse 37. But he who stands firm in his heart, and is not compelled by necessity, but has power over his own will, and has determined this in his heart, to keep his virgin, does well.

units.la: Altera pars responsionis, ex suppositione etiam triplici: 1. Si parens persuasum habeat se nullâ injuriâ filiam asfecifle, à matrimonio eam retinens: 2. Si filia donum continentiæ habeat, & nulla neces-sitas ab ipsa patris voluntatem movere possit, ut ei maritum quærat, ita ut statuere possit parens de filia, sicut ipsi lubet: 3. Si decrevit filiam suam in cælibatu retinere; bene inquit, statuit, id est, in filiæ suæ commodum.
units.tr: The second part of the answer also rests on a threefold supposition: (1) if the parent is persuaded that he does the daughter no wrong by keeping her from marriage; (2) if the daughter has the gift of continency, and no necessity can move the father's own will so that he seeks a husband for her, so that the parent may decide about the daughter as he pleases; (3) if he has decided to keep his daughter in celibacy. He decides well, he says, that is, for the daughter's advantage.

units.la: Verf. 38 Itaque qui dat nuptum, benè facit, qui verò non dat nuptum, melius facit.
units.tr: Verse 38. So then he who gives her in marriage does well, but he who does not give her in marriage does better.

units.la: Unde concludit in primo casu parentem benè facere, seu ad filiæ utilitatem: in altero verò casu, parentem melius facere, seu magis consulere filiæ suæ commodo; interim pronunciat neutrum peccare. Verf. 39. Uxor alligata est lege quandiu vivit vir ipsius : quod si obdormierit vir ipsius, libera est ad cui velit nubendum : tantum in Domino.
units.tr: Hence he concludes that in the first case the parent does well, that is, for the daughter's benefit; but in the other case the parent does better, that is, he better consults his daughter's advantage. Meanwhile he pronounces that neither sins. Verse 39. A wife is bound by law as long as her husband lives; but if her husband falls asleep, she is free to marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord.

units.la: Quæsitum quintum: an secundæ nuptiæ viduarum fœminarum licitæ sint an non? Responsionis duæ sunt partes: 1. Licere ait cum limitatione, modo pio affectu fiant nuptiæ, & cum persona fideli, & cui per DEI legem nubere licet; hoc enim est in Domino nubere, ita nubere ut DEI benedictio expectari possit.
units.tr: Fifth question: whether second marriages of widows are lawful or not. The answer has two parts. (1) He says they are lawful, with a limitation: provided the marriage is made with a godly affection, and with a believing person whom it is lawful to marry by God's law. For this is to marry in the Lord, to marry in such a way that God's blessing may be expected.

units.la: Vers. 40. Sed beatior est si ita maneat, secundum meam sententiam: videor autem mihi, & ego Spiritum Dei habere.
units.tr: Verse 40. But she is happier if she so remains, according to my judgment; and I think that I also have the Spirit of God.

units.la: Secundò respondet, etiamsi liceat, non tamen expedire plerunque, præsertim in persecutionis periculo, seu necessitate præsenti; quia beatior erit si manserit vidua, id est, tranquillius vivet, & molestiis carebit, quas secundæ nuptiæ ipsi essent creaturæ.
units.tr: Second, he answers that even if it is lawful, it is nevertheless usually not expedient, especially in the danger of persecution or present necessity. For she will be happier if she remains a widow, that is, she will live more quietly and be free from the troubles which a second marriage would itself bring upon her.

units.la: Hoc consilium de commoditate, divinum esse modestè insinuans, validissimè asserit, ad commoditatem certissimè facere; plus enim dicitur quam si sine μεριμνᾶν hoc dixisset.
units.tr: Gently suggesting that this counsel concerning convenience is divine, he most strongly affirms that it certainly serves convenience; for more is said than if he had said it without anxiety [μεριμνᾶν].

units.la: Caput octavum.
units.tr: Chapter 8.

units.la: Articulus sextus de Idolothytis vitandis.
units.tr: Sixth article, on avoiding things sacrificed to idols.

units.la: Equitur sextus Epistolæ articulus, de Idolothytis, vitandis, Capitibus 8, 9, 10.
units.tr: The sixth article of the Epistle follows, concerning things sacrificed to idols, which are to be avoided, in chapters 8, 9 and 10.

units.la: Vers. 1. Cæterum de iis quæ idolis immolantur, scimus nos omnes notitiâ esse præditos. Notitia inflat, charitas verò ædificat.
units.tr: Vers. 1. Now as touching things offered unto idols, we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth.

units.la: Disputatio quæ hoc capite continetur constat solutione trium objectionum: unde apparet non licere simpliciter Idolothytis vesci.
units.tr: The discussion contained in this chapter consists in the answering of three objections, from which it appears that it is not lawful simply to eat things sacrificed to idols.

units.la: Prima objectio: Satis instructi sumus scientiâ, de licito Idolothytorum usu; Ergo de iis licite possumus edere. Respondet, concessione, & correctione, in hunc sensum, etiamsi quis sciat libertatem suam in idolothytis utendis, non sufficit scientia nuda, nisi in usu & praxi cum charitate. tate jungatur: Quia scientia sine charitate inflat, & superbos fratrum despectores sciolos reddit: cum charitate vero conjuncta ædificat, id est, accommodat se in bonum aliorum.
units.tr: First objection: We are sufficiently instructed in knowledge of the lawful use of things sacrificed to idols; therefore we may lawfully eat of them. He answers by granting and correcting, in this sense: even if someone knows his liberty in using things sacrificed to idols, bare knowledge is not enough, unless it is joined with charity in the use and practice. For knowledge without charity puffs up and makes the conceited despisers of their brethren; but joined with charity it edifies, that is, it accommodates itself to the good of others.

units.la: Verf. 2. Quod si quis sibi videtur aliquid scire, nondum quic-quam novit sicut oportet nosse.
units.tr: Vers. 2. And if any man think that he knoweth any thing, he knoweth nothing yet as he ought to know.

units.la: Verf. 3. Sed si quis diligit Deum, hic cognitus fuit ab eo.
units.tr: Vers. 3. But if any man love God, the same is known of him.

units.la: Dictum explicat, distinctione scientis cum superbia, & scientis cum charitate Dei & proximi: Ille, qui scientiam habet cum superbia junctam, quia inflatur vana opinione suæ scientiæ, solidè nihil scit: hic vero, qui scientiam cum dilectione junctam habet, sicut à Deo edoctus est, ita à Deo approbatur ut verè sciens.
units.tr: He explains the saying by distinguishing knowledge joined with pride from knowledge joined with love of God and neighbour. The one who has knowledge joined with pride, because he is puffed up with the empty opinion of his own knowledge, really knows nothing at all; but the one who has knowledge joined with love, as he is taught by God, is so approved by God as one who truly knows.

units.la: Verf. 4. De esu igitur eorum quæ idolis immolantur, scimus idolum nihil esse in mundo, & nullum esse Deum alium nisi unum.
units.tr: Vers. 4. As concerning therefore the eating of those things that are offered in sacrifice unto idols, we know that an idol is nothing in the world, and that there is none other God but one.

units.la: Secunda objectio; Scimus idolum sive externum sive internum nihil habere divinitatis, quæ ab Idololatris ei inesse putatur, aut in eo repræsentari fingitur: scimus etiam quod non sit Deus ullus præter unum: Ergo quum à figmentis hominum non possint nobis pollui Dei creaturæ, idolothytis licet vesci.
units.tr: Second objection: We know that an idol, whether external or internal, has no divinity such as the idolaters suppose to be in it or pretend is represented in it; we also know that there is no God besides the one. Therefore, since God's creatures cannot be polluted for us by men's fictions, it is lawful to eat idol-offerings.

units.la: Verf. 5. Nam etiamsi sint qui dicantur Dii, & in cælo & in terra (sicut sunt dij multi, & Domini multi.)
units.tr: Vers. 5. For though there be that are called gods, whether in heaven or in earth, (as there be gods many, and lords many,)

units.la: Verf. 6 Nobis tamen unus est Deus Pater ille, à quo omnia, & nos in ipso: & unus Dominus Iesus Christus: per quem omnia, & nos per ipsum.
units.tr: Vers. 6. But to us there is but one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things, and we by him.

units.la: Respondet primò per concessionem & confirmationem antecedentis ab objicientibus positi, Quod etiamsi verbis & opinione hominum sint, & vocentur dii cœlestes & terrestres, & Domini multi, unus tamen est Deus & Dominus, nempe pater, (quo nomine ducimur ad reliquas personas, Filium videlicet & Spiritum sanctum, qui sunt unus Deus, principium omnium creaturarum à quo, & finis omnium ad quem, potissimum respectu nostri, qui fideles & in illius gloriam confecti sumus) & unus MEDIATOR IESUS CHRISTUS, idem cum patre Deus, per quem ut per verbum Patris omnia creata sunt, & nos fideles per eum, scilicet redempti, qui ideo DOMINUS dicitur, & creationis, & redemptionis nomine.
units.tr: He answers first by granting and confirming the antecedent put forward by the objectors: even if, in words and in the opinion of men, there are those who are called gods in heaven and on earth, and many lords, yet there is one God and one Lord, namely the Father (by which name we are led to the remaining persons, namely the Son and the Holy Spirit, who are one God, the principle of all creatures from which, and the end of all to which, chiefly with respect to us, who are believers and have been made for his glory), and one MEDIATOR, JESUS CHRIST, the same God as the Father, through whom, as the Word of the Father, all things were created, and we believers through him, that is, redeemed; who is therefore called LORD, both in the name of creation and in the name of redemption.

units.la: Verf. 7. Sed non in omnibus est ea cognitio, nonnulli enim cum cum conscientia idoli usque ad hoc tempus, ut idolis immolatum edunt: & conscientia eorum, infirma quum sit, inquinatur.
units.tr: Vers. 7. Howbeit there is not in every man that knowledge: for some with conscience of the idol unto this hour eat it as a thing offered unto an idol; and their conscience being weak is defiled.

units.la: Secundo respondet per limitationem; Negando hanc scientiæ mensuram esse in omnibus conversis, quia aliqui veterem opinionem de Idolis nondum plane depositerunt, sed reverentia quadam Idoli tanguntur, dum Idolothyta edunt, & sic polluuntur conscientiæ infirmæ, dubitantes an recte faciant: idcirco Idolothytis non licet vesci simpliciter.
units.tr: Secondly he answers by limitation, denying that this measure of knowledge is found in all converts, because some have not yet fully put away the old opinion about idols, but are still moved by a certain reverence for the idol when they eat things offered to idols; and so their weak consciences, doubting whether they act rightly, are defiled. Therefore it is not lawful simply to eat idol-offerings.

units.la: Verf. 8. Cæterum esca nos non commendat Deo: neque enim si edamus, amplius habemus: neque si non edamus, minus habemus.
units.tr: Vers. 8. But meat commendeth us not to God: for neither, if we eat, are we the better; neither, if we eat not, are we the worse.

units.la: Tertia objectio; At cibórum comestio est in indifferentibus, & extra religionem positis, in quibus libertas nobis datur; siquidem Deo non minus placemus edentes, quam non edentes; nam perinde est ad salutem, sive edamus hunc cibum, sive alium: Ergo libertas hic nobis non est auferenda.
units.tr: Third objection: But the eating of food belongs to indifferent things, placed outside religion, in which liberty is given to us; for we please God no less when we eat than when we do not eat, since it makes no difference to salvation whether we eat this food or another. Therefore this liberty is not to be taken away from us here.

units.la: Verf. 9. Sed videte ne quo ipsud quod vobis licitum est, impingendi causa fiat infirmis.
units.tr: Vers. 9. But take heed lest by any means this liberty of yours become a stumblingblock to them that are weak.

units.la: Respondet verum quidem hoc esse, extra casum scandali, peccare tamen eum, qui libertate utitur cum infirmi fratris offendiculo.
units.tr: He answers that this is indeed true outside the case of scandal, but that the one who uses his liberty to the offence of a weak brother nevertheless sins.

units.la: Verf. 10 Etenim si quis viderit te, illa cognitione præditum, in idoleio accumbere, nonne conscientia ipsius qui infirmus est, instruetur ad edendum ea quæ sunt idolis mactata?
units.tr: Vers. 10. For if any man see thee which hast knowledge sit at meat in the idol's temple, shall not the conscience of him which is weak be emboldened to eat those things which are offered to idols?

units.la: Hoc probat quatuor rationibus: Prima, quia in præsuppositio casu, infirmus animatur, & male instruitur exemplo edentis in idoleio cum scientia sine charitate, ad polluendum se idolothytorum esu: Ergo non licet simpliciter idolothytis vesci.
units.tr: He proves this by four reasons. The first: because in the supposed case the weak one is emboldened and badly instructed by the example of one who eats in the idol's temple with knowledge but without charity, to defile himself by eating idol-offerings; therefore it is not lawful simply to eat idol-offerings.

units.la: Verf. 11. Et tua ista cognitione frater ille infirmus propter quem Christus est mortuus, peribit?
units.tr: Vers. 11. And through thy knowledge shall the weak brother perish, for whom Christ died?

units.la: Ratio 2. Quia tali facto destruitur is pro quo mortuus est Christus, quantum scilicet per operis intentionem & procurationem comedentium fieri potest: Ergo, non licet simpliciter idolothytis vesci.
units.tr: The second reason: because by such an act he for whom Christ died is destroyed, as far as this can be done by the intention and effort of those who eat; therefore it is not lawful simply to eat idol-offerings.

units.la: Verf. 12 Ita autem peccantes in fratres, & vulnerantes ipsorum conscientiam infirmam, in Christum peccatis.
units.tr: Vers. 12. But when ye sin so against the brethren, and wound their weak conscience, ye sin against Christ.

units.la: Ratio 3 Quia tali facto peccatur non in fratres tantum, quorum conscientia vulneratur, sed etiam adversus Christum; quia factum tendit eo, ut frustetur Christus fine mortis suæ, quatenus scilicet quem Christus redemit ut servetur, edens cum scandalo operam dat, quantum in ipso est, ut perdatur: Ergo, &c.
units.tr: The third reason: because by such an act sin is committed not only against the brethren whose conscience is wounded, but also against Christ; for the act tends to frustrate Christ of the purpose of his death, since, whom Christ redeemed that he might be saved, the one who eats with scandal labours, as far as in him lies, that he be lost; therefore, etc.

units.la: Vers. 13. Quapropter si esca offendiculo est fratri meo, non edam carnes in æternum, ne sim offendiculo fratri meo.
units.tr: Vers. 13. Wherefore, if meat make my brother to offend, I will eat no flesh while the world standeth, lest I make my brother to offend.

units.la: Ratio 4. Quia satius est privari libertate edendi carnes in perpetuum, quam edere cum scandalo ; quod ostendit Apostolus in voti sui exemplo: Ergo, &c.
units.tr: The fourth reason: because it is better to be deprived forever of the liberty of eating flesh than to eat with scandal; which the Apostle shows in the example of his own vow; therefore, etc.

units.la: Caput nonum.
units.tr: Chapter 9.

units.la: DErgit de Idolothytis agere; exemplum suum proponebat sub finem superioris capitis: hortatur hoc capite ab exemplo suo, ut sibi temperent in usu libertatis suæ, potissimùm in illis quæ gulam spectabant, & nominatim in idolothytorum esu: Argumenti summa hæc est, Ego Apostolus non minus liber quàm quisquam alius, non solùm abstineo à licitis & commodis, sed etiam me omnium accommodo infirmitatibus, imo meipsum macero continentiâ in bonum Euangelii, similiter ergo & vos facite. Antecedens habetur, ad vers. 23. consequens est hortatio, ad finem.
units.tr: Having dealt with the things offered to idols, he had proposed his own example at the end of the previous chapter. In this chapter he urges the Corinthians, from his example, to moderate their use of their liberty, especially in matters that concern the appetite, and particularly in eating meat offered to idols. The substance of his argument is this: I, the apostle, am no less free than anyone else, yet I not only abstain from things lawful and convenient, but also accommodate myself to the weaknesses of all, and even mortify myself by continence for the good of the Gospel. So you too should act likewise. The antecedent is found up to verse 23; the consequent is the exhortation, to the end.

units.la: Vers. 1. NOnne sum Apostolus? nonne sum liber? Nonne Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum vidi? nonne opus meum vos estis in Domino?
units.tr: Verse 1. Am I not an apostle? Am I not free? Have I not seen Jesus Christ our Lord? Are you not my work in the Lord?

units.la: Vers. 2. Si aliis non sum Apostolus at certè vobis sum, nam sigillum apostolatus mei vos estis in Domino.
units.tr: Verse 2. If I am not an apostle to others, yet at least I am to you; for you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.

units.la: Vers. 3. Mea defensio apud eos qui in me inquirunt hæc est.
units.tr: Verse 3. This is my defence to those who examine me.

units.la: Antecedens per partes prosequitur; & primum, non postremum sibi deberi locum in libertate Christiana, probat tribus rationibus. 1. Quia Apostolus erat: 2. Quia aspectu Domini honoratus, & immediate vocatus erat: 3. Quia in Testimonium Apostolatus habebat Corinthiorum conversionem, vers 1. qui fructus, tanquam sigillum, Apostolatum confirmaret, saltem apud Corinthios, vers. 2. & defensionem Apostolo, saltem apud Corinthios, suppeditaret adversus eos, qui Apostolatum ejus in dubium vocarent, vers. 3.
units.tr: He pursues the antecedent part by part. First, he proves by three reasons that he should not be given the last place in Christian liberty: (1) because he was an apostle; (2) because he was honoured with the sight of the Lord and was called immediately; (3) because he had as the testimony of his apostleship the conversion of the Corinthians (verse 1), a fruit which, like a seal, confirmed his apostleship, at least among the Corinthians (verse 2), and supplied him with a defence against those who called his apostleship into doubt (verse 3).

units.la: Verf. 4. Annon licet nobis edere & bibere?
units.tr: Verse 4. Have we not the right to eat and drink?

units.la: Verf. 5. Annon licet nobis sororem uxorem circumducere, ut & reliquis Apostolis & fratribus Domini, & Cephas?
units.tr: Verse 5. Have we not the right to lead about a sister, a wife, as the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas do?

units.la: Verf. 6. An soli mihi & Barnabæ non licet non operari?
units.tr: Verse 6. Or is it only I and Barnabas who have no right not to work?

units.la: Deinde hanc suam libertatem applicat, Primum ad esculenta & poculenta, quibus liberè uti poterat, si quisquam, verf. 4. Secundò, ad matrimonium contrahendum, ejusque beneficio utendum; quod probat ab exemplo aliorum Apostolorum, verf. 5. Tertiò, ad abstinendum à laboribus manuariis; & per consequens, ad stipendium exigendum ab Ecclesiis; quod suum jus probat septem argumentis: Argumentum primum, ab exemplo aliorum Apostolorum, & Ministrorum; Aliis Apostolis licet. Ergo mihi & Barnabæ licet.
units.tr: Next he applies this liberty of his: first, to food and drink, which he could freely use if anyone could (verse 4); second, to contracting marriage and enjoying its benefits, which he proves from the example of the other apostles (verse 5); third, to abstaining from manual labour, and consequently to claiming maintenance from the churches. He proves this right of his by seven arguments. The first argument is from the example of the other apostles and ministers: the other apostles are allowed it; therefore I and Barnabas are allowed it.

units.la: Verf. 7. Quis militat propriis stipendiis unquam? quis plantat vineam, & de fructu ejus non edit? aut quis pascit gregem, & de lacte gregis non edit?
units.tr: Verse 7. Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Or who feeds a flock and does not eat of the flock's milk?

units.la: Arg. 2. A jure Gentium, in exemplo triplici propositum, militum, vinitorum, & pastorum; Milites, vinitores, & pastores pecudum, alluntur ex fructu laborum, in munere cuique suo. Ergo & nos Ministri Euangelii ali debemus ex fructu laborum nostrorum in Euangelio.
units.tr: Argument 2. From the law of nations, set out in a threefold example: soldiers, vinedressers and shepherds of flocks are fed from the fruit of their labours, each in the office that is his. Therefore we ministers of the Gospel too ought to be fed from the fruit of our labours in the Gospel.

units.la: Verf. 8. Num secundum hominem hæc dico? nonne etiam Lex hæc dicit?
units.tr: Verse 8. Do I say these things as a man? Does not the Law also say the same?

units.la: Verf. 9. Nam in Mosis Lege scriptum est, Non obligabis os bovi trituranti, num boves curæ sunt Deo?
units.tr: Verse 9. For it is written in the Law of Moses, You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain. Is it oxen that God cares for?

units.la: Verf. 10. An hoc propter nos omnino dicit? propter nos enim hoc scriptum est, nam sub spe debet is qui arat, arare: & qui triturat sub spe, spei suæ particeps esse.
units.tr: Verse 10. Or does he say this altogether on our account? For it was written on our account, because he who ploughs ought to plough in hope, and he who threshes in hope should share in his hope.

units.la: Arg. 3. A testimonio legis, de pabulo bovi triturant dando: quod ostendit dictum esse, in gratiam omnium laborantium in aliorum usum, potissimum in ministerio. Bos triturans alitur ex frumento quod pedibus excutit: Ergo omnes laborantes, arantes, triturantes, & per consequens laborantes in Euangelio, ali debent ex fructu laborum suorum. Nam si qui arat, & triturat sub spe præmii, particeps est sperati præmii, quidni etiam laborantes in Euangelio participes sint fructus laborum suorum?
units.tr: Argument 3. From the testimony of the Law concerning giving fodder to the ox that treads out the grain. This shows that it was said for the benefit of all who labour for the use of others, especially in the ministry. The ox that treads out the grain is fed from the wheat which it shakes out with its feet. Therefore all who labour, who plough and thresh, ought to be fed from the fruit of their labours, and consequently those who labour in the Gospel. For if he who ploughs and threshes in hope of reward shares in the reward hoped for, why should not those who labour in the Gospel share in the fruit of their labours?

units.la: Verf. 11. Si nos vobis spiritualia seminavimus, magnum est si nos vestra carnalia messuerimus.
units.tr: Verse 11. If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great thing if we reap your material things?

units.la: Arg. 4. A regula justitiæ; Si nos ministravimus vobis spiritualia, vicem vix rependitis cum nobis ministratis temporalia.
units.tr: Argument 4. From the rule of justice: if we have ministered spiritual things to you, you hardly repay us with a return when you minister temporal things to us.

units.la: Vers. 12. Si alii sui in vos juris sunt compotes, an non potius nos? atqui non usi sumus jure isto quod nobis licebat: sed omnia tegimus, ne interrumpamus Euangelium Christi.
units.tr: Verse 12. If others have the right over you, do not we rather? But we have not used this right which was ours; but we bear all things, lest we hinder the Gospel of Christ.

units.la: Arg. 5. A pari exemplo doctorum, qui Corinthi tum prædicabant, quorum exemplum in jure allegat, sed in facto negat se secutum, ut Euangelii commodum promoveret, Doctores illi vestri vestris sumptibus aluntur. Ergo æquum est ut nos quoque alamur, etiamsi decretum sit jure nostro non uti.
units.tr: Argument 5. From the parallel example of the teachers who were then preaching at Corinth. He cites their example as regards right, but says that he did not follow it in fact, so as to advance the benefit of the Gospel. Those teachers of yours are supported at your expense. Therefore it is fair that we too should be supported, even though it has been decided not to use our right.

units.la: Vers. 13 An nescitis eos qui sacris operantur, ea quæ ex sacrario sunt edere? & qui altari assident, cum altari participare.
units.tr: Verse 13. Do you not know that those who serve at the sacred things eat of the things from the temple, and those who wait at the altar share in the altar?

units.la: Arg. 6. Ab exemplo Levitarum, quibus pro ministerio dabatur alimonia, & sacrificiorum portio: vivebant ex altari Levitæ, Ergo ex Euangelio vivere debemus nos Ministri Euangelii.
units.tr: Argument 6. From the example of the Levites, to whom food and a portion of the sacrifices were given for their ministry. The Levites lived from the altar. Therefore we ministers of the Gospel ought to live from the Gospel.

units.la: Vers. 14. Ita & Dominus constituit iis qui Euangelium annuntiant? ut ex Euangelio vivant.
units.tr: Verse 14. So also the Lord ordained for those who proclaim the Gospel that they should live from the Gospel.

units.la: Arg 7. Christus mandatum dedit de sustinendis, ab Ecclesia Euangelii Ministris: Ergo ex Euangelio vivere debemus.
units.tr: Argument 7. Christ gave the command that the ministers of the Gospel should be sustained by the Church. Therefore we ought to live from the Gospel.

units.la: Vers. 15 Ego tamen nullo horum usus sum: Neque vero hæc scripsi ut ita fiat in me, nam bonum est mihi mori potius quam ut gloriationem meam aliquis inanem reddat.
units.tr: Verse 15. Yet I have used none of these things. Nor have I written these things so that it should be done in my case; for it is better for me to die than that anyone should make my boasting empty.

units.la: Jus suum asseruit; Jam moderationem suam, & abstinentiam à libertatis prædictæ usu proponit, Primum in stipendii negotio, & simul constans propositum suum de abstinendo in futuro ostendit: à quo proposito, priusquam cum detrimento Euangelii divertatur, inedia mori malle se dicit; cujus rationem reddit à fine, ut gloriari posset adversus calumniantes, qui dicerent forte Apostolum stipendii causa docere.
units.tr: He has asserted his right; now he sets forth his moderation and abstinence from the use of the said liberty. First, in the matter of maintenance, and at the same time he shows his firm purpose of abstaining in future. From this purpose he says he would rather die of hunger than turn aside from it at the cost of the Gospel. He gives the reason for this from the end in view: so that he might have something to boast of against slanderers, who might perhaps say that the apostle preached for the sake of pay.

units.la: Vers. 16 Etenim si euangelizem, non est quod glorier: necessitas enim mihi incumbit. Væ autem mihi est nisi euangelizem.
units.tr: Verse 16. For if I preach the Gospel, I have nothing to boast of; for necessity is laid upon me. Woe is me if I do not preach the Gospel.

units.la: Exponit gloriationem hanc non esse in mera Euangelii prædicatione, quia ad eam, necessitate officii & mandati, & metu iræ Dei nisi prædicaret, adigebatur.
units.tr: He explains that this boasting does not lie in the mere preaching of the Gospel, because by the necessity of his office and command, and by fear of the wrath of God if he did not preach, he was driven to it.

units.la: Vers. 17 Nam si volens hoc faciam, mercedem habeo: sin invitus, dispensatio credita est mihi. Prædicatio (inquit) mea, si voluntaria fuerit, mercedem habitura est, sin invita vero, à me tamen esset obeunda, propter dispensationem mihi impositam ex Dei mandato, eaque sine gloria voluntariæ meæ prædicationis futura esset, si invitus prædicarem, sicut illis accidit, qui non ex amore Dei, & studio convertendarum animarum, sed turpis lucri vel ambitionis suæ gratia, ministerium exercent.
units.tr: Verse 17. For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, a stewardship has been entrusted to me. My preaching, he says, if it were voluntary, would have a reward; but if it were unwilling, I would still have to discharge it, because of the stewardship laid upon me by God's command. And that would be without the glory of my voluntary preaching, if I preached unwillingly, as happens to those who exercise the ministry not from love of God and zeal for converting souls, but for the sake of shameful gain or their own ambition.

units.la: Vers. 18. Quæ igitur mihi est merces? ut evangelizando gratuitum constituam Evangelium Christi, ut ne abutar jure meo in Evangelio.
units.tr: Verse 18. What then is my reward? That in preaching the Gospel I may offer it free of charge, so that I do not abuse my right in the Gospel.

units.la: Nunc vero pro mercede abstinentiæ seu stipendii loco, dicit se habere gloriandi materiam, adversus calumniatores, quod ministraverint Evangelium Corinthiis, sine ipsorum sumptibus; Cui subnectit rationem aliam, ne si stipendium exegisset illic, ubi calumniatores insidias struebant ipsius famæ, quasi lucri causa prædicaret, tunc abusus fuisset sua libertate.
units.tr: Now, instead of a reward for abstinence or a stipend, he says that he has matter for boasting against the slanderers, because he ministered the Gospel to the Corinthians without any expense to them. To this he adds another reason: if he had claimed a stipend there, where the slanderers were laying snares for his good name, as if he preached for the sake of gain, he would then have abused his liberty.

units.la: Vers. 19. Nam quamvis liber sim ab omnibus, omnibus meipsum servum feci, ut plures lucrifaciam.
units.tr: Verse 19. For although I am free from all, I have made myself a slave to all, so that I might win more.

units.la: Libertatis suæ moderationem extendit ad totum genus rerum mediarum, in quibus non sibi, sed aliis servivit, ut eos lucrifaceret.
units.tr: He extends the moderation of his liberty to the whole class of indifferent things, in which he served not himself but others, so that he might win them.

units.la: Vers. 20. Et factus sum Judæis ut Judæus, ut Judæos lucri facerem: iis qui sub Lege sunt, ut si esset sub Lege, ut eos qui sub Lege sunt lucrifacerem.
units.tr: Verse 20. And I became to the Jews as a Jew, so that I might win the Jews; to those who are under the Law, as one under the Law, so that I might win those who are under the Law.

units.la: Id explicat particulatim in tribus; Primum, Quod Judæis, ceremoniali jugo, (ut illi putabant) ligatis se accommodaverit, ceremonias Moysaicas, pro loco & tempore observans, ut res requirebat, quasi suisset sub jugo ceremoniarum. Idque faciebat ex sententia Synodi Hierosolymitanæ, quæ Judæis sub jugo natis, ex quibus fuit Apostolus, liberum usum Ceremoniarum, ad tempus relinquebat: Gentibus vero minime, Act. 21, 21, 25.
units.tr: He explains this in three particulars. First, that he accommodated himself to the Jews, who were bound under the yoke of ceremonies (as they supposed), observing the Mosaic ceremonies according to place and time, as the situation required, as though he himself were under the yoke of ceremonies. He did this in accordance with the decision of the Synod of Jerusalem, which left the free use of the ceremonies, for a time, to the Jews born under the yoke, from whom the Apostle came, but not to the Gentiles at all: Acts 21:21, 25.

units.la: Vers. 21. Exlegibus ut exlex, (non tamen ut exlex Deo, sed sublex Christo) ut lucrifacerem exleges.
units.tr: Verse 21. To those without law I became as one without law (not indeed being without law toward God, but under the law toward Christ), that I might gain those without law.

units.la: Secundum est, quod gentibus quæ sine illa lege erant, se accommodans à ceremoniis abstinuerit, ut à lege solutus; Legem exponit interim se intelligere non moralem, seu dilectionis, quæ est Dei & Christi perpetua Lex, à qua non potuit solvi, sed Legem ceremonialem à qua reipsa solvebatur, ut libere in commodum Euangelii ceremoniis uteretur, vel abstineret.
units.tr: Second, that accommodating himself to the Gentiles, who were without that law, he abstained from the ceremonies as one released from the law. Meanwhile he explains that by "law" he understands not the moral law, that is, the law of love, which is the perpetual law of God and of Christ and from which he could not be released, but the ceremonial law, from which in fact he was released, so that he might use or abstain from the ceremonies freely for the advancement of the gospel.

units.la: Verf. 22 Factus sum infirmis ut infirmus, ut infirmos lucrifacerem : omnibus factus sum omnia, ut omnino aliquos servarem.
units.tr: Verse 22. To the weak I became as weak, that I might gain the weak. I have become all things to all men, that by all means I might save some.

units.la: Tertium, Quod dubitantibus de libertate se accommodaverit, abstinens scilicet à licitis, sicut illi abstinebant: Denique in omnibus rebus mediis, se omnibus accommodans, tres ob causas: Prima, ut lucrifaceret quam posset plurimos, vel saltem aliquos.
units.tr: Third, that he accommodated himself to those who doubted about liberty, abstaining, namely, from things lawful, just as they abstained; and finally, in all indifferent matters, he accommodated himself to everyone, for three reasons. The first was that he might gain as many as possible, or at least some.

units.la: Verf. 23. Hoc autem facio propter Euangelium, ut consors ejus fiam.
units.tr: Verse 23. And this I do for the gospel's sake, that I may be partaker thereof with you.

units.la: Secunda causa, Ut Euangelii doctrina melius audiret apud omnes, per ipsius moderationem. Tertia causa, ut serviens Euangelii commodis, ipse servaretur, particeps factus Euangelii cum aliis credentibus.
units.tr: The second reason was that the doctrine of the gospel might be heard more readily by all, through his own moderation. The third reason was that, serving the advantage of the gospel, he himself might be preserved, made a partaker of the gospel together with the other believers.

units.la: Verf. 24. An ignoratis eos qui in stadio currunt, omnes quidem currere, sed unum accipere praemium? sic currite ut comprehendatis.
units.tr: Verse 24. Know you not that they which run in a race all run, but one receives the prize? So run that you may obtain.

units.la: Hactenus exemplum suum propositi, tanquam antecedens argumenti, sequitur exempli vis, seu consequens, seu conclusio hortatoria, scilicet, ut Corinthii, temperantiae studeant, & ne ita indulgeant gulae, ut Idolothyta comedant, cum scandalo: Hunc in finem currendum illis in stadio Christiano ostendit, in quo currentes secundum DEI leges omnes (non unus tantum ut in ipsorum ludis usu veniebat,) coronandi erant.
units.tr: Hitherto he has set forth his own example as the antecedent of the argument; there follows the force of the example, that is, its consequent or hortatory conclusion: namely, that the Corinthians should strive for temperance, and not indulge their appetite so far as to eat meat offered to idols, to the offence of others. To this end he shows them that they must run in the Christian stadium, in which all who run according to the laws of God (not only one, as happened in their games) are to be crowned.

units.la: Verf. 25. Porro quisquis certat, in omnibus est continens. Illi quidem itaque ut corruptibilem coronam accipiant, sunt continentes: nos autem, ut incorruptam.
units.tr: Verse 25. Furthermore, every man that strives for mastery is temperate in all things. Now they indeed do it to receive a corruptible crown, are temperate; but we an incorruptible one.

units.la: Et quomodo istud fiat ostendit, nempe, si exemplo certantium in ludis illis nobilibus, (sive cursu, sive pugillatu, &c.) prope Corinthum celebrari solitis, gulae & voluptatibus non indulserint, sed in omnibus continentes fuerint, omnia tolerantes, quibus corona victrix obtineri poterat. In ludis Isthmicis seu Corinthiacis, Cursores & athletae solebant temperantissima victus ratione servata, ad certamina se praeparare, sicut nunc parantur equi ad currendum: victores in his ludis, lauro vel hedera coronabantur, vel simile aliquod praemium reportabant: Similiter Apostolus vult Christianos, moderatissime uti rebus hujus seculi, & ab omnibus, quæ cursum Christianum remorari, pugnamve impedire possent abstinere, idque ut incorruptibilem, id est, æternam coronam, (in Cælo repositam iis qui bene certaverint, & cursum consummaverint,) assequantur: Argumenta hortationis adjicit tria: Argumentum primum: Quia nobilior corona, quam corruptibilis illa ludentium in gymnasticis illis ludis vobis athletis Christianis expectanda est, Ergo & vos etiam sic currite ut comprehendatis.
units.tr: And he shows how this is to be done, namely, if, following the example of those competing in those noble games (whether the race, or boxing, etc.) customarily celebrated near Corinth, they did not indulge in gluttony and pleasures, but were temperate in all things, enduring everything by which the victor's crown could be obtained. In the Isthmian or Corinthian games, runners and athletes were accustomed, keeping the strictest regimen of diet, to prepare themselves for the contests, just as horses are now prepared for racing. Victors in these games were crowned with laurel or ivy, or received some similar prize. Likewise the Apostle wants Christians to use the things of this age most moderately, and to abstain from everything that could hinder the Christian course or impede the fight, so that they may obtain the incorruptible crown, that is, the eternal one, laid up in heaven for those who have fought well and finished the course. He adds three arguments for this exhortation. The first argument: because the crown is more noble than the corruptible one awaited by those who compete in those gymnastic games, therefore you Christian athletes also run in such a way that you may obtain it.

units.la: Verf. 26. Ego igitur ita curro, ut non in incertum: ita pugilem ago ut non aerem cædens.
units.tr: Verse 26. I therefore so run, not as uncertainly; so fight I, not as one that beats the air.

units.la: Verf. 27. Sed contundo corpus meum, & in servitutem redigo: ne quo modo, quum aliis prædicarim, ipse rejectaneus fiam.
units.tr: Verse 27. But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection, lest by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should become rejected.

units.la: Arg. 2. Ab exemplo sui ipsius currentis, & pugilem agentis, & adversarium ferientis, certò, & serió: Ego corpus peccati seu veterem hominem & carnis appetitus serió contundo ut mactentur, & ut serviat corpus proprie dictum Spiritui meo disciplinæ spiritualis vi cogo. Idem ergo & vos facite. Sic enim Apostolus nutrivit corpus proprie dictum, ut laboribus, vigiliis, & jejuniis in officio ipsum continuerit, ne adversus Spiritum lasciviret; corpus vero peccati (quantum poterat) destruebat.
units.tr: Second argument: from his own example, as one who runs, fights as a boxer, and strikes his adversary, certainly and in earnest: I earnestly bruise the body of sin, that is, the old man and the appetites of the flesh, so that they may be put to death; and I compel the body properly so called to serve my spirit by the force of spiritual discipline. Therefore you do the same. For so the Apostle nourished the body properly so called, while keeping it in duty by labours, watchings and fastings, lest it grow wanton against the Spirit; but the body of sin he destroyed as far as he could.

units.la: Ne quo ] Arg. 3. A fine, Ego contundo corpus peccati, seu veterem hominem, ne si aliter viverem, quam præcipio aliis vivendum, rejectaneus essem, seu ex numero Sanctorum tanquam hypocrita expungendus essem. Ergo idem vos facite quod ego, & in eundem finem.
units.tr: "Lest by any means": third argument, from the end. I bruise the body of sin, or the old man, lest, if I lived otherwise than I command others to live, I should be rejected, or struck from the number of the saints as a hypocrite. Therefore you do the same thing as I do, and to the same end.

units.la: Non opponit hic Apostolus Reprobum electo, sed probato, nam sicut Scriptura vocat reprobum argentum, quod verum & genuinum non est, & probatum quod syncerum: Sic Apostolus reprobum, seu rejectaneum vocat, qui professioni non respondet, qui sincerus non est, vel qui talem se experientiâ non ostendit, qualem esse oportebat. Si fingeremus eum hic reprobum absolute sumere, nihil attendendum nobis esset, præter connexionis necessitatem inter vitam profanam (si præsupponatur perpetuata in finem) & reprobationem; nam quicunque in peccatis moritur reprobus demonstratur. Absurdum enim est, & scriptis Apostoli nostri minime consentaneum, affirmare, quod Apostolus de electione sua dubitaverit, vel mutabile existimaverit decretum electionis suæ: Contra enim quia persuasum habebat, se & electum & regenitum fuisse, perfuasionis suæ documentum, & demonstrationem dare statuebat in vitæ sanctitate, studiose
units.tr: Here the Apostle does not oppose "reprobate" to "elect" but to "approved." For just as Scripture calls reprobate silver that which is not true and genuine, and approved that which is sincere, so the Apostle calls reprobate, or rejected, one who does not answer to his profession, who is not sincere, or who does not show by his experience that he is such as he ought to be. If we were to take "reprobate" here in an absolute sense, we would have to consider nothing but the necessary connection between a profane life (if it be presupposed to continue to the end) and reprobation; for whoever dies in sins is shown to be reprobate. For it is absurd, and by no means consistent with the writings of our Apostle, to affirm that the Apostle doubted his own election, or thought the decree of his election mutable. On the contrary, since he was persuaded that he had been both elected and regenerated, he resolved to give proof and demonstration of his persuasion in the holiness of his life, carefully

units.la: [illegible, ~8 letters] diosè cavens ne malè vivendo, vel hypocriseos signa in se ostenderet; nedum reprobationis.
units.tr: [illegible, about 8 letters] carefully taking care not to show in himself, by living badly, the signs of hypocrisy, much less of reprobation.

units.la: Caput decimum.
units.tr: Chapter 10.
