units.tr: Verse 16. And if the ear should say, "Because I am not an eye, I am not of the body," is it therefore not of the body?

units.la: Arg. 10. Cum ratio corporis requirat necessariò pluralitatem membrorum, & per consequens diversitatem, sequetur infima officia in minimis donis tam esle de corpore, quam excellentissima officia & dona: Et quod si se excluderent, non minus stolide facerent, quam si pes manum se negans, vel auris se oculum negans, propterea concluderet se non esse de corpore. Ergo propter diversitatem donorum, non debet esse inter vos dissensio.
units.tr: Argument 10. Since the nature of a body necessarily requires a plurality of members, and therefore a diversity of them, it follows that the lowliest offices and the least gifts are just as much part of the body as the most excellent offices and gifts. And if these lesser members were to exclude themselves, they would act no less foolishly than if a foot refused to be a hand, or an ear refused to be an eye, and therefore concluded that it was not part of the body. Therefore, because of the diversity of gifts, there ought to be no dissension among you.

units.la: Vers. 17 Si totum corpus oculus, ubi auditus? si totum auditus, ubi odoratus.
units.tr: Verse 17. If the whole body were an eye, where would the hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would the smelling be?

units.la: Vers. 18. Nunc autem Deus collocavit membra, singula sigillatim in corpore sicut voluit.
units.tr: Verse 18. But now God has set the members, each one of them, in the body as he pleased.

units.la: Vers. 19 Quod si essent omnia unum membrum, ubi corpus?
units.tr: Verse 19. If they were all one member, where would the body be?

units.la: Vers. 20. Nunc verò multa quidem membra sunt, unum ve- to corpus.
units.tr: Verse 20. But now there are indeed many members, yet one body.

units.la: Arg. II. Sicut si totum corpus esset unum membrum, sequerentur tria incommoda: Primò, excluderentur reliqua membra, & sensus nobiliores, verf. 17. Secundò, mutatio fieret contra DeI sapientem dispensationem, qui aliter de multiplicitate membrorum statuit, verf. 18. Tertiò, Mutatio fieret contra corporis organici naturam: nam corpus ipsum organicum tolleretur, verf. 19. Quia Deus corpus organicum fecit unum, ex pluralitate membrorum, verf. 20. Sic in functionibus Ecclesiasticis, si una esset functio, sequerentur tria incommoda. 1. tollerentur reliquæ functiones: 2. everteretur Dei dispensatio: 3. Ecclesia ipsa organica destrueretur, quæ nunc ex variis officiis, in unum corpus coagmentatis consistit: Colenda ergo concordia.
units.tr: Argument 11. If the whole body were one member, three inconveniences would follow. First, the remaining members and the nobler senses would be excluded (verse 17). Second, a change would be made against God's wise arrangement, who has decided otherwise about the multiplicity of members (verse 18). Third, a change would be made against the nature of the organic body, for the organic body itself would be taken away (verse 19). Because God made the organic body one out of a plurality of members (verse 20), so too in ecclesiastical functions, if there were only one function, three inconveniences would follow: (1) the remaining functions would be taken away; (2) God's arrangement would be overturned; (3) the Church itself, as an organic body, would be destroyed, which now consists of various offices joined into one body. Concord, therefore, is to be cultivated.

units.la: Verf. 21. Non potest autem oculus dicere manui, Non est mihi opus te: aut rursum caput pedibus, Non est mihi vobis opus.
units.tr: Verse 21. But the eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you; or again the head to the feet, I have no need of you.

units.la: Verf. 22. Imò multo potius, quæ videntur membra corporis infirmissima esse, necessaria sunt.
units.tr: Verse 22. On the contrary, much rather those members of the body which seem to be the weakest are necessary.

units.la: Arg. 12. Sicut in corpore Physico, membra superiora & excellentiora, non possunt inferioribus carere, inferiora autem & debiliora sunt maximè necessaria, ideoque inter se amicitiam colunt: sic in functionibus Ecclesiasticis se res habet: Idcirco concorditer conspirare debent.
units.tr: Argument 12. As in the physical body the higher and more excellent members cannot do without the lower ones, and the lower and weaker ones are most necessary, and therefore they cultivate friendship with one another, so it is with ecclesiastical functions. Therefore they ought to agree together in harmony.

units.la: Verf, 23. Et quæ putamus membra corporis maximè esse inhonesta, honesta, iis honorem ampliorem circumponimus: & quæ sunt in nobis indecora, copiosiorem decorem habent.
units.tr: Verse 23. And those members of the body which we think to be least honourable, we clothe with greater honour; and those which are unseemly in us have a fuller comeliness.

units.la: Verf. 24. Nam quæ sunt in nobis decora, iis decore non est opus: sed Deus simul temperavit corpus, ei cui deerat, copiosiore tributo honor{ }.
units.tr: Verse 24. For those which are comely in us have no need of comeliness; but God has so tempered the body that to that which lacked he gave more abundant honour.

units.la: Arg. 13. Sicut in corpore Physico, ut fiat concordia, honorantur maxime quæ infirmiora sunt membra, & necessaria ex Dei voluntate: sic debet fieri, in functionibus Ecclesiasticis. Ergo in Diaconis potius quam Pastoribus eligendis, curandum ut cæteris paribus, lautioris fortunæ homines, qui infimum hoc officium ornent, eligantur.
units.tr: Argument 13. As in the physical body, so that there may be concord, those members which are weaker and necessary by the will of God are most honoured, so it ought to be in ecclesiastical functions. Therefore, in choosing deacons rather than ministers, care should be taken that, other things being equal, men of more comfortable circumstances, who will adorn this lowest office, are chosen.

units.la: Verf. 25. Ut ne sit dissidium in corpore, sed membra idem curent alia pro aliis.
units.tr: Verse 25. So that there may be no division in the body, but that the members may have the same care one for another.

units.la: Arg. 14. Sicut rueret ex schismate corpus Physicum, si membra inter se contenderent, & se mutuo non curarent: sic in functionibus Ecclesiasticis; concordia ergo colenda.
units.tr: Argument 14. Just as the physical body would fall apart through schism if the members contended among themselves and did not care for one another, so it is in ecclesiastical functions; concord, therefore, is to be cultivated.

units.la: Verf. 26. Itaque sive patitur unum membrum, simul dolent omnia membra: sive honore afficitur unum membrum, simul gaudent omnia membra.
units.tr: Verse 26. So whether one member suffers, all the members suffer together; or if one member is honoured, all the members rejoice together.

units.la: Verf. 27. Vos autem estis corpus CHRISTI, & membra ex parte.
units.tr: Verse 27. Now you are the body of CHRIST, and members in part.

units.la: Arg. 15. Sicut inter membra corporis superiora & inferiora, συμπάθεια est in dolore & gaudio, ita inter Ecclesiæ Gubernatores, seu Ministros Ecclesiasticos esse debet: Ergo & summa concordia: Rationem reddit, quia vos, inquit, estis corpus Christi & membra speciatim: id est; qui ut membra toti corpori Ecclesiæ & vobis invicem consentire debetis; Et hic habetur apodosis communis totius similitudinis, à corpore sumptæ à versu 12. usque ad 27.
units.tr: Argument 15. As among the members of the body, higher and lower alike, there is συμπάθεια [sympatheia] in suffering and rejoicing, so there ought to be among the governors of the Church, or ecclesiastical ministers; therefore also the highest concord. He gives the reason: because you, he says, are the body of Christ and members in particular. That is, as members you ought to agree with the whole body of the Church and with one another. And here is stated the common application of the whole comparison, taken from the body, from verse 12 to verse 27.

units.la: Verf. 28. Et alios quidem constituit Deus in Ecclesia, primum Apostolos, deinde Prophetas, tertio doctores, deinde constituit potestates, deinde dona sanationum, opitulationes, gubernationes, genera linguarum.
units.tr: Verse 28. And God has set some in the Church: first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then powers, then gifts of healings, helps, governments, kinds of tongues.

units.la: Jam recenset ordine ministros Ecclesiæ, quantum ad æmulationem & invidiam inter Corinthios compescendam sufficiebat: Apostolorum & Pauli nominatim authoritas, ab argutulis & disertis, apud Corinthios (ut ex secunda Epistola liquet) Doctoribus, labefactabatur. Idcirco Apostolorum dignitatem primo loco asserit, & Apostolos primùm à Deo constitutos, quia illi omnibus ecclesiis fundamentum jaciunt. De Euangelistis & Prophetis extraordinariis, vel non erat inter illos quæstio, vel assertâ dignitate ministrorum Euangelii extra ordinem, in officii Apostolici vindicatione, etiam de authoritate & dignitate Euangelistarum & prophetarum extraordinariorum (quorum ministerium erat ex æquo omnibus Ecclesiis commune, & Apostolorum ulibus adjunctum) satis constabat.
units.tr: Now he enumerates in order the ministers of the Church, as far as was sufficient to restrain emulation and envy among the Corinthians. The authority of the apostles and of Paul himself was being undermined among the Corinthians by clever and eloquent teachers (as is clear from the second Epistle). Therefore he first asserts the dignity of the apostles, and says that apostles were first established by God, because they lay the foundation for all churches. Concerning the evangelists and the extraordinary prophets, there was either no question among them, or, since the dignity of the extraordinary ministers of the gospel was asserted in the vindication of the apostolic office, it was sufficiently established also concerning the authority and dignity of the evangelists and extraordinary prophets (whose ministry was equally common to all churches and was joined to the apostles' work).

units.la: Secundo loco statuit Prophetas, quo nomine, ut posteà patebit Cap. 14. intelligit Pastores, qui doctrinam ad usum pro concione applicabant, quorum donum erat sermo sapientiæ, supra verf. 8. Tertio loco nominat Doctores, qui licet eloquentia & prudentia ad applicandam doctrinam, in omnes usus Ecclesiæ, non pollebant, habebant tamen sermonem Scientiæ, ut possent generalem doctrinam ad captum Ecclesiæ applicare. Hæ sunt functiones, quæ in Verbo & Doctrina occupantur, ideoque insigniores. Quarto loco ponit eos, qui in primitiva Ecclesia, ad confirmationem fidei auditorum, donabantur potestate miraculorum multa genera, & signa seu portenta, edendi in amplissima mensura. Quinto loco ponit eos qui morbos miraculose sanare poterant, in quibus donum miraculorum coarctabatur magis, & ad hanc unam speciem restringebatur. Post hæc sexto loco dona & officia ordinaria nominat, nempe opitulationes, seu functiones Diaconorum, quorum opera, de stipendiis Ministrorum & Sanctorum necessitatibus prospiciebatur, & Ecclesiæ publicæ facultates dispensabantur, quod officium licet infimum videri posset, in honore non parvo videtur fuisse tamen, & viris non infimis impositum, sed viris, & spectatæ fidei, & potentioribus, seu lautioris fortunæ, secundum verf. 22, 23, 24. Idque propter necessarium ejus usum, quia absque functionis hujus opitulatione, opus Ministerii multum impediretur; nisi enim opitulationes seu Diaconi sint, qui stipendii colligendi curam in se suscipiant, ut Ministri liberius operi Domini vacare possint, necesse est ut Ministri cum Levitis, Nehem. 13. quibus portio designata non dabatur, ad agrum & negotia sua fugiant, vel secularibus negotiis, immo & contentionibus forensibus de stipendio debito impliciti, perdant laborandi in Domini vinea zelum; vel laborum suorum fructum. Post hos (nisi forte quia de hisofficiis inferioribus, non erat contentio, de ordine amplius plius non est solicitus Apostolus, nominat gubernationes seu presbyteros gubernantes, qui mores Populi observant, & disciplinæ præsides cum pastoribus & doctoribus in Senatu Ecclesiastico scandalis tollendis invigilant: Ultimo loco ponit donum linguarum, scilicet solitarium, quo quis vel loquebatur quæ interpretari non poterat, idiomate populo cognito, vel interpretari poterat, loqui verò ignota lingua non poterat: quod donum, quia admirationem præ aliis donis excitabat, videtur affectatum fuisse à Corinthiis aliis, & materiam fuisse gloriationis aliis.
units.tr: In second place he sets prophets, by which name, as will later be clear in Chapter 14, he understands ministers who applied doctrine to practical use in preaching, and whose gift was the word of wisdom, see above verse 8. In third place he names teachers, who, although they did not excel in eloquence and prudence for applying doctrine to every use of the Church, nevertheless had the word of knowledge, so that they could apply general doctrine to the understanding of the Church. These are the functions which are occupied with the Word and doctrine, and therefore more distinguished. In fourth place he sets those who in the primitive Church were endowed, for the confirmation of the faith of the hearers, with the power of many kinds of miracles, and of performing signs or portents in the greatest measure. In fifth place he sets those who could heal diseases miraculously, in which the gift of miracles was more restricted and confined to this one kind. After these, in sixth place, he names the ordinary gifts and offices, namely helps, or the functions of deacons, by whose work provision was made for the stipends of ministers and the needs of the saints, and the public resources of the Church were distributed. Although this office might seem the lowest, it nevertheless seems to have been of no small honour, and was laid not on the lowest men but on men of proven faith and of more influence, or of more comfortable fortune, according to verses 22, 23, 24. And this was because of its necessary use, since without the help of this function the work of the ministry would be much hindered. For unless there were helps or deacons who took upon themselves the care of collecting the stipends, so that ministers could devote themselves more freely to the work of the Lord, it would be necessary for the ministers, like the Levites (Nehem. 13.), to whom no designated portion was given, to flee to their fields and private affairs, or to be entangled in secular business, or even in lawsuits over the stipend due to them, and so to lose their zeal for labouring in the Lord's vineyard, or the fruit of their labours. After these (unless perhaps because there was no dispute about these lower offices, the apostle is no longer concerned about the order), he names governments, or elders who govern, who observe the morals of the people and preside over discipline, watching with the pastors and teachers in the ecclesiastical senate to remove scandals. Last of all he sets the gift of tongues, namely the solitary kind, by which someone either spoke in a language he could not interpret, known to the people, or could interpret but could not speak in an unknown tongue. This gift, because it aroused admiration above the other gifts, seems to have been coveted by some of the Corinthians, and to have been a matter of boasting for others.

units.la: Verf. 29: Num omnes, Apostoli? num omnes, Prophetæ? num omnes, doctores? num omnes lunt potestates?
units.tr: Verse 29. Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Are all powers?

units.la: Verf. 30. Num omnes donum habent sanationum? num omnes linguis loquuntur? num omnes interpretantur?
units.tr: Verse 30. Do all have the gift of healings? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret?

units.la: Quibus omnibus recitatis, vellicat & sugillat acriter æmulationem & invidiam inferiorum, quasi vellent omnes, dona eminentissima, & functiones excellentiores habere, quod à ratione alienissimum erat, prout interrogationes, repetitæ ad pungendas ipsorum conscientias ostendunt.
units.tr: When all these have been recited, he sharply lashes and rebukes the emulation and envy of the lesser members, as if they all wished to have the most eminent gifts and the more excellent offices. That is most alien to reason, as the questions, repeated to prick their consciences, show.

units.la: Verf. 31. Sed ambite dona potiora. Et porrò iter ad excellentiam vobis indicabo.
units.tr: Verse 31. But covet the better gifts. And moreover I will show you a way to excellence.

units.la: Arg. 16. Suasionis, ne fit æmultatio prava de donis: æmulatio melius collocari poflet, ambiendo dona excellentissima, nempe salvifica, seu quæ salutem comitari solent, quale donum est imprimis Charitas Christiana; per quam fides salvifica efficax est (de qua dicturum le pollicetur:) Ergo æmulatio prava de donis & officiis Ecclesiasticis, seu spiritualibus cavenda est.
units.tr: Argument 16, of persuasion: let there be no evil emulation about the gifts. Emulation would be better directed by coveting the most excellent gifts, namely those that bring salvation or are usually accompanied by it, of which the chief is Christian charity, through which saving faith is effective (he promises to speak of this). Therefore evil emulation concerning the ecclesiastical and spiritual gifts and offices is to be avoided.

units.la: Caput
units.tr: Chapter

units.la: Iam illam excellentiorem, de qua versu ultimo superi-oris Capitis dixit, ostendit esse viam Charitatis, & probat Charitatis donum dignißimum esse, quod supra omnia alia affeƫent, argumentis quatuor.
units.tr: Now he shows that the more excellent way, which he mentioned in the last verse of the previous chapter, is the way of charity, and he proves by four arguments that the gift of charity is more worthy than all the others.

units.la: Vers. 1. Si linguis hominum loquar, & angelorum, charitatem autem non habeam, factus sum as resonans, aut symbalum tinniens.
units.tr: Verse 1. If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not charity, I am become sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.

units.la: Argumentum primum. Dona quæ vos ambitis nihil sunt sine Charitate; quinque autem dona enumerat, quibus Charitatem præfert: Primum, Donum linguarum in summo gradu, (quale esset, si quis omnibus linguis loqui posset, aut qualis esset Angelorum loquendi ratio, si linguis loquerentur) quod sine Charitate ad salutem nihil faceret, plus quam inutilis sonus.
units.tr: First argument. The gifts you covet are nothing without charity. He lists five gifts, which he sets below charity. The first is the gift of tongues at its highest degree (such as one would have if he could speak in all languages, or the manner of speaking of the angels if they spoke in tongues). Without charity this would do nothing for salvation, being no more than an empty sound.

units.la: Vers. 2. Et si habeam prophetiam, & noverim mysteria omnia, omnemque scientiam: & si habeam totam fidem, adeò ut montes transferam, charitatem autem non habeam, nihil sum.
units.tr: Verse 2. And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, but have not charity, I am nothing.

units.la: Donum secundum, est donum Prophetiæ in summo gradu cum scientia & sapientia conjunctum, quod ad salutem Prophetæ sine Charitate nihil faceret: Donum 3. est fidei miraculosæ in summo gradu, ad operandum quæ maximè impossibilia sunt, quod si daretur, etiam nihil esset sine Charitate.
units.tr: The second gift is the gift of prophecy at its highest degree, joined with knowledge and wisdom; without charity it would do nothing for the salvation of the prophet. The third gift is miraculous faith at its highest degree, for accomplishing what is most impossible; even if it were given, it would be nothing without charity.

units.la: Vers. 3. Et si insumam alendis egenis omnes facultates meas, & si tradam corpus meum ut comburar, charitatem autem non habeam, hoc nihil mihi prodest.
units.tr: Verse 3. And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, but have not charity, it profits me nothing.

units.la: Donum 4. Est liberalitas in pauperes summa, quæ fingi potest: Donum 5. fortitudo Martyrij maxima, quantam quis imaginari poterit, quæ omnia sine charitate, nihil prodessent ad salutem: Ergo charitas donum est dignißimum quod affectetis.
units.tr: The fourth gift is the greatest liberality towards the poor that can be imagined; the fifth is the greatest courage of martyrdom that anyone can conceive. Without charity all these would profit nothing for salvation. Therefore charity is the most worthy gift that you should desire.

units.la: Vers. 4. Charitas patiens est, comis est: Charitas non invidet: charitas non agit perperam, non inflatur.
units.tr: Verse 4. Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up.

units.la: Arg. 2. A proprietatibus seu effectis Charitatis eximiis, qualia quindecim enumerat: 1. Charitas patiens est: 2. Et benigne agit: 3. Non invidiosa est: 4. Non est proterva: 5. Non inflatur arroganti opinione bonorum suorum.
units.tr: Second argument, from the outstanding properties or effects of charity, of which he lists fifteen: 1. Charity suffers long. 2. And acts kindly. 3. Is not envious. 4. Is not forward. 5. Is not puffed up with the arrogant opinion of its own good qualities.

units.la: Verf. 5. Non agit indecore, non quærit quæ sua sunt, non irritatur, non cogitat malum.
units.tr: Verse 5. Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil.

units.la: 6. Neque dehonestat se neque proximum, indecorè agendo: 7. Non injuste studet suis privatis commodis, sed in aliorum bonum oculos intentos tenet: 8. Non irritatur ut malum malo rependat: 9. Non est injuste suspicax.
units.tr: 6. It dishonours neither itself nor its neighbour by acting unseemly. 7. It does not unjustly pursue its private advantages, but keeps its eyes fixed on the good of others. 8. It is not provoked to repay evil with evil. 9. It is not unjustly suspicious.

units.la: Vers. 6. Non gaudet injustitia, gratulatur autem veritati:
units.tr: Verse 6. Rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth.

units.la: Vers. 7. Omnia suffert, omnia credit, omnia sperat, omnia sustinet.
units.tr: Verse 7. Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.

units.la: 10. Non lætatur cum fit injustitia: 11. Lætatur successibus aliorum bonis: 12. Fortiter perfert labores & difficultates in officio fungendo: 13. Optima quæque de omnibus credit, quantum patitur veritas: 14. Optima quæque sperat de omnium emendatione, quantum patitur prudentia. 15. Omnes aliorum infirmitates tolerat: Ergo charitas donum dignissimum est quod affectetis.
units.tr: 10. It does not rejoice when injustice occurs. 11. It rejoices in the good successes of others. 12. It bears bravely the labours and difficulties of discharging its office. 13. It believes the best of everyone, as far as truth allows. 14. It hopes the best of everyone's amendment, as far as prudence allows. 15. It tolerates the weaknesses of all others. Therefore charity is the most worthy gift that you should desire.

units.la: Vers. 8. Charitas nunquam excidit: & prophetia vero abolebuntur: & lingua cessabunt: & cognitio abolebitur.
units.tr: Verse 8. Charity never faileth; but whether there be prophecies, they shall fail; whether there be tongues, they shall cease; whether there be knowledge, it shall vanish away.

units.la: Arg. 3. Charitas nunquam excidit: Ergo excellentissima est & dignissima quam affectetis: Hanc proprietatem illustrat comparatione cum aliis donis: primò cum prophetia & linguis; quæ, quia non erit earum usus in vita sequenti, ut media, amplius non necessaria cessabunt: 2. Charitatem cum ipsa cognitione comparat, & præfert eam cognitioni, quia cognitio abolenda est, ea scilicet mediata, seu ratio cognoscendi, qualis nunc habetur per libros, per auditionem, meditationem, &c. Ergo, Charitas excellentissimum donum est quod affectetis.
units.tr: Third argument. Charity never fails; therefore it is the most excellent and most worthy gift that you should desire. He illustrates this property by comparison with the other gifts. First with prophecy and tongues: since there will be no use of them in the life to come, they will cease as means that are no longer necessary. Second, he compares charity with knowledge itself and prefers charity to it, because knowledge must be abolished, namely that mediated knowledge, or the way of knowing that now obtains through books, hearing, meditation, and so on. Therefore charity is the most excellent gift that you should desire.

units.la: Vers. 9. Ex parte enim cognoscimus, & ex parte prophetamus: Quod probat, Quia cognitio jam est ex parte & imperfecta, non tantum respectu mensuræ, sic enim etiam charitas est imperfecta, sed potissimùm ratione modi cognoscendi, per media scilicet, quod genus cognoscendi quia mediatum est, imperfectum est.
units.tr: Verse 9. For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. He proves this, because knowledge is now partial and imperfect, not only with respect to its measure (for charity too is imperfect in that sense), but chiefly by reason of its mode of knowing, namely through means. Since this kind of knowing is mediated, it is imperfect.

units.la: Vers. 10 Postquam autem advenerit quod perfectum est, tunc quod ex parte est, abolebitur.
units.tr: Verse 10. But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away.

units.la: Hic modus cognoscendi, mediatè scilicet, plane abolebitur, cum venerit cognitionis modus perfectus, nempe immediatus: Charitas autem licet quo ad mensuram imperfecta sit, quo ad modum diligendi tamen perfecta est, nam immediate fertur in Deum, & idcirco hic modus diligendi nunquam abolebitur, sed augebitur potius.
units.tr: This mode of knowing, namely mediated knowing, will be plainly abolished when the perfect mode of knowing, namely immediate knowing, has come. Charity, however, although imperfect as to measure, is perfect as to the mode of loving, for it is directed immediately to God; therefore this mode of loving will never be abolished, but will rather be increased.

units.la: Vers. 11. Quum essem infans, ut infans loquebar, ut infans cogitabam, ut infans sentiebam: postquam autem factus sum vir, abolevi quae infantis erant.
units.tr: Verse 11. When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things.

units.la: Ostendit praesentem cognitionis modum abolendum esse, per similitudinem abolitionis ludicrorum & puerilium, cum adoleverit aliquis in virum.
units.tr: He shows that the present mode of knowing must be abolished, by the likeness of the abolition of childish and puerile things when someone grows up into a man.

units.la: Vers. 12. Cernimus enim nunc per speculum, & per aenigma: tunc autem coram cernemus: nunc cognosco ex parte, tunc vero cognoscam prout edoctus fuero.
units.tr: Verse 12. For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.

units.la: Alia similitudine idem ostendit, comparans praesentem cognoscendi modum, cognitioni per speculum & aenigma, qui modus mediatus est, cognitionem vero futuram, cognitioni per aspectum immediatum, quo aliquis cognoscit intuitive, quia in vita futura mens nostra a Deo immediate illustrabitur, & nos immediate videbimus seu cognoscemus Deum.
units.tr: By another likeness he shows the same thing, comparing the present mode of knowing with knowledge through a mirror and a riddle, which is a mediated mode, and comparing future knowledge with knowledge by immediate sight, by which one knows intuitively. For in the future life our mind will be illumined immediately by God, and we shall see or know God immediately.

units.la: Vers. 13. Nunc vero manet fides, spes, charitas, tria haec: maxima autem harum, charitas.
units.tr: Verse 13. And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.

units.la: Arg. 4. Charitas fide & spe (quae gratiae sunt salvificae, & dona <bl>excellentior est</bl>: Ergo dignissima: Quia charitas nunquam excidet, sed manebit etiam in vita futura, cum fides & spes jam functae officio cessabunt: interim meminerimus aliis respectibus, fidem potiorem esse charitate, quia fides est causa dilectionis: Gal. 5. 6. Fide justificamur & pacem habemus erga Deum, Rom. 5. 1. Et per fidem habitat Christus in cordibus nostris, qui charitatem in nobis operatur: Ephes. 3. 17. Sed Apostolus concordiam, & Ecclesiae aedificationem respiciens, charitatem Jure extollit, quantum ad propositum suum attinet: sciebat etiam neminem ampliandae charitati Christianae studere posse, quin simul studeat augendae fidei, quae dilectionis causa est.
units.tr: Fourth argument. Charity is more excellent than faith and hope (which are saving graces and gifts); therefore it is most worthy. Because charity will never fail, but will remain even in the life to come, when faith and hope, having discharged their office, will cease. Meanwhile let us remember that, in other respects, faith is greater than charity, because faith is the cause of love: Gal. 5:6, By faith we are justified and have peace towards God; Rom. 5:1; And through faith Christ dwells in our hearts, who works charity in us: Eph. 3:17. But the Apostle, looking to concord and the edification of the Church, rightly extols charity, so far as his purpose requires. He also knew that no one can strive to increase Christian charity without at the same time striving to increase faith, which is the cause of love.

units.la: Caput decimumquartum.
units.tr: Chapter 14.

units.la: Pergit, de donis spiritualibus, & eorum recto Usu agere.
units.tr: He continues to speak of spiritual gifts and their right use.

units.la: Capitis dua sunt partes: In priori præfert donum prophetiæ dono linguarum, ad verf. 26. In altera præcepta dat de εὐταξίᾳ observanda in Cœtibus Ecclesiasticis, ad finem.
units.tr: The chapter has two parts. In the first, he puts the gift of prophecy before the gift of tongues, down to verse 26. In the second, he gives precepts on observing good order [εὐταξίᾳ] in ecclesiastical assemblies, to the end.

units.la: Verf. 1. Sectamini charitatem, ambite autem spiritualia, magis tamen ut prophetetis.
units.tr: Verse 1. Follow after charity, and desire spiritual gifts, but rather that you may prophesy.

units.la: Probavit superiori Capite Charitatem donum esse excellentissimum, Initio hujus capitis infert pro conclusione hortationem, ut eam affectent, & omnia tum dona tum officia spiritualia, in honore habeant: Sed quia dono linguarum superbiebant aliqui, & plerique præhoc dono, pastorale donum despiciebant, donum vero linguarum admirabantur nimium, Idcirco confert hæc inter se dona, & donum Prophetiæ seu exhortationis probat præstantius esse dono linguarum, ab interpretationis dono segregatum: Rationes reddit tredecim.
units.tr: In the previous chapter he proved that charity is the most excellent gift. At the beginning of this chapter he draws from it, as a conclusion, an exhortation that they should pursue it and hold in honour all gifts and spiritual offices, both gifts and duties. But since some were puffed up over the gift of tongues, and most admired that gift too much while despising the gift of pastoral teaching, he now compares these gifts with one another. He shows that the gift of prophecy, that is, of exhortation, is more excellent than the gift of tongues, which is separated from the gift of interpretation. He gives thirteen reasons.

units.la: Verf. 2. Nam qui loquitur lingua, non hominibus loquitur, sed Deo, nullus enim audit, spiritu vero loquitur mysteria.
units.tr: Verse 2. For he who speaks in a tongue does not speak to men, but to God, for no one hears; yet in the Spirit he speaks mysteries.

units.la: Verf. 3. Qui autem prophetat, hominibus loquitur ædificationem, & exhortationem, & consolationem.
units.tr: Verse 3. But he who prophesies speaks to men for edification, exhortation and consolation.

units.la: Prima ratio, Qui lingua ignota loquitur etiamsi ex dono Spiritus loquatur mysteria DEI, tamen sine fructu loquitur, quia à solo DEO intelligitur, & non ab hominibus: Propheta vero seu Pastor cognita lingua loquens, docet, hortatur, consolatur auditores, & sic cum fructu loquitur: Ergo præstantior est prophetia dono linguarum.
units.tr: First reason: he who speaks in an unknown tongue, even if by the gift of the Spirit he speaks the mysteries of God, nevertheless speaks without fruit, because he is understood by God alone and not by men. But the prophet, or pastor, speaking in a known tongue, teaches, exhorts and comforts his hearers, and so speaks with fruit. Therefore prophecy is more excellent than the gift of tongues.

units.la: Verf. 4. Qui loquitur lingua, seipsum ædificat: qui vero prophetat, Ecclesiam ædificat.
units.tr: Verse 4. He who speaks in a tongue edifies himself; but he who prophesies edifies the Church.

units.la: Ratio 2. Qui lingua ignota loquitur, nullum ædificat præter seipsum, Propheta vero totam Ecclesiam seu Cœtum: præstantior Ergo prophetia.
units.tr: Reason 2. He who speaks in an unknown tongue edifies no one but himself, but the prophet edifies the whole Church or assembly. Therefore prophecy is more excellent.

units.la: Verf. 5. Velim autem omnes vos loqui linguis, magis tamen ut prophetetis, major enim est qui prophetat quàm qui loquitur linguis nisi si interpretetur, ut Ecclesia œdificationem accipiat.
units.tr: Verse 5. I would have you all speak with tongues, but rather that you prophesy; for he who prophesies is greater than he who speaks with tongues, unless he interprets, so that the Church may receive edification.

units.la: Ut rectius intelligatur, ostendit se non derogare linguis, licet prophetam præferat loquenti lingua ignota.
units.tr: So that this may be understood more correctly, he shows that he does not disparage tongues, although he prefers the prophet to the one who speaks in an unknown language.

units.la: Verf. 6. Nunc verò, fratres, si veniam ad vos linguis loquens, quid vos juvabo, nisi vobis loquar aut per revelationem, aut per cognitionem, aut per prophetiam, aut per doctrinam.
units.tr: Verse 6. But now, brethren, if I come to you speaking in tongues, what shall I profit you, unless I speak to you by revelation, or by knowledge, or by prophecy, or by doctrine?

units.la: Ratio 3. A suo exemplo: Etiam ipsius Apostoli ministerium non esset ipsis profuturum, nisi per prophetiam extraordinariam, ex revelatione vel ex cognitione ordinariâ, lingua cognita ipsis loqueretur, vel prophetando seu hortando ut pastor, vel docendo ut doctor; Ergo inferius est donum linguarum dono prophetiæ.
units.tr: Reason 3. From his own example: even the Apostle's ministry would not benefit them unless he spoke to them, in a language they knew, by extraordinary prophecy, by revelation, or by ordinary knowledge, either prophesying or exhorting as a pastor, or teaching as a teacher. Therefore the gift of tongues is inferior to the gift of prophecy.

units.la: Verf. 7. At qui inanima quæ sonum edunt, sive tibia sit, sive cithara, nisi distinctionem tonis dederint, quomodo cognoscetur quid tibia canitur aut cithara.
units.tr: Verse 7. Even things without life that give a sound, whether a flute or a harp, unless they give a distinction in the notes, how shall it be known what is played on the flute or the harp?

units.la: Verf. 8. Etenim si incertum sonum tuba dederit, quis apparabitur ad bellum?
units.tr: Verse 8. For if the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who will prepare himself for battle?

units.la: Verf. 9. Ita & vos nisi per linguam bene significantem sermonem edideritis, quomodo intelligetur quod dicitur? eritis enim in aerem loquentes.
units.tr: Verse 9. So also you, unless you utter by the tongue speech that is easily understood, how will what is said be known? For you will be speaking into the air.

units.la: Ratio 4. Sicut tuba aut instrumentum aliud quodvis sive tactile, sive flatile, incondite sonans, inutilem & ingratum sonum edit, sic etiam lingua, non intellecta nihil præter sonum incertum & inutilem reddit: Prophetæ vero cognita lingua loquuntur in prophetia sua: Ergo inferius est donum linguarum, dono prophetiæ.
units.tr: Reason 4. Just as a trumpet, or any other instrument, whether struck or blown, sounding confusedly, makes a useless and unpleasant noise, so also a tongue not understood yields nothing but an uncertain and useless sound. But prophets speak in their prophecy in a known tongue. Therefore the gift of tongues is inferior to the gift of prophecy.

units.la: Verf. 10. Tot, prout inciderit, genera vocum sunt in mundo, & nihil est mutum
units.tr: Verse 10. There are, as it happens, so many kinds of voices in the world, and none of them is without meaning.

units.la: Ratio 5. Brutorum voces plurimæ sunt, quarum nulla adeò inarticulata est, quin certam animalis speciem audientibus repræsentet: Turpe est ergo ita prolituere donum Spiritus, ut non plus prosit, sed & minoris æstimetur, quam brutus aliquis balatus: Non sic in prophetia: Ergo inferius est donum linguarum dono prophetiæ.
units.tr: Reason 5. The voices of brute beasts are very many, and none of them is so inarticulate that it does not present to the hearers a definite kind of animal. It is shameful, then, for a gift of the Spirit to be displayed so that it not only benefits no one but is valued less than the bleating of some brute. It is not so with prophecy. Therefore the gift of tongues is inferior to the gift of prophecy.

units.la: Verf. 11. Nisi igitur sciero vim vocis, ero ei qui loquitur barbarus: & qui loquitur, apud me barbarus fuerit.
units.tr: Verse 11. Unless, then, I know the meaning of the voice, I shall be a barbarian to him who speaks, and he who speaks will be a barbarian to me.

units.la: Ratio 6. Quia loqui non intellecta, doctorem & auditores sibi invicem reddit ut barbaros, qui se mutuo non intelligunt: Ergo.
units.tr: Reason 6. Speaking in a language not understood makes the speaker and the hearers barbarians to one another, since they do not understand each other. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Verf. 12. Ita & vos quandoquidem Spiritus ambitis, ad aedificationem Ecclesiae quaerite ut excellatis.
units.tr: Verse 12. So also you, since you are zealous for spiritual gifts, seek to excel in order to edify the Church.

units.la: Verf. 13. Quapropter qui loquitur lingua, precetur ut interpretetur.
units.tr: Verse 13. Wherefore let him who speaks in a tongue pray that he may interpret.

units.la: Ex praedictis infert hortationem, ut prophetiae donum ad Ecclesiae bonum ambiant, In eumque finem, ut qui donum linguae incognitae habet, precetur, ut etiam habeat donum interpretandi illam linguam.
units.tr: From what has been said he draws the exhortation that they should desire the gift of prophecy for the good of the Church, and to this end, that whoever has the gift of an unknown tongue should pray that he may also have the gift of interpreting that language.

units.la: Verf. 14. Nam si precer lingua, Spiritus meus precatur, sed intelligentia mea est infructuosa.
units.tr: Verse 14. For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays, but my understanding is unfruitful.

units.la: Ratio 7. Si Deum alloquatur quisquam publice precando lingua ignota perperam facit, quia licet ipse orans intelligat, audientibus tamen & non intelligentibus infructuosus erit precantis intellectus; & multo magis perperam facit, qui publice homines alloquitur lingua non intellecta: Ergo inferius est donum linguarum dono prophetiae.
units.tr: Reason 7. If anyone addresses God in public prayer in an unknown tongue, he acts amiss, because although the one praying understands, the understanding of the prayer will be unfruitful for the hearers who do not understand. Much more does he act amiss who addresses men publicly in a language they do not understand. Therefore the gift of tongues is inferior to the gift of prophecy.

units.la: Verf. 15 Quid est igitur? precabor Spiritu, sed precabor etiam intelligentia: Psallam Spiritu, sed psallam etiam intelligentia.
units.tr: Verse 15. What is it then? I will pray with the Spirit, but I will pray also with the understanding; I will sing with the Spirit, but I will sing also with the understanding.

units.la: Hinc hortationem deducit, Quia ex his qui linguarum exoticarum dono instruebantur, alii miraculose differendi de mysteriis divinis facultate pollebant, alii facultate precandi valebant, alii linguis illis exoticis psallebant, alii denique gratiarum actiones concipiebant, & diversa erant haec dona & ad diversa; omnia haec ita exerceri jubet, ut ab audientibus intelligantur: nam si oret quis Spiritu seu ex Spiritus dono, quid proderit Ecclesiae, nisi oret etiam intelligentia, id est ita ut auditores intelligant.
units.tr: From this he draws an exhortation. Of those who were equipped with the gift of foreign tongues, some had the miraculous power of speaking about divine mysteries, some the power of praying, some sang in those foreign tongues, and others finally offered thanksgivings. These gifts were diverse and for different purposes. He orders that all of these be exercised in such a way that they are understood by the hearers. For if someone prays by the Spirit, or by the gift of the Spirit, what will it profit the Church unless he prays also with the understanding, that is, so that the hearers understand.

units.la: Verf. 16. Quandoquidem si benedixeris Spiritu, is qui implet locum idiotae, quomodo dicturus est Amen ad tuam gratiarum actionem? nam quid dicas nescit.
units.tr: Verse 16. For if you bless with the Spirit, how will he who fills the place of the unlearned say Amen to your thanksgiving? For he does not know what you say.

units.la: Hoc confirmat & addit rationem octavam ab incommodo: Quia quando aliquis per donum Spiritus benedicit, illi qui privatorum locum occupant in Ecclesia, id est, reliqui auditores in coetu non poterunt sua vota conjungere aut comprecari, vel Amen dicere, nisi cognita lingua loquatur, non sic in prophetia res se habet, ubi omnia, lingua cognita proferuntur: Ergo, &c.
units.tr: He confirms this and adds an eighth reason from inconvenience: when someone blesses by the gift of the Spirit, those who occupy the place of the laity in the Church, that is, the other hearers in the assembly, cannot join in or make their own prayers, or say Amen, unless he speaks in a known tongue. It is not so in prophecy, where everything is delivered in a known tongue. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Verf. 17. Nam tu quidem bene gratias agis, sed alius non edificatur.
units.tr: Verse 17. For you indeed give thanks well, but the other is not edified.

units.la: Causam reddit, Quia auditores in Ecclesia non intelligunt, nec aedificantur, etiam si id quod dicitur, excellentissimum sit.
units.tr: He gives the cause: the hearers in the Church do not understand, nor are they edified, even if what is said is most excellent.

units.la: Verf. 18. Gratias ago Deo meo, quod magis quam vos omnes linguis loquar.
units.tr: Verse 18. I thank my God that I speak in tongues more than you all.

units.la: Verf. 19. Sed in Ecclesia malim quinque verba ex intelligentia mea loqui, ut & alios instituam, quam decem millia verborum lingua.
units.tr: Verse 19. But in the Church I would rather speak five words with my understanding, so that I may also instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue.

units.la: Ratio 9. Ab exemplo suo, qui dono linguarum erat instructissimus, & tamen malebat paucissima verba proloqui, quae intelligerentur ab auditoribus, quam plurima in lingua populo incognita. Ergo praestantior est prophetia dono linguarum.
units.tr: Reason 9. From his own example: he who was most richly endowed with the gift of tongues nevertheless preferred to utter a very few words that the hearers could understand, rather than very many in a language unknown to the people. Therefore prophecy is more excellent than the gift of tongues.

units.la: Verf. 20. Fratres, ne estote pueri intelligentia: sed malitia pueri, intelligentia vero adulti estote.
units.tr: Verse 20. Brethren, do not be children in understanding, but be children in malice, and be mature in understanding.

units.la: Ratio 10. Praecepto vestita: Quod hic abusus doni linguarum exoticarum sine utilitate audientium, ut puerilis & stolida ostentatio, quum deceat eos pueros quidem agere, respectu innocentiae, non vero cognitionis.
units.tr: Reason 10, drawn from a precept: the abuse of the gift of foreign tongues, without benefit to the hearers, is a childish and foolish display. They ought to act as children in innocence, but not in knowledge.

units.la: Verf. 21. In Lege scriptum est, Propterea per diversa linguas homines, & alia labra loquar populo huic: & ita quoque me non audient, dicit Dominus.
units.tr: Verse 21. It is written in the Law: By men of other tongues and by other lips I will speak to this people, and even so they will not hear me, says the Lord.

units.la: Verf. 22. Linguae igitur sunt signum, non iis qui credunt, sed infidelibus: prophetia vero non infidelibus, sed credentibus.
units.tr: Verse 22. Tongues, therefore, are a sign, not for those who believe, but for unbelievers; but prophecy is not for unbelievers, but for believers.

units.la: Ratio 11. Ex Isaiae 28. 11. & Jer. 5. 15. Quia loqui linguis non intellectis in Ecclesia, pro comminatione poenae infidelitatis a Deo petitur, prophetia vero fidelibus aedificandis inservit: cessant igitur ex Ecclesia linguae non intellectae, & praeferatur prophetia.
units.tr: Reason 11. From Isaiah 28:11 and Jeremiah 5:15. Speaking in unknown tongues in the Church is demanded by God as a threat of punishment for unbelief, whereas prophecy serves to build up the faithful. Therefore unknown tongues cease in the Church, and prophecy is to be preferred.

units.la: Verf. 23. Itaque si eodem convenerit tota Ecclesia, & omnes linguis loquantur, ingrediantur autem idiotae vel infideles, nonne dicent vos furere.
units.tr: Verse 23. So if the whole Church comes together in one place and all speak in tongues, and unlearned or unbelieving people enter, will they not say that you are mad?

units.la: Ratio 12. A scandalo vitando: Infideles, vel privatae conditionis profecflores professores, alienabuntur à fide, dicentque & præconem & populum inlanire, literatur tempus publico cultui dicatum in sermonis incognitæ auditione: Ergo inferius est donum linguarum dono prophetiæ.
units.tr: Reason 12. To avoid giving offence: unbelievers, or those of private standing, will be alienated from the faith and will say that both the preacher and the people are mad, wasting the time set apart for public worship by listening to a speech they do not understand. Therefore the gift of tongues is inferior to the gift of prophecy.

units.la: Vers. 24 Sed si omnes prophetent, ingrediatur autem infidelis quispiam, aut idiota, arguitur ab omnibus, dijudicatur ab omnibus.
units.tr: Verse 24. But if all prophesy, and some unbeliever or unlearned person enters, he is convicted by all and judged by all.

units.la: Vers. 25. Et ita occulta cordis ejus manifesta fiunt, atque ita procidens in faciem, adorabit Deum, renuntians Deum verè in vobis esse.
units.tr: Verse 25. And so the secrets of his heart are made manifest, and so, falling on his face, he will worship God, declaring that God is truly among you.

units.la: Ratio 13. A speciali fructu, qui sequuturus erat, si missis linguis exoticis, omnes Prophetæ scilicet (nam Fideles omnes in Ecclesia esse Prophetas negavit, Cap. 12. vers. 29.) prophetaverint, id est, Prophetarum oracula, & doctrinam in ædificationem populi proposuerint; In hoc casu enim, si infidelis aliquis ingrediens, vel privatus Christianus ex auditoribus unus, audiat prophetantes, arguitur peccati, & condemnatur ex sententia Legis ab omnibus prophetantibus, & latentia in corde ipsius peccata ipsi aperiuntur, quæ ubi videt auditor, & simul DEI gratiam, in Evangelio patefactam à Prophetis observat; procidit in faciem, DEUM adorat, & serio testimonium dat de DEI præsentia cum Prophetis in Ecclesia: Ergo præstantior est Prophetia dono linguarum.
units.tr: Reason 13. From the special fruit that was to follow if, with foreign tongues set aside, all the prophets (for he denied that all the faithful in the Church are prophets, ch. 12, verse 29) prophesied, that is, set forth the oracles and teaching of the prophets for the edification of the people. For in this case, if some unbeliever entering, or some private Christian among the hearers, listens to those prophesying, he is convicted of sin and condemned by the sentence of the Law by all the prophesying, and the sins hidden in his heart are laid open to him. When the hearer sees this, and at the same time observes God's grace revealed in the Gospel by the prophets, he falls on his face, worships God, and gives serious witness to the presence of God with the prophets in the Church. Therefore prophecy is more excellent than the gift of tongues.

units.la: Secunda Pars.
units.tr: Second Part.

units.la: Vers. 26. Quid igitur est, fratres? quoties convenitis quisque vestrum canticum habet, doctrinam habet, linguam habet, revelationem habet, interpretationem habet: omnia ad ædificationem fiant.
units.tr: Verse 26. What then is it, brothers? Whenever you come together, each one of you has a psalm, has a teaching, has a tongue, has a revelation, has an interpretation. Let all things be done for edification.

units.la: Altera pars Capitis, in qua præcepta dat de εὐλαξία, septem: Primum est, ut si Spiritus suggesserit alicui ex Prophetis piam aliquam cantionem ad DEI laudem, vel doctrinam aliquam, vel linguæ exoticæ expressionem in usum Ecclesiæ, vel revelationem rei futuræ, aut mysterii non prius observati, vel interpretationem linguæ exoticæ, vel Scripturæ; præcipit ut exercitium horum omnium disponatur ad Ecclesiæ ædificationem, ut omnes abeant ex conventu auditiores quam accesserant.
units.tr: The second part of the chapter, in which he gives seven precepts concerning good order [εὐταξία]. The first is that if the Spirit inspires any of the prophets to a pious song in praise of God, or some teaching, or the utterance of a foreign tongue for the use of the Church, or a revelation of a future matter or of a mystery not previously noticed, or the interpretation of a foreign tongue or of Scripture, he commands that the exercise of all these be arranged for the building up of the Church, so that all depart from the gathering having been edified more than when they came.

units.la: Vers. 27. Sive lingua quis loquitur, fiat per binos, aut ad plurimum ternos, & vicissim: unus autem interpretetur.
units.tr: Verse 27. If anyone speaks in a tongue, let it be done by two, or at most three, and in turn, and let one interpret.

units.la: Vers. 28. Quod si non fit interpres, taceat in Ecclesia qui loquitur linguâ, sibiipsi verò loquatur & Deo.
units.tr: Verse 28. But if there is no interpreter, let the one who speaks in a tongue keep silent in the Church, and speak to himself and to God.

units.la: Præceptum 2. Ut ex iis qui linguarum dono instructi erant, in uno conventu non loquantur plures quam duo aut tres, idque ordine, alius post alium, & non nisi adesset interpres aliquis, qui exponeret dicta: alioqui silendum erat illis in Ecclesia.
units.tr: Precept 2. That of those who were endowed with the gift of tongues, no more than two or three should speak in one assembly, and this in order, one after another, and only if some interpreter was present to explain what was said; otherwise they were to keep silent in the Church.

units.la: Vers. 29. Prophetæ autem duo aut tres loquantur, & alii dijudicent.
units.tr: Verse 29. Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others judge.

units.la: Præceptum 3. Ut Prophetæ ordinarii, id est, Pastores loquantur in uno conventu, duo vel tres, de quorum doctrina reliqui Prophetæ judicent examinantes eam ad regulam Verbi.
units.tr: Precept 3. That the ordinary prophets, that is, the ministers, should speak in one assembly, two or three of them, and the remaining prophets should judge their teaching, examining it by the rule of the Word.

units.la: Vers. 30. Quod si quid alii patefactum fuerit assidenti, prior taceat.
units.tr: Verse 30. But if something is revealed to another who is sitting by, let the first be silent.

units.la: Præceptum 4. Si (ut illis temporibus usu venire poterat) aliquis alius Propheta Spiritu afflatus, extra ordinem audiri cupiebat, jubet ut prior taceat, ut tempus alteri concedatur, ad loquendum.
units.tr: Precept 4. If (as could happen in those times) some other prophet, inspired by the Spirit, wished to be heard out of turn, he orders that the first be silent, so that time to speak is granted to the other.

units.la: Vers. 31. Potestis enim sigillatim omnes prophetare, ut omnes discant, & omnes consolationem accipiant.
units.tr: Verse 31. For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all may receive comfort.

units.la: Rationes præcepti subjungit quinque: 1. Quia in tali casu plures, imo omnes Prophetæ audiri poterant (non hic intelligit promiscuè Fideles, sed Prophetas, & quidem Spiritu extra ordinem afflatos) in quo casu omnes audiendi erant, ordine tamen servato.
units.tr: He adds five reasons for the precept. 1. Because in such a case several, indeed all, the prophets could be heard (he does not here mean the faithful indiscriminately, but the prophets, and indeed those moved by the Spirit beyond the ordinary course), and in that case all were to be heard, yet with order preserved.

units.la: Ut omnes ] Ratio 2. Quia sic promoveri poterit cognitio, & consolatio Ecclesiæ, & ipsorum etiam Prophetarum, si plures per vices audiantur.
units.tr: So that all] Reason 2. Because in this way knowledge and the comfort of the Church, and of the prophets themselves too, can be advanced, if several are heard in turn.

units.la: Vers. 32. Et Spiritus prophetarum Prophetis subjiciuntur.
units.tr: Verse 32. And the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets.

units.la: Ratio 3. Quia Spiritus prophetarum examinandi & dijudicandi sunt à reliquis prophetis, qui de auditis postea ferre poterant sententiam, utrum quis tempestive alterum interpellaverit, & an verbo Dei consentaneum fuerit, quod ab eo prolatum est, ideoque non erat periculum si prior loquens cederet modestè interpellanti, & sic plures ordine loquerentur. Cum Prophetis defert judicium de Spiritu, seu doctrina quam Propheta à Spiritu profert, non excludit homines spirituales, id est, reliquos Ecclesiæ gubernatores, qui in spiritualibus cognoscendis ac dijudicandis eruditi sunt, quales debent esse omnes in Senatu Ecclesiastico: his enim, vers. 37. una cum Prophetis, seu Verbi Ministris præcipit, ut pro Ecclesiastica suâ autoritate agnoscant, & defendant itam doctrinam in Ecclesia sua, ut secundum eam de immorigeris judicent & statuant.
units.tr: Reason 3. Because the spirits of the prophets are to be examined and judged by the other prophets, who could afterwards pass sentence on what was heard, whether someone interrupted the other at the right time, and whether what was uttered by him agreed with the Word of God. Therefore there was no danger if the first speaker yielded modestly to the one interrupting, and so several would speak in order. In entrusting judgement on the spirit, or on the teaching which the prophet delivers by the Spirit, to the prophets, he does not exclude spiritual men, that is, the remaining governors of the Church, who are learned in discerning and judging spiritual matters, as all should be in the ecclesiastical senate. For to these, in verse 37, together with the prophets, or ministers of the Word, he commands that they acknowledge and defend such teaching in their Church by their ecclesiastical authority, so that according to it they may judge and decide concerning the disobedient.

units.la: Verf. 33. Non enim est seditionis author Deus, sed pacis, ut in omnibus Ecclesiis sanctorum.
units.tr: Verse 33. For God is not the author of confusion but of peace, as in all the churches of the saints.

units.la: Ratio 4. Quia alioqui oriretur tumultus, dum plures scilicet loquerentur, qui Deo odiosus est: Ordine ergo alius potest alium in Casu praedicto, loquatur. Ut in Ratio 5. Quia sic usu receptum est in omnibus Sanctorum Ecclesiis, & idcirco sic inter ipsos fieri debet, ut alius post alium ordine loquatur.
units.tr: Reason 4. Because otherwise a tumult would arise while several spoke at once, which is hateful to God. In the aforementioned case, then, one may speak after another in order. Let ... Reason 5. Because this is the custom received in all the churches of the saints, and therefore it ought to be done among you as well, so that one speaks after another in order.

units.la: Vers. 34. Mulieres vestrae in conventibus sileant: nec enim permissum est eis ut loquantur, sed imperatur ut subditae sint, sicut & Lex dicit.
units.tr: Verse 34. Let your women keep silent in the assemblies, for it is not permitted for them to speak, but they are commanded to be subject, as the Law also says.

units.la: Praeceptum 5. Quo prohibet ne mulieres loquantur in Ecclesia, hoc est, doceant publice vel quaestiones agitent, quia subjectio naturalis sexus foeminei Verbo Dei sancita, Gen. 3. 16. illud exigit.
units.tr: Precept 5. By which he forbids women to speak in the Church, that is, to teach publicly or to raise questions, because the natural subjection of the female sex, sanctioned by the Word of God, Gen. 3:16, requires this.

units.la: Vers 35. Quod si quid discere volunt, domi suos viros interrogent, nam turpe est mulieribus in conventu loqui.
units.tr: Verse 35. But if they wish to learn anything, let them ask their own husbands at home, for it is shameful for women to speak in the assembly.

units.la: Ut occurrat objectioni, domi jubet eas discere privatim à maritis suis, vel aliunde, quod publice sciscitari voluissent, addita alia ratione praecepti, quod sit indecorum mulierem loqui in Ecclesia.
units.tr: To meet an objection, he bids them learn at home, in private, from their husbands or elsewhere, whatever they would have wished to ask publicly, adding another reason for the precept: that it is unseemly for a woman to speak in the Church.

units.la: Vers. 36. An à vobis sermo Dei profectus est: an ad vos solos devenit?
units.tr: Verse 36. Did the word of God go out from you? Or did it come to you alone?

units.la: Quia aegre laturos sciebat sciolos, se cancellis horum praeceptorum concludi, cohibet responsaturos quatuor modis: 1. Ostendendo, quod illi qui his praeceptis se non subjiciunt, ita se gerant, quasi se Apostolis aequarent, à quibus prodiit Christi voluntas in mundum: 2. Quod ita se gerant quasi soli sint Christiani, ad quos missi sint Apostoli, & ad quos solos judicium de ordine & decoro pertineat.
units.tr: Since he knew that the conceited would take it badly to be shut in by the bars of these precepts, he restrains those who would reply in four ways: (1) by showing that those who do not submit to these precepts behave as if they were equal to the Apostles, from whom Christ's will went out into the world; (2) by showing that they behave as if they alone were Christians, to whom the Apostles were sent, and to whom alone judgement about order and decorum belongs.

units.la: Vers 37. Si quis videtur Propheta esse, aut spiritualis, agnoscat quae scribo vobis, esse Domini mandata.
units.tr: Verse 37. If anyone seems to be a prophet, or spiritual, let him acknowledge that what I write to you is the commandment of the Lord.

units.la: Tertiò affirmando haec praecepta esse Domini, & jubendo, ut non solum illi qui in Ecclesia verè Prophetae sunt, vel verè spirituales, id est, qui tales sunt, & officio & merito, agnoscant ea divina esse, sed etiam ut qui propter officium & dona quaedam Spiritus, sibi videntur esse. Prophetae, vel spirituales, seu eruditi in spiritualibus discernendis, vel qui pro talibus habentur in Ecclesia, propter præfecturam suam in rebus spiritualibus curandis, agrolcant secundùm officii sui rationem scilicet, hæc præcepta pro Divinis, & per consequens, ut in contemptores horum præceptorum, judicium Ecclesiasticum exerceant, ut in eos qui Deo sunt rebelles. Quod autem nomine spiritualium insigniebantur Ecclesiasticæ disciplinæ præfecti patet, Galat. 6. 1. & 1 Cor. 12. 1. ubi Ecclesiastica omnia officia & dona, nomine spiritualium comprehendit.
units.tr: Thirdly, by affirming that these precepts are the Lord's, and by commanding that not only those who are truly prophets in the Church, or truly spiritual (that is, those who are such both by office and by merit), acknowledge them to be divine, but also that those who seem to themselves to be prophets, or spiritual, by reason of their office and certain gifts of the Spirit, or who are held to be such in the Church because of their charge over spiritual affairs, or who are learned in discerning spiritual matters, acknowledge them, in accordance with the nature of their office, as divine precepts, and consequently that they exercise ecclesiastical judgement against the despisers of these precepts, as against those who are rebels against God. That the rulers of ecclesiastical discipline were distinguished by the name of spiritual men is clear from Galatians 6:1 and 1 Corinthians 12:1, where he comprehends all ecclesiastical offices and gifts under the name of spiritual things.

units.la: Vers. 38, Qui vero ignarus est, ignarus esto.
units.tr: Verse 38: "But if anyone is ignorant, let him be ignorant."

units.la: Quartò, Contemnendo judicium affectatæ ignorantiæ, & post præceptum jam datum Ecclesiæ Gubernatoribus, ut illi agnoscant hæc præcepta Divina, relegando ignaros, & contemptores horum præceptorum, ad Disciplinæ Moderatores; ut secundum judicium Apostoli, & Ecclesiæ suæ judicantis secundum regulam Apostoli, suo periculo ignorent, vel contemnant hæc præcepta.
units.tr: Fourthly, by condemning the judgment of wilful ignorance: once the rule has been given to the governors of the Church that they should acknowledge these divine precepts, those who are ignorant and those who despise these precepts are to be referred to the moderators of discipline, so that, according to the judgment of the Apostle, and of the Church judging according to the Apostle's rule, they may remain ignorant of or despise these precepts at their own peril.

units.la: Vers. 39. Itaque fratres, hoc ambite, ut prophetetis, & loquι linguis ne prohibetis.
units.tr: Verse 39: "Therefore, brethren, covet to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking with tongues."

units.la: Præceptum 6. Usum ostendens superioris doctrinæ: ut omni ratione foveant, & ambiant donum Prophetiæ, sed citra contemptum aut neglectum linguarum.
units.tr: Precept 6. Showing the use of the preceding teaching: that they should by every means foster and covet the gift of prophecy, but without contempt or neglect of tongues.

units.la: Vers. 40. Omnia verò decenter & ordine fiant.
units.tr: Verse 40: "But let all things be done decently and in order."

units.la: Præceptum 7. Ut decorum observetur in personis ad publicum conventum Ecclesiæ accedentibus, & in rebus ad publicum cultum necessariis: ut omnia cum gravitate, & modestia, sine superstitione, & sordibus peragantur; & partes cultus Divini inter se ita ordinentur, & temporibus suis disponantur, ut Dei gloriæ, & ædificationi Ecclesiæ inserviant maximè.
units.tr: Precept 7. That decorum be observed in the persons who come to the public assembly of the Church, and in the things necessary for public worship: that everything be carried out with gravity and modesty, without superstition and slovenliness; and that the parts of divine worship be so ordered among themselves and arranged in their proper times that they may serve most of all the glory of God and the edification of the Church.

units.la: Caput decimumquintum.
units.tr: Chapter 15.

units.la: Articulus nonus de Resurrectione.
units.tr: The ninth article, on the Resurrection.

units.la: Onus Epistolæ articulus, de Resurrectionis doctrinæ confirmanda, quam aliqui inter ipsos in dubium vocabant.
units.tr: The burden of this article of the Epistle is to confirm the doctrine of the resurrection, which some among them were calling into doubt.

units.la: Capitis tres sunt partes. In prima confirmat Corinthios in fide Evangelii, & nominatim articuli de Resurrectione Christi, ad vers. 12. In secunda, confirmat resurrectionis corporum nostrorum doctrinam, ad vers. 35. In tertia refutat objectiones adversus hanc fidem, ut fideles confirmati constantiores sint, ad finem.
units.tr: The chapter has three parts. In the first, he confirms the Corinthians in the faith of the Gospel, and in particular the article of Christ's resurrection, up to verse 12. In the second, he confirms the doctrine of the resurrection of our bodies, from verse 35. In the third, he refutes the objections against this faith, so that the faithful, once confirmed, may be more steadfast, to the end.

units.la: Verf. 1. Ecce porro vobis declaro, fratres, Euangelium quod euangelizavi vobis, & quod accepistis, in quo etiam statis.
units.tr: Verse 1. Moreover, brethren, I declare to you the gospel which I preached to you, which you also received, and in which you stand.

units.la: Quod ad primam attinet, Quia per resurrectionis negationem Euangelium totum subverti sciebat, primo confirmat Corinthios in fide Euangelii in genere, tacitè monens, ne ab illo deficiant, adhibitis quinque argumentis: Argumentum primum. Ego vobis Euangelium constanter praedicavi: Ergo firmiter tenete meam doctrinam.
units.tr: As to the first part: since he knew that by denying the resurrection the whole Gospel would be overthrown, he first confirms the Corinthians in the faith of the Gospel in general, tacitly warning them not to fall away, and he uses five arguments. The first argument: I preached the Gospel to you constantly; therefore hold firmly to my teaching.

units.la: Verf. 2. Per quod etiam, si retinetis quo sermone vobis euangelizaverim, servamini: nisi si frustrà credidistis.
units.tr: Verse 2. By which also you are saved, if you hold fast the word which I preached to you, unless you believed in vain.

units.la: Arg. 4. Per hoc Euangelium salutem estis consequuturi, nisi fides vestra fuerit hypocritica: Tenete ergo
units.tr: Argument 4. Through this Gospel you are to obtain salvation, unless your faith was hypocritical; therefore hold fast.

units.la: Verf. 3 Tradidi enim vobis in primis quod & acceperam, Christum videlicet mortuum esse pro peccatis nostris, secundùm Scripturas:
units.tr: Verse 3. For I delivered to you first of all what I also received, namely that Christ died for our sins, according to the Scriptures.

units.la: Verf. 4. Et sepultum fuisse, & excitatum tertio die, secundùm Scripturas:
units.tr: Verse 4. And that he was buried, and that he was raised on the third day, according to the Scriptures.

units.la: Arg. 5. Confirmans etiam praecedens: Quia quod praedicatum est, & à vobis creditum de CHRISTI morte & resurrectione, &c. Divinitus revelatum est: Tenete ergo.
units.tr: Argument 5. Confirming what goes before: because what was preached and believed by you concerning the death and resurrection of Christ, etc., was revealed by God; therefore hold fast.

units.la: Verf. 5. Et visum fuisse Cephae, deinde duodecim illis.
units.tr: Verse 5. And that he was seen by Cephas, then by the twelve.

units.la: Verf. 6. Postea visus est amplius quam quingentis fratribus semel, ex quibus plerique manent usque adhuc, quidam autem obdormierunt.
units.tr: Verse 6. Afterwards he was seen by more than five hundred brethren at once, of whom many remain until now, but some have fallen asleep.

units.la: Verf. 7. Postea visus est Iacobo, deinde Apostolis omnibus.
units.tr: Verse 7. Afterwards he was seen by James, then by all the apostles.

units.la: 2. Testimonium est Petri Apostoli qui redivivum Christum viderat.
units.tr: 2. There is the testimony of Peter the apostle, who had seen Christ risen again.

units.la: 3. Testimonium est duodecim Apostolorum simul congregatorum.
units.tr: 3. There is the testimony of the twelve apostles gathered together.

units.la: 4. Testimonium est quingentorum Fratrum, quorum multi tum vivebant.
units.tr: 4. There is the testimony of the five hundred brethren, many of whom were still living at that time.

units.la: 5. Testimonium est Jacobi.
units.tr: 5. There is the testimony of James.

units.la: 6. Testimonium est Apostolorum omnium, qui secunda vice omnes simul Christum redivivum viderunt.
units.tr: 6. There is the testimony of all the apostles, who together saw Christ risen again on a second occasion.

units.la: Vers. 8. Ultimo vero omnium, velut abortivo visus est etiam mihi.
units.tr: Verse 8. And last of all, as to one born out of due time, he was seen by me also.

units.la: Vers. 9. Ego enim sum minimus Apostolorum, qui non sum dignus vocari Apostolus, propterea quòd persequutus sum Ecclesiam Dei.
units.tr: Verse 9. For I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God.

units.la: Vers. 10. Sed gratia Dei sum id quod sum: & gratia ejus erga me non fuit inanis, sed amplius quam illi omnes laboravi: non ego tamen, sed gratia Dei quæ mecum est.
units.tr: Verse 10. But by the grace of God I am what I am; and his grace toward me was not in vain, but I laboured more abundantly than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which is with me.

units.la: 7. Est ipsius Pauli Testimonium, quod etiamsi ab aliquibus elevari posse videbat, propterea quod post Christi obitum, & abitum in Cœlum, subitò quasi fœtus abortivus ipse extrusus esset in lucem Euangelii, simul etiam, quod propter vitam præcedentem in naturæ statu, minimus Apostolorum censeri merito posset: gratiæ tamen in se collatæ respectu, ostendit suum Testimonium comparari posse cum Testimonio reliquorum: quia gratia Dei tantò clarius erga ipsum quam erga alios Apostolos manifestabatur, quanto ipsius conversio, reliquorum Apostolorum conversione mirabilior fuit, & quanto gratia Dei, operatione in ipso, & per ipsum, & ipsius amplissimos labores in Euangelio testatior, & illustrior erat illâ, quæ in aliis Apostolis se exeruit, effectorum respectu: Hujus excellentiæ laudem totam, in solidum tribuit Dei gratiæ, sibi verò nullam gloriæ partem.
units.tr: 7. There is the testimony of Paul himself. Although he saw that some might cast it aside, because after Christ's death and ascension into heaven he had been suddenly thrust forth into the light of the Gospel like an abortive birth, and also because on account of his earlier life, lived in the state of nature, he could rightly be counted the least of the apostles, nevertheless, with respect to the grace bestowed on him, he shows that his testimony can be compared with that of the rest. For the grace of God was made manifest in him all the more clearly than in the other apostles, in proportion as his conversion was more wonderful than the conversion of the other apostles, and as the grace of God, working in him and through him, and the very great labours he undertook in the Gospel, was more evident and more striking than that grace which showed itself in the other apostles, in respect of the results. He ascribes the whole praise of this excellence, wholly and entirely, to the grace of God, and to himself no share of glory at all.

units.la: Vers. 11, Et ego igitur & illi ita prædicamus, & ita credidistis.
units.tr: Verse 11. Whether therefore it be I or they, so we preach, and so you believed.

units.la: Testimonium 8. Est consensus Pauli & reliquorum Apostolorum in prædicatione resurrectionis Christi, quibus omnibus testimoniis, suam fidem pro Sigillo appenderant Corinthii.
units.tr: Testimony 8. There is the agreement of Paul and the other apostles in preaching the resurrection of Christ; by all these testimonies the Corinthians had set their faith as a seal.

units.la: Secunda Pars.
units.tr: The second part.

units.la: Verf. 12. Quod si Christus prædicatur ex mortuis excitatus esse, quomodo dicunt quidam inter vos non esse resurrectionem mortuorum?
units.tr: Verse 12. Now if Christ is preached, that he rose from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?

units.la: Secunda pars Capitis, in qua probat doctrinam resurrectionis ipsis prius traditam, veram esse, & dogma negantium resurrectionem esse falsum. Thesis proponitur hoc versu: argumenta ad probationem affert 15. quorum septem priora ducuntur ab absurdo septuplici.
units.tr: The second part of the chapter, in which he proves that the doctrine of the resurrection, previously delivered to them, is true, and that the teaching of those who deny the resurrection is false. The thesis is set out in this verse; he brings fifteen arguments to prove it, of which the first seven are drawn from a sevenfold absurdity.

units.la: Verf. 13. Nam si resurrectio mortuorum non est, Christus quoque non est excitatus.
units.tr: Verse 13. For if there is no resurrection of the dead, neither is Christ risen.

units.la: Primum argumentum, & absurdum primum; Ex ipsorum dogmate sequitur Christum non resurrexisse. Falsum ergo est: nam inter Christum caput & fideles qui membra sunt, ea est connexio, ut negata resurrectione horum, negetur etiam illius resurrectio, & contra.
units.tr: The first argument, and the first absurdity: it follows from their doctrine that Christ has not risen. This is false, for between Christ the head and the faithful, who are the members, there is such a connection that if the resurrection of the members is denied, the resurrection of the head is denied too, and conversely.

units.la: Verf. 14. Quod si Christus non est excitatus, inanis videlicet est prædicatio nostra, inanis autem est etiam fides vestra.
units.tr: Verse 14. And if Christ is not risen, then our preaching is vain, and your faith is also vain.

units.la: 2. Absurdum & Arg. 2. per consequens, Sequitur prædicationem Apostolorum inanem esse, ex ipsorum dogmate: falsum est ergo.
units.tr: 2. Absurdity and argument 2: by consequence, it follows from their doctrine that the preaching of the apostles is empty. This is false, therefore their doctrine is false.

units.la: Vana ] Absurdum 3. & Arg. 3. sequeretur (inquit) fidem vestram inanem esse, Ergo falsum est dogma: nisi enim Christus resurrexisset, neque justitia, neque vita æterna, neque ulla alia resurrectionis Christi effecta, expectanda essent.
units.tr: Vain: the third absurdity and argument 3. It would follow, he says, that your faith is empty; therefore the doctrine is false. For unless Christ had risen, neither righteousness, nor eternal life, nor any other effect of Christ's resurrection could be expected.

units.la: Verf. 15. Reperimur autem etiam falsi testes Dei, quoniam de Deo testificati sumus, eum excitasse Christum: quem non excitavit, si videlicet mortui non excitantur.
units.tr: Verse 15. Yea, and we are found false witnesses of God, because we have testified of God that he raised up Christ, whom he did not raise up, if so be that the dead rise not.

units.la: Absurdum 4. & Arg. 4. Sequeretur nos falsum testimonium dixisse, non tantum de Christo, sed etiam de Deo suscitatore Christi, qui suscitator Christi non est, si resurrectio non est. Ergo falsum est eorum dogma.
units.tr: Absurdity 4 and argument 4. It would follow that we have borne false witness, not only concerning Christ but also concerning God, who raised up Christ, and who did not raise Christ if there is no resurrection. Therefore their doctrine is false.

units.la: Verf. 16. Nam si mortui non excitantur, Christus quoque non est excitatus.
units.tr: Verse 16. For if the dead rise not, neither is Christ raised.

units.la: Ratio est, Quia si doctrina resurrectionis nostræ falsa est, etiam & doctrina de resurrectione Christi falsa est, nec consistere potest.
units.tr: The reason is that if the doctrine of our resurrection is false, then the doctrine of Christ's resurrection is also false, and the two cannot stand apart.

units.la: Verf. 17. Quod si Christus non est excitatus, inanis est fides vestra: adhuc estis in peccatis vestris. Absurdum 5. & Arg. 5. Sequeretur etiam ex eorum dogmate, præter fidei vestræ vanitatem vos adhuc in peccatis jacere, sine redemptione, falsum est ergo: nam nisi redemptus resurrexerit, redemptio nulla est, nec tolluntur peccata.
units.tr: Verse 17. And if Christ is not raised, your faith is vain; you are yet in your sins. Absurdity 5 and argument 5. It would also follow from their doctrine, besides the emptiness of your faith, that you still lie in your sins without redemption. This is false, for unless the Redeemer had risen, there is no redemption, and sins are not taken away.

units.la: Vers. 18. Nempe & qui obdormierunt in Christo perierunt.
units.tr: Verse 18. Then also they who are fallen asleep in Christ are perished.

units.la: Absurdum 6. & Arg. 6 Sequeretur ex eorum dogmate qui negant resurrectionem Sanctos demortuos periisse: Ergo falsum est.
units.tr: Absurdity 6 and argument 6. It would follow from the doctrine of those who deny the resurrection that the saints who have died have perished. Therefore it is false.

units.la: Vers. 19 Si in hac solùm vita speramus in Christum, miserrimi omnium hominum sumus.
units.tr: Verse 19. If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable.

units.la: Absurdum 7. & Arg. 7. Sequeretur ex eorum dogmate Christianos esse omnium hominum miserrimos: Quia non tantùm in vita futura, per hunc errorem præciditur illis spes beatitudinis, sed etiam in vita præsenti, quia seipsos volentes religionis causa, stolidissimè plurimis incommodis objiciunt & commoditatibus privant, si resurrectio futura non esset: falsum ergo & absurdum est dogma negantium resurrectionem.
units.tr: Absurdity 7 and argument 7. It would follow from their doctrine that Christians are of all men the most miserable. For by this error they are deprived of the hope of blessedness not only in the future life, but also in the present life, since for the sake of religion they foolishly expose themselves to many inconveniences and deprive themselves of comforts, if there were no future resurrection. Therefore the doctrine of those who deny the resurrection is false and absurd.

units.la: Vers. 20 Nunc autem Christus excitatus est ex mortuis: & primitiæ eorum qui obdormierunt factus est.
units.tr: Verse 20. But now Christ is risen from the dead, and has become the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.

units.la: Arg. 8. Ut primitiæ pignora sunt & arrha messis futuræ, ita Christi resurrectio pignus & arrha est resurrectionis sanctorum demortuorum omnium.
units.tr: Argument 8. As firstfruits are the pledge and earnest of the future harvest, so Christ's resurrection is the pledge and earnest of the resurrection of all the dead saints.

units.la: Vers. 21. Quia enim per hominem mors, per hominem quoque resurrectio mortuorum.
units.tr: Verse 21. For since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead.

units.la: Arg. 9.
