Quia non minus convenit Dei bonitati & sapientiæ, filios gratiæ omnes restituere à morte per Christum hominem, quam convenit justitiæ & sapientiæ ejus, per hominem Adamum, mortem intromittere in omnes filios naturæ, & contra, sicut per Adamum mors fuit, sic per Christum resurrectio à mortuis futura est: Vera ergo nostra doctrina de resurrectione.
units.tr: Argument 9. It agrees no less with the goodness and wisdom of God to restore all the sons of grace from death through Christ the man, than it agrees with his justice and wisdom to bring death, through the man Adam, upon all the sons of nature; and conversely, just as through Adam came death, so through Christ the resurrection from the dead is to come. Our doctrine of the resurrection is therefore true.

units.la: Vers. 22. Sicut enim in Adam omnes moriuntur, ita & in Christo omnes vivificabuntur,
units.tr: Verse 22. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.

units.la: Arg. 10. Quia sicut in Adamo mortui sunt omnes ejus posteri, Primo, judicialiter & tandem facto, Ita in Christo omnes ipsius filii seu liberi, id est, fideles, judicialiter resurrexerunt, & tandem facto resurgent: Par enim ratio est sententiæ judicis, & executionis sententiæ utrobique.
units.tr: Argument 10. Just as all his posterity died in Adam, first judicially and when the time comes actually, so all his sons or children, that is, the faithful, rose judicially in Christ and will rise actually when the time comes. For the reasoning of the judge's sentence and of its execution is the same in both cases.

units.la: Verf. 23. Unusquisque autem suo ordine: primitiæ Christus, postea qui sunt Christi in adventu ipsius.
units.tr: Verse 23. But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, afterward those who are Christ's at his coming.

units.la: Arg. II. Quo etiam occurrit quæstioni: Cur <bl>Christo</bl> suscitato mortui illi qui sunt Christi, nondum resurrexerint: responsio est & argumentum undecimum, oportere ordinem à Deo constitutum observari, id est, ut primum Christus instar primitiarum resurgeret, & postea messis Christianorum per Christum, in secundo ejus adventu: Christus (ut primitiæ) resurrexit primus, Ergo ejus membra, id est, omnes fideles (ut messis reliqua) resurgent.
units.tr: Argument 11. This also meets the question why, with Christ already raised, those who belong to Christ have not yet risen. The answer, and the eleventh argument, is that the order established by God must be observed: first Christ rises as the firstfruits, and afterward the harvest of Christians through Christ, at his second coming. Christ rose first as the firstfruits; therefore his members, that is all the faithful, will rise as the rest of the harvest.

units.la: Verf. 24. Deinde erit finis, quum tradiderit regnum Deo et Patri: quum aboleverit omne imperium, & omnem potentiam & virtutem.
units.tr: Verse 24. Then comes the end, when he shall have delivered up the kingdom to God and the Father, when he shall have abolished all rule, and all authority and power.

units.la: Hoc argumentum declarat, ostendendo ex instituto Dei, duo connexa esse tempore cum fine mundi, Traditionem regni scilicet à Filio, in manus Patris, & Abolitionem omnis imperii, potentiæ & virtutis adversariæ: Cujus loci hic est sensus, Postquam Christus profravenit, & evacuaverit omnes adversarias potestates, ut diabolum, mundum, reliquasque, cujuscunque demum ordinis fuerint, etiam eas potestates abolebit, eousque ut ipsius membris non poterint quicquam mali inferre, omnibus in infernum detrusis scilicet: deinde Ecclesiam omnibus numeris absolutam, quæ dicitur Christi regnum à Patre ipsi datum, præsentabit Christus, & in manus quasi tradet Patri: Tertió, regnandi modum, per media quæ jam adhibet in Ecclesia colligenda, & gubernanda deponet, quasi jam perfunctus officio Mediatoris: Quartò, Peractis omnibus quæ Ipsi peragenda commissa erant à Patre, commissum etiam sibi regnum, in omnia quæ in mundo sunt, ad Redemptionis opus peragendum, Regnum (inquam) mediatorium tradet, & resignabit Deo suo, secundum humanitatem, & Patri suo, secundum Divinitatem, non ut desinat immediatè regere, sed ut ceslet, mediatè, & sic regere ut prius: non ut desinat cum Patre regnare, sed ut cessel tanquam deputatus à Patre regnare, cum hostibus conflictari, aut laboriosam, seu tumultuosam provinciam in colligenda Ecclesia amplius administrare; alioqui enim regni ejus non est finis, imo vero gloriosior erit quam nunc est, regnandi ratio, cum devictis adversariis, sine Ministerio Angelorum vel Hominum, unà cum Patre & Spiritu, luce, dilectione, vita, & virtute suâ immediate implebit, & gubernabit omnes suos.
units.tr: This argument declares, by showing from God's appointment, that two things are joined in time with the end of the world: the handing over of the kingdom by the Son into the hands of the Father, and the abolition of every hostile rule, power and might. The sense of the passage is this. After Christ has overcome and emptied all hostile powers, such as the devil, the world, and whatever others there are of whatever order, he will also abolish those powers, so that they can inflict no harm on his members, all of them having been thrust down into hell. Then Christ will present the Church, complete in every respect, which is called the kingdom given to him by the Father, and will as it were hand it over to the Father. Third, having finished the office of Mediator, he will lay down the manner of ruling by the means he now uses to gather and govern the Church. Fourth, when all the things committed to him by the Father to be carried out have been completed, he will hand over and resign to God his God and to his Father the kingdom committed to him, the mediatorial kingdom (I mean) over all things in the world, for the carrying out of the work of redemption: according to his humanity to his God, and according to his divinity to his Father. This does not mean he will cease to rule directly, but that he will cease to rule mediately, and so rule as before. He will not cease to reign with the Father, but cease to be the one appointed by the Father to reign, to contend with enemies, or to administer any longer the laborious or turbulent task of gathering the Church. Otherwise there would be no end to his kingdom; indeed the manner of his reign will be more glorious than it is now. With his adversaries overcome, without the ministry of angels or men, he will fill and govern all his own immediately, together with the Father and the Spirit, by his light, love, life and power.

units.la: Verf. 25. Nam oportet eum regnare usque quo omnes inimicos subjecerit pedibus ejus.
units.tr: Verse 25. For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet.

units.la: Verf. 26 Ultimus autem hostis aboletur mors:
units.tr: Verse 26. The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death.

units.la: Arg. 12. Confirmans sensum datum, oportet CHRISTUM regnare, donec aboleat omnes hostes suos, & mortem ut hostem ultimum. Ergo abolebit mortem, & per consequens erit resurrectio.
units.tr: Argument 12. Confirming the sense given: Christ must reign until he has abolished all his enemies, and death as the last enemy. Therefore he will abolish death, and consequently there will be a resurrection.

units.la: Verf. 27. Nam omnia subjecit sub pedes ejus. Quum autem dicit omnia esse ei subjecta, palam est hoc dici excepto eo qui subjecit ei omnia.
units.tr: Verse 27. For he hath put all things under his feet. But when he says that all things are put under him, it is manifest that this is said except him who put all things under him.

units.la: Ne quis cavilletur in voce Omnia, excipit Deum e numero Omnium subjiciendorum CHRISTO, quia Deus est qui reliqua omnia, praeter seipsum, CHRISTO subjicit.
units.tr: Lest anyone quibble over the word "all", he excepts God from the number of "all things" to be subjected to Christ, because it is God who subjects all other things to Christ, apart from himself.

units.la: Verf. 28 Postquam vero subjecta fuerint ei omnia, tunc & ipse Filius subjicietur ei qui subjecit ipsi omnia, ut Deus sit omnia in omnibus.
units.tr: Verse 28. And when all things shall be subdued unto him, then shall the Son also himself be subject unto him that put all things under him, that God may be all in all.

units.la: Quod porro illustrat, Quia tradito & depos ito regno CHRISTI meditatorio, ut jam dictum, ipse FILIUS est subjiciendus DEO, qui subjecit IPSI omnia, ut DEUS sit omnia in omnibus, id est, CHRISTUS qua Homo, depositā legatione Mediatoriā, manifestabit plenissimè omnia quae per se, ut hominem, facta sunt, DEI potentiā, authoritate, & nomine facta esse, seque qua Homo est, Patre minorem esse, & cum corpore suo, seu Ecclesia in aeternum adunatum, PATRI subjectum esse; ut mediatione, & mediis, & instrumentis, & adjumentis quae nunc adhibentur remotis, Deus Triunus, Pater, Filius, & Spiritus Sanctus, immediate omnibus Sanctorum necessitatibus subveniat, & virtute sit omnia media in omnibus Sanctis, omninoque omnium mediorum, instrumentorum, & adjumentorum necessitatem plenissimè praesentiā suā immediatā, in perpetuum, ab omnibus Sanctis depellat: quorum omnium vicem plus quam supplebit; & ipse erit, virtute & effectu, plus quam omnia illa, & quaecunque desiderari possunt alia ad felicitatem felicissimam, in omnibus Sanctis.
units.tr: He goes on to illustrate this: when the mediatorial kingdom of Christ has been handed over and laid down, as already said, the Son himself is to be subjected to God, who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all. That is, Christ as man, with his mediatorial embassy laid down, will show most fully that all the things made through him as man were made by the power, authority and name of God, and that as man he is less than the Father, and that, united with his body, that is the Church, for ever, he is subject to the Father. Then, with mediation, means, instruments and helps, which are now used, removed, the triune God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, will bring aid immediately to all the needs of the saints, and by his power will be "all means" in all the saints. Thus he will banish for ever from all the saints the need for all means, instruments and helps, by his own immediate presence, fully supplying their place more than abundantly. He himself will be, in power and effect, more than all those things, and whatever else may be desired for the most blessed happiness, in all the saints.

units.la: Verf. 29. Alioqui quid facient qui baptizantur pro mortuis, si omnino mortui non excitantur, & cur baptizantur pro mortuis?
units.tr: Verse 29. Otherwise what will those do who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise at all? Why then are they baptized for the dead?

units.la: Arg. 13. Ad probandam resurrectionem futuram, in hunc sensum: Nisi resurrectio futura sit mortuorum, quem fructum reportabunt illi qui afflictionibus persecutionis merguntur, pro mortuis aliquibus, id est, pro Christo, & Sanctis demortuis, quorum resurrectionem defendentes CHRISTI resurrectionem jam factam, & Sanctorum omnium futuram profitentur & defendunt. (Ita enim Verbum Baptizari sumitur; Marc. 10. 38. & Praepositio pro, Act. 9. 16) absurdum autem est Martyrium patientes pro defensione resurrectionis mortuorum, frustrari spe sua: Ergo erit resurrectio.
units.tr: Argument 13. To prove the future resurrection, in this sense: unless there is to be a future resurrection of the dead, what fruit will those reap who are plunged into the afflictions of persecution for some dead ones, that is, for Christ and the saints who have died, whose resurrection they defend, professing and maintaining that Christ's resurrection has already happened and that all the saints' will come. (For the word "baptized" is taken in this way at Mark 10:38, and the preposition "for" at Acts 9:16.) It is absurd, however, that those who suffer martyrdom in defence of the resurrection of the dead should be disappointed in their hope. Therefore there will be a resurrection.

units.la: Verf. 30. Et cur nos periclitamur omni momento?
units.tr: Verse 30. And why do we stand in peril every hour?

units.la: Confirmans sensum praecedentis argumenti: Si absurdum non videtur operam ludere alios Martyres, absurdum existimabunt saltem omnes Christiani, nos Apostolos etiam operam ludere, qui praedicantes & sperantes resurrectionem mortuorum, in continuis vitae periculis versamur: Ergo resurrectio erit.
units.tr: Confirming the sense of the preceding argument: if it does not seem absurd that other martyrs should labour in vain, at least all Christians will judge it absurd that we apostles too should labour in vain, who, preaching and hoping for the resurrection of the dead, live in constant dangers to life. Therefore there will be a resurrection.

units.la: Verf. 31. Indies morior, per gloriationem nostram, quam habeo in Christo Iesu Domino nostro.
units.tr: Verse 31. I die daily, by the rejoicing I have in Christ Jesus our Lord.

units.la: Hoc argumentum confirmat suae experientiae testimonio, serio affirmans, quam certo gloriabantur illi, & Corinthii in CHRISTO, tam certo se indies aliam atque aliam quasi mortem obire pro Evangelio, in novam capitis pericula indies conjectum.
units.tr: This argument confirms the point by the testimony of his own experience, seriously affirming that, as surely as those Corinthians too boasted in Christ, so surely he himself each day met a kind of death, one after another, for the Gospel, and was daily exposed to new perils to his life.

units.la: Verf. 32. Si secundum hominem adversus bestias pugnavi Ephesi, quae mihi utilitas, si mortui non excitantur? Edamus & bibamus? cras enim morimur.
units.tr: Verse 32. If after the manner of men I have fought with beasts at Ephesus, what does it profit me if the dead do not rise? Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.

units.la: Verf. 33. Ne erratis; Mores bonos commercia corrumpunt mala.
units.tr: Verse 33. Do not be deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners.

units.la: In specie profert exemplum periculi notabilis, in pugna cum bestiis Ephesi, in simplici sensu, & sicut homines accipiunt hanc phrasin ordinario: damnare enim ad bestias usitatum erat mortis genus, quo etiam affectos fuisse Christianos comitat ex historiis: hoc periculum adiisse Apostolum quid opus fuisset? quid juvisset, nisi resurrectio speranda & defendenda fuisset?
units.tr: He cites in particular an example of a notable danger, the fight with beasts at Ephesus, in its plain sense, and as people ordinarily take this phrase. For condemnation to the beasts was a usual kind of death, and the histories tell that Christians too were subjected to it. What need was there for the Apostle to face this danger? What would it have profited him, unless the resurrection was to be hoped for and defended?

units.la: Comedamus Si mortui non resurgunt, optima esset gulosa Epicureorum religio, edamus, bibamus, cras moriemur, sicut aliqui inter ipsos porci jam grunnire incipiebant: At hoc absurdum. Ergo mortui resurgent. Vice assumptionis vetat: 1. Ne attendant putidis ejusmodi loquutionibus, quae ipsos possent, vel falsa doctrina, vel vitiosis moribus inficere.
units.tr: "Let us eat." If the dead do not rise, the religion of the gluttonous Epicureans would be best: "let us eat, let us drink, for tomorrow we die", as some among them were already beginning to grunt like pigs. But this is absurd. Therefore the dead will rise. The assumption is met by a prohibition: (1) that they not give heed to filthy speeches of this kind, which could infect them either with false doctrine or with corrupt morals.

units.la: Verf. 34. Evigilate juste, & ne peccate: quidam enim Deum nescunt, ad pudorem vobis incutiendum loquor.
units.tr: Verse 34. Awake to righteousness, and sin not; for some have not the knowledge of God: I speak this to your shame.

units.la: Deinde insinuando authores hujus erroris & fautores inter eos, sterte-re in ignorantiâ Deı, & in intemperantia cum corporali tum spirituali, hujus mundi voluptatibus inebriatos, idcirco hortatur ut justè expergiscantur, id est, ut qui ad rem suam satis attenti erant, & sibi place-bant in acumine suo, excutiant socordiam, ingeniumque ad res bonas, & sanctas convertant potius, interim ut pudendum omnibus objiciens quod ferrent atheos illos erroris hujus doctores.
units.tr: Then, hinting that the authors of this error and their supporters among them were sunk in ignorance of God, and drunk with intemperance, both bodily and spiritual, with the pleasures of this world, he urges them to wake up rightly, that is, to shake off their drowsiness, those who were fairly attentive to their own affairs and pleased themselves with their own cleverness, and to turn their wit rather to good and holy things, while at the same time setting before all, to their shame, the atheists who were teachers of this error.

units.la: Verf. 35. At dicet aliquis, quomodo suscitantur mortui? quali autem corpore prodeunt?
units.tr: Verse 35. But someone will say, How are the dead raised? And with what kind of body do they come?

units.la: Tertia pars capitis, in qua solvit tres objectiones adversariorum: Prima, Videtur impossibile ut resurgant mortui: quomodo enim fiet? Objectio 2. Describere nemo poterit quali corpore sint resurrecturi: Objectio 3. verf 51. Quid fiet viventibus in adventu Domini, illi enim quia non morientur, non poterunt resurgere?
units.tr: The third part of the chapter, in which he answers the three objections of the adversaries. First: it seems impossible that the dead should rise, for how will it happen? Objection 2: no one will be able to describe with what kind of body they will rise. Objection 3, verse 51: What will happen to the living at the Lord's coming? For since they will not die, they will not be able to rise.

units.la: Verf 35. Demens, quod tu feminas, non viviscit, nisi mortu-um fuerit.
units.tr: Verse 35. Fool, what you sow is not quickened unless it dies.

units.la: Ad primam objectionem: Respondet, non esse impossibilem resurrectionem mortuorum, quia semen quotannis moritur, & quasi resurgit.
units.tr: To the first objection he replies that the resurrection of the dead is not impossible, because seed dies every year and in a manner rises again.

units.la: Verf. 37. Et quod feminas, non corpus oriturum feminas, sed nudum granum, prout inciderit, tritici aut alicujus ex reliquis granis.
units.tr: Verse 37. And you do not sow the body that will be, but a bare grain, such as may chance to be wheat or one of the other grains.

units.la: Verf. 38. Sed Deus ei dat corpus ut voluit, & singulis feminibus suum corpus.
units.tr: Verse 38. But God gives it a body as he has willed, and to each seed its own body.

units.la: Ad secundam objectionem, Respondet, corpora substantiâ eadem, sed qualitate diversa resurrectura: id confirmat quatuor modis: Primum exemplo granorum, sicut granum nudum, aridum, durum, &c. suscïtatur in substantiâ, & specie idem, sed qualitatibus diversum, sic etiam corpora substantiâ eadem, sed qualitatibus diversissima resurgent.
units.tr: To the second objection he replies that bodies will rise with the same substance but with different qualities. He confirms this in four ways. First, by the example of grains: just as a bare grain, dry, hard, and so on, rises in the same substance and species but with different qualities, so also bodies will rise with the same substance but with very different qualities.

units.la: Verf. 39. Non omnis caro, eadem caro: sed alia quidem caro hominum, alia verò caro pecorum, alia vero piscium, alia vero volucrium.
units.tr: Verse 39. Not all flesh is the same flesh: but there is one flesh of men, another flesh of beasts, another of fishes, and another of birds.

units.la: Secundò, A pari exemplo carnium: Sicut Deus potest producere, & quotidie producit non tantùm diversa femina, sed etiam, carnes di-versas specie, nam omnis caro non est ejusdem speciei, sic carnem can-dem ejusdem hominis potest resuscitare, & qualitates ejus mutare.
units.tr: Second, by a like example of flesh: just as God can produce, and daily does produce, not only different seeds but also flesh of different species (for not all flesh is of the same species), so he can raise the same flesh of the same man and change its qualities.

units.la: Verf. 40. Et sunt corpora cœlestia, & sunt corpora terrestria: sed alia quidem cœlestium gloria, alia verò terrestrium.
units.tr: Verse 40. There are celestial bodies, and there are terrestrial bodies: but the glory of the celestial is one, and that of the terrestrial another.

units.la: Verf. 41. Alia gloria Solis, & alia gloria Lunæ, & alia gloria Stellarum, stella enim à stella differt in gloria.
units.tr: Verse 41. There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars: for one star differs from another in glory.

units.la: Verf. 42. Ita & resurrectio mortuorum: seminatur corpus corruptioni obnoxium, excitatur incorruptibile:
units.tr: Verse 42. So also is the resurrection of the dead: it is sown a body subject to corruption, it is raised incorruptible.

units.la: Verf. 43. Seminatur ignominiosum, excitatur gloriosum: seminatur infirmum, excitatur potens.
units.tr: Verse 43. It is sown in dishonour, it is raised in glory: it is sown in weakness, it is raised in power.

units.la: Verf. 44. Seminatur corpus animale, excitatur corpus spirituale: est corpus animale, & est corpus spirituale.
units.tr: Verse 44. It is sown a natural body, it is raised a spiritual body: there is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body.

units.la: Tertiò, A pari stellarum & corporum terrestrium differentia: Sicut Deus Cœlestia corpora Cœlesti, & terrestria terrestri gloriâ formata ornavit, & Cœlestia corpora à se invicem gloriâ differentia constituit, ut in sole, luna, & stellis est videre; sic etiam in resurrectione corpus, resurgens gloriâ differet à corpore cadente, sicut incorruptibile à corruptibili, decorum à fœdo, potens ab infirmo, & spirituale ab animali; animale corpus dicitur quod ab anima, animantium more, per media ciborum, elementorum, &c. vegetatur; spirituale vero corpus, quod retinens animam, à Spiritu Dei sustentatur sine mediis, sicut Angeli.
units.tr: Third, from the difference between the stars and terrestrial bodies: just as God has adorned celestial bodies with a celestial glory and terrestrial bodies with a terrestrial glory, and has made celestial bodies differ from one another in glory, as can be seen in the sun, moon and stars, so also in the resurrection the body that rises will differ in glory from the body that falls, as the incorruptible from the corruptible, the comely from the foul, the powerful from the weak, and the spiritual from the animal. A body is called animal when it is nourished by the soul, after the manner of living creatures, through the intermediate means of food, the elements, and so on. A spiritual body, however, is one which, while retaining the soul, is sustained by the Spirit of God without intermediate means, as the angels are.

units.la: Verf. 45. Ita etiam scriptum est, Factus est prior homo Adam anima vivens: posterior autem Adam factus est Spiritus vivificus.
units.tr: Verse 45. So also it is written, The first man Adam was made a living soul; the last Adam was made a life-giving spirit.

units.la: Ultimam hanc differentiam corporis animalis & spiritualis repetitam explicat, & probat, (quia phrasis durior videri posset,) ducendo nos ad primum Adamum, ut ad originem primi status in corpore animali, & ad Christum, secundum Adamum, ut ad originem secundi status in corpore spirituali, & comparat hos duos tripliciter: Prima comparatio, est in statu oppositio corporis animalis & spiritualis: Primus Adam factus est in animam viventem, non vivificantem, quæ vitam quidem haberet, sed sustentatam ut in aliis animantibus, cibo, potu, &c. Non vero quæ vitam continuaret corpori sine alimentis; Sed Christus ultimus Adam factus est in Spiritum vivificantem, qui virtutem posset sus, per Spiritum suum communicare, ut sine alimentis corporis, animæ cum corpore unio felicissima conservari possit.
units.tr: He explains and proves this last difference between the animal and the spiritual body, which he repeats, since the phrase might seem harsh, by leading us to the first Adam, as the origin of the first state in an animal body, and to Christ, the second Adam, as the origin of the second state in a spiritual body. He compares these two in three ways. The first comparison is in the state: the first Adam was made a living soul, not a life-giving one; he had life indeed, but sustained as in other living creatures by food, drink, and so on, and not such as could preserve life in the body without nourishment. But Christ, the last Adam, was made a life-giving Spirit, who by his own Spirit can communicate power, so that the most blessed union of soul with body can be preserved without the nourishment of the body.

units.la: Verf. 46. At spirituale non est prius: sed animale, deinde spirituale.
units.tr: Verse 46. But the spiritual is not first, but the animal, and then the spiritual.

units.la: Secunda comparatio in ordine; Primus Adam tempore præcessit in naturali seu animali statu corporis; Secundus Adam posterior fuit in spiritutuali statu corporis: imperfectior enim status debuit praecedere, sic enim solet Deus progredi ad perfectissima. Non dicit quod simpliciter Adam sit prior Christo, sed quod animalis status primi Adami, sit tempore prior in Adamo, in Christo & in nobis. Spiritualis vero status qui est à Christo, posterior est.
units.tr: The second comparison is in order: the first Adam preceded in time in the natural or animal state of the body; the second Adam came later in the spiritual state of the body. For the more imperfect state ought to come first, since God usually advances to what is most perfect. He does not say that Adam is simply prior to Christ, but that the animal state of the first Adam is prior in time in Adam, in Christ, and in us. The spiritual state, which comes from Christ, is later.

units.la: Verf. 47. Primus homo è terra, pulvereus: secundus homo, ipse Dominus è cœlo.
units.tr: Verse 47. The first man is of the earth, earthy; the second man is the Lord from heaven.

units.la: Tertia comparatio in ordine & dignitate personæ: Primus homo, merus homo, de terra terrenus est, cujus corpus de terra ortum, & in terram resolutum est, & substractis alimentis necessario resolvendum erat, unde nobis nihil aliud praeter terrenam vitam communicari poterat; secundus Adam vero, & homo est & Deus de cœlo, qui licet corpus de terra habeat, quia tamen etiam Deus est de Cœlo, eoque nomine cœlestis dicitur, sicut corpus suum (alioqui natura sua terrenum & in pulverem resolubile) potuit conservare, ne videret corruptionem, & sicut ex sepulchro suscitatum, Immortale seu Cœleste, terrenorum subsidiorum minime indigum, & omni ex parte gloriosum reddidit: Sic similiter etiam corpora nostra poterit talia reddere.
units.tr: The third comparison is in the order and dignity of the person. The first man, a mere man, is earthly from the earth, whose body arose from the earth and was dissolved into the earth, and which, once its nourishment was withdrawn, had of necessity to be dissolved; hence nothing but an earthly life could be communicated to us from him. But the second Adam is both man and God, from heaven. Although he has a body from the earth, yet because he is also God from heaven, and is therefore called heavenly by that name, he was able to preserve his body (which by its nature was earthly and capable of dissolution into dust) so that it did not see corruption, and, when it was raised from the tomb, made it immortal or heavenly, in no way needing earthly supports, and glorious in every respect. So likewise he will be able to make our bodies such.

units.la: Verf. 48. Qualis pulvereus, tales & qui pulverei, & qualis ille cœlestis, tales & cœlestes.
units.tr: Verse 48. As is the earthy, such are they also that are earthy; and as is the heavenly, such are they also that are heavenly.

units.la: Ex his probat futuram mutationem qualitatum corporis, à terrenis qualitatibus ad Cœlestes; ab animalibus ad spirituales, quatuor argumentis.
units.tr: From these things he proves the future change of the qualities of the body, from earthly qualities to heavenly ones, and from animal to spiritual, by four arguments.

units.la: Argumentum primum, Qualis erat terrenus Adam, princeps generis nostri, secundum carnalem propagationem, tales nos ex terreno natos esse oportet, nempe mortales: Ergo qualis Adam Cœlestis, (princeps noster secundum regenerationem & glorificationem,) post resurrectionem est, nempe spiritualis, gloriosus, incorruptibilis, immortalis, tales nos ab eo regenitos post resurrectionem esse oportet.
units.tr: The first argument: just as the earthly Adam, the head of our race, according to carnal propagation, was such that we had of necessity to be born of earthly stock, namely mortal, so the heavenly Adam (our head according to regeneration and glorification) is, after the resurrection, spiritual, glorious, incorruptible and immortal; such, then, we must be after the resurrection, regenerated by him.

units.la: Verf. 49. Et sicut gestavimus imaginem terreni, gestabimus etiam imaginem Cœlestis.
units.tr: Verse 49. And as we have borne the image of the earthy, we shall also bear the image of the heavenly.

units.la: Arg. 2. De certitudine quod hoc sit futurum: Quam certò gestavimus imaginem primi Adami, in substantiæ qualitatibus, conformes ei facti animo, & corpore tam certo imaginem geremus secundi Adami, in substantiæ qualitatibus gloriosis.
units.tr: Second argument, concerning the certainty that this will come to pass: just as surely as we have borne the image of the first Adam in the qualities of the substance, being made like him in soul and body, so surely shall we bear the image of the second Adam in his glorious qualities of substance.

units.la: Verf. 50. Hoc autem dico, fratres, carnem & sanguinem non posse regni Dei hæreditatem consequi, neque corruptionem consequi incorruptæ naturæ hæreditatem,
units.tr: Verse 50. Now this I say, brethren, that flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, neither does corruption inherit incorruption.

units.la: Arg. 3. Promissiones de nostris corporibus glorificandis, seu de nobis in regnum Dei gloriosum introducendis, compleri oportet. At caro & sanguis, hoc est, corpora nostra, ut nunc sunt corruptibilia, regnum Dei ingredi, seu in regnum gloriosum introduci non possunt, nisi aptata ad Coelestem illum statum: Ergo corpora nostra mutatis qualitatibus aptabuntur, ut in regnum gloriæ ingrediantur.
units.tr: Third argument: the promises concerning the glorifying of our bodies, or concerning our introduction into the glorious kingdom of God, must be fulfilled. But flesh and blood, that is, our bodies as they now are, corruptible, cannot enter the kingdom of God, or be introduced into the glorious kingdom, unless they are fitted for that heavenly state. Therefore our bodies, with their qualities changed, will be fitted to enter the kingdom of glory.

units.la: Corruptio ] Hanc rationem confirmans addit Arg. 4. Corruptio seu corruptibile non poterit hæreditate consequi, & possidere incorruptibilitatem: Ergo necesse est ut corpora in qualitatibus mutentur à corruptibilitate ad incorruptibilitatem:
units.tr: Corruption: Confirming this reason, he adds a fourth argument. What is corruptible cannot inherit and possess incorruptibility; therefore it is necessary that bodies be changed in their qualities from corruptibility to incorruptibility.

units.la: Verf. 51. Ecce, mysterium vobis dico, Non omnes quidem obdormiemus, sed omnes mutabimur.
units.tr: Verse 51. Behold, I tell you a mystery: We shall not all indeed sleep, but we shall all be changed.

units.la: Objectio 3. Quid fiet viventibus in adventu Domini? Quomodo resurgent, qui non morientur, sed vivi comperientur à Judice in eius adventu? Respondet aperiendo mysterium: nempe non omnes morituros, nec omnes resurrecturos, sed excipiendos esse eos, qui superstites sunt futuri in adventu Domini, qui mutabuntur omnes in statum immortalem perpetuò duraturum, vel in gloria, vel in cruciatibus, quæ mutatio futura est vice mortis & resurrectionis.
units.tr: Objection 3: What will happen to the living at the coming of the Lord? How will they rise, who will not die, but will be found alive by the Judge at his coming? He answers by opening up the mystery: namely, that not all will die, nor all rise, but that those who will be found surviving at the coming of the Lord are to be taken up, and all of them will be changed into an immortal state that will last for ever, whether in glory or in torments; and this change will take place in place of death and resurrection.

units.la: Verf 52. Momento & ictu oculi, ad ultimam tubam (canet enim tuba) & mortui suscitabuntur incorrupti, & nos mutabimur.
units.tr: Verse 52. "In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet (for the trumpet will sound), and the dead will be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed."

units.la: Modum ostendit, quod mutatio hæc futura fit in jactu, vel in ictu oculi, hoc est, momento, omnibus vivis & mortuis horrendo classico citatis ad Dei judicium.
units.tr: He shows the manner: this change will take place in a flash, or in the twinkling of an eye, that is, in a moment, when all the living and the dead are summoned by the dreadful trumpet call to God's judgment.

units.la: Verf. 53. Oportet enim hoc corruptioni obnoxium induere incorruptam naturam, & mortale hoc induere immortalitatem,
units.tr: Verse 53. "For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality."

units.la: Hujus mutationis duas reddit rationes: Prima, Quia oportet mortalitatem absorberi ab immortalitate, & mortale corpus induere immortalitatem: Ergo mutabuntur qui vivi comperientur in adventu DOMINI.
units.tr: He gives two reasons for this change. The first: because mortality must be swallowed up by immortality, and the mortal body must put on immortality. Therefore those who are found alive at the coming of the Lord will be changed.

units.la: Verf. 54. Quum autem hoc corruptioni obnoxium induerit incorruptam naturam, & mortale hoc induerit immortalitatem, tunc fiet illud quod scriptum est, Absorpta est mors ad victoriam.
units.tr: Verse 54. "But when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying that is written: Death is swallowed up in victory."

units.la: Verf. 55. Ubi tua, O mors, victoria? ubi tuum, O sepulchrum, stimulus?
units.tr: Verse 55. "O death, where is your victory? O grave, where is your sting?"

units.la: Ratio 2. Quia oportet impleri vaticinium Prophetæ Hosea, Cap. 13. verf. 14. qui plenam victoriam de morte & sepulchro reportandam prædixit: Ergo mutationem patientur vivi in adventu Domini, quæ vicem mortis supplebit.
units.tr: The second reason: the prophecy of the prophet Hosea, chapter 13, verse 14, must be fulfilled, which foretold that a full victory over death and the grave would be won. Therefore those who are alive at the coming of the Lord will undergo a change which will take the place of death.

units.la: Verf. 56. Stimulus verò mortis est peccatum: vis autem peccati, Lex.
units.tr: Verse 56. "Now the sting of death is sin; but the strength of sin is the Law."

units.la: Ut hæc victoria major appareat, insinuat victoriam reportandam esse etiam de peccato & Lege, absque quibus nihil posset in nos sepulchrum, nihil mors; nam nisi Legi satisfiat, manet peccatum, manet ira, manet mors. Postquam autem Legi est satisfactum pro nobis, tollitur ira & peccatum, quo solo ut aculeo armatur mors, ad lethalem punctionem nobis infligendam: exarmata autem mors, triumphatur & aboletur.
units.tr: So that this victory may appear greater, he hints that the victory is to be won also over sin and the Law, without which the grave would have nothing over us and death nothing. For unless the Law is satisfied, sin remains, wrath remains, death remains. But once the Law has been satisfied on our behalf, wrath and sin are taken away, and death, which is armed only with sin as its sting for inflicting a deadly wound upon us, is disarmed; and disarmed death is conquered and abolished.

units.la: Verf. 57. Sed Deo sit gratia, qui dedit nobis victoriam per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum.
units.tr: Verse 57. "But thanks be to God, who has given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ."

units.la: Hujus victoriæ duplicem usum ostendit: primus est, ut gratiæ agantur Deo, qui per Christum concessit nobis victoriam in mortem, peccatum, & Legem, imò verò Christi victoriam imputavit nobis, & fecit nostram, nam pro nobis mortuus est, & pro nobis per resurrectionem, victoriam de morte consequutus est, ut nos victores redderet.
units.tr: He shows the twofold use of this victory. The first is that thanks be given to God, who through Christ has granted us victory over death, sin and the Law. Indeed, Christ's victory has been imputed to us and made ours: for he died for us, and through the resurrection he gained the victory over death for us, so that he might make us victors.

units.la: Verf. 58 Itaque, fratres mei dilecti, firmi estote, immoti, abundantes in opere Domini semper, quum sciatis laborem vestrum non esse inanem in Domino.
units.tr: Verse 58. "Therefore, my beloved brethren, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, since you know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord."

units.la: Alter usus hujus doctrinæ est, ut sub spe præmii gratuitò donandi, in die resurrectionis, constantes perseveremus in fide Evangelii, & gnaviter incumbamus fructibus fidei ferendis, quia in resurrectione retribuet nobis Dominus, quod apud homines deperditum est, videlicet operum bonorum præmium.
units.tr: The other use of this doctrine is that, under the hope of a reward freely bestowed on the day of resurrection, we may persevere constantly in the faith of the Gospel and diligently devote ourselves to bearing the fruits of faith, because at the resurrection the Lord will repay us what was lost among men, namely the reward of good works.

units.la: Caput decimumsextum.
units.tr: Chapter 16.

units.la: Ultimi Capitis tres sunt partes: in prima continetur ultimus Epistolae articulus, de collecta in usum pauperum Judaeorum faciendá, ad versum 5. In secunda habetur Conclusio, continens res magna ex parte familiares, ad verf. 19. In tertia salutationes Sanctorum commemorantur, ad finem.
units.tr: The last chapter has three parts. The first, up to verse 5, contains the final article of the Epistle, concerning the making of a collection for the relief of the poor Jews. The second, to verse 19, contains the Conclusion, which deals largely with private matters. The third, at the end, recalls the greetings of the saints.

units.la: Verf. 1. Porro de collecta in Sanctos, quemadmodum constitui Ecclesiis Galatiae, ita & vos facite.
units.tr: Verse 1. Now concerning the collection for the saints, as I ordered the churches of Galatia, so also do you.

units.la: Quod ad collectam attinet; fames praedicta ab Agabo, Act. 11. 28. & simul persecutio, urgebant Ecclesias in Judaea degentes, quapropter hortati sunt Apostoli qui Hierosolymis agebant, Paulum & Barnabam, ut collectam fieri curarent inter gentes, ad necessitates pauperum Judaeorum sublevandas, Galat. 2. 20. de hac collecta hic agit, jubens, ut Die Dominico, quo Christiani omnes vacabant à laboribus, & publice convenie-bant ad Dei cultum, in aerarium publicum singuli per se conferrent, absque pompa, pro unusquisque facultate.
units.tr: As to the collection: the famine foretold by Agabus (Acts 11:28), together with persecution, was pressing upon the churches living in Judea. For this reason the Apostles who were at Jerusalem urged Paul and Barnabas to take care that a collection was made among the Gentiles to relieve the needs of the poor Jews (Gal. 2:10). Here he deals with that collection, directing that on the Lord's Day, when all Christians were free from their labours and gathered publicly for the worship of God, each should put into the public treasury, without display, according to his means.

units.la: Rationes suasionis sunt sex: Prima ratio ab exemplo aliarum Ecclesiarum, nominatim earum quae erant in Galatia, quibus idem officium incumbebat, eademque praecepta data sunt.
units.tr: There are six reasons for his urging. The first is the example of the other churches, especially those in Galatia, to whom the same duty had fallen and to whom the same instructions had been given.

units.la: Verf. 2. Primo quoque die hebdomadis unusquisque vestrum apud se reponat, recondens quod pro Dei benignitate licuerit: ne quum venero, tunc collectae fiant.
units.tr: Verse 2. On the first day of the week let each of you lay something aside at home, storing up whatever he has been able to gain by God's kindness, so that when I come the collections need not then be made.

units.la: Ratio 2. Quia nihil requiritur quod ipsis sit grave vel iniquum, sed ut singulis septimanis semel, tempore & loco ad rem opportuno, quisque conferat pro suae prosperitatis (quam à Deo obtinuerit) mensura; facilis autem erat ratio qua collecta fieret publice diebus Dominicis, & tamen singuli apud se, id est, nemine de summa conscio, eleemosynam seponerent, nempe si judicaverimus imitatos esse exemplum veteris Ecclesiae in collectis faciendis, posita cista perforata in aditu domus, in qua ad Dei cultum conveniebant.
units.tr: The second reason: nothing is required of them that is burdensome or unfair. They are asked only that once a week, at a suitable time and place, each should give according to the measure of his prosperity, which he has received from God. The arrangement was also easy: the collection could be made publicly on the Lord's Day, while each person set aside his alms at home, that is, without anyone else knowing the sum. This is the plan, if we judge that they imitated the practice of the ancient Church in making collections: a box with a hole in it was placed at the entrance of the house in which they gathered for the worship of God.

units.la: Ne cum venero Ratio 3. Quia ipse ad eos venturus erat, cognituros de ipsorum obedientia: Hic etiam habetur ratio 4. Ne si rem neglexerint, vel distulerint, imparati inveniantur, cum Apostolus venerit, & tempore minus idoneo collectam faciant, majori cum difficultate & dispendio.
units.tr: When I come: the third reason. He himself was going to come to them, and would learn of their obedience. Here also is the fourth reason: lest, if they neglected or postponed the matter, they should be found unprepared when the Apostle arrived, and should make the collection at an unsuitable time, with greater difficulty and expense.

units.la: Verf. 3. Postquam autem accessero, quoscunque probaveritis per Epistolas, hos mittam, ut perferant beneficentiam vestram in Hierusalem.
units.tr: Verse 3. But when I have arrived, I will send those whom you approve by letters, to carry your gift to Jerusalem.

units.la: Ratio 5. Objectioni occurrens, quia ne metus sit de collecta recte impendendâ, Ecce deferendam Hierosolymas, collectam committam solis probatis viris, à vobisipsis eligendis, quos ego unà vobiscum mittam cum Epistolis.
units.tr: The fifth reason, meeting an objection so that there may be no fear that the collection will not be properly spent: when it is taken to Jerusalem, I will entrust it only to men of proven character, chosen by yourselves, and I will send them with you, together with the letters.

units.la: Verf. 4. Quòd si res digna fuerit ut, & ipse proficiscar, mecum proficiscentur.
units.tr: Verse 4. But if it is worth while that I also should go, they shall go with me.

units.la: Ratio 6. Quia res haec adeo mihi est cordi, ut paratus sim non modo legatos vestros per Epistolam commendare Ecclesiis quae sunt in Judaea, sed si operae pretium futurum fuerit, etiam cum iis quibus negotium commiseritis, profici ipse statui.
units.tr: The sixth reason: the matter is so dear to me that I am ready not only to commend your delegates by letter to the churches in Judea, but, if it proves worth the effort, to go myself with those to whom you have entrusted the business.

units.la: Secunda Pars.
units.tr: Second Part.

units.la: Verf. 5. Veniam autem ad vos quum Macedoniam transiero: (Macedoniam enim pertransibo.)
units.tr: Verse 5. But I will come to you when I have passed through Macedonia (for I am passing through Macedonia).

units.la: Verf. 6. Apud vos autem fortasse permanebo, aut etiam hybernabo: ut vos me prosequamini quocunque profecifcar.
units.tr: Verse 6. Perhaps I will stay with you, or even spend the winter, so that you may send me on whatever way I go.

units.la: Verf. 7. Nolo enim vos nunc in transcursu videre: sed spero temporis aliquantum mansurum me apud vos, si Dominus permiserit.
units.tr: Verse 7. For I do not want to see you now in passing; but I hope to remain with you for some time, if the Lord permits.

units.la: Secunda pars Capitis est Epilogus Epistolæ, continens magna ex parte res familiares, quæ etiam ad Corinthiorum ædificationem spectabant: Articuli hujus conclusionis sunt sex; Primus articulus de ipsius ad eos adventu, cujus spem facit, verf. 5. & suæ apud eos commorationis, in amicitiæ mutuæ confirmandæ, & ipsorum consolationis occasionem, si voluerit Deus, verf. 6, 7.
units.tr: The second part of the chapter is the Epilogue of the Epistle. It deals largely with private matters, which also concerned the building up of the Corinthians. This conclusion has six articles. The first concerns his coming to them, the hope of which he holds out: verse 5, and of his staying with them, to strengthen mutual friendship and to give an opportunity for their encouragement, if God wills, verses 6, 7.

units.la: Verf. 8. Permanebo autem Ephesi, usque ad Pentecosten.
units.tr: Verse 8. But I will stay at Ephesus until Pentecost.

units.la: Verf. 9. Nam ostium mihi apertum est magnum, & efficax, & adversarii multi.
units.tr: Verse 9. For a great and effective door has been opened to me, and there are many adversaries.

units.la: Cur differat adventum, & Ephesi porrò subsistere cogitet, usque ad Festi Judaici tempus, quod in eum usque diem observabant Judaizantes, rationes reddit duas: 1. Quia Deus apertum ostium magnum, seu occasionem amplam & paratam, multos lucrifaciendi, seu ad Euangelium convertendi obtulerat, & laboribus ipsius perspicuè benedicebat, quod vocat ostium efficax: Altera ratio, quia propter adversariorum tur-bam ipsius præsentia maximè requirebatur, & Satan ipło absente multùm nocuisset.
units.tr: He gives two reasons why he postpones his coming and intends to remain at Ephesus until the time of the Jewish feast, which the Judaizers observed up to that day. (1) God had opened a great door, that is, a large and ready opportunity of winning many people, or of converting them to the Gospel, and he clearly blessed his labours; this he calls an effective door. (2) Because of the crowd of adversaries, his presence was especially needed, and Satan would have done much harm in his absence.

units.la: Vers. 10. Quòd si venerit Timotheus, videte ut tuto sit apud vos: opus enim Domini operatur, ut & ego.
units.tr: Verse 10. Now if Timothy comes, see that he is safe among you, for he works the work of the Lord, as I do.

units.la: Vers. 11. Ne quis igitur illum pro nihilo habeat: sed profequtmini eum cum pace, ut veniat ad me: expecto enim eum cum fratribus.
units.tr: Verse 11. Therefore let no one despise him, but send him on his way in peace, so that he may come to me, for I am expecting him with the brothers.

units.la: Articulus 2. In quo studiose commendat ipsis Timotheum, si ad ipsos veniet, tanquam charissimum filium suum, (qui filius dicitur Apostoli, quia in Euangelio prædicando insistebat vestigiis Apostoli, Deo sanctè serviens, sicut Ille) ut eum ab injuriis tutarentur, honorificè tractarent, deducerent revertentem, custodirent à periculis in via, ut ad se salvus reverteretur.
units.tr: Article 2. In which he earnestly commends Timothy to them, should he come to them, as his most beloved son (who is called the Apostle's son because in preaching the Gospel he followed closely in the Apostle's footsteps, serving God faithfully as the Apostle did), asking that they protect him from injuries, treat him with honour, escort him on his return, guard him from dangers on the road, so that he may return safely to him.

units.la: Vers. 12. Porrò de Apollo fratre multum precatus sum eum, ut iret ad vos cum fratribus: sed omnino non fuit ergo voluntas nunc eun-di: venturus est autem quum tempus opportunum habuerit.
units.tr: Verse 12. Now concerning our brother Apollos, I strongly urged him to go to you with the brethren, but he was altogether unwilling to go now; he will come when he has opportunity.

units.la: Articulus 3. In quo ne ægrius ferrent Corinthii, quod Apostolus dum ipse veniret, non miserit Apollo Euangelistam, hominem ipsis familiarem, qui rigaverat plantationem Apostoli inter ipsos, purgat se, quod per se non steterit, quominus venerit, sed spem facit interim ipsius adventus, cum occasio opportuna oblata fuerit.
units.tr: Article 3. In which, lest the Corinthians take it too hard that the Apostle, while he himself was coming, did not send Apollos, a man familiar to them who had watered the planting of the Apostle among them, he clears himself: it was not through any fault of his own that he did not come, but he holds out hope of his coming meanwhile, when a suitable opportunity has been offered.

units.la: Verf. 13. Vigilate, state in fide, viriliter agite, estote fortes.
units.tr: Verse 13. Watch, stand fast in the faith, act manfully, be strong.

units.la: Vers. 14. Omnia vestra cum charitate fiant.
units.tr: Verse 14. Let all your things be done in charity.

units.la: Articulus 4. In quo hortatur ad officia Christianorum militum quinq;
units.tr: Article 4. In which he exhorts to the duties of Christian soldiers, in five respects:

units.la: 1. Ut etiamsi neque ipse, neque Apollo venturus fuerit, interea perpetuas excubias agant, ne Satan socordes, vel terrenis curis inebriatos, incautos opprimat: 2. Ut in fide constantes sint, doctrinæ veritatem firmiter tenentes, & Christo per fidem agglutinati: 3 Ut se viros præstent in omni certamine adversus adversarios fidei & salutis suæ: 4. Ut in Dei virtute animi robur colligant, ne fracti malis unquam succumbant: 5. Ut rerum omnium cum Ecclesiasticarum, tum civilium, inter se moderatricem statuant charitatem, publicæ utilitati in omnibus servientes.
units.tr: 1. That, even if neither he himself nor Apollos should come, they keep constant watch in the meantime, lest Satan overtake them unwary, when they are careless or drunk with earthly cares; 2. That they be steadfast in the faith, holding firmly to the truth of doctrine and bound to Christ through faith; 3. That they show themselves men in every struggle against the adversaries of their faith and their salvation; 4. That they gather strength of spirit in the power of God, so that, broken by evils, they never give way; 5. That they set up mutual charity as the moderator of all things, both ecclesiastical and civil, serving public utility in all things.

units.la: Vers. 15. Precor autem vos, fratres, nostri familiam Stephanæ esse primiesse primitias Achaiæ, & se se in ministerium sanctũ addixisse:
units.tr: Verse 15. Now I beseech you, brethren, you know the household of Stephanas, that it is the firstfruits of Achaia, and that they have devoted themselves to the holy ministry:

units.la: Vers. 16. Ut & vos subjiciamini talibus, & omnibus operam suam conferentibus & laborantibus.
units.tr: Verse 16. That you also submit yourselves to such, and to everyone who contributes effort and labours.

units.la: Articulus 5. In quo commendat illis Stephanam cum familia ejus, quæ in Diaconatus munere exequendo ipsum adjuvabat, ut in honore habeant ipsum & familiam ipsius: Primò, Quia inter primos nomina dederant Christo: 2. Quia ultro suum servitium obtulerant Ecclesiæ Corinthiacæ in Diaconatu, idque ordine observato, qui in Diaconis constituendis requirebatur, sicut verbi vis insinuat: rogat igitur Apostolus, ut his subjecti, honorem debitum, seu convenientem ipsorum ministeriis exhibeant; Subjectionem hic non tam politicam, respectu muneris, quam moralem intelligit, qua reverentes & obsequentes nos præbemus iis, qui virtute præstant; interim non excludimus subjectionem quæ muneris causa debetur diaconis, qui una cum reliquis presbyteris res Ecclesiasticas administrant, in quibus rebus Stephanas cum familia sua serviebat.
units.tr: Article 5. In which he commends to them Stephanas with his household, who helped him in discharging the office of deacon, that they should hold him and his household in honour: First, because they were among the first to give their names to Christ; second, because they had offered their service of their own accord to the Corinthian Church in the diaconate, and this in the order that was required in appointing deacons, as the force of the word suggests. The Apostle therefore asks that they show subjection to these men, and give the honour due or fitting to their ministries. He understands this subjection not so much as political, with respect to office, as moral, by which we show ourselves reverent and obedient to those who excel in virtue. Meanwhile we do not exclude the subjection that is owed for the sake of office to the deacons, who together with the other elders administer church affairs, in which affairs Stephanas with his household was serving.

units.la: Vers. 17. Gaudeo verò de adventu Stephanæ Fortunati & Achaici, quoniam absentiam vestram hi supplêverunt.
units.tr: Verse 17. I rejoice indeed at the coming of Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus, because these men have supplied your absence.

units.la: Vers. 18. Refecerunt enim spiritum meum ac vestrum. Agnoscite itaque qui sunt hujusmodi.
units.tr: Verse 18. For they have refreshed my spirit and yours. Acknowledge therefore those who are such.

units.la: Articulus 6. In quo laudat missionem trium fratrum à Corinthiis ad se, quia vices Corinthiorum in ipsius visitatione suppleverant; Refocillasse dicuntur Spiritum & Apostoli & Corinthiorum, quia sicut gratum fecerant Corinthiis qui eos miserant, sic & Apostolo etiam ad quem missi sunt, quapropter æstimari vult tantò pluris & hos, & similes ipsorum.
units.tr: Article 6. In which he praises the sending of three brethren from the Corinthians to him, because they had supplied the place of the Corinthians in visiting him. They are said to have refreshed the spirit both of the Apostle and of the Corinthians: as they had been a pleasure to the Corinthians who sent them, so also to the Apostle to whom they were sent. Wherefore he wishes these men, and others like them, to be valued all the more highly.

units.la: Tertia Pars.
units.tr: Third Part.

units.la: Vers. 19. Salutant vos Ecclesiæ Asiæ, Salutant vos in Domino multum Aquila & Priscilla, cum Ecclesia quæ est domi ipsorum.
units.tr: Ver. 19. The churches of Asia salute you. Aquila and Priscilla salute you warmly in the Lord, together with the church that meets in their house.

units.la: Vers. 20. Salutant vos fratres omnes. Salutate alij alios osculo sancto.
units.tr: Ver. 20. All the brethren salute you. Greet one another with a holy kiss.

units.la: Tertia pars capitis, in qua post salutatos Corinthios: 1. Nomine Ephesiorum & reliquarum Ecclesiarum in Asia: 2. Nomine Priscillæ & Aquilæ & familiæ ipsorum, versu 19. 3. Nomine fratrum comitum suorum, qui in ipsius consortio degebant. Jubet, prout orientalibus moserat, ut se invicem salutantes osculo, sicut nos dextrarum conjunctione, sine dolo aut dissimulatione, sancte id præstent, & reliqua mutuæ dilectionis signa.
units.tr: This is the third part of the chapter, in which, after the greetings to the Corinthians: (1) he sends greetings in the name of the Ephesians and the other churches in Asia; (2) in the name of Priscilla, Aquila and their household, ver. 19; (3) in the name of the brethren who were his companions and lived with him. He bids them, as was the custom of the Easterners, to greet one another with a kiss, as we greet with a handshake, and to do so holily, without deceit or pretence, and to give the other signs of mutual love.

units.la: Verf. 21. Salutatio manu mea Pauli,
units.tr: Ver. 21. The salutation with my own hand, Paul's.

units.la: Deinde Epistolam hanc ab amanuensi descriptam, cum salutatione sua, manu propria obsignat, ut genuina cognoscatur; Quia enim ipsius temporibus fictæ erant Epistolæ Apostolorum nomine, 2 Thess. 2. 1. Idcirco opus erat ut signo aliquo, Ecclesiis manifesto, discernerentur.
units.tr: Next, having had this Epistle written down by an amanuensis, he seals it with his own hand, together with his own greeting, so that it may be recognised as genuine. For in his own time letters were forged in the names of the Apostles, 2 Thess. 2. 1. Therefore it was necessary that they be distinguished by some sign that was plain to the churches.

units.la: Verf. 22. Si quis non amat Dominum Iesum Christum, sit anathema maranatha.
units.tr: Ver. 22. If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema maranatha.

units.la: In Epistolæ clausula, osoribus & inimicis CHRISTI occultis, & apertis, maledicit Apostolica authoritate, idque usitatis extremæ execrationis vocibus; hac enim solenni formula, Maranatha, id est, DOMINUS venit, Ecclesia testata est se omnibus officii sui partibus erga virum ejusmodi perfunctam esse: Deinceps ab eo de communi consilio abstinere, eumque DEI judicio extremo, seu adventui DOMINI, ut deploratæ inter homines spei, permittere; Interim Apostolus his verbis non excommunicat hypocritas ab externa societate Ecclesiæ, sed minatur extremum exitium, nisi resipiscant.
units.tr: At the close of the Epistle, he pronounces a curse with apostolic authority upon the haters and enemies of Christ, both hidden and open, and does so in the customary words of the most solemn execration. For by this formula, Maranatha, that is, "the Lord comes," the Church bears witness that it has discharged every part of its duty towards such a man: thereafter it is to abstain from common counsel with him, and to leave him to the final judgment of God, or to the coming of the Lord, as one whose hope among men is despaired of. Meanwhile the Apostle, by these words, does not excommunicate the hypocrites from the external fellowship of the Church, but threatens them with utter destruction unless they repent.

units.la: Verf 23 Gratia Domini Iesu Christi sit vobiscum.
units.tr: Ver. 23. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

units.la: Verf. 24. Charitas mea cum omnibus vobis in Christo Iesu. Amen.
units.tr: Ver. 24. My love be with you all in Christ Jesus. Amen.

units.la: Denique post Apostolicam benedictionem, pro authoritate sua Corinthiorum Ecclesiæ applicatam, specialem amorem suum erga eos significat, ut apud se statuere possent, omnia quæ in hac Epistola descripta sunt, sive in ipsorum reprehensionem, sive exhortationem, à dilectione profecta esse.
units.tr: Finally, after the apostolic benediction, which is addressed to the church of Corinth in his own authority, he expresses his special love towards them, so that they may be assured within themselves that everything written in this Epistle, whether by way of rebuke or exhortation, has proceeded from love.

units.la: EXPOSITIO
units.tr: EXPOSITION

units.la: EXPOSITIO ANALYTICA Epistolæ Pauli Posterioris, ad Corinthios, Summarium.
units.tr: Analytical Exposition of Paul's Second Epistle to the Corinthians, Summary.

units.la: NON caruerat prior Epistola suo fructu apud Corinthios plerosque, sed erant tamen aliqui, præsertim vaniloqui Doctores, qui perstiterunt in sui contumacia, & Apostoli authoritatem non tantùm ipsi contempserunt, sed etiam publicè ausi sunt se cum illo comparare, & seipsos illi præferre, Apostolique dignitatem cum detrimento Euangelii, apud populum quantum poterant imminuere. Hos ut compesceret, & omnia in Corinthiorum Ecclesia melius constituta inveniret in suo adventu, scripsit hanc secundam Epistolam, quæ tota ferè apologetica est.
units.tr: The first Epistle had not been without its fruit among many of the Corinthians, but there were still some, especially vain-talking teachers, who persisted in their obstinacy. Not only did they despise the authority of the Apostle, but they even dared publicly to compare themselves with him and to prefer themselves to him, and as far as they could, they diminished the dignity of the Apostle in the eyes of the people, to the detriment of the Gospel. To restrain these men, and so that on his arrival he might find everything in the Church of the Corinthians better settled, he wrote this second Epistle, which is almost entirely apologetic.

units.la: Præter exordium & epilogum, Epistolæ tres sunt partes: In prima, postquam removit scandalum crucis sibi impositæ, & suspicionem alienati sui animi à Corinthiis, Cap. 1. & 2. defendit ministerium suum, Cap. 2. & Cap. 3. Suamque in Ministerio constantiam & fidelitatem probat, Cap. 4. & Cap. 5. addità hortatione ut Ministerii sui fructus ferant, Cap. 6. deque sua in ipsos benevolentia sibi persuadeant, Cap. 7.
units.tr: Apart from the introduction and the conclusion, the Epistle has three parts. In the first, after he has removed the scandal of the cross laid upon him and the suspicion that his mind was estranged from the Corinthians (chapters 1 and 2), he defends his ministry (chapter 2 and chapter 3), and proves his constancy and faithfulness in the ministry (chapters 4 and 5), with an added exhortation that they bear the fruits of his ministry (chapter 6), and that they persuade themselves of his good will towards them (chapter 7).

units.la: In secunda parte Epistolæ hortatur, ut collectam faciant in usum afflictorum, fratrum Judæorum, Cap. 8. & 9.
units.tr: In the second part he exhorts them to make a collection for the relief of the afflicted brethren, the Jews (chapters 8 and 9).

units.la: In tertia parte authoritatem suam vendicat, à contemptu & aspersionibus falsorum doctorum, qui ut Apostolus vilesceret, apud Corinthios laborabant, Cap. 10. & sanctè adversus eos gloriatur, Cap. 11. & 12. Suamque authoritatem formidabilem, simul & amabilem Corinthiis studet reddere, Cap. 13.
units.tr: In the third part he vindicates his authority against the contempt and calumnies of the false teachers, who were labouring among the Corinthians to make the Apostle seem contemptible (chapter 10), and he boldly glories against them (chapters 11 and 12). He also strives to make his authority both formidable and lovable to the Corinthians (chapter 13).

units.la: Caput Primum.
units.tr: Chapter 1.

units.la: CApitis duæ sunt partes præter inscriptionem Epistolæ: In priori removet scandalum crucis & afflictionum, quibus non its primdem premebatur, ad verf. 12. In secunda parte, removet suspicionem alienati sui animi à Corinthiis, ad finem.
units.tr: Apart from the inscription of the letter, the chapter has two parts. In the first, he removes the scandal of the cross and of afflictions, by which he was not less oppressed, as far as verse 12. In the second part, he removes the suspicion that his mind had become estranged from the Corinthians, to the end.

units.la: Inscriptio Epistolæ quæ vicem supplet exordii, verf. 1. & 2. parandis Corinthiorum animis ad rectè accipiendum quæ scribebat, inservit, quinque in eum finem insinuatis rationibus.
units.tr: The inscription of the letter, which takes the place of an exordium, verses 1 and 2, serves to prepare the minds of the Corinthians to receive rightly what he writes, through five reasons suggested to that end.

units.la: Verf. 1. PAulus Apostolus Iesu Christi per Dei voluntatem, & Timotheus frater, Ecclesiæ Dei quæ est Corinthi, unà cum sanctis omnibus qui sunt in tota Achaia:
units.tr: Verse 1. Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, to the Church of God which is at Corinth, together with all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia:

units.la: Ratio prima : Quia Paulus author Epistolæ, erat Apostolus Iesu Christi, & summæ in Ecclesia authoritatis : Ratio 2. Quia non assumpsit hunc sibi honorem (sicut falsi aliqui fratres mentiebantur se esse servos Christi, cum à Deo non essent missi) sed speciali Dei voluntate consequutus erat hunc honorem. Ratio 3. Quia Timotheum secum testem vocaverat adversus eos, nisi hanc Dei veritatem à se scriptam admitterent. Ratio 4. Quia quod scripturus erat, non ad Ecclesiam Corinthiacam tantùm, sed ad omnes Ecclesias & Sanctos in reliqua Achaia pertinebat, nempe assertam hanc quam scripturus erat veritatem cognoscere.
units.tr: Reason 1: because Paul, the author of the letter, was an apostle of Jesus Christ and held the highest authority in the Church. Reason 2: because he did not assume this honour for himself (as certain false brothers, who had not been sent by God, falsely claimed to be servants of Christ), but obtained this honour by the special will of God. Reason 3: because he had called Timothy to be a witness with him against those who would not admit this truth of God which he had written. Reason 4: because what he was about to write pertained not only to the Corinthian Church but to all the churches and saints in the rest of Achaia, namely, that they should come to know the truth he was about to assert.

units.la: Verf. 2. Gratia sit vobis & pax à Deo patre nostro, & Domino Iesu Christo.
units.tr: Verse 2. Grace be to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: Ratio 5. In salutatione, seu benedictione Apostolicâ, comprehensa: Quia Paulus author Epistolæ, dignitatem Ecclesiæ Corinthiacæ, nolebat inminu' quovis modo, etiamsi corruptissimos sciret homines, in illius Ecclesiæ societate, non latere tantùm, sed etiam aperte se ipsius Apostoli inimicos prodere: sed Ecclesiam quæ erat Corinthi pro vera Ecclesia constanter habebat, cui pro authoritate sua, Evangelii benedictionem applicare, eique omnia bona comprecari non dubitabat. Idcirco ea quæ scribebat, cum ea animi submissione & benevolentia qua par erat, accipere tenebantur.
units.tr: Reason 5, contained in the apostolic salutation or blessing: because Paul, the author of the letter, did not wish in any way to diminish the dignity of the Corinthian Church, even though he knew that very corrupt men were present in its fellowship, men who not only lay hidden but openly showed themselves to be enemies of the Apostle himself. Rather, he steadfastly regarded the church at Corinth as a true Church, and by virtue of his authority he did not hesitate to apply to it the blessing of the Gospel and to wish it every good thing. Therefore they were bound to receive what he wrote with the submissiveness and goodwill that were fitting.

units.la: Prima Pars.
units.tr: First Part.

units.la: Verf. 3. Benedictus Deus ac Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, Pater inquam ille misericordiarum: & Deus omnis consolationis Author:
units.tr: Verse 3. Blessed be God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father, I say, of mercies, and the God of all consolation:

units.la: Prima pars Capitis, in qua probat Apostolus Corinthios non debere ipsum, crucis vel miseriarum nomine despicere, idque argumentis duodecim.
units.tr: The first part of the chapter, in which the Apostle proves that the Corinthians ought not to despise him on account of the cross or his miseries, and does so by twelve arguments.

units.la: Argumentum primum, In mediis afflictionibus compertum habeo DEUM Patrem maximè misericordem, & consolatione omnigenâ abundantissimum, adeo ut causam potiùs habeam benedicendi Deo, quam quærendi de calamitatibus, à Deo immissis. Ergo afflictionum nomine non debetis offendi, vel me despicere.
units.tr: First argument: I have found that in the midst of afflictions God the Father is most merciful and most abundant in every kind of consolation, so that I have more cause to bless God than to complain about the calamities sent by God. Therefore you ought not to be offended by my afflictions, nor to despise me.

units.la: Vers. 4 Consolans nos in omni oppressione nostra, ut possimus positos in quavis oppressione consolari, ea ipsa consolatione qua nos ipsos Deus consolatur.
units.tr: Verse 4. Comforting us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction with the same comfort by which God himself comforts us.

units.la: Arg. 2. Per hanc in afflictionibus experientiam, aptior redditus sum ad consolationem ministrandam aliis afflictis: Ergo non debetis in me offendi, &c.
units.tr: Argument 2. Through this experience of affliction I have been made better fitted to bring consolation to others who are afflicted. Therefore you ought not to be offended in me, etc.

units.la: Vers. 5. Nam sicut abundant perpessiones Christi in nobis, ita per Christum abundat etiam, consolatio nostra.
units.tr: Verse 5. For as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds.

units.la: Arg. 3. Afflictiones sunt Martyrii pars, & pro Evangelio, seu CHRI-STO cum honore mihi inflictæ, ita ut CHRISTI afflictiones dici possint, participativè: Nam quæ Martyribus infliguntur, CHRISTUS sibi imputat, ut Act. 9. Saul, Saul, cur me persequeris? Ergo, &c.
units.tr: Argument 3. The afflictions are part of martyrdom, and have been inflicted on me, with honour, for the Gospel, or for CHRIST, so that they may be called the afflictions of CHRIST by participation. For what is inflicted on the martyrs, CHRIST counts as done to himself, as in Acts 9: "Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?" Therefore, etc.

units.la: Arg. 4. CHRISTUS testimonium tulit (ex tempestiva & superabundanti mensura consolationis in meipsum, collatâ in afflictionibus,) ærumnas, quas perpetior, propter Evangelii defensionem inflictas esse mihi: Ergo non debetis, &c.
units.tr: Argument 4. CHRIST has borne witness (from the timely and overflowing measure of consolation poured into me in my afflictions) that the hardships I endure have been inflicted on me for the defence of the Gospel. Therefore you ought not, etc.

units.la: Vers. 6. Sive autem premimur, id fit pro vestra consolatione ac salute, quæ efficitur in tolerantia earundem perpessionum, quibus & nos afficimur: sive consolationem accipimus, id fit pro vestra consolatione ac salute: & spes nostra firma est de vobis:
units.tr: Verse 6. But whether we are afflicted, it is for your consolation and salvation, which is brought about by the endurance of the same sufferings which we also undergo; or whether we receive consolation, it is for your consolation and salvation: and our hope for you is firm:

units.la: Arg. 5. Illæ afflictiones, & similiter consolationes tendebant ad utilitatem Corinthiorum, qui in fide confirmari, & variis modis ædificari ad salutem, & nominatim consolationem capere, per experientiam Apostoli poterant: Ergo non debebant in Apostoli cruce offendi.
units.tr: Argument 5. Those afflictions, and likewise the consolations, tended to the profit of the Corinthians, who, through the Apostle's experience, could be confirmed in faith, built up in various ways to salvation, and especially receive consolation. Therefore they ought not to have been offended at the Apostle's cross.

units.la: Arg. 6. Quia salus Corinthiorum efficaciter promovenda erat, per ejusdem generis afflictionum tolerantiam, per quas afflictiones, ut per viam, ad gratis datam salutem, ipsis contendendum erat: Ergo tenebantur Corinthii Apostolum propter afflictiones, quas patiebatur minimè despicere.
units.tr: Argument 6. Because the salvation of the Corinthians was to be effectively promoted through the endurance of afflictions of the same kind, by which afflictions, as by a way, they had to press on to the salvation freely given. Therefore the Corinthians were bound not to despise the Apostle at all on account of the afflictions which he suffered.

units.la: Arg. 7, Spes certa est de vobis quod neque sitis nos despe-cturi cturi, neque afflictiones quas perpetiemini male laturi; Tenemini ergo nostram de vobis spem non frustrare.
units.tr: Argument 7. There is a sure hope concerning you that you will neither despise us nor take ill the afflictions which you will suffer. You are bound, therefore, not to disappoint our hope of you.

units.la: Vers. 7. Quod sciamus vos sicut socii estis perpessionum, ita etiam socios fore consolationis.
units.tr: Verse 7. Knowing that as you are partners in the sufferings, so also you will be in the consolation.

units.la: Arg. 8. Novi vos & confortes factos esse nostarum afflictionum per sympathiam, & confortes futuros consolationum nostrarum: Ergo tenemini nos ob afflictiones quas perpetimur minime despicere.
units.tr: Argument 8. I know that you have become sharers in our afflictions through sympathy, and will be sharers in our consolations. Therefore you are bound not to despise us on account of the afflictions which we undergo.

units.la: Vers. 8. Non enim volumus vos ignorare fratres, de oppressione nostra quæ nobis evenit in Asia, nos summè gravatos suisse supra vires, adeò ut prorsus animi penderemus etiam quod ad vitam,
units.tr: Verse 8. For we would not have you ignorant, brethren, of our affliction which befell us in Asia: that we were weighed down exceedingly, beyond our strength, so that we despaired even of life;

units.la: Vers. 9 Sed ipsi apud nos decretum mortis habuimus, ne consideremus in nobisipsis, sed in Deo qui mortuos excitat:
units.tr: Verse 9. But we ourselves had the sentence of death within ourselves, so that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God who raises the dead:

units.la: Vers. 10. Quique ex tanta morte liberavit, & liberat, in quo speramus nos adhuc etiam liberatum iri:
units.tr: Verse 10. Who delivered us from so great a death, and does deliver us, in whom we hope that we shall be delivered again:

units.la: Arg. 9. A speciali exemplo & nupera sua experientia in Asia, Tantùm abest, ut me pudeat afflictionum mearum, ut cupiam earum magnitudinem ab omnibus intelligi, & meam etiam in illis infirmitatem, ut Deus magis glorificetur: Ergo non debetis me ob afflictiones despicere. Afflictionis magnitudinem, & suam infirmitatem manifestat in eo, quod in Ephesino tumultu, de quo Act. 19. 23. vel simili aliquo periculo, inops fuerit consilii, quomodo vitæ periculum evaderet, ut qui intus, & in animo suo certam mortem expectabat.
units.tr: Argument 9. From a special example and his recent experience in Asia: I am so far from being ashamed of my afflictions that I desire their greatness to be understood by all, and my weakness in them too, so that God may be the more glorified. Therefore you ought not to despise me on account of my afflictions. He shows the greatness of the affliction and his own weakness in this: in the Ephesian tumult, of which we read in Acts 19:23, or in some similar danger, he was without counsel as to how he might escape the peril to life, since he inwardly and in his own mind expected certain death.

units.la: Ne consideremus Arg. 10. Didici ex hac experientia & similibus, mihi ipsi diffidere, & Deo soli inniti, qui ex præsentissima morte eripere potest morientes, & mortuos etiam excitare, in quem etiam finem Deus me in periculum conjecit: Ergo non debetis meam afflictionem despicere.
units.tr: Not to consider ourselves Argument 10. I have learned from this experience and similar ones to distrust myself and to rest on God alone, who can snatch the dying from imminent death and raise up the dead; to this end God also brought me into danger. Therefore you ought not to despise my affliction.

units.la: Speramus Arg. 11. Experientiâ hac nuperâ, & similibus, excitavit in me Deus firmam spem, de liberatione mea in tempore futuro, etiam si in novas calamitates inciderem: Ergo ob præteritas afflictiones non debetis me despicere.
units.tr: We hope Argument 11. By this recent experience and similar ones, God has stirred up in me a firm hope of my deliverance in time to come, even if I fall into new calamities. Therefore you ought not to despise me on account of past afflictions.

units.la: Vers. 11. Vobis etiam unà pro nobis operam conferentibus adeprecandum, ut donum ex multis personis in nos collatum, per multos celebretur gratiarum actione pro nobis. Arg. 11. Quia cognitio periculi & liberationis excitatura erat Corinthios inter alios ad precandum pro ipso, & sic ad impetrandum à Deo ipsius liberationem in futuro, & per consequens etiam ad gratiarum actionem ampliorem, per multos Deo reddendam: Quibus argumentis consideratis non poterant Corinthii Paulum ob afflictiones quas passus erat, contemnere, saltem non debebant in eo offendi.
units.tr: Verse 11. You also helping together with us by prayer, so that the gift bestowed upon us by many persons may be celebrated through many in thanksgiving on our behalf. Argument 11: Because the knowledge of the danger and of the deliverance was going to move the Corinthians, among others, to pray for him, and so to obtain from God his deliverance in future, and consequently also to give greater thanks to God, offered by many. Considering these arguments, the Corinthians could not despise Paul on account of the afflictions he had suffered; at least they ought not to have been offended in him.

units.la: Secunda Pars.
units.tr: Second Part.

units.la: Verf. 12. Nam gloriatio nostra hæc est, testimonium videlicet conscientiæ nostræ, quòd cum simplicitate & sinceritate Dei, non cum sapientia carnali, sed cum gratia Dei versati sumus in mundo, potissimum autem apud vos.
units.tr: Verse 12. For our rejoicing is this, the testimony of our conscience, that in simplicity and godly sincerity, not with fleshly wisdom but by the grace of God, we have had our conversation in the world, and most abundantly toward you.

units.la: Secunda pars Capitis, in qua suspicionem alienati sui à Corinthiis animi (quam excitasse, & frivolis argumentis fovisse videntur ipsius adversarii pseudapostoli) removet, & probat non debere eos suspicari morum ipsius mutationem, aut animum ab ipsis alieniorem, idque sex argumentis, post quæ solvit objectiones quæ contrà afferebantur ab adversariis, duas vel tres.
units.tr: The second part of the chapter, in which he removes the suspicion of an alienated mind toward the Corinthians (which his adversaries, the false apostles, seem to have aroused and fed with trivial arguments). He proves that they ought not to suspect a change in his conduct or a mind more estranged from them. He does this with six arguments, after which he answers two or three objections that the adversaries raised against him.

units.la: Argumentum primum, In quo simul reddit rationem, cur ipsius salus debeat omnibus esse commendata, & simul probat se eundem manere quem Corinthii experti erant, tot mensium probatione, quot ipse inter eos commoratus erat; In simplicitate & synceritate sancta, constanter ita me gessi, ut qui Deo & conscientiæ meæ, & omnium hominum me probaverim. Ergo non est quod suspicemini morum meorum, aut affectus erga vos mutationem.
units.tr: The first argument, in which he at the same time gives the reason why his salvation ought to be commended to everyone, and shows that he remains the same man the Corinthians knew through the trial of as many months as he had stayed among them. In holy simplicity and sincerity I have conducted myself constantly, so that I have approved myself to God, to my conscience, and to all men. Therefore there is no reason for you to suspect a change in my conduct or in my affection toward you.
