units.la: Articuli autem hujus partis septem sunt: 1. Est de adventu Timothei, quem (si Ephesi jam erat) revocat Epheso, postquam satis ibi hæsisse visus est.
units.tr: The articles of this part are seven. 1. It concerns the coming of Timothy, whom he recalls from Ephesus (if he was already there), since he seems to have stayed there long enough.

units.la: Versf. 10 Nam Demas me dereliquit, amplexus præsens seculum, & profectus est Thessalonicam: Crescens in Galatiam, Titus in Dalmatiam.
units.tr: Verse 10. For Demas has forsaken me, having loved this present world, and has gone to Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia.

units.la: Versf. 11. Lucas mecum est solus. Marcum assumptum adduc tecum: est enim mihi perutilis ad ministerium:
units.tr: Verse 11. Luke alone is with me. Take Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me for the ministry.

units.la: Maturandi adventum Timothei rationes reddit tres: Prima à paucitate comitum & adjutorum, quibus jam destituebatur: Nam Demas pertæsus periculorum & afflictionum, quibus Pauli comites obnoxii erant, & crebrò exercebantur sui otii & securitatis gratia, & hujus vitæ commodorum amore ductus, Pauli & Evangelii ab eo jam publicè lice defensi,curam privatis commodis postposuit, Thessalonicam profectus, ubi securius poflet agere. Crescens legatus in Galatiam profectus fuit, & Titus in Dalmatiam, Euangelii propagandi causa: Ita ut solum Lucam medicum in comitatu haberet; Advenientem autem Timotheum jubet secum adducere Marcum Barnabae consobrinum, vel nepotem ex sorore, qui usibus Apostoli commode inservire poterat.
units.tr: He gives three reasons for hastening Timothy's coming. The first is drawn from the small number of companions and helpers he now lacked. For Demas, weary of the dangers and afflictions to which Paul's companions were constantly exposed, and led by love of the comforts of this life and of his own ease and safety, put his private advantage before Paul and the gospel, which Paul had now openly defended, and went to Thessalonica, where he could act more safely. Crescens went as an envoy to Galatia, and Titus to Dalmatia, for the sake of spreading the gospel; so that he had only Luke the physician in his company. He orders Timothy, on his arrival, to bring with him Mark, the cousin of Barnabas (or his nephew through a sister), who could serve the Apostle usefully.

units.la: Vers. 12. Porro Tychicum misi Ephesum.
units.tr: Verse 12. Now I have sent Tychicus to Ephesus.

units.la: Ratio 1 Quia Tychicum miserat Ephesum, quod dicitur sine relatione ad Timothei commorationem in eo oppido, unde dubitari potest an Ephesi tunc fuerit Timotheus, dum haec scriberentur.
units.tr: Reason 1: because he had sent Tychicus to Ephesus. This is said without reference to Timothy's stay in that town, so it may be doubted whether Timothy was at Ephesus when these things were written.

units.la: Vers. 13. Penulam quam reliqui Troade apud Carpum, adfer quum venies, & libros, maxime membranas.
units.tr: Verse 13. The cloak which I left at Troas with Carpus, bring when you come, and the books, especially the parchments.

units.la: Denique, rationem adventus tertiam reddens, jubet advenientem Timotheum, pallium, sive arculam in qua asservabantur libri, vel membranae secum afferre, quibus tum opus habebat. Utrum vero pallium, an arculam intelligamus, non multum interest, modo Iciamus Deum, nec dedignari res suorum servorum minimas curare, nec locum in quo mentio ipsarum fiat, in libro suo, recusare.
units.tr: Finally, giving the third reason for his coming, he bids Timothy, when he arrives, to bring with him the cloak, or the chest in which the books or parchments were kept, which he then needed. Whether we understand a cloak or a chest does not much matter, provided we acknowledge that God does not disdain to care for the smallest things belonging to his servants, nor refuse to record in his book the place where mention of them is made.

units.la: Vers. 14. Alexander faber ararius multa mala mihi exhibuit: reddat ei Dominus secundum facta ipsius. Vers. 15. Quem & tu cave, vehementer enim restitit sermonibus nostris.
units.tr: Verse 14. Alexander the coppersmith did me much harm; the Lord will repay him according to his works. Verse 15. Beware of him too, for he strongly opposed our words.

units.la: Articulus 2. Alexandrum fabrum Euangelii hostem spectat, qui Apostolo praedicanti vehementer restitit, Apostolumque vexavit, cui ex zelo recte composito, in Spiritu Dei, imprecatur divinam ultionem, ut hosti malitioso & obstinato; Timotheumque monet, ut caveat sibi ab eo, ne simili ab eo injuria afficeretur.
units.tr: Article 2. It concerns Alexander the coppersmith, an enemy of the gospel, who strongly resisted the Apostle as he preached and harassed him. Out of a zeal rightly ordered, in the Spirit of God, the Apostle calls down divine vengeance on him as a malicious and obstinate enemy, and warns Timothy to beware of him, lest he suffer a similar injury at his hands.

units.la: Vers. 16. In prima mea defensione nemo mihi adfuit, sed omnes me deseruerunt: (ne illis imputetur)
units.tr: Verse 16. At my first defence no one stood by me, but all deserted me; may it not be laid to their charge.

units.la: Articulus 3. Commemorat notabilia tria, quae sibi contigerunt in prima sua defensione, quando primum omnium ad Tribunal Neronis causam dixit: Primum est, quod nullus in Romana Ecclesia sit auxiliatus sibi, aut patrocinium sibi praestiterit (quod indicio esse potest Petrum non ibi suisse, nedum Episcopum Romae fuisse,) quam desertionem sui ex infirmitate Romanorum profectam interpretatur, ideoque se intercessorem apud Deum opponit pro iis, ad veniam illis impetrandam.
units.tr: Article 3. He recalls three noteworthy things that happened to him at his first defence, when he first of all pleaded his cause before the tribunal of Nero. The first is that no one in the Roman Church helped him or gave him support (which may be an indication that Peter was not there, let alone that he was Bishop of Rome). He interprets this desertion of himself as arising from the weakness of the Romans, and therefore he sets himself forward as an intercessor before God on their behalf, that pardon might be obtained for them.

units.la: Verf. 17. Sed Dominus mihi adfuit, & corroboravit me: ut per me fieret fides praeconii quod audirent omnes Gentes: & ereptus fui ex ore leonis.
units.tr: Verse 17. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the preaching might be fully proclaimed and all the Gentiles might hear; and I was rescued from the mouth of the lion.

units.la: Alterum est, quod Dominus ei auxilio fuerit, in defensione causae suae, & gratia sua eum adversus omnes accusationes sustinuerit, cujus rationem reddit, ut sic Dominus praedicationem Euangelii apud Gentes illustrius confirmaret, & commendatam daret.
units.tr: The second is that the Lord stood by him in the defence of his cause, and by his grace sustained him against all accusations. He gives the reason for this: that the Lord might thus more brightly confirm the preaching of the gospel among the Gentiles and give it commendation.

units.la: Ex ore ] Tertium est, Quod eripuerit eum Deus ex praesenti periculo mortis, (seu ex crudelitate Neronis, & adversariorum, qui ipsum accusabant,) tanquam ex ore Leonis.
units.tr: From the mouth: the third is that God rescued him from the present danger of death (or from the cruelty of Nero and of his adversaries who accused him), as if from the mouth of a lion.

units.la: Verf. 18. Et eripiet me Dominus ab omni opere malo, servabitque regno suo caelesti: cui gloria in saecula saeculorum. Amen.
units.tr: Verse 18. And the Lord will deliver me from every evil work and will preserve me for his heavenly kingdom; to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: Quartum est, Quod hoc experimento confirmaverit ipsi fidem Deus, fore ut conservaretur, ne periculo quovis territus, ullo malo opere se polueret, usque dum in coelestem gloriam Deus ipsum transferret, quo nomine Deo gratias agit cum fiducia.
units.tr: The fourth is that by this experience God confirmed his faith, that he would be preserved, so that, frightened by no danger, he would defile himself with no evil deed, until God should carry him up into heavenly glory; for which he gives thanks to God with confidence.

units.la: Verf. 19. Saluta Priscam & Aquilam, & Onesiphori familiam.
units.tr: Verse 19. Greet Prisca and Aquila, and the household of Onesiphorus.

units.la: Verf. 20. Erastus mansit Corinthi: Trophimum autem reliqui Mileti egrotantem.
units.tr: Verse 20. Erastus remained at Corinth, but Trophimus I left sick at Miletus.

units.la: Verf. 21. Stude venire ante hyemem. Salutant te Eubulus & Pudens, & Linus, & Claudia, & fratres omnes.
units.tr: Verse 21. Make haste to come before winter. Eubulus, Pudens, Linus, Claudia and all the brethren salute you.

units.la: Articulus 4. Continet salutationes missas ad Priscam, seu Priscillam, & maritum ejus Aquilam, & ad Onesiphori familiam.
units.tr: Article 4. It contains greetings sent to Prisca, or Priscilla, and her husband Aquila, and to the household of Onesiphorus.

units.la: Trophimum ] Articulus 5. In quo ad maturandum iter Timothei, facit mentionem absentiae Erasti & Trophimi, qui ipsi ministrare, & Timothei vicem supplere potuissent.
units.tr: Trophimus: Article 5. In it, to hasten Timothy's journey, he mentions the absence of Erastus and Trophimus, who could have ministered to him and taken Timothy's place.

units.la: Salutat ] Articulus 6. Salutationes continet missas ab aliquot Sanctis, qui Romae, & cum Apostolo erant dum haec scriberet.
units.tr: Salutes: Article 6. It contains greetings sent by some saints who were at Rome, and with the Apostle, while he was writing these things.

units.la: Verf. 22. Dominus Iesus Christus sit cum spiritu tuo. Gratia ejus sit vobiscum. Amen.
units.tr: Verse 22. The Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. His grace be with you. Amen.

units.la: Articulus 7. Claudit Epistolam optans praesentiam Christi cum Spiritu seu Anima Timothei: & gratiam comprecatur toti Ecclesiae, cujus intererat scire doctrinam in hac Epistola descriptam, ut majori cum reverentia Timothei ministerium admitteret, & autoritatem agnosceret.
units.tr: Article 7. He closes the Epistle by wishing the presence of Christ with the spirit, or soul, of Timothy, and by praying for grace upon the whole Church, whose concern it was to know the doctrine described in this Epistle, so that they might receive Timothy's ministry with greater reverence and acknowledge his authority.

units.la: EXPOSITIO
units.tr: EXPOSITION

units.la: EXPOSITIO ANALYTICA EPISTOLAE PAULI, AD TITVM. Summarium.
units.tr: ANALYTICAL EXPOSITION OF PAUL'S EPISTLE TO TITUS. Summary.

units.la: CUM in Creta Insula, quæ & Candia dicitur, Ecclesiæ fundamenta tantùm jecisset Paulus, alio properans, sicut Gentium Apostolum oportebat, Tito prosequendi operis partes, tanquam Euangelistæ mandaverat. Verùm quum Paulus sciret eum à quibusdam contemni, & in contemptum à refractariis adduci porro potuisse, tanquam aliquem ex vulgo Pastorum, Paulus autoritatem ei conciliat, & suam ei quasi personam imponit, tam in creandis ministris, quam in tota reliqua Ecclesiæ administratione, eumque ad opus DOMINI peragendum instruit & animat. Epistolæ, præter Præsationem & Conclusionem, tres sunt partes, pro numero Capitum. Prima est de electione Ministrorum, Capite primo. Secunda est de officiis singulorum ordinum in familia, Capite secundo. Tertia est de communibus officiis omnium Christianorum, Capite tertio,
units.tr: When Paul had only laid the foundations of the Church in the island of Crete, also called Candia, he hurried on elsewhere, as an Apostle of the Gentiles had to do, and had entrusted to Titus, as an evangelist, the task of carrying on the work. But since Paul knew that Titus was despised by some, and that the stubborn might be led to despise him further, as though he were one of the common run of ministers, Paul lends him authority and puts his own person, as it were, upon him, both in appointing ministers and in the whole rest of the administration of the Church, and he instructs and encourages him to carry out the work of the LORD. Apart from the Preface and the Conclusion, the epistle has three parts, corresponding to the number of chapters. The first concerns the election of ministers, in chapter one. The second concerns the duties of the individual orders within the household, in chapter two. The third concerns the common duties of all Christians, in chapter three.

units.la: Caput Primum.
units.tr: Chapter One.

units.la: POST Præfationem, ad versum quintum, instituit Titum de Pastorum delectu balendo; ostendens qui sint admittendi, ad versum decimum: qui verò repudiandi, ad finem.
units.tr: After the Preface, down to verse 5, Paul instructs Titus about choosing ministers. He shows who are to be admitted, down to verse 10, and who are to be rejected, at the end.

units.la: Verf. 1. PAulus servus Dei, Apostolus autem Iesu Christi secundùm fidem electorum Dei, & agnitionem veritatis quæ est secundùm pietatem:
units.tr: Verse 1. Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, according to the faith of God's elect and the knowledge of the truth which is according to godliness:

units.la: Præfatio tria continet: Primo, Descriptionem Scriptoris, verf. 1, 2, 3. Secundo descriptionem illius ad quem scribitur; & tertiò, Salutationem cum benedictione Apostolica, verf. 3, 4. In descriptione scribentis Pauli, authoritas ejus asseritur ex his octo: 1. Quod sit servus Dei, idque affirmatur contra Judaeos, qui defectorem Patriae religionis eum calumniabantur: 2. Quod sit Apostolus Iesu Christi, qui immediata legatione ad omnes nationes, supremum Ministerii gradum in Ecclesia tenebat: 3. Quod ipsius doctrina congruat cum fide Abrahae & Patrum, omniumque Electorum, quam nemo Electus non recipieret, nemo nisi reprobus rejiceret, quippe quae nihil praeter agnitam & compertam ab Electis veritatem contineat, quae homines ad pietatem, & purum Dei cultum instituit.
units.tr: The Preface contains three things: first, the description of the writer, vv. 1, 2, 3; second, the description of the one to whom he writes; and third, the greeting with apostolic blessing, vv. 3, 4. In the description of the writer, Paul, his authority is asserted on these grounds: 1. that he is a servant of God, which is affirmed against the Jews, who accused him of being a defector from the religion of his homeland; 2. that he is an apostle of Jesus Christ, who, by immediate commission to all nations, held the highest grade of the ministry in the Church; 3. that his doctrine agrees with the faith of Abraham and of the Fathers and of all the elect, which no elect person would refuse and no one but a reprobate would reject, since it contains nothing but the truth recognised and grasped by the elect, which establishes men in godliness and in the pure worship of God.

units.la: Vers. 2. Ad spem vitae aeternae, quam promisit Deus ille mentiri nescius, ante tempora saecularia, patefecit autem temporibus suis:
units.tr: Verse 2. In hope of eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, promised before the ages of the world, but has manifested in his own times:

units.la: Doctrinae suae elogia & suae authoritatis argumenta reliqua addit: 4. est, Quod vivam ipsem vitae aeternae affert credentibus. 5. est, Quod nitatur testimonio Dei, qui nescit mentiri, seu quem impossibile est mentiri, sive dicendo quod non est, sive non efficiendo ut sit quod dicit: 6. Quod antiquissima sit hujus veritatis origo, quatenus Deus promisit vitam aeternam, non tantum initio mundi praedicando eam primis parentibus in Paradiso, sed etiam pacisc endo de ea ante conditum mundum cum Filio designato Mediatore nostro, in foedere redemptionis: 7. Quod prudentissime revelata sit haec veritas, hoc est, quod gradatim, & prout temporibus accommodatum Deo videbatur innotuerit, nunc vero in apertum producta sit per praedicationem Euangelii.
units.tr: He adds further commendations of his doctrine and further arguments for his authority: 4. it brings the living hope of eternal life to believers; 5. it rests on the testimony of God, who knows not how to lie, that is, whom it is impossible to lie, either by saying what is not so, or by failing to bring about what he says; 6. the origin of this truth is most ancient, inasmuch as God promised eternal life not only at the beginning of the world, when he proclaimed it to the first parents in Paradise, but also by covenanting about it before the world was made, with the Son designated as our Mediator, in the covenant of redemption; 7. this truth was revealed most wisely, that is, it became known gradually and as God saw fit for the times, but now has been brought into the open through the preaching of the Gospel.

units.la: Vers. 3. Videlicet sermonem illum suum, per praedicationem quae concredita est mihi ex mandato Servatoris nostri Dei; Tito germano filio in communi fide.
units.tr: Verse 3. Namely, his word, through the preaching which has been entrusted to me by the command of God our Saviour; to Titus, my true son in the common faith:

units.la: 8. Quod hujus doctrinae praedicandae provincia ex speciali ordinatione & delegatione Servatoris nostri Christi, concredita sit sibi; Atque haec descriptio est Pauli scriptoris Epistolae: Sequitur descriptio Titi ad quem scribitur, qui filius germanus Pauli vocatur, non secundum carnem, sed Primo secundum communem fidem, quam hausit ex Apostoli doctrina, cujus etiam discipulus fuit, & in ipsius comitatu quotidianus Auditor: Deinde, quia impressionem fidei ab Apostolo praedicatae, & plene receperat, & in Doctrina sua ad vivum expresserat: denique, quia vitae instituto, & moribus, Paulum quasi in imagine referebat.
units.tr: 8. The province of preaching this doctrine was entrusted to him by the special ordination and delegation of Christ our Saviour. This is the description of Paul, the writer of the Epistle. Next follows the description of Titus, to whom it is written, who is called a true son of Paul, not according to the flesh, but first according to the common faith which he drew from the apostle's teaching, of which he was also a disciple and a daily hearer in his company; then because he had fully received the impression of the faith preached by the apostle and had expressed it to the life in his own teaching; and lastly because in his manner of life and conduct he represented Paul, as in an image.

units.la: Vers. 4.
units.tr: Verse 4.

units.la: Vers. 4 Gratia sit tibi, misericordia, & pax à Deo Patre, & Domino Iesu Christo Servatore nostro.
units.tr: Verse 4. Grace be to you, mercy, and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ our Saviour.

units.la: In salutatione benedicit Tito, à Deo per Christum, optando & applicando ipsi, Primo gratiam, id est, dona Spiritus Sancti, & ad salutem, & ad vocationem in Ministerio necessaria: 2. Misericordiam, id est, remissionem peccatorum, seu defectuum in exercitio donorum ipsi datorum: 3. Pacem, id est, felicitatem gradatim ex fonte gratiae per dona salutifera, perficiendam.
units.tr: In the greeting he blesses Titus from God through Christ, wishing and applying to him: first, grace, that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, both for salvation and for the calling necessary in the ministry; 2. mercy, that is, forgiveness of sins or failings in the exercise of the gifts given to him; 3. peace, that is, happiness to be brought to completion step by step from the fountain of grace through the saving gifts.

units.la: Vers. 5. Hujus rei gratia reliqui te in Creta, ut quae reliqua sunt pergas corrigere, & constituas oppidatim presbyteros, sicut ego tibi mandavi:
units.tr: Verse 5. For this reason I left you in Crete, that you should go on correcting what remains, and should appoint elders in every town, as I commanded you:

units.la: Praemissa hac praefatione, ut de eligendis Ministris instituat Titum, primo loco repetit mandata tria quae discedens à Creta Tito dederat in genere: 1. Ut Titus absolvat in Ecclesiarum constitutione, quod ab Apostolo inchoatum erat: Deinde ut oppidatim in unaquaque civitate, in qua fideles nuper converti habitabant, constituat Presbyteros, id est, omnes Ecclesiae gubernatores ordinarios: 3. Ut in hoc negotio non agat pro libitu suo, sed regulam sequatur ab Apostolo praescriptam, sicut ille ordinaverat.
units.tr: Having laid down this preface, so that he may instruct Titus about choosing ministers, he first repeats in general the three commands which he gave Titus when leaving Crete: 1. that Titus should complete the establishment of the churches, which the apostle had begun; then that in each town in which the recently converted faithful lived, he should appoint elders, that is, all the ordinary governors of the Church; 3. that in this business he should not act as he pleases, but follow the rule prescribed by the apostle, as he himself had ordained.

units.la: Vers. 6 Si quis est inculpatus, unius uxoris vir, liberos habens fideles, non obnoxios crimini luxus, vel qui non sint refractarii
units.tr: Verse 6. If anyone is blameless, the husband of one wife, having faithful children, not open to accusation of debauchery or disobedience.

units.la: Secundo loco Presbyterorum sive Gubernantium tantum, sive praeterea docentium, requisita ponit tria: 1. Ut nulla infamia notentur, quae illis auctoritatem derogaret, Deinde ne Polygamias vitio (iis temporibus nimis frequenti) laborent: Et denique, ut totam suam domum habeant honestae, & caste disciplinae speculum, id est, liberos in fide educatos, temperantiae & frugalitati assuefactos, alienos à luxu profuso, & qui obedientiae exemplaria essent: ad componendam enim familiam Presbyteri multum facere existimabat, si uxor & liberi intelligerent, ex ipsorum malis moribus conjecturâ factâ, aliceri posse Patrem familias ab omni Ecclesiastico munere.
units.tr: Second, he sets down three requirements for elders, whether they only govern or also teach: 1. that they be not marked by any infamy which would diminish their authority; then that they not be afflicted with the vice of polygamy, too frequent in those times; and finally, that they keep their whole household as a mirror of honest and chaste discipline, that is, children brought up in the faith, accustomed to temperance and thrift, far from wasteful luxury, and who are examples of obedience. For he thought that an elder did much to put his household in order if his wife and children understood that, from their own bad conduct, it could be concluded that the father of the family might be removed from every ecclesiastical office.

units.la: Vers. 7 Oportet enim Episcopum inculpatum esse, tanquam Dei dispensatorem: non sibi pertinaciter placentem, non iracundum, non vinosum, non percussorem, non turpiter lucri cupidum.
units.tr: Verse 7. For a bishop must be blameless, as God's steward: not self-pleasing, not quick-tempered, not given to wine, not a striker, not greedy for base gain.

units.la: Tertio loco, Quia ex Presbyteris, illi qui laborant in Verbo & Doctrina strina praecipuum tenent locum: proprietates hujus presbyteri, quem Episcopum vocat, recitat duodecim, de quibus in Epistola priori ad Timoth. 1. Oportet à criminatione justa esse immunem, ne autoritate destituatur, imo vero adeo immunem, ut nihil in eo reperiatur indignum œconomo Dei, qui tanto longius à crimine debet abesse, quam alii, quanto sanctius est hoc officium: 2. Oportet esse minime præfractum, vel qui sibi pertinaciter placeat: quia qui sibi nimium placet, paratus est ad aliis omnibus displicendum: 3. Oportet non esse iracundum, quia infirmitates populi Dei non poterit ferre, vel curare is qui iracundus est: 4. Oportet alienum esse ab ebrietate & compotationibus: 5. Et alienum à contentionibus & pugna: 6. Et alienum ab avaritia.
units.tr: Third, since among the elders those who labour in the Word and doctrine hold the chief place, he recites the qualities of this elder, whom he calls bishop, twelve in number, concerning which see the first Epistle to Timothy. 1. He must be free from just accusation, so that he is not deprived of authority; indeed so free that nothing unworthy of God's steward is found in him, who ought to be as far from crime as his office is holier than others. 2. He must not be stubborn, or self-pleasing, for he who pleases himself too much is ready to displease everyone else. 3. He must not be quick-tempered, for one who is irascible cannot bear or heal the infirmities of God's people. 4. He must be free from drunkenness and drinking bouts. 5. And free from quarrels and fighting. 6. And free from covetousness.

units.la: Vers. 8. Sed hospitalem, bonorum amantem, temperantem, justum, pium, continentem.
units.tr: Verse 8. But hospitable, a lover of good men, temperate, just, holy, continent.

units.la: Hoc confirmat, quia requiritur ut pro facultatibus paratus sit excipiendis peregrinantibus, aut exulibus Dei servis: 7. Ut bonos seu probos, qui prae aliis eminent in pretio habeat. Indicium enim est hominis minime probi, qui probos quovis praetextu odit: 8. Ut sit in omnibus modestus, sobrius, sanae mentis seu prudens: 9. Ut sit justus; qui unicuique suum cupiat reddere: 10. Ut sit pius & sanctus, qui vita & conversatione sanctitatem alios doceat: 11. Ut sit continens & temperans, qui dominium exerceat in suos affectus & appetitus.
units.tr: This confirms the list: it is required that he be ready, according to his means, to receive travellers or exiles who are servants of God; 7. that he hold good or upright men in high esteem, above others, for it is a sign of a man who is not upright that he hates upright men on any pretext; 8. that he be in all things modest, sober, and sound of mind or prudent; 9. that he be just, desiring to render to each his due; 10. that he be holy and pious, teaching others holiness by his life and conduct; 11. that he be continent and temperate, exercising mastery over his own passions and appetites.

units.la: Vers. 9. Tenacem fidelis illius sermonis qui ad doctrinam facit, ut possit etiam exhortari per doctrinam sanam, & contradicentes convincere.
units.tr: Verse 9. Holding fast the faithful word which accords with the doctrine, so that he may be able both to exhort by sound doctrine and to convict those who contradict.

units.la: 12. Ut non tantum consultus sit Theologiae, sed ut per fidem veritati firmiter adhaereat, ut non tantum pascere possit gregem, sed obturare os lupis oggannientibus.
units.tr: 12. That he be not only versed in theology, but hold firmly to the truth through faith, so that he can not only feed the flock but also stop the mouths of the snarling wolves.

units.la: Secunda pars Capitis.
units.tr: The second part of the chapter.

units.la: Vers. 10. Sunt enim multi refractarii, & vaniloqui, & mentium deceptores, maxime ii qui sunt ex Circumcisione.
units.tr: Ver. 10. For there are many unruly and vain talkers and deceivers of minds, especially those of the circumcision.

units.la: Altera capitis pars, in qua simul rationem reddit tantae diligentiae & curae, in eligendis Pastoribus habendae, nempe, quia abundabant tum temporis falsi doctores: simul etiam describit eos quos rejici vellet ab hoc munere, hoc numere, ex quibus sunt: 1. Immorigeri, seu refractarii, qui in ordinem se cogi non sustinent, & subjectionis jugum excutiunt, sive Presbyterii, sive alius alicujus legitimi judicii, vel qui se subtrahunt auctoritati sive naturali, sive politicae, cui se subjicere in Domino debent: 2. Vaniloqui, qui ambitiosae ostentationi dediti, inanes tantum argutias sectantur, vel speculationes frigidas & nugatorias, quae ad pietatem, & Dei timorem nihil conducunt. 3. Deceptores, seu mentium seductores, qui vel corrupta sua doctrina Euangelium adulterant, vel illecebris suis rhetoricis & scholasticis, mentes hominum ita demulcent, & quasi incantant, ut non amplius admittant salubrem docendi modum: Cujus generis, Exempli causa, Doctores Judaeos indigetat, qui Cretae indigenae erant.
units.tr: The second part of the chapter gives the reason why such great diligence and care must be taken in choosing ministers, namely, that false teachers abounded at that time. At the same time it describes those whom Paul wished to be excluded from this office, from this list, and they are: (1) the unruly or refractory, who will not submit to being brought into order and throw off the yoke of subjection, whether to the eldership or to any other lawful judgement, or who withdraw from authority, whether natural or political, to which they ought to submit in the Lord; (2) the vain talkers, who, given over to empty display, pursue only idle subtleties or cold and trifling speculations, which contribute nothing to piety and the fear of God; (3) the deceivers, or seducers of minds, who either adulterate the Gospel with their corrupt teaching, or by their rhetorical and scholastic allurements so soothe and, as it were, enchant the minds of men that they no longer admit the wholesome manner of teaching. Of this kind, for example, he points to the Jewish teachers, who were natives of Crete.

units.la: Vers. 11. Quibus oportet os obturare: qui totas domos subvertunt, docentes quae non oportet, turpis lucri gratia.
units.tr: Ver. 11. Whose mouths must be stopped, who subvert whole households, teaching things they ought not, for the sake of filthy lucre.

units.la: Hos non refutandos tantum monet, sed etiam prohibendos, ne publice vel privatim doceant. Rationes reddit septem; Ratio prima, Quia familias totas a sana doctrina alienabant, & in perditionem devolvebant, idque vel docendo errores, vel generalem doctrinam male applicando ad hominum cupiditates fovendas, idque turpis lucri causa.
units.tr: He not only instructs that such men must be refuted but also forbidden to teach, whether in public or in private. He gives seven reasons. The first reason: because they were turning whole families away from sound doctrine and plunging them into ruin, and this either by teaching errors or by misapplying general doctrine to indulge men's lusts, and this for the sake of filthy lucre.

units.la: Vers. 12. Dixit quidam ex ipsis, proprius ipsorum propheta, Cretenses semper mendaces, mala fera, ventres pigri.
units.tr: Ver. 12. One of themselves, a prophet of their own, said, The Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies.

units.la: Ratio 2. Quia ingenium Gentis suae sequebantur, mentientes, otio dediti, ventri & gulae servientes, ut bestiae. Quod probat Testimonio Poetae Cretensis, Callimachi vel Epimenidis, cui Testimonio Paulus ipse suffragatur.
units.tr: Reason 2: because they followed the character of their own nation, being liars, given over to idleness, slaves to the belly and to gluttony, like beasts. This Paul proves by the testimony of a Cretan poet, either Callimachus or Epimenides, to which testimony Paul himself lends his support.

units.la: Vers. 13. Testimonium hoc est verum: quam ob causam eos redarguito praecise, ut sani sint in fide.
units.tr: Ver. 13. This testimony is true. For this cause rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith.

units.la: Ratio 3. Quia severa castigatio ejusmodi Doctorum & Discipulorum Cretensium eis adhaerentium, conducebat ad sanitatem fidei ipsorum procurandam & conservandam. Ergo arguendi & severe castigandi erant.
units.tr: Reason 3: because a severe reproof of such teachers, and of the Cretan disciples who adhered to them, served to secure and preserve the soundness of their faith. Therefore they had to be confronted and severely rebuked.

units.la: Vers. 14. Non attendendo Judaicis fabulis, & mandatis hominum aversantium veritatem.
units.tr: Ver. 14. Not giving heed to Jewish fables and commandments of men who turn away from the truth.

units.la: Ratio 4. Ne alioqui Cretenses attenderent traditionibus fabulosis, & commentis Judaicis de legalibus Ceremoniis, & praeceptis ejusmodi hominum, qui puram CHRISTI doctrinam non poterant ferre, sed fermento suo corrumpere eam studebant.
units.tr: Reason 4: lest the Cretans otherwise give heed to fabulous traditions and Jewish inventions about legal ceremonies, and to the precepts of men who could not bear the pure doctrine of Christ, but strove to corrupt it with their leaven.

units.la: Verl. 15. Omnia quidem pura purís: pollutis autem & infidelibus nihil est purum, sed polluta est eorum & mens & conscientia.
units.tr: Ver. 15. To the pure all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure, but both their mind and their conscience are defiled.

units.la: Ratio 5. Quia Christiana veritas contraria statuit doctorum Judaizantium praeceptis, pronuncians scilicet, puris omnia esse pura, id est, Christianis purgatis per fidem in CHRISTUM à peccatis suis, omnes cibos reliquasque creaturas, quae lege ceremoniali immundae erant, jam possit CHRISTI exhibitionem licere, ut bona conscientia possint fideles iis uti.
units.tr: Reason 5: because Christian truth stands against the precepts of the Judaizing teachers, declaring, namely, that to the pure all things are pure, that is, that to Christians cleansed from their sins through faith in Christ, all foods and the other creatures which were unclean under the ceremonial law are now permitted, through the revelation of Christ, so that the faithful may use them with a good conscience.

units.la: Ratio 6. Quia eadem veritas docet, nihil pure usurpari posse ab iis, qui per fidem in CHRISTUM non justificantur, sed pollutas esse etiam ipsorum mentes non renovatas, & conscientias, quae falso ipsos absolvunt; atque ita vanitatis arguit eos, qui ex ceremoniarum observatione sanctitatem studebant comparare.
units.tr: Reason 6: because the same truth teaches that nothing can be used purely by those who are not justified through faith in Christ, but that their minds, not renewed, and their consciences are defiled, and that these falsely absolve them; and thus it exposes the vanity of those who sought to acquire holiness by observing ceremonies.

units.la: Verf. 16. Deum profitentur se scire, sed factis negant, quum sint abominandi, & rebelles, & ad omne opus bonum reprobi.
units.tr: Ver. 16. They profess that they know God, but by their works they deny him, being abominable, disobedient, and reprobate for every good work.

units.la: Ratio 7. Quia etiamsi Doctores illi profiterentur se cultores esse DEI, factis tamen negabant, quia justitiae quae est per fidem, & fructibus Spiritus adversarii erant, abominandi quippe hypocritae, adversus DEI veritatem rebelles, & inepti, per quos ullum opus bonum perageretur. Ex quibus rationibus conficitur falsos istos Doctores coercendos, ne publice vel privatim docere possent.
units.tr: Reason 7: because even though those teachers professed to be worshippers of God, they nevertheless denied him by their works, since they were opposed to the righteousness which is through faith and to the fruits of the Spirit. They were indeed abominable hypocrites, rebellious against the truth of God, and unfit for any good work to be carried out through them. From these reasons it follows that such false teachers must be restrained, so that they could not teach either in public or in private.

units.la: Caput Secundum.
units.tr: Chapter Two.

units.la: HOC Capite agitur de inculcanda salubri doctrina, omnibus secundum aetatem, sexum, & ordinem, uniuscujusque in familia, & per quam formari debeat ipsorum vita ad sanctitatem, ad verf. 11. Et qua firmari posset ipsorum fides in DEI gratia, ex qua (tanquam ex fonte) promanare vult fructus obedientiae in ipsorum conversatione, ad finem.
units.tr: This chapter treats of inculcating wholesome teaching for everyone according to age, sex and station, within each household, and by which their lives ought to be formed to holiness; see verse 11. It also treats of how their faith may be strengthened in the grace of God, from which (as from a fountain) he wills the fruit of obedience to flow in their conduct, to the end.

units.la: Verf. 1. AT tu loquere quae decent sanam doctrinam.
units.tr: Verse 1. But speak thou the things which become sound doctrine.

units.la: Ut Doctorum vanitati facto se opponat, praecipit in genere, ut Titus inculcet doctrinam quæ ad sanctitatem & salutem conducat.
units.tr: Setting himself against the vanity of the teachers, he commands in general that Titus inculcate doctrine that leads to holiness and salvation.

units.la: Vers. 2. Ut senes sobrii sint, venerandi, temperantes, sani fide, charitate, tolerantia.
units.tr: Verse 2. That the aged men be sober, grave, temperate, sound in faith, in charity, in patience.

units.la: In specie quinque præcipit; Primo, de viris ætate provectis, ut doceat seniores, & ætate jam grandes hæc quatuor: 1. Ut virtutibus suæ ætati convenientibus senectam suam ornent, nempe ut Sobrii sint, à temulentia sibi caventes: 2. Ut sint graves & venerandi, & à juvenili lascivia alieni: 3. Ut sint temperantes, prudentes, id est, ut in omni actione moderatè se gerant: 4. Ut in fide, charitate, & spe per patientiam manifestata, sani & minimè simulati sint.
units.tr: He gives five precepts in particular. First, concerning men advanced in years, that he should teach the elders and those now old these four things: (1) that they adorn their old age with virtues suited to their years, namely that they be sober, guarding themselves against drunkenness; (2) that they be grave and venerable, and free from youthful wantonness; (3) that they be temperate and prudent, that is, that they conduct themselves with moderation in every action; (4) that they be sound in faith, charity, and hope, shown through patience, and not feigned.

units.la: Vers. 3. Anus itidem, ut sint habitu qui sanctimoniam decent, non calumniatrices, non vino multo servientes, honestatis magistræ, Secundò de fœminis natu grandioribus præcipit, ut doceat matro- nas hæc quinque officia: ut, 1. in amictu incessu, & toto corporis gestu, decorum servent: 2. Ne calumniatrices sint, quæ aliorum famæ suis men- daciis noceant: 3. Ne bibaces sint: 4. Ut Juniores doceant non aniles fabulas, sed ea quæ bona & honesta sunt.
units.tr: Verse 3. The aged women likewise, that they be in behaviour as becometh holiness, not false accusers, not given to much wine, teachers of good things. Second, he commands him to teach the older women five duties: (1) to keep decorum in dress, bearing and the whole demeanour of the body; (2) not to be slanderers, who harm the reputation of others with their lies; (3) not to be given to drink; (4) to teach the younger women not old wives' tales but what is good and honest.

units.la: Vers. 4. Ut ad sapientiam instruant adolescentulas, ut maritos suos diligant, ut liberos ament:
units.tr: Verse 4. That they may train the younger women in wisdom, to love their husbands, to love their children:

units.la: Vers. 5. Ut temperantes sint, pură, domi manentes, bona, subjecta suis viris: ne sermo Dei blasphemetur.
units.tr: Verse 5. To be discreet, chaste, keepers at home, good, obedient to their own husbands, that the word of God be not blasphemed.

units.la: Officium 5. Ut uxores juniores (ad quas accedere possent familiarius, quam Ministri) doceant prudentiam & modestiam, utque diligant viros suos, & liberos suos amore ordinato & Christiano: Utque sint temperantes, castæ, domus custodes, non vagantes extra familiam, benignæ, & suis maritis obedientes, ne doctrina Christiana male audiat propter eas.
units.tr: Duty 5. That they teach the younger wives (whom they may approach more familiarly than the ministers) prudence and modesty, and that they love their husbands and children with an ordered and Christian love; and that they be temperate, chaste, keepers of the house, not wandering outside the family, kind, and obedient to their husbands, lest Christian doctrine be spoken ill of because of them.

units.la: Vers. 6. Adolescentes itidem adhortare, ut sint temperantes.
units.tr: Verse 6. Likewise exhort the young men to be sober-minded.

units.la: Tertio loco, De adolescentibus præcipit Tito, ut hortetur adolescentes ad temperantiam.
units.tr: In the third place, concerning young men, he commands Titus to exhort them to temperance.

units.la: Vers. 7. Per omnia teipsum præbens exemplar bonorum operum, in doctrina, integritatem, gravitatem,
units.tr: Verse 7. In all things showing thyself a pattern of good works: in doctrine showing uncorruptness, gravity,

units.la: Vers. 8. Sermonem sanum, qui damnari non possit: ut qui, se ex adverso opponit, erubescat, nihil habens quod de vobis dicat malì.
units.tr: Verse 8. Sound speech that cannot be condemned; that he who is of the contrary part may be ashamed, having nothing evil to say of you.

units.la: Quarto loco, De Pastoribus in persona Titi, in eum finem, Ut melius reciperetur ipsorum doctrina, præcipit ut Titus seipsum præbeat in omni bono opere exemplar, aliis imitandum; speciatim vero, ut in doctrina ostendat integritatem purræ veritatis, gravitatem autoritatis, & loquendi modum ædificationi auditorum accommodatum teneat, ne adversarius possit aliquid in ipso carpere merito.
units.tr: In the fourth place, concerning the ministers, in the person of Titus, with the aim that their doctrine be better received, he commands that Titus present himself as an example in every good work for others to imitate; and specifically, that in his teaching he show the integrity of pure truth and the gravity of authority, and keep a manner of speaking suited to the edification of his hearers, so that the opponent may find nothing justly to carp at in him.

units.la: Verf. 9. Servos hortare ut suis Dominis subjiciant se, ut in omnibus sint eis accepti, non respondatores:
units.tr: Verse 9. Exhort servants to be obedient unto their own masters, and to please them well in all things; not answering again;

units.la: Verf. 10. Nihil intervertentes, sed omnem bonam fidem ostendentes, ut doctrinam Servatoris nostri Dei ornent in omnibus,
units.tr: Verse 10. Not purloining, but shewing all good fidelity; that they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things.

units.la: Quinto loco de servis præcipit, Ut servos instituat de officiis: 1 Ut suis dominis (licet infidelibus) se subjiciant, in omnibus licitis eis morem gerentes: 2. Ut servi studeant heris suis placere, seu grata facere, nec illis respondeant, quando mandata ipsis dant duriora, aut severius quam æquum esset ipsos objurgant: 3. Denique, ne quid furrurentur ab heris, sed Fideles se præstent in omnibus. Cujus rationem addit, ut doctrina Euangelii ornetur ab iis in omnibus, & agnoscatur esse divina, utpote quæ adeo efficax sit, ut etiam homines in durissima conditione servitutis positos, conditionis suæ patientes, & in vocatione probos & fideles reddat.
units.tr: In the fifth place, concerning servants, he commands that servants be instructed in their duties: (1) that they submit to their masters (even unbelieving ones), obeying them in all lawful things; (2) that servants strive to please their masters and do what is agreeable to them, and not answer back when masters give harsher commands or rebuke them more severely than is fair; (3) finally, that they not steal anything from their masters, but show themselves faithful in all things. He adds the reason: that the doctrine of the Gospel be adorned by them in all things and acknowledged as divine, since it is so effective that it makes even men placed in the hardest condition of slavery patient in their lot, and upright and faithful in their calling.

units.la: Secunda pars Capitis,
units.tr: Second Part of the Chapter.

units.la: Verf. 11, Illuxit enim gratia illa Dei salutifera omnibus hominibus.
units.tr: Verse 11. For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men.

units.la: Altera pars Capitis de doctrina Fidei, quam subnectit quasi fontem, unde hauriatur virtus ad præstandum prædicta officia: nam officia Christiana esse non possunt, nisi ex Christo per fidem hauriatur gratia ad præstandum ea. Hoc enim interest inter opera materialiter bona renatorum, & irregenitorum. Quod horum opera fiant à Dei inimicis, ex liberi arbitrii corruptis viribus, propter fines carnales, absque voluntatis, vel gloriæ Divinæ intuitu: illorum vero opera fiant à servis Dei per fidem reconciliatis, ex fonte salutaris gratiæ Christi, cognitione & virtute ad agendum haultâ. Proponitur autem hæc fidei doctrina, per modum confirmationis præceptorum, seu doctrinæ de moribus. Rationes auones autem sunt quatuor, quae omnes probant praedictis virtutibus studendum esse.
units.tr: The second part of the chapter concerns the doctrine of faith, which he adds as a fountain from which the power to perform the aforesaid duties is drawn; for Christian duties cannot be performed unless grace to perform them is drawn from Christ through faith. For this is the difference between the materially good works of the regenerate and of the unregenerate: the works of the latter are done by enemies of God, from the corrupt powers of free will, for carnal ends, without regard to the will or glory of God; but the works of the former are done by servants of God reconciled through faith, from the fountain of Christ's saving grace, with knowledge and power to act drawn from it. This doctrine of faith is set forth by way of confirming the precepts, or the doctrine of morals. There are four reasons, all of which prove that one must strive for the aforesaid virtues.

units.la: Illuxit ] Ratio prima, Quia Euangelium gratiae DEI afferens salutem omnis generis hominibus, promulgatum seu patefactum, illuxit omnis generis hominibus. Ergo aequum est, ut omnis ordinis homines gratitudinem erga DEUM in sancta conversatione ostendant, praedictis virtutibus studendo.
units.tr: Illuxit] First reason: because the Gospel of the grace of God, bringing salvation to men of every kind, has been published and made manifest, and has shone upon men of every kind. Therefore it is fitting that men of every rank show gratitude to God in holy conduct, by striving for the aforesaid virtues.

units.la: Verf. 12. Erudiens nos ut abnegata impietate & mundanis cupiditatibus, temperanter, & juste, & pie vivamus in praesenti seculo:
units.tr: Verse 12. Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world:

units.la: Secunda Ratio, Quia hoc DEI Euangelium non solum docet nos quae officia praestare teneamur, sed etiam instituit quomodo vires hauriamus ex fonte gratiae CHRISTI, ex fonte mortis & resurrectionis ipsius, ad abnegandam impietatem, & mundanas cupiditates, & ad vivendum temperanter, quod ad nosipsos attinet, juste quod ad proximos, & pie quod ad DEUM spectat: Ideo his officiis praestandis accingere nos debemus.
units.tr: Second reason: because this Gospel of God not only teaches us what duties we are bound to perform, but also shows us how to draw strength from the fountain of Christ's grace, from the fountain of his death and resurrection, to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts, and to live soberly as regards ourselves, righteously as regards our neighbours, and godly as regards God. Therefore we ought to gird ourselves to perform these duties.

units.la: Verf. 13. Expectantes beatam illam spem & illustrem illum adventum gloriae magni illius Dei ac Servatoris nostri, nempe IESV CHRISTI:
units.tr: Verse 13. Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour, namely Jesus Christ:

units.la: Ratio 3. Quia expectamus vitam aeternam in secundo adventu CHRISTI, qui est magnus DEUS, unus cum PATRE ac SPIRITU Sancto, & Servator noster. Ergo animari & excitari decet nos ad studendum, praedictis & omnibus bonis operibus, quae DEUS requirit a nobis.
units.tr: Third reason: because we look for eternal life at the second coming of Christ, who is the great God, one with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and our Saviour. Therefore it is fitting that we be stirred and roused to strive for the aforesaid and all the good works which God requires of us.

units.la: Verf. 13. Qui dedit semetipsum pro nobis, ut redimeret nos ab omni iniquitate, & purificavit sibi ipsi populum peculiarem studiosum bonorum operum.
units.tr: Verse 13. Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works.

units.la: Ratio 4. Quia ideo se obtulit pro nobis CHRISTUS, ut nos redimeret efficaciter a peccati servitute, & acquireret nos sibi quasi in peculium, ut studiosi essemus bonorum operum: Ergo nisi redemptionem velemus irritam esse erga nos, necessario renunciandum est peccato, & studendum praedictis virtutibus, & omnigenae vitae novitati.
units.tr: Fourth reason: because Christ therefore offered himself for us, that he might effectually redeem us from the slavery of sin and acquire us for himself as a special possession, zealous of good works. Therefore, unless we wish his redemption to be made void toward us, we must necessarily renounce sin and strive for the aforesaid virtues and for newness of life in every kind.

units.la: Verf. 15. Haec loquere & exhortare, & argue cum omni imperio, nemo te despiciat. Repetit mandatum de doctrina curanda, jubens, ut in his insistat, & immoretur, id est, ut aculeos addat hortationum & objurgationum cum auctoritate: Quam auctoritatem ne despiciat quisquam ex Professoribus, vetat, & ne ipse Titus quicquam admittat quod eum contemptui exponeret.
units.tr: Verse 15. These things speak, and exhort, and rebuke with all authority. Let no man despise thee. He repeats the command to take care over doctrine, bidding him persist and dwell in these things, that is, to add the goads of exhortation and rebuke with authority; and he forbids any of the teachers to despise this authority, and forbids Titus himself to admit anything that would expose him to contempt.

units.la: Caput Tertium.
units.tr: Chapter Three.

units.la: DErgit Titum in officio instituere, in quem supra addit alia octo mandata.
units.tr: He instructs Titus in his duty, to whom he adds eight further commands above.

units.la: Verf. 1. Suggere ipsis, ut sese subjiciant principibus, ac potestatibus, ut obtemperent, ut ad omne opus bonum sint parati:
units.tr: Verse 1. Remind them to submit themselves to rulers and authorities, to obey them, and to be ready for every good work:

units.la: Primum mandatum, ut praecipiat Christianis omnibus, ut placide colant ordinem politicum, id est, Ut subjiciant se supremo Magistratui & Potestati inferiori, seu magistratibus inferioribus, ut obediant edictis & legibus politicis, & ad omne opus bonum, cui promovendo constituuntur Magistratus, alacres se praestent & paratos.
units.tr: The first command: that he should instruct all Christians to live peacefully under the civil order, that is, to submit themselves to the supreme magistrate and to the lesser authorities, or inferior magistrates, obeying their edicts and civil laws, and showing themselves eager and ready for every good work, to whose advancement the magistrates are appointed.

units.la: Verf. 2 Ne cujus famam laedant, ut sint à pugnis alieni, moderati, omnem exhibentes lenitatem erga quosvis homines.
units.tr: Verse 2. Let them speak evil of no one, be peaceable, not quarrelsome, showing all gentleness towards all people.

units.la: Secundum mandatum de officiis charitatis erga quosvis extra Ecclesiam, vel intra eam: officia haec sunt quatuor: 1. Ut aliorum famae consulant nemini maledicentes: 2. Ut sint à contentione & pugnis alieni: 3. Ut moderationi & aequitati studeant, parati (ubi opus est) cedere de suo privato jure: 4. Ut mansuetudinem & lenitatem oltendant erga quosvis homines etiam pessimos.
units.tr: The second command concerns the duties of charity towards all, whether outside the Church or within it. These duties are four: (1) to care for the reputation of others, speaking evil of no one; (2) to keep away from strife and quarrels; (3) to aim at moderation and fairness, being ready (where necessary) to give up their own private right; (4) to show meekness and gentleness towards all people, even the most wicked.

units.la: Verf. 3. Nam eramus quondam & nos amentes, rebelles, errantes, servientes cupiditatibus ac voluptatibus variis, in malitia & invidia degentes, odiosi, alii alios odio prosequentes:
units.tr: Verse 3. For we too were once foolish, disobedient, deceived, slaves to various desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, hating one another:

units.la: Rationes mansuetudinis exercendae erga quosvis reddit duas.
units.tr: He gives two reasons for practising gentleness towards all.

units.la: Ratio prima, Quia nos quoque ante conversionem tales eramus, quales nunc sunt illi, nempe eramus omnes per naturam multis nominibus culpandi interim tamen cupiebamus humaniter & leniter tractari ab omnibus: Ergo pari ratione agamus cum iis qui nondum conversi sunt. Morbos naturæ enumerat quinque: 1. Eramus amentes, qua mera vanitas elt tota hominum sapientia, quandiu Deum non cognoscimus, ignoramus enim rectam regulam, & fontem verum, & debitum finem actionum nostrarum: 2. rebelles, Quia nihil eorum quæ vel Deus, vel conscientia præcipit, faciunt homines per naturam, sed quod sibi, ipsis placet tantùm: 3. Errantes nempe à vera via quæ ducit ad vitam æternam, & erroribus decepti longius à Deo indies recedentes 4. Servientes cum delectatione cupiditatibus & voluptatibus variis, quæ regnant simul, & quasi per vices imperium oltentant in omnibus irregenitis: 5. Destituti eramus verâ dilectione Dei & proximi, degentes in malitia & invidia, lætantes de malo, & tristantes de bono proximorum; alii alios odio habentes, interim omnes & singuli odio Dei dignissimi eramus.
units.tr: The first reason: because we too, before our conversion, were such as those now are, indeed we were all by nature open to blame in many ways, yet we wished to be treated kindly and gently by everyone. Therefore, by the same reasoning, let us act in this way towards those who are not yet converted. He lists five diseases of nature: (1) we were foolish, since all human wisdom is mere vanity as long as we do not know God; for we are ignorant of the right rule, the true fountain, and the proper end of our actions; (2) disobedient, because by nature men do nothing that either God or conscience commands, but only what pleases themselves; (3) deceived, namely straying from the true way that leads to eternal life, and, deceived by errors, withdrawing further from God every day; (4) slaves with delight to various desires and pleasures, which reign together and by turns exercise dominion over all the unregenerate; (5) destitute; we lacked true love of God and neighbour, living in malice and envy, rejoicing in our neighbours' misfortunes and grieving at their good, hating one another; and meanwhile each and all of us deserved the hatred of God.

units.la: Verf. 4. Sed postquam bonitas & erga homines amor apparuit Servatoris nostri Dei,
units.tr: Verse 4. But when the kindness and love of God our Saviour towards mankind appeared,

units.la: Ratio 2. Quia nos quantumvis perversi fuerimus, tandem per Dei gratiam tamen converti sumus. Ergo debemus lenitatem erga non conversos exercere, & bene de iis sperare, qui eâdem divinâ gratiâ poterint similiter converti.
units.tr: The second reason: however perverse we were, we have nevertheless at last been converted by the grace of God. Therefore we ought to show gentleness towards those who are not converted, and to hope well of those who, by that same divine grace, may likewise be converted.

units.la: Benignitas ] Hanc rationem explicat, & gratiam nobis factam in conversione commendat, & probat undecim rationibus: 1. Ex causa remotiori bonitate (scilicet & benignitate Dei, quæ in commodum nostrum gaudet se exerere & nobis bonum communicare· 2. Ex causa propinquiori, quæ est φιλανθρωπια, seu dilectio illa quâ Deus prosequitur humanum genus supra omnes alias creaturas: 3. Ex instrumentali causa, seu modo revelationis Euangelii, quod non minus gratiosè nobis illuxit, & sine nostra procuratione, vel opera editum est, quam Sol (unde similitudo illucescendi ducitur) oritur sine opera nostra super nos: 4. A causa proxima conversionis, quæ est efficax manifestatio Dei, ut Salvatoris, facta nobis qui simul ac cordibus nostris se manifestat, non ut judicem nostrum qui nos condemnet, sed ut Servatorem nostrum, qui nos salvos præstet illico, per hanc sui manifestationem trahit cor nostrum ad se, & convertit nos.
units.tr: Kindness. He explains this reason, commends the grace shown to us in our conversion, and proves it by eleven arguments: (1) from the more remote cause, the goodness (namely the kindness of God, which delights to show itself for our benefit and to communicate good to us); (2) from the nearer cause, which is philanthropy, or that love by which God regards the human race above all other creatures; (3) from the instrumental cause, that is, the manner in which the gospel was revealed, which shone upon us no less graciously and was published without any effort or work of ours, just as the sun (from which the image of shining is taken) rises upon us without our labour; (4) from the proximate cause of conversion, which is the effective manifestation of God as Saviour, made to us, who, as soon as he reveals himself to our hearts, not as a judge who would condemn us but as our Saviour who would at once make us safe, draws our heart to himself and converts us through this manifestation of himself.

units.la: Verf. 5. Non ex operibus justis quæ fecerimus nos, sed ex sua misericordia misericordia servavit nos per lavacrum regenerationis, & renovationem Spiritus sancti:
units.tr: Verse 5. Not by works of righteousness which we had done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit:

units.la: Ratio quinta à remotione omnium operum nostrorum, & omnis meriti in nobis, aut nostris operibus, quae vel tempore praecesserunt efficacem vocationem nostri, vel quae praevideri, & quasi fecisse mus, considerari poterant: 6. Expresse affirmando misericordiam esse causam salutis: 7. Deum Autorem statuendo Sacramentorum, seu mediorum Salutis externorum, & simul etiam Autorem regenerationis, seu renovationis nostri; atque ita mediorum salutis internorum, per quae perducimur ad salutem (idem intellige de aliis mediis) quae non sunt à nobis, sed à Spiritu Sancto, seu Deo solo Autore: Qui solus sine nobis lavacrum Baptismi instituit pro Sacramento, & gratiam obsignatam per Baptismum (nempe ablutionem à lordibus peccatorum, & renovationem imaginis Dei, in sanctitate & justitia) solus operatur in nobis.
units.tr: The fifth reason, drawn from the removal of all our works and all merit in us or in our works, which either came before the effectual calling of us, or which could be foreseen and, as it were, considered as already done. (6) By expressly affirming that mercy is the cause of salvation; (7) by declaring God to be the author both of the sacraments, or external means of salvation, and at the same time also the author of our regeneration or renewal, and thus of the internal means of salvation through which we are led to salvation (understand the same of other means), which are not from us but from the Holy Spirit, or from God alone as author. He alone, without us, instituted the washing of baptism as a sacrament, and he alone works in us the grace sealed through baptism (namely the cleansing from the filth of sins and the renewal of the image of God in holiness and righteousness).

units.la: Verf. 6. Quem effudit in nos copiose per Iesum Christum servatorem nostrum:
units.tr: Verse 6. Which he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Saviour:

units.la: 8. A gratiarum Spiritus Sancti in nos copiose effusarum causa meritoria, quae est, Iesus Christus Servator noster: & fons à quo, & canalis per quem, gratia Dei ad nos derivatur.
units.tr: (8) From the meritorious cause of the gifts of the Holy Spirit poured out upon us abundantly, which is Jesus Christ our Saviour, and the fountain from which, and the channel through which, the grace of God flows down to us.

units.la: Verf. 7. Ut justificati ipsius gratia, haeredes efficeremur secundum spem vitae aeternae.
units.tr: Verse 7. That, being justified by his grace, we should be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life.

units.la: 9. A natura justificationis gratuitae, siquidem non ex operibus justificamur sed ex Christi gratia: 10. A modo adeundi vitam aeternam, ad cujus possessionem, non ut emptores, seu mercatores, sed ut haeredes constituti, admittimur: 11. A causa instrumentali, spe, seu fide, quae promissionibus Dei gratuitis nititur, (non meritis ullis nostris) & opera nostra prorsus excludit, siquidem haeredes efficimur vitae, secundum spem, quam Dei promissiones nobis fecerunt.
units.tr: (9) From the nature of free justification, since we are justified not by works but by the grace of Christ; (10) from the manner of obtaining eternal life, to the possession of which we are admitted not as buyers or merchants but as appointed heirs; (11) from the instrumental cause, hope or faith, which rests on the free promises of God (not on any merits of ours), and utterly excludes our works, since we are made heirs of life according to the hope which God's promises have given us.

units.la: Verf. 8. Fidus est hic sermo, & haec volo te affirmare, ut studeant bona opera tueri qui crediderunt Deo, id est quae sunt honesta & hominibus utilia.
units.tr: Verse 8. This is a faithful saying, and these things I want you to affirm, so that those who have believed God may be careful to maintain good works, that is, things which are honourable and useful to men.

units.la: Verf. 9 Stultas autem quaestiones, & genealogias & contentiones ac pugnas legales cohibe; sunt enim inutiles & vanae.
units.tr: Verse 9. But avoid foolish questions, genealogies, contentions and legal strifes; for they are unprofitable and vain.

units.la: Tertium mandatum, Ut cum doctrina fidei conjungat, & pro auctoritate urgeat, doctrinam bonorum operum ex fontibus fidei educendorum, curetque ut fideles, Patroni sint bonorum operum, siquidem gratis donati sunt vitâ. Rationes mandati addit duas: Ratio 1. Quia termo de hoc mandato fide dignus est, & maximè necessarius, & verus seu fidelis, qui obedientes minimè frustretur, aut fallat.
units.tr: The third command: that he should join the teaching of good works, drawn from the fountains of faith, with the doctrine of faith, and press it with authority, and see to it that believers are patrons of good works, since they have been freely given life. He adds two reasons for the command. Reason 1: because the matter of this command is trustworthy and very necessary, and true or faithful, which will not disappoint or deceive those who obey it.

units.la: Ratio 2, Quia hujus generis doctrina bona est, & utilis hominibus, quia ad Deum glorificandum, & ad seipsos confirmandum, de certitudine salutis, & ad alios in fide ædificandum, & ad infideles convertendum, conducit.
units.tr: Reason 2: because this kind of teaching is good and useful to men, since it serves to glorify God, to strengthen themselves in the certainty of their salvation, to build up others in faith, and to convert unbelievers.

units.la: Mandatum 4. Ut compescat curiosas quæstiones, quibus homines solent se intricare & impedire, ne quid fixum in veritate agnita teneant: quales sunt quæstiones Genealogicæ, seu Chronologicæ: & Eristicæ disputationes, & pugnæ de legalibus ceremoniis, & similes.
units.tr: The fourth command: that he should restrain curious questions, in which men are accustomed to entangle and hinder themselves, so that they do not hold anything fixed in the truth they have acknowledged. Such are genealogical or chronological questions, contentious disputes, quarrels about legal ceremonies, and the like.

units.la: Rationem addit. Quia etiamsi illæ quæstiones sapientiam præ se ferant, stultæ tamen sunt & vanæ & inutiles, siquidem ad ædificationem in fide & sanctitate vitæ nihil conducunt.
units.tr: He adds a reason: even if those questions show a kind of wisdom, they are nevertheless foolish, vain and unprofitable, since they contribute nothing to edification in faith and holiness of life.

units.la: Vers. 10. Hæreticum hominem post unam & alteram admonitionem rejice:
units.tr: Verse 10. Reject a heretical man after one or two warnings.

units.la: Mandatum 5. In quo præcipit Apostolus Tito, vt hæreticum homi-nem, seu eum qui sanæ doctrinæ contrarium tenet, & in Ecclesia sestam facsitat, seu unitatem Ecclesiæ errore aliquo suo rumpit (publicè convictum coram Presbyterio, & admonitum semel atque iterum) per excommunicationem tandem rejiciat, nec se & Ecclesiam plus quam satis est istiusmodi hominum disputationibus fatiget, vel tempus docendæ Ec-clesiæ destinatum amittat, frustra cum perversis hominibus disputando.
units.tr: The fifth command, in which the Apostle orders Titus to finally reject by excommunication a heretical man, that is, one who holds something contrary to sound doctrine and makes a schism in the Church, or breaks the unity of the Church by some error of his (having been publicly convicted before the presbytery and admonished once and again), and not to weary himself and the Church more than enough with disputes of such men, or lose the time destined for teaching the Church, by disputing in vain with perverse men.

units.la: Vers. 11. Vt qui norit eversum esse eum qui sit ejusmodi, & peccare, & qui suo prejudicio sit condemnatus.
units.tr: Verse 11. That he who is such a man knows that he has been overturned, and sins, and has been condemned by his own judgment.

units.la: Rationem addit, Quia frustra disputatur adversus pervicacitatis jam convictum; nam à veritate cecidit, & eversus est ita, ut non patiatur se ædificari amplius, & respuendo lucem in admonitionibus oblatam, con-scientiæ suæ vim se facere manifestum facit.
units.tr: He adds the reason: because it is in vain to dispute against one who is already convicted of obstinacy; for he has fallen from the truth and has been overturned, so that he no longer allows himself to be built up, and by rejecting the light offered in admonitions he makes it plain that he does violence to his own conscience.

units.la: Vers. 12. Cum misero Artemas ad te aut Tychicum, stude venire ad me Nicopolin; nam illic decrevi hybernare.
units.tr: Verse 12. When I send Artemas to you, or Tychicus, make haste to come to me at Nicopolis; for I have decided to winter there.

units.la: Mandatum 6. privatum est, Quo revocat Titum ex Creta, & jubet eum Nicopolin venire, ubi Apostolus non videtur fuisse, quum hæc scriberet (sicut adjectio imperiti librarii alicujus post Epistolam, statuit) sed ibi hiematurus erat.
units.tr: Command 6, considered private. By it he recalls Titus from Crete and bids him come to Nicopolis, where the Apostle does not seem to have been when he wrote these things (as the addition of some unskilled copyist after the Epistle asserts), but where he was going to spend the winter.

units.la: Verf. 13. Zenam legisperitum & Apollo sedulo educito, ne-quid illis desit.
units.tr: Verse 13. Diligently send on Zenas the lawyer and Apollos, so that nothing is lacking to them.

units.la: Mandatum 7. etiam privatum, Ut viaticum suppeditetur Zenæ & Apollo, viris Scripturarum consultis, sed minimè opulentis.
units.tr: Command 7, also private: that provision for the journey be supplied to Zenas and Apollos, men versed in the Scriptures, but by no means wealthy.

units.la: Verf. 14. Discant autem & nostri bona opera tueri ad necessarios usus, ut non sint infrugiferi.
units.tr: Verse 14. And let our people also learn to maintain good works for necessary uses, so that they may not be unfruitful.

units.la: Mandatum 8. Ut doceat non solum fideles de populo, sed etiam Evangelii prædicatores, seu eos qui Pastoralis sunt ordinis, ut exemplo suo aliis præeant ex facultatibus suis contribuendo, ubi necessitas requirit: Cujus ratio additur, ne dum alios hortantur ad bona opera, ipsi fructibus carere videantur.
units.tr: Command 8: that he should teach not only the faithful of the people, but also the preachers of the Gospel, that is, those who belong to the pastoral order, so that by their example they may go before others, contributing from their means where need requires. The reason is added: lest, while they exhort others to good works, they themselves seem to lack fruits.

units.la: Verf. 14. Salutant te qui mecum sunt omnes, Saluta eos qui diligunt nos in fide. Gratia Dei sit cum omnibus vobis. Amen.
units.tr: Verse 14. All who are with me greet you. Greet those who love us in the faith. The grace of God be with you all. Amen.

units.la: Concludit Epistolam: 1. Missis salutationibus à fratribus ad Titum: 2. Salutationibus à se missis, ad fideles Cretenses: 3. Benedictione Apostolicâ, quâ non Titum solum complectitur, sed Ecclesias etiam in quarum usum Scripta est hæc Epistola, votum suum, & veritatem totius doctrinæ obsignans suo, AMEN.
units.tr: He concludes the Epistle: (1) with greetings sent by the brothers to Titus; (2) with greetings sent by himself to the faithful Cretans; (3) with the apostolic blessing, by which he embraces not Titus alone but also the churches for whose use this Epistle was written, sealing his prayer and the truth of the whole doctrine with his AMEN.

units.la: EXPOSITIO ANALYTICA EPISTOLÆ PAULI, AD PHILEMONEM.
units.tr: Analytical Exposition of Paul's Epistle to Philemon.

units.la: EX Tasforibus Colossensibus unus Philemon, servum habebat Onesimum, qui furto admisso, fugitivus Romam venit, & speciali DEI providentiâ, audito Paulo qui in vinculis Romæ prædicabat Euangelium, conversus est ad fidem. Hunc Onesimum remittit Apostolus ad Dominum suum Philemonem, & multis Argumentis veniam illi dandam precatus, contendit, ut in gratiam reciperetur. Quoniam autem Spiritus Sanctus in Onesimi negotio specimen extare voluit, & divinæ dilectionis suæ, & officii nostri erga pœnitentes, licet fortis inter homines abjectissimæ, idcirco in communem & perpetuam Ecclesiæ ædificationem, locum huic Epistolæ inter reliquas canonicas concedi voluit Deus.
units.tr: Philemon, one of the Colossians, had a slave named Onesimus, who, having committed a theft, fled to Rome. By a special providence of God, he heard Paul preaching the gospel there while in chains, and was converted to the faith. The Apostle sends this Onesimus back to his master Philemon, and, asking with many arguments that he be pardoned, urges that he be received back into favour. Since the Holy Spirit wished to set forth in the affair of Onesimus an example both of his own divine love and of our duty toward penitents, however lowly the man is among men, God willed that this Epistle be given a place among the other canonical books, for the common and lasting edification of the Church.

units.la: Partes Epistolæ sunt tres: Prima est præfatio accommodata ad propositum, ad versum octavum, Altera continet petitionis Argumenta, ut restituatur Onesimus, ad versum 21. Tertia est Epilogus.
units.tr: The Epistle has three parts: the first is a preface suited to the purpose, up to verse 8; the second contains the arguments for petitioning that Onesimus be restored, up to verse 21; the third is the conclusion.

units.la: Versus 1. Paulus captivus Iesu Christi, & Timotheus frater, Philemoni dilecto, & adjutori nostro,
units.tr: Verse 1. Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, and Timothy our brother, to Philemon our beloved and fellow-worker,

units.la: Directio Epistolæ eosdem habet salutantes cum Epistola ad Colossenses, quæ una cum hac, scripta & missa esse videtur per Tychicum, & hunc Onesimum, quem Apostolus jam conversum ad fidem, commendat Ecclesiæ Colossensi, Cap. 4. verf. 7, 8. 9.
units.tr: The address of the Epistle greets the same persons as the Epistle to the Colossians, which together with this one seems to have been written and sent by Tychicus and this Onesimus, whom the Apostle now commends, as one already converted to the faith, to the Colossian Church. Chap. 4, verses 7, 8, 9.

units.la: De Pauli Apostolatu non dubitabat Philemon, ideo de eo hic non loquitur Apostolus, sed de vinculis suis, propter Euangelium Christi honorificis; adjungit Timotheum fratrem, ut socium petitionis futurum. Vocat Philemonem primo Dilectum; deinde Cooperarium, scilicet in Euangelii prædicatione, ut viam pararet ad demulcendum Philemonis animum.
units.tr: Philemon did not doubt Paul's apostleship, so the Apostle does not speak of it here, but of his chains, which were an honour because of the gospel of Christ. He adds Timothy as a brother, so that he would be a partner in the petition. He calls Philemon first "beloved," then "fellow-worker," namely in the preaching of the gospel, in order to prepare the way for soothing Philemon's spirit.

units.la: Versus 2. Et Apphiæ dilectæ, & Archippo commilitoni nostro, & quæ domi tuæ est Ecclesiæ:
units.tr: Verse 2. And to Apphia our beloved, and Archippus our fellow-soldier, and to the Church in your house:

units.la: Versus 3. Gratia sit vobis & pax à Deo Patre nostro, & Domino Iesu Christo.
units.tr: Verse 3. Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

units.la: Uxorem Philemonis Appiam ut in Christo dilectam salutat, quippe cujus negotium commune cum marito agebatur in recipiendo servo fugitivo, addit & totam familiam, quam Philemon, ut Ecclesiam regebat: Et Archippum Pastorem Ecclesiæ, & Collegam Philemonis, ut plures haberet qui in petitione auxiliarios se præstarent, quos omnes in salutatione simul complectitur Apostolicæ benedictionis gremio.
units.tr: He greets Philemon's wife Apphia as beloved in Christ, since she shared with her husband the business of receiving the runaway slave. He adds the whole household, which Philemon governed as a Church. And he greets Archippus, the minister of the Church and colleague of Philemon, so that Philemon would have more helpers to support the petition. He embraces them all together in the bosom of the Apostolic blessing.

units.la: Versus 4. Gratias ago Deo meo, semper mentionem tui faciens in precibus meis,
units.tr: Verse 4. I thank my God, always making mention of you in my prayers,

units.la: Conciliat porro Philemonis benevolentiam, reliqua proœmii parte quatuor argumentis: 1. Quod simul gratias agat pro donis Spiritus Sancti Philemoni datis, simul etiam precetur pro donorum incremento.
units.tr: Further, he wins Philemon's goodwill in the rest of the preface by four arguments: 1. He gives thanks for the gifts of the Holy Spirit bestowed on Philemon, and at the same time prays for the increase of those gifts.

units.la: Verf. 5. Audiam tuam charitatem, ac fidem quam habes erga Dominum Iesum, & erga omnes sanctos:
units.tr: Verse 5. I hear of your love and the faith which you have toward the Lord Jesus, and toward all the saints:

units.la: Arg. 2. Specialius à commendatione fidei ipsius in CHRISTUM, & charitatis inde profluentis erga omnes homines, præcipuè verò erga Sanctos: quæ duo totam hominis Christiani perfectionem continent, & hæc est gratiarum actionis pro Philemone materia.
units.tr: Argument 2. More specifically, he commends Philemon's faith in Christ and the love flowing from it toward all men, and especially toward the saints. These two make up the whole perfection of a Christian man, and this is the matter of thanksgiving for Philemon.

units.la: Verf. 6. Ut communicatio fidei tuæ efficax fiat, ut agnoscatur quicquid boni est in vobis per Christum Iesum.
units.tr: Verse 6. That the fellowship of your faith may become effective, so that every good thing among you in Christ Jesus may be acknowledged.

units.la: Arg. 3. à voto, Ut fides ipsius per bonos fructus efficaciam suam ita demonstraret, ut in honorem CHRISTI ab omnibus magis magisque agnosceretur, sincera gratia CHRISTI in ipso, & uxore ipsius latens, & hæc est precationis pro Philemone, materia.
units.tr: Argument 3, from his prayer: that Philemon's faith might show its effectiveness through good fruits, so that it might be more and more acknowledged by all to the honour of Christ, the sincere grace of Christ being hidden in him and in his wife. This is the matter of the prayer for Philemon.

units.la: Verf. 7. Gaudium enim habemus multum, & consolationem super dilectione tua, quod viscera sanctorum refocillata sunt per te, frater.
units.tr: Verse 7. For we have great joy and consolation in your love, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you, brother.

units.la: Arg. 4. Ex lætitia quam habebat ex eo quod Philemon piorum necessitatibus opem ita tulerit, ut omnes se ab ipso recreatos ex intimis quasi visceribus agnoverint.
units.tr: Argument 4, from the joy he had because Philemon had brought help to the needs of the godly in such a way that all acknowledged themselves refreshed by him from their very inmost hearts.

units.la: Secunda pars.
units.tr: Second part.

units.la: Verf. 8. Quapropter quamvis multam in Christo libertatem habeam mandandi tibi quod officii tui est,
units.tr: Verse 8. Wherefore, though in Christ I have much liberty to command you what is your duty,

units.la: Secunda pars Epistolæ, in qua Apostolus petit, ut Philemon in gratiam recipiat Onesimum, fugitivum servum suum. Argumenta sunt in hunc finem 14: Argumentum primum, Pro jure Apostolatus imperare possum, quod tui est officii: Ergo recipiendus est in Gratiam Onesimus, ubi officium in hoc negotio tibi ostendero.
units.tr: The second part of the Epistle, in which the Apostle asks that Philemon receive Onesimus, his runaway slave, back into favour. There are fourteen arguments to this end. The first argument: I could command by the right of my apostleship what is your duty; therefore Onesimus is to be received into favour, when I show you what your duty in this matter is.

units.la: Verf. 9. Tamen propter charitatem potius precor, quum talis sim, nempe Paulus senex, nunc autem etiam captivus Iesu Christi.
units.tr: Verse 9. Yet for love's sake I rather beg, since I am such a one, namely Paul, an old man, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ.

units.la: Arg. 2. Etiamsi possem tibi imperare in hoc negotio, malo tamen ex dilectione tui, imperio abstinere, & humiliter te rogare: Ergo concedendum est quod peto de Onesimo.
units.tr: Argument 2. Even if I could command you in this matter, I prefer nevertheless, out of love for you, to refrain from commanding and to ask you humbly. Therefore what I ask concerning Onesimus must be granted.

units.la: Talis Arg. 3. Seni jam Paulo, & Christi in vinculis captivo, & humiliter à te petenti id quod honestum & factu facile est, annuere debes, & quod gratum ei esse posset, facere. Concedendum ergo quod de Onesimo requiro.
units.tr: Such Argument 3. You ought to grant, as an old man now, a prisoner in Christ's chains, asking you humbly, what is honourable and easy to do, and to do what could be pleasing to him. Therefore what I request concerning Onesimus must be granted.

units.la: Verf. 10. Precor autem pro filio meo, quem genui in vinculis meis, Onesimo:
units.tr: Verse 10. I beg you for my son, whom I begot in my chains, Onesimus:

units.la: Arg. 4. Petitio mea est pro Onesimo servo tuo, quem in vinculis jacens, ex vinculis Satanæ per Euangelium ad CHRISTI fidem liberavi, & quem non minùs charum habeo, quam genuinum filium meum. Ergo eum recipe.
units.tr: Argument 4. My request is for Onesimus your slave, whom, lying in chains, I freed from the chains of Satan through the gospel to the faith of Christ, and whom I hold no less dear than my own begotten son. Therefore receive him.

units.la: Verf. 11. Quondam tibi inutili, nunc verò tibi & mihi perutili, quem remisi:
