units.la: Verf. 7. Nonne blasphemant praeclarum illud nomen a quo estis cognominati?
units.tr: Verse 7. Do not they blaspheme that worthy name by which ye are called?

units.la: Arg. 4. Hac prosopolepsia dedecore afficitis Pauperes, quos Deus honoravit, eligendo eos in haeredes regni sui, ornando eos divitiis melioribus quam sunt hae mundanae; divitiis nempe fidei & dilectionis Dei, & promissionibus haereditatis coelorum, quae gratiae sunt salvisicae. Ergo prosopolepsia vitanda est.
units.tr: Fourth argument: By this partiality you put shame upon the poor, whom God has honoured by choosing them as heirs of his kingdom, adorning them with better riches than these worldly ones: namely, the riches of faith and of the love of God, and the promises of the inheritance of heaven, which are the gifts of saving grace. Therefore partiality is to be avoided.

units.la: Nonne Divites] Arg. 5. Quia per hanc prosopolepsiam, eousque inconsiderationis provecti estis, ut honoretis publicos Euangelii hostes, (qui neque Magistratus respectu, nec ullo alio quam Divitiarum nomine honorabiles sunt, sed tyrannice usurpant in vos jus non datum ipsis, opprimunt vos, deferunt vestra nomina ad judices, & corpora ad tribunalia trahunt, & blasphemant Christi nomen gloriosum, unde vos denominamini Christiani) quae summa est stultitia. Ergo prosopolepsia, est vitanda.
units.tr: Do not the rich] Fifth argument: Through this partiality you have advanced so far in thoughtlessness that you honour the public enemies of the Gospel. These men are not honourable by reason of any magistracy, nor by any name other than that of wealth; rather they usurp tyrannically a right not given to them, oppress you, bring your names before judges, drag your persons to the tribunals, and blaspheme the glorious name of Christ, from which you are named Christians. This is the height of folly. Therefore partiality is to be avoided.

units.la: Verf. 8. Siquidem Legem regiam praestatis secundum Scripturam, Diliges proximum tuum ut teipsum, bene facitis.
units.tr: Verse 8. If ye fulfil the royal law according to the Scripture, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself, ye do well.

units.la: Verf. 9 Sin vero personam respicitis, peccatum committitis, & redarguimini a Lege, veluti transgressores.
units.tr: Verse 9. But if ye have respect to persons, ye commit sin, and are convicted of the law as transgressors.

units.la: Arg. 6. Per occupationem objectionis, Quia in hac prosopolepsia redarguimini a lege, ut transgressores. Nam in respectum illum civilem, qui communiter debetur unicuique, secundum conditionem externam & civilem, & secundum merita uniuscujusque distribueretis, excusari potestis, si lautioris fortunae hominibus, quod aequum est, daretis, & fratribus vestris fidelibus, quod aequum est, non detrahueretis, servientes regiae legi Dei regis regum, secundum communem regulam dilectionis mensuram communicando aliis, sicut ipsi justam mensuram expectare potestis ab aliis, tum quidem absolvi potestis, Verf. 8. Sed cum indebitum honorem datis divitibus; pauperibus vero fidelibus debitum respectum non datis, jam personas accipitis, & peccati rei tenemini, & legis transgressores estis: Ergo prosopolepsia vitanda est.
units.tr: Sixth argument, by anticipating an objection: In this partiality you are convicted by the law as transgressors. For you could be excused from that civil respect which is owed commonly to everyone according to outward and civil condition and the merits of each, if you gave to men of better fortune what is fitting, and did not withhold from your faithful brethren what is fitting too, serving the royal law of God, the King of kings, by communicating to others, according to the common rule of love, the measure you yourselves may expect from others. Then indeed you could be acquitted (verse 8). But since you give undue honour to the rich, and do not give due respect to the poor believers, you now accept persons, are held guilty of sin, and are transgressors of the law. Therefore partiality is to be avoided.

units.la: Verf. 10. Quisquis enim totam Legem servaverit, offenderit autem in uno, omnibus tenetur.
units.tr: Verse 10. For whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all.

units.la: Arg. 7. confirmans superius, Si indulgeatis vobis in una hac Prosopolepsia, in pauperum fidelium contemptu, rei peragendi eritis totius Legis, etiamsi prae vobis feratis observationem omnium reliquorum praeceptorum, excepto hoc unico, Quia quisquis offenderit in unico praecepto, tenetur violationis omnium reus, non quod in uno peccato concurrant omnia, sed quia est copulatio praeceptorum omnium in una justitiae regula, & eadem authoritas Dei in omnibus violatur in aliquo uno; & ita reatus generalis omnium legum, seu maledictio Dei attrahitur per unius legis violationem, etiamsi in specialibus gradibus reatus & maledictionis discrimen maneat. Ergo Prosopolepsia vitanda est.
units.tr: Seventh argument, confirming what was said above: If you indulge yourselves in this one partiality, in contempt of poor believers, you will be guilty of the whole law, even if you profess to observe all the other precepts, with the exception of this one. For whoever offends in one precept is guilty of violating all, not because all sins meet in one sin, but because all the precepts are linked together in one rule of righteousness, and the single authority of God is violated in any one of them. Thus the general guilt of all the laws, or the curse of God, is incurred by the violation of one law, even though in the particular degrees there remains a difference of guilt and of curse. Therefore partiality is to be avoided.

units.la: Verf. 11. Nam qui dixit, Ne moecheris, dixit etiam, Ne occidas. Quod si non fueris moechatus, occideris autem, factus es transgressor Legis.
units.tr: Verse 11. For he that said, Do not commit adultery, said also, Do not kill. Now if thou commit no adultery, yet if thou kill, thou art become a transgressor of the law.

units.la: Confirmat hoc Argumentum in exemplo sexti & septimi mandati, in quorum alterius violatione, violatur authoritas mandantis utrumque.
units.tr: He confirms this argument by the example of the sixth and seventh commandments, in the violation of either of which the authority of the one commanding both is violated.

units.la: Verf. 12. Ita loquimini & ita facite ut per Legem libertatis judicandi.
units.tr: Verse 12. So speak ye, and so do, as they that shall be judged by the law of liberty.

units.la: Arg. 8. per modum hortationis propositum, Sic loquendum & faciendum vobis est erga pauperes fideles praecipue, ut judicandos vos sciatis sine acceptione personarum, secundum doctrinam Euangelii quae prosopolepsiam prohibet: Ergo.
units.tr: Eighth argument, put forward by way of exhortation: So you must speak and act towards your poor believers especially, knowing that you are to be judged without acceptance of persons, according to the doctrine of the Gospel, which forbids partiality. Therefore...

units.la: Verf. 13. Nam damnatio absque misericordia erit ei qui non praestiterit misericordiam, & gloriatur misericordia adversus damnationem.
units.tr: Verse 13. For he shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy; and mercy rejoiceth against judgment.

units.la: Arg. 9. Nisi misericordiam exerceatis, praecipue erga fratres vestros pauperes & afflictos, metuendum vobis erit judicium sine misericordia. Ergo cavenda Prosopolepsia.
units.tr: Ninth argument: Unless you exercise mercy, especially towards your poor and afflicted brethren, you will have reason to fear judgment without mercy. Therefore partiality is to be guarded against.

units.la: Gloriatur Arg. 10. & ultimum, Si misericordiam exerceatis, praecipue erga pauperes & afflictos fratres, prout Euangelium requirit, non erit quod metuat s iram seu judicium sine misericordia, sed de misericordia Dei ex hoc signo certi esse poteritis, quâ freti gloriari vobis licebit contrà judicii meri severitatem, utpote à qua per misericordiam Dei liberati estis. Ergo nisi misericordiae renunciare, & judicio vosmet obnoxios reddere vultis, cavenda vobis est haec cum crudelitate iuncta prosopolepsia.
units.tr: Rejoiceth] Tenth and last argument: If you exercise mercy, especially towards your poor and afflicted brethren, as the Gospel requires, you will have no cause to fear wrath or judgment without mercy. From this sign you will be able to be certain of the mercy of God, and relying on it you may rightly glory against the severity of strict judgment, since through the mercy of God you have been delivered from it. Therefore, unless you wish to renounce mercy and make yourselves liable to judgment, this partiality, joined as it is with cruelty, must be avoided.

units.la: Secunda pars.
units.tr: The second part.

units.la: Verf. 14. Quae utilitas, fratres mei, si fidem dicat aliquis habere se, opera vero non habeat? num poterit fides illa eum servare?
units.tr: Verse 14. What good is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can that faith save him?

units.la: Altera admonitio ad vitandam vanitatem iactantiae de fide otiosa: Propositio statuitur primis verbis, Quod inutilis seu vana sit professio fidei, quae destituitur operibus. Hanc probat Argumentis novem. Arg. 1. Quia fides istiusmodi quae destituitur fructibus, non potest iactantem de fide hac inani servare. Ergo vana est ejus professio.
units.tr: This is the second warning, against the vanity of boasting of an idle faith. The proposition is laid down in the first words: a profession of faith that lacks works is useless or vain. He proves it by nine arguments. Argument 1: faith of this kind, which lacks fruits, cannot save the one who boasts of this empty faith. Therefore its profession is vain.

units.la: Verf. 15. Quod si frater aut soror nudi fuerint, & egentes quotidiano victu:
units.tr: Verse 15. If a brother or sister is naked and lacks daily food,

units.la: Verf. 16 Dicat autem eis aliquis vestrum, Abite cum pace, calescite & saturamini: non tamen dederitis eis quae sunt apta corpori, quae erit utilitas?
units.tr: Verse 16. and one of you says to them, Go in peace, be warmed and filled, yet you do not give them what the body needs, what good is that?

units.la: Arg. 2. à pari, Verbalis professio charitatis otiosae, est inanis & inutilis, & profitenti, & famelico: cui verba pro cibo dantur. Ergo etiam & professio fidei otiosa, inanis est.
units.tr: Argument 2, from parity: a merely verbal profession of idle charity is empty and useless, both to the one who professes it and to the hungry person, to whom words are given in place of food. Therefore an idle profession of faith is empty too.

units.la: Verf. 17. Ita quoque fides, si opera non habeat, mortua est per se.
units.tr: Verse 17. So also faith, if it does not have works, is dead in itself.

units.la: Arg. 3. Charitas quae consistit tantum in orali professione, mortua est: Ergo etiam & fides quae consistit in orali professione, sine operibus, mortua est & inanis.
units.tr: Argument 3: charity that consists only in an spoken profession is dead. Therefore faith too, which consists in a spoken profession without works, is dead and empty.

units.la: Verf. 18. Quinimo dicet aliquis, Tu fidem habes, & ego opera habeo: ostende mihi fidem tuam ex operibus tuis, & ego ostendam tibi ex operibus meis fidem meam,
units.tr: Verse 18. Indeed someone will say, You have faith, and I have works: show me your faith without your works, and I will show you my faith from my works.

units.la: Arg. 4. Talis fidei professio convincitur vanitatis cum ad examen ventum fuerit, ut apparet in suppositione Dialogi instituti inter vere fidelem, qui fidem potest suam ex operibus ostendere, & iactabundum hypocritam, qui ex vita & operibus non potest fidem suam demonstrare. Ergo ista fidei iactantia est vana & inutilis.
units.tr: Argument 4: a profession of such faith is convicted of vanity when it is brought to the test, as appears from the imagined dialogue set up between the truly faithful man, who can show his faith from his works, and the boastful hypocrite, who cannot demonstrate his faith from his life and works. Therefore this boasting about faith is vain and useless.

units.la: Verf. 19. Tu credis Deum unum esse, recte facis: & daemonia credunt, & horrescunt.
units.tr: Verse 19. You believe that God is one; you do well. The demons also believe, and shudder.

units.la: Arg. 5. Fides quae dicitur historica, qua creditur veritati articulorum fidei de unitate Dei & similibus, licet hactenus bona sit, non sufficit ad salutem, non est salvifica fides; quia & Dæmones veritati Verbi Divini credunt, & contremiscunt. Ergo multò minus prodest ad salutem, vana fidei professio, quæ operibus destituitur.
units.tr: Argument 5: the faith called historical, by which one believes the truth of the articles of faith concerning the unity of God and similar matters, though good so far as it goes, does not suffice for salvation; it is not saving faith, because the demons too believe the truth of the Word of God and tremble. Therefore a vain profession of faith that is destitute of works is much less profitable for salvation.

units.la: Verf. 20 Vis verò nosse, homo vane, fidem illam quæ est absque operibus, mortuam esse?
units.tr: Verse 20. But do you wish to know, vain man, that faith without works is dead?

units.la: Arg. 6. per colloquutionem propositum, Qui nititur vel gloriatur tali fide quæ otiosa est, ignorans eam esse mortuam, homo vanus est & inanis, sicut vas, quo magis vacuum est, eo majorem sonitum edens: Et hic sibi parat viam ad Argumentum septimum.
units.tr: Argument 6, proposed by way of address: the one who relies on or boasts of an idle faith, not knowing that it is dead, is a vain and empty man, like a vessel that, the emptier it is, the louder the noise it makes. And here he prepares his way to the seventh argument.

units.la: Verf. 21. Abraham pater ille noster, nonne ex operibus justificatus est, quum obtulisset Isaac filium suum super altare?
units.tr: Verse 21. Was not our father Abraham justified by works, when he offered his son Isaac upon the altar?

units.la: Arg. 7. Probans fidem sine operibus esse mortuam, & per consequens vanam esse professionem fidei quæ caret operibus, ab exemplo Abrahami, qui in causa prædicta de fide demonstranda, vivane an mortua esset, justus compertus & declaratus est ex operibus, & hic per interrogationem urget conscientiam hypocritæ. Abraham Pater Fidelium justificatus est coram toto mundo, quod fides ejus non fuerit mortua, sed viva, ex operibus ejus, cum obtulisset Isaac filium suum super altare, in testimonium sinceritatis fidei ipsius, seu quod vivâ fide crediderit in Deum, & non placuerit sibi in vanâ professione otiosæ seu mortuæ fidei, sicut multi faciunt. Ergo fides quæ est sine operibus est fides mortua & inanis. Atque ita Jacobo optimè convenit cum Paulo; nam Rom 4. 2 Paulus sic ratiocinatur, Si Abraham justificatus est ex operibus, habuit de quo gloriaretur, sed non coram Deo, subaudi, habuit de quo gloriatur. Ergo coram Deo non est justificatus operibus. Jacobus verò sic ratiocinatur, Abraham justificatus est ex operibus coram hominibus, qui dicerent ei, Ostende mihi fidem tuam per opera tua; seu, Demonstra mihi quod tua fides non sit mortua, sed viva: Ex quo Antecedente sequitur non tantum, Ergo fides sine operibus est mortua, sed etiam Conclusio consentiens cum Pauli Conclusione. Ergo Abraham justificatus est coram Deo, non fide illâ mortuâ, & operibus cassâ, sed fide vivâ, & in operibus efficaci: atque ita optimè convenit inter Apostolos.
units.tr: Argument 7: proving from the example of Abraham that faith without works is dead, and consequently that a profession of faith lacking works is vain. In the matter of demonstrating faith, whether it is living or dead, Abraham was found and declared righteous by his works. Here he presses the conscience of the hypocrite by a question. Abraham, father of the faithful, was justified before the whole world, showing that his faith was not dead but living, by his works, when he offered his son Isaac upon the altar, as a testimony to the sincerity of his faith, that is, that he believed in God with a living faith and did not take pleasure in the empty profession of an idle or dead faith, as many do. Therefore faith that is without works is dead and empty. And so James agrees very well with Paul. For Paul reasons thus in Rom. 4. 2: If Abraham was justified by works, he had something to boast of, but not before God; understand, he has something to boast of. Therefore he was not justified before God by works. James, however, reasons thus: Abraham was justified by works before men, who would say to him, Show me your faith by your works; that is, prove to me that your faith is not dead but living. From this antecedent follows not only the conclusion, Therefore faith without works is dead, but also a conclusion agreeing with Paul's conclusion. Therefore Abraham was justified before God not by that dead faith, emptied of works, but by a living faith that is effective in works. And so the Apostles agree very well.

units.la: Verf. 22 Vides fidem administram fuisse operum ipsius, & ex operibus fidem perfectam fuisse?
units.tr: Verse 22. You see that faith was active together with his works, and that by his works faith was made perfect?

units.la: Hanc esse mentem Jacobi ipse declarat convincendo jactabundum hypocritam gloriantem de mortua fide, ex eo quod Abrahæ fides una cum professione fidei junxerit opera, ita ut ex operibus fides ejus perfecta, non inanis seu mortua inventa, & declarata sit.
units.tr: James himself declares that this is his meaning, when he convicts the boastful hypocrite who glories in a dead faith: Abraham's faith, joined with the profession of faith, also brought forth works, so that by those works his faith was found and declared to be perfect, not empty or dead.

units.la: Verf. 23. Itaque impleta est Scriptura quae dicit, Credidit autem Abraham Deo, & imputatum est ei ad justitiam, & amicus Dei vocatus est.
units.tr: Verse 23. And so the Scripture was fulfilled which says, Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness, and he was called the friend of God.

units.la: Hinc etiam infert expositionem Scripturae, quam citat Paulus in causa justificationis per fidem; atque ita consensum suum cum Paulo plene demonstrat. Cum fides Abrahae perfecte declarata est ex operibus, seu fructibus ejus, tum plana declaratum est quam vere Scriptura dixerit, Credidit, &c. Atque ita cum dicitur fides imputata esse Abrahamo ad justitiam conflat, intelligendam esse fidem non mortuam, sed vivam illam, & operibus efficacem, & hanc expositionem Scripturae esse impletionem, seu hunc esse plenum sensum illius Scripturae, Iacobus hic ostendit; Dicit Abrahamum vocatum esse Dei amicum, ut intelligamus solidam cum Deo reconciliationem, per fidem effici, & veram amicitiam, per fidei manifestationem in operibus obedientiae, demonstrari.
units.tr: From this he also draws an explanation of the Scripture, which Paul cites in the matter of justification by faith; and so he fully demonstrates his agreement with Paul. Since Abraham's faith was perfectly declared by his works, or fruits, it is plainly shown how truly the Scripture said, He believed, etc. And so when it is said that faith was imputed to Abraham for righteousness, it is clear that it must be understood as the living faith, not the dead one, the faith that is effective in works; and James shows that this explanation of the Scripture is its fulfilment, or its full sense. He says that Abraham was called the friend of God, so that we may understand that a solid reconciliation with God is effected through faith, and that true friendship is demonstrated through the manifestation of faith in works of obedience.

units.la: Verf. 24. Videtis igitur ex operibus justificari hominem, & non ex fide tantum?
units.tr: Verse 24. You see then that a man is justified by works, and not by faith only?

units.la: Ex his sequitur conclusio, contra jactantiam hypocritarum, de inani sua fide, quod omnes fidem profitentes coram hominibus, justificentur ex operibus, & non ex fidei professione tantum, seu non ex mortua & inani fide, quam vos hypocritae jactatis.
units.tr: From these things follows the conclusion, against the boasting of hypocrites about their empty faith: all who profess faith before men are justified by works, and not by a mere profession of faith, that is, not by the dead and empty faith that you hypocrites boast of.

units.la: Verf. 25. Similiter autem etiam Rahab illa meretrix, annon ex operibus justificata est, quum excepisset nuntios, & alia via emisisset?
units.tr: Verse 25. Likewise also Rahab the harlot, was she not justified by works, when she received the messengers and sent them out by another way?

units.la: Arg 8. Rahab meretrix justificata est (coram Israele, scilicet, quod vere crediderit in Deum, & vere conversa fuerit) ex operibus; cum excepisset hospitio nuncios Israelis, & salvos dimisisset. Ergo inanis est professio otiosae fidei. Quod Iacobus justificationem non aliter accipiat quam diximus, apparet ex eo quod Rahab meretricem vocet, seu foedis libidinibus prostitutam, quam idcirco impossibile fuit coram Deo justificari ex operibus, sed tantum ex fide vera quae operibus se veram ostendit.
units.tr: Argument 8: Rahab the harlot was justified (before Israel, that is, in that she truly believed in God and was truly converted) by works, in that she received the messengers of Israel into her house and sent them away safe. Therefore the profession of an idle faith is empty. That James does not understand justification otherwise than we have said appears from the fact that he calls Rahab a harlot, that is, one prostituted to foul lusts; for it was therefore impossible for her to be justified before God by works, but only by a true faith, which showed itself true by its works.

units.la: Verf. 26. Nam sicut corpus absque spiritu mortuum est, ita & fides illa quae est absque operibus, mortua est:
units.tr: Verse 26. For as the body without the spirit is dead, so also faith without works is dead.

units.la: Arg. 9. Quemadmodum corpus animalis, si non spirat, mortuum est: ita fides, si non producit opera, mortua est: Ergo inanis est illiusmodi fidei mortuæ jactantia, in qua sibi hypocritæ placent.
units.tr: Argument 9: just as the body of an animal, if it does not breathe, is dead, so faith, if it does not produce works, is dead. Therefore the boasting of such dead faith, in which hypocrites take pleasure, is empty.

units.la: Caput Tertium.
units.tr: Chapter Three.

units.la: HOC capite habentur duæ admonitiones: Prima, de gubernanda lingua, ad versi. 13. Altera de sapientiâ, quæ malam linguæ compescit, & rixas seu contentiones vitat, ad finem.
units.tr: In this chapter there are two admonitions: the first, about governing the tongue, at verse 13; the second, about wisdom, which restrains the evil tongue and avoids quarrels and strife, to the end.

units.la: Vers. 1. NE sitis multi magistri, fratres mei scientes, ut gravius judicium auferamus.
units.tr: Verse 1. Be not many masters, my brethren, knowing that we shall receive the greater judgment.

units.la: Quod ad primam admonitionem, frænari linguam & cohiberi jubet nominatim ab invectivis & rigidis alienorum vitiorum, vel infirmitatum exaggerationibus. Ne estote, inquit, multi magistri, id est, ne arrogate vobis magisterii in alios autoritatem, & nimiam quævis carpendi licentiam, ut multi faciunt, sed frænate linguas vestras. Admonitionem confirmat argumentis decem.
units.tr: As to the first admonition, he orders the tongue to be bridled and restrained, especially from invectives and harsh exaggerations of other people's faults and weaknesses. Be not, he says, many masters, that is, do not arrogate to yourselves authority to teach others, nor take excessive licence to find fault with everything, as many do, but bridle your tongues. He confirms this admonition with ten arguments.

units.la: Scientes ] Argumentum primum, Quia iniqui censores gravius judicium auferent à Deo Vindice injuriarum: Frænanda igitur lingua, nisi gravius auferre judicium vultis.
units.tr: Knowing] First argument: because unfair critics will receive a greater judgment from God, the Avenger of wrongs. The tongue must therefore be bridled, unless you wish to incur the greater judgment.

units.la: Vers. 2. In multis enim labimur omnes. Si quis in sermone non labitur, hic perfectus est vir, ut qui possit frano moderari totum etiam corpus.
units.tr: Verse 2. For in many things we all offend. If anyone offends not in word, the same is a perfect man, and able also to bridle the whole body.

units.la: Arg. 2. Cum omnes obnoxii simus multis lapsibus, clementius decet nos agere cum aliorum infirmitatibus, nec judicandi autoritatem arrogare sine vocatione, nec in judicio iniquiores nos ostendere.
units.tr: Argument 2. Since we are all liable to many falls, it becomes us to deal more gently with the weaknesses of others, neither to arrogate the authority of judging without a calling, nor to show ourselves more unjust in judgment.

units.la: Si quis ] Arg. 3. Si quis modum linguæ ponere novit, argumentum habet perfecti, seu sinceri hominis, qui moderari potest omnes actiones suas, & contrà, qui linguam suam non potest cohibere, quin carpat in omnibus, aliorum mores, indicium habet hypocritæ: Frænanda ergo lingua.
units.tr: If anyone] Argument 3. If anyone knows how to set a limit to his tongue, that is a sign of a perfect or sincere man, who can govern all his actions. On the contrary, the man who cannot restrain his tongue, but carps at the conduct of others in everything, has the mark of a hypocrite. The tongue must therefore be bridled.

units.la: Vers. 3. Ecce, equis frena in ora immittimus, ut obediant nobis, & totum corpus eorum circumagimus:
units.tr: Verse 3. Behold, we put bits into the mouths of horses, that they may obey us, and we turn about their whole body.

units.la: RRRR Verf. 4. Ecce, naves quoque, quum tanta sint, & à ventis favis agantur, circumaguntur à minimo gubernaculo quocunque libet ab gubernatoris voluntate:
units.tr: Verse 4. Behold, the ships also, though they are so great and are driven by strong winds, are turned about by a very small helm, wherever the will of the steersman pleases.

units.la: Verf. 5. Ita & lingua pusillum membrum est, & magna jactat. Ecce, exiguus ignis quantam materiam incendit.
units.tr: Verse 5. So the tongue also is a little member, and boasts great things. Behold, how small a fire kindles how great a matter!

units.la: Verf. 6 Lingua etiam flamma est, & mundus iniquitatis: ita inquam lingua constituta est inter membra nostra, maculans totum corpus, inflammans orbem conditum, & inflammata à gehenna.
units.tr: Verse 6. The tongue also is a fire, a world of iniquity. So is the tongue placed among our members, defiling the whole body, setting on fire the course of nature, and set on fire by hell.

units.la: Arg. 4 confirmans superius, Sicut si regas frænum, etiam regas equum, & si clavum regas, etiam & navim; Sic etiam si linguam recte gubernaveris, etiam totum corpus, & externas actiones gubernabis; licet instrumenta pusilla sint illa, & pusillum membrum lingua. Frænanda ergo.
units.tr: Argument 4, confirming what was said above: just as, if you govern the bit, you also govern the horse, and if you govern the helm, you also govern the ship, so too, if you govern the tongue rightly, you will govern the whole body and its outward actions, although those instruments are small and the tongue is a little member. It must therefore be bridled.

units.la: Et sese ] Arg. 5. Lingua effert se magnifice, & jactat se gloriose quod pollit in utramque partem, & multum boni in veritate, constantia, taciturnitate, urbanitate, & similibus præstare; & multum etiam mali, immendaciis, conviciis, calumniis, & similibus. Ergo summa cura regenda & gubernanda est.
units.tr: And boasts] Argument 5. The tongue puffs itself up magnificently and vaunts itself boldly, since it can work in either direction: it can accomplish much good by truthfulness, steadfastness, silence, courtesy and the like, and also much evil by lies, reproaches, calumnies and the like. It must therefore be ruled and governed with the greatest care.

units.la: Ignis ] Arg. 6. Quia sicut ignis exiguus quantumvis materiæ accendere & depascere potest, sic lingua nisi compescatur, & frænetur, mundum malorum excitare, infinita peccata procreare potest: & cum corporis exigua sit pars, potest reliqua omnia membra, & totum corpus sceleribus involvere & fœdare, & rotam naturalium facultatum omnium, suis vitiis inflammare. Ergo studiose gubernanda est.
units.tr: Fire] Argument 6. Just as a small fire can kindle and consume any amount of matter, so the tongue, unless it is restrained and bridled, can stir up a world of evils and beget endless sins. Since it is only a small part of the body, it can entangle and defile all the remaining members and the whole body in wickedness, and set on fire the whole wheel of our natural faculties by its vices. It must therefore be governed diligently.

units.la: A Gehenna ] Arg. 7. Linguæ malæ cum inferno & Diabolo affinitas quædam est, cui lingua servire parata est, & ab eo flammam mendaciorum, calumniarum, & rixarum ad totum orbem accendendum transmittere. Magno ergo studio ad eam regendam opus est.
units.tr: From hell] Argument 7. The evil tongue has a certain kinship with hell and the Devil, whom the tongue is ready to serve, and from whom it sends forth the flame of lies, calumnies and quarrels to set the whole world on fire. Great zeal is therefore needed to rule it.

units.la: Verf. 7. Omnis enim natura & ferarum & volucrum, serpentiumque & marinorum, domatur, & domita est à natura humana.
units.tr: Verse 7. For every nature of beasts, and of birds, and of serpents, and of things in the sea, is tamed and has been tamed by human nature.

units.la: Verf. 8 Linguam autem nullus hominum domare potest, malum est quod coercere non possis: plena est veneno mortifero.
units.tr: Verse 8. But the tongue no man can tame; it is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison.

units.la: Arg. 8. Nullum est genus animalium quod domari non possit ab humana ratione, seu arte: & experientia docet omnis generis aliqua, ab hominibus cicurata esse, verf. 7 Verum linguam nulla humana ratio, seu ars cicurare potest, quia malum inquietum & indomitum suâ natura est, plena veneno mortifero, quo aliis lethales noxas infert, & inferre parata est. Ergo ut gratiâ Dei supernaturali frænetur lingua studiosius curandum est.
units.tr: Argument 8. There is no kind of animal that cannot be tamed by human reason or skill, and experience teaches that animals of every kind have been domesticated by men (verse 7). But no human reason or art can tame the tongue, since by its nature it is a restless and untamable evil, full of deadly poison, by which it inflicts, and is ready to inflict, lethal harm on others. Therefore, that the tongue may be bridled by the supernatural grace of God, we must take more earnest care.

units.la: Verf. 9. Per ipsam benedicimus Deo & Patri, & per ipsam maledicimus hominibus qui ad similitudinem Dei conditi sunt.
units.tr: Verse 9. With it we bless God, even the Father, and with it we curse men, who are made after the similitude of God.

units.la: Verf. 10. Ex eodem ore procedit benedictio & maledictio. Non oportet, fratres mei, hæc ita fieri.
units.tr: Verse 10. Out of the same mouth proceeds blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be.

units.la: Arg. 9. Lingua varia, subdola, versipellis est, nunc fe simulans optimam, Deo benedicendo; nunc naturam suam aperte prodens, expresse maledicendo hominibus, Deo vero obliquè, ad cujus similitudinem homines facti sunt, ex eodem ore emittens nunc benedictionem, nunc maledictionem, verf. 9. At hoc absurdum est, & monstri simile, quod minimè tolerandum est, verf. 10 Ergo gubernandæ linguæ necessario studendum est.
units.tr: Argument 9. The tongue is changeable, deceitful and fickle: sometimes it feigns itself most excellent by blessing God; sometimes, betraying its own nature openly, it expressly curses men, and God only indirectly, although men were made in his likeness, pouring out from the same mouth now blessing, now cursing (verse 9). But this is absurd and monstrous and in no way to be tolerated (verse 10). Therefore we must necessarily give diligence to governing the tongue.

units.la: Verf. 11. Nunquid fons ex eodem foramine manat dulcem & amaram aquam?
units.tr: Verse 11. Does a fountain send out from the same opening sweet water and bitter?

units.la: Verf. 12. Nunquid potest, fratres mei, ficus oleas edere, aut vitis ficus? ita nullus fons falsam & dulcem aquam potest edere.
units.tr: Verse 12. Can the fig tree, my brethren, bear olives, or a vine figs? So no fountain can yield both salt and sweet water.

units.la: Arg. 10. Confirmans superius, per quadruplex simile fontis, ficus, vitis, & maris. Argumentatur autem ab eo, quod est impossibile fecundùm naturam, ad absurdum in moribus: Quemadmodum natura non patitur, ut ex eodem fontis foramine, emanet dulcis aqua & amara, vel ut ficus uvas ferat, & vitis ficus, vel idem fons marinus fallam & dulcem aquam reddat: Ita ratio non finit ut credamus eam esse renovati hominis linguam, quæ licet aliquando benedicat, eftrænis tamen fertur alias ad maledicendum: Arbor enim mala non fert fructus bonos. Ergo decet regenitos simplicitatem sanctitatis in sermone sectari, & frænandæ linguæ operam dare.
units.tr: Argument 10, confirming what was said above by the fourfold likeness of a fountain, a fig tree, a vine and the sea. It argues from what is impossible according to nature to an absurdity in morals. Just as nature does not allow sweet and bitter water to flow from the same opening of a spring, or a fig tree to bear grapes, or a vine figs, or the same sea to yield salt and sweet water, so reason does not allow us to believe that the tongue of a regenerate man is such that, although it sometimes blesses, it is nevertheless carried at other times to cursing. For a bad tree does not bear good fruit. Therefore regenerate persons ought to pursue simplicity and holiness in speech, and to take pains to bridle the tongue.

units.la: Secunda pars.
units.tr: Second Part.

units.la: Verf. 13. Quis sapiens & scientia præditus est inter vos? demonstret ex bona conversatione opera sua, cum mansuetudine sapientiæ.
units.tr: Verse 13. Who among you is wise and endowed with knowledge? Let him show his works by good conduct, in the meekness of wisdom.

units.la: Altera admonitio, in qua hortatur ad sapientiam, cum mansuetudine conjunctam, quæ malis linguæ & æmulationibus afferat remedium. Propositio ponitur hoc versu, Si quis fe prudentem Christianum vult ostendere, innocentiæ & mansuetudinis operibus id ostendere debet, Argumenta sunt sex.
units.tr: This is the second admonition, in which he urges wisdom joined with meekness, which provides a remedy for the evils of the tongue and for rivalries. The proposition is laid down in this verse: if anyone wishes to show himself a wise Christian, he ought to demonstrate it by works of innocence and meekness. There are six arguments.

units.la: Ves. 14. Quòd si invidiam amaram habetis, & irritationem, in corde vestro, ne gloriamini, & ne mendaces estote adversus veritatem.
units.tr: Verse 14. But if you have bitter envy and rivalry in your hearts, do not boast, and do not be liars against the truth.

units.la: Argumentum primum, Si quis omissâ mansuetudine, foveat in corde contraria vitia, æmulationem & contentionem, non est quod glorietur de tali sapientia, sed quod pudesiat potius. Ergo sapientiæ mansuetæ studendum,
units.tr: First argument: if someone, having set aside meekness, nurtures contrary vices in his heart, namely rivalry and contention, he has no reason to boast of such wisdom, but rather reason to be ashamed. Therefore wisdom must be pursued together with meekness.

units.la: Mendaces ] Arg. 2. Qui omissâ mansuetudine in cordibus fovent æmulationem & contentionem, mendaces sunt adversus veritatem, id est, falsò jactitant se omninò sapere, vel Christianos esse, qui operè se improbos demonstrant: Ergo sapientiæ cum mansuetudine junctæ studendum est.
units.tr: Liars: Arg. 2. Those who, having set aside meekness, nurture rivalry and contention in their hearts, are liars against the truth; that is, they falsely claim that they are wise in every way, or that they are Christians, when by their deeds they show themselves wicked. Therefore wisdom joined with meekness must be pursued.

units.la: Vers. 15. Non est enim ista sapientia superne descendens, sed terrena, animalis, dæmoniaca.
units.tr: Verse 15. For this wisdom does not come down from above, but is earthly, animal, demonic.

units.la: Arg. 3. Sapientia rixandi, invidendi, injurias privatas vindicandi, non est illa quæ cœlitus descendit à Deo, sed terrena, animalis, diabolica, à corruptâ naturâ, & diabolo originem habens. Ergo sapientiæ mansuetæ studendum est.
units.tr: Arg. 3. The wisdom that quarrels, envies, and avenges private injuries is not that wisdom which comes down from heaven from God, but is earthly, animal, diabolical, having its origin in corrupt nature and in the devil. Therefore wisdom joined with meekness must be pursued.

units.la: Vers 16 Ubi enim invidia est & irritatio, ibi tumultuatio, & omne opus pravum.
units.tr: Verse 16. For where there is envy and rivalry, there is tumult and every wicked work.

units.la: Arg. 4. confirmans superius, Ubi non est sapientia cum mansuetudine, sed invidia & contentio, ibi tumultus, seditiones, & omne scelus regnat. Ergo sapientiæ cum mansuetudine studendum est.
units.tr: Arg. 4, confirming the above: where there is not wisdom with meekness, but envy and contention, there tumults, seditions, and every crime hold sway. Therefore wisdom with meekness must be pursued.

units.la: Vers. 17. Quæ autem superne est sapientia primum quidem pura est, deinde pacifica, moderata, tractabilis, plena misericordiâ & fructuum bonorum, absque dijudicatione, sine simulatione.
units.tr: Verse 17. But the wisdom that is from above is first indeed pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, without hypocrisy.

units.la: Arg 5. Ab octo proprietatibus cœlestis sapientiæ illius, quæ cum mansuetudine conjungitur, Sapientia cum mansuetudine conjuncta, 1. Pura & casta est, i. tenax veritatis & sanctitatis, ne quovis modo poluatur: 2. Pacifica, & abhorrens à contentionibus: 3. Æquitatis studiosa: 4 Facilè cedens rationi rectæ: 5. Plena misericordiâ erga errantes & peccantes: 6. Plena bonorum fructuum, nihil omittens eorum quæ bonum & pium virum decent: 7. Non inquirens in aliorum nævos sufpiciosè: 8. Sine simulatione, quâ carnalis sapientia delectatur maximè. Ergo sapientiæ cum mansuetudine junctæ studendum est.
units.tr: Arg. 5. From the eight properties of that heavenly wisdom which is joined with meekness: wisdom joined with meekness (1) is pure and chaste, that is, holds fast to truth and holiness, lest it be polluted in any way; (2) is peaceable and abhors contentions; (3) is eager for fairness; (4) readily yields to right reason; (5) is full of mercy toward the erring and sinning; (6) is full of good fruits, omitting nothing that befits a good and pious man; (7) does not suspiciously pry into the faults of others; (8) is without hypocrisy, in which carnal wisdom takes the greatest delight. Therefore wisdom joined with meekness must be pursued.

units.la: Vers. 18, Fructus autem justitiæ cum pace seritur iis qui dant operam paci.
units.tr: Verse 18. But the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who work for peace.

units.la: Arg. 6. Qui huic sapientiæ cum mansuetudine junctæ student, dum student pacem facere, seu pacifici esle ipsi: 1. In pace sunt: 2. Justitiam operantur, seu sanctitatem suam augent: 3. Sementem faciunt sibi ipsis in tempus futurum, & in vitam æternam, ut fructum justitiæ metant tempore destinato: Ergo huic sapientiæ studendum est.
units.tr: Arg. 6. Those who strive for this wisdom joined with meekness, while they strive to make peace, or to be peacemakers themselves: (1) they are in peace; (2) they work righteousness, or increase their own holiness; (3) they make a sowing for themselves for the time to come and for eternal life, so that they may reap the fruit of righteousness at the appointed time. Therefore this wisdom must be pursued.

units.la: Caput Quartum.
units.tr: Chapter Four.

units.la: Res hoc capite continentur admonitiones: Prima, ad curandum morbum carnalium cupiditatum, ad vers. 11. Secunda, ad diminutionem & lœsionem famæ fratrum vitandam, ad vers. 13. Tertia, ad corrigendum contemptum di-vinæ providentiæ, in negotiis & consiliis exequendis.
units.tr: This chapter contains admonitions. The first, to cure the disease of carnal desires, is on verse 11; the second, to avoid diminishing and harming the reputation of brothers, is on verse 13; the third, to correct contempt of divine providence in carrying out affairs and plans.

units.la: Vers. 1. Unde bella, & lites inter vos? nonne hinc, nimirum ex voluptatibus vestris, quæ militant in membris vestris.
units.tr: Verse 1. Whence come wars and quarrels among you? Do they not come from this, namely from your pleasures, which wage war in your members?

units.la: Quod ad primam attinet, Argumenta dehortationis à carnalibus cupiditatibus sunt novem: ex quibus, sex priora malum ostendunt, tria postrema remedia continent.
units.tr: As far as the first admonition is concerned, the arguments for dissuasion from carnal desires are nine. Of these, the first six show the evil, and the last three contain the remedies.

units.la: Argumentum primum, Ex cupiditatibus, quæ intus in visceribus inter se quasi digladiantur, & militant adversus salutem & corporis & animæ, oriuntur rixæ, contentiones, & bella inter homines, quales cupiditates sunt avaritia, ambitio, libido, & similes. Ergo ab iis cavendum est.
units.tr: First argument: from desires which fight among themselves within the inner parts, as if with swords, and wage war against the health of both body and soul, arise quarrels, contentions, and wars among men. Such desires are avarice, ambition, lust, and the like. Therefore one must beware of them.

units.la: Vers. 2. Concupiscitis, & non habetis: invidetis & studiosè assectatis, nec potestis assequi: pugnatis & bellatis, non tamen obtinetis, propterea quòd non petitis.
units.tr: Verse 2. You desire and do not have; you envy and eagerly pursue, and cannot attain; you fight and make war, yet do not obtain, because you do not ask.

units.la: Arg. 2. Cupiditates fatigant vos laboribus inutilibus, cruciant vestros animos, in discrimen vitæ multiplex impellunt, à Deo legitimisque mediis, quibus aliquid obtinere potuissetis, avellunt: Ergo ab iis vobis cavendum est. Verf. 3. Petitis, & non accipitis, eo quòd male petatis, ut in voluptates vestras insumatis,
units.tr: Arg. 2. Desires wear you out with fruitless labours, torment your minds, drive you into manifold dangers to life, and tear you away from God and from the lawful means by which you could have obtained something. Therefore you must beware of them. Verse 3. You ask and do not receive, because you ask badly, so that you may spend it on your pleasures.

units.la: Arg. 3. Si quando licitis & probatis mediis utimini: Exempli causa, In precatione ad Deum, cupiditates sese pro fine precationum vestrarum obtrudentes, preces vestras, & omnia reliqua media vitiant, polluunt, & fructu omni vos privant. Ergo ab iis vobis cavendum est
units.tr: Arg. 3. If at any time you use lawful and approved means: for example, in prayer to God, desires thrusting themselves forward as the goal of your prayers corrupt and defile your prayers and all the other means, and deprive you of all fruit. Therefore you must beware of them.

units.la: Verf. 4. Adulteri & adulterae, nescitis amicitiam mundi, inimicitiam esse cum Deo? Quicunque ergo voluerit amicus esse mundi, inimicus Dei constituitur.
units.tr: Verse 4. Adulterers and adulteresses, do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God? Whoever therefore wishes to be a friend of the world is made an enemy of God.

units.la: Arg. 4. Cupiditates amorem hujus mundi in vobis excitantes, in spirituale adulterium animas vestras pertrahunt, adulterosque, & adulteras reddunt vos, qui spirituali connubio Deo conjecrati estis. Ergo ab iis cavendum.
units.tr: Arg. 4. Desires that stir up love of this world in you draw your souls into spiritual adultery, and make you adulterers and adulteresses, you who have been joined to God in spiritual marriage. Therefore one must beware of them.

units.la: Quicunque ] Arg. 5. Carnales cupiditates internae dum vos in amorem & amicitiam hujus mundi trahunt, conjiciunt in odium & inimicitias Dei; siquidem quicunque sibi placere in animum induxerit, vel mundanis hominibus ipsorum moribus se conformando gratum facere statuerit, bellum adversus Deum suscipit, & militat in adversariis castris. Ergo ab iis vobis cavendum est.
units.tr: Whoever: Arg. 5. Inner carnal desires, while they draw you into love and friendship with this world, cast you into hatred and enmity with God. For whoever has resolved in his mind to please himself, or has determined to make himself agreeable by conforming his manners to worldly men, takes up war against God and fights in the enemy's camp. Therefore you must beware of them.

units.la: Verf. 5. An putatis Scripturam inaniter dicere, Ad invidiam fertur spiritus qui habitat in nobis?
units.tr: Verse 5. Or do you think that Scripture speaks in vain: the spirit that dwells in us tends toward envy?

units.la: Arg. 6. confirmans superius, Spiritus ille veteris hominis, (unde omnes carnales cupiditates excitantur) qui per naturam habitat in nobis, naturali suo impetu, & diaboli impulsu, fertur in invidiam seu odium, & Dei & proximi, sicut non frustra multis in locis docet Scriptura, de corrupta hominis natura, loquens. Sequitur ergo amicos mundi, inservientes cupiditatibus carnis esse, inimicos Dei, & cupiditates etiam illas carnales a pravo spiritu ortum ducere.
units.tr: Arg. 6, confirming the above: that spirit of the old man (from which all carnal desires are stirred up), which dwells in us by nature, by its natural impulse and at the devil's prompting, tends toward envy or hatred both of God and of neighbour. Scripture, speaking of corrupt human nature, teaches this in many places, and not without reason. It follows that friends of the world, who serve the desires of the flesh, are enemies of God, and that those carnal desires also draw their origin from a wicked spirit.

units.la: Verf. 6. Sed majorem offert gratiam, quia dicit, Deus superbis resistit, modestis autem dat gratiam.
units.tr: Verse 6. But he gives greater grace, for it says: God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.

units.la: Arg. 7. Deus jam, (postquam scilicet renati & conversi estis ad fidem Christi) dat majorem gratiam quam ut veteri inhabitante spiritu feramini in invidiam, seu odium Dei & proximi. Quod probat ex Scriptura, docente, quod sicut Deus irregenitis, superbis, & veteri Spiritu adversariis, resistit, & se opponit adversarium: sic etiam regenitis nitis resipiscentibus, & humilibus dat gratiam & auxilium, ut cupiditates carnales possint cohibere. Ergo carnales cupiditates vobis sunt fugiendæ. Hoc primum adversus carnales cupiditates remedium est.
units.tr: Arg. 7. God now (namely, after you have been reborn and converted to the faith of Christ) gives greater grace than to let you be carried away by the indwelling old spirit into envy, or hatred of God and neighbour. He proves this from Scripture, which teaches that just as God resists the unregenerate, the proud, and those opposed to the old Spirit, and sets himself against them as an adversary, so also he gives grace and help to the regenerate, the repentant, and the humble, so that they may be able to restrain carnal desires. Therefore carnal desires are to be fled from by you. This is the first remedy against carnal desires.

units.la: Verl. 7 Subjicite igitur vos DEO, resistite Diabolo, & fugiet à vobis.
units.tr: Verse 7. Submit therefore to God, resist the devil, and he will flee from you.

units.la: Arg. 8. Hortationis modo propositum, Si ut regenitos decet, amicitiam Dei ambiatis, & humiliati vos Deo regendos subjiciatis, & Diabolo resistatis, qui ducit agmen carnalium cupiditatum adversus animas vestras militantium, futurum est, ut diabolus dux cupiditatum infugam conjiciatur, atque ita cupiditates ei militantes dislipentur. Ergo carnales cupiditates vobis cohibendæ sunt: Hoc alterum est remedium.
units.tr: Arg. 8. Proposed by way of exhortation: if, as the regenerate ought, you seek the friendship of God, and humbly submit yourselves to be governed by God, and resist the devil, who leads the army of carnal desires warring against your souls, then it will come about that the devil, the leader of the desires, is put to flight, and thus the desires that fight for him are scattered. Therefore carnal desires must be restrained by you. This is the second remedy.

units.la: Verl. 8. Appropinquate Deo, & appropinquabit vobis: emundate manus, vos peccatores; & purificate corda, vos duplices animo.
units.tr: Verse 8. Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners; and purify your hearts, you double-minded.

units.la: Arg. 9. hortationis modo propositum; Si resipueritis, & ad Dominum (ut fideles decet) accesseritis, implorantes ejus auxilium, Deus appropinquaturus est vobis, & auxilium vobis laturus in hac pugna adversus cupiditates vestras, & in omnibus aliis necessitatibus, Ergo utendum est hoc remedio contra carnales cupiditates, quod tertium est remedium.
units.tr: Arg. 9. Proposed by way of exhortation: if you repent and approach the Lord (as faithful people ought), imploring his help, God is about to draw near to you and bring you help in this struggle against your desires, and in all other necessities. Therefore this remedy must be used against carnal desires; it is the third remedy.

units.la: Purificate ] Prosequitur hoc remedium specialius, hortando ut agnoscentes se peccatores esle, studeant manuum seu actionum suarum puritati: & agnoscentes se hypocritas per naturam esse, studeant puritati cordis.
units.tr: Purify yourselves: He pursues this remedy more specifically, exhorting those who acknowledge themselves to be sinners to strive for the purity of their hands and their actions; and those who acknowledge themselves to be hypocrites by nature to strive for the purity of heart.

units.la: Verl. 9 Affligimini & lugete, & flete: risus vester in luctum convertatur, & gaudium in mærorem.
units.tr: Verse 9. Be afflicted, and mourn, and weep: let your laughter be turned into mourning, and your joy into heaviness.

units.la: Prosequitur adhuc specialius hortationem ad resipiscentiam, præscribendo exercitia resipiscentiæ externa, jejunium, fletum, & reliqua quæ minimè fucatam resipiscentiam ostendant, & quæ reipsa carnales cupiditates mortificent.
units.tr: He pursues the exhortation to repentance still more specifically, prescribing outward exercises of repentance: fasting, weeping, and the rest, which show repentance not to be feigned and which in fact mortify carnal lusts.

units.la: Verl. 10. Summittite vos in conspectu Domini, & exaltabit vos.
units.tr: Verse 10. Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up.

units.la: Denique, ne in externis exercitiis acquiescant, exhortationem ad humilitatem inculcat, additâ promissione de exaltatione gratiosa, in qua victoriam adversus omnes hostes, & insuper gaudium & gloriam reportaturi sint.
units.tr: Finally, lest they rest in outward exercises, he inculcates an exhortation to humility, adding the promise of a gracious exaltation, in which they are to win victory over all enemies and, besides, to obtain joy and glory.

units.la: Secunda pars Capitis.
units.tr: The second part of the chapter.

units.la: Verf. 11. Ne alii aduersus alios loquimini, fratres: qui loquitur contra fratrem, quique damnat fratrem suum, loquitur contra Legem, & damnat Legem: quòd si damnas Legem, non es obseruator Legis, sed judex.
units.tr: Verse 11. Speak not evil one of another, brethren: he that speaks against a brother, and judges his brother, speaks against the Law and judges the Law: but if you judge the Law, you are not a doer of the Law, but a judge.

units.la: Specialis hortatio de cohibenda libidine detrahendi famæ fratris: Argumenta dehortationis sunt quinque.
units.tr: A special exhortation to restrain the lust of slandering a brother's reputation. The arguments against it are five.

units.la: Obloquitur ] Argumentum primum, Qui detrahit famæ fratris sui: judicat eum, & damnat eum: quia talem eum pronunciat ac si judex esset: Ergo non detrahendum famæ fratrum.
units.tr: Speaks evil: The first argument: he who slanders the reputation of his brother judges him and condemns him, because he pronounces him such as if he were a judge. Therefore one must not slander the reputation of brethren.

units.la: Damnat ] Arg. 2. Qui detrahit fratris famæ, & judicat fratrem seu condemnat eum, etiam detrahit legi, & judicat, seu condemnat legem. Ratio est, Quia lex, temerarias judicia & obloquutiones prohibet & damnat: detractor vero contrà, ipso facto dum detrahit aliorum famæ, actionem illam probat quasi bonam, & hic contraria legi loquitur & facit, legemque nec bonam nec dignam cui obtemperetur, pronunciat.
units.tr: Condemns: The second argument: he who slanders a brother's reputation and judges his brother, or condemns him, also slanders the law and judges or condemns the law. The reason is this: the law forbids and condemns rash judgments and evil speaking; but the slanderer, on the contrary, by the very fact that he slanders the reputation of others, approves that action as good, and so he speaks and acts against the law, and pronounces the law neither good nor worthy to be obeyed.

units.la: Obseruator ] Arg. 3. Quia qui fratri detrahit, non est obediens legis obseruator, sed legis & violator, & condemnator, ut patet ex superioribus: Ergo non detrahendum famæ fratris.
units.tr: Doer: The third argument: because he who slanders a brother is not an obedient doer of the law, but a violator and condemner of the law, as is clear from what has gone before. Therefore one must not slander the reputation of a brother.

units.la: Verf. 12. Vnus est Legislator qui potest seruare & perdere: tu quis es qui judicas alium?
units.tr: Verse 12. There is one Lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy: who are you that judge another?

units.la: Arg. 4. Pertinet ad unum Deum Judicis partes exercere, quid est ergo homuncio, qui partes Judicis Dei non datas inuadat.
units.tr: The fourth argument: it belongs to the one God to exercise the office of Judge. What then is a mere mortal, who usurps the office of God the Judge, which has not been given to him?

units.la: Solus ] Arg. 5. Deus solus, ut potest seruare, si detractor resipuerit, ita & etiam perdere, nisi de hoc & aliis peccatis resipiscendo, Dei admonitionibus obtemperaverit. Non igitur indulgendum huic peccato.
units.tr: Alone: The fifth argument: God alone, as he is able to save if the slanderer repents, so also is able to destroy, unless he obeys God's admonitions by repenting of this and other sins. Therefore this sin is not to be indulged.

units.la: Tertia pars.
units.tr: The third part.

units.la: Verf. 13. Age nunc qui dicitis, Hodie vel cras ibimus in illam urbem, & agemus ibi annum unum, & mercabimur, & lucrabimur:
units.tr: Verse 13. Come now, you who say, Today or tomorrow we will go into such a city, and spend a year there, and trade, and make gain:

units.la: Tertia admonitio ad mercatores potissimum, de corrigendo socordi Diuinæ providentiæ neglectu in negotiis suscipiendis. Peccati hujus ipsos convincit ex dictis ἐμμηλύσεις propositis. Argumenta hortationis sunt sex.
units.tr: The third admonition, chiefly to merchants, to correct the careless neglect of divine providence in undertaking business. He convicts them of this sin by means of the words set forth, the ἐμμηλύσεις. The arguments of the exhortation are six.

units.la: Argumentum primum, In formula citationis ad Tribunal Dei continetur, Age, &c. Quasi diceret, hic profanus & impius deliberandi modus, qui Deum providentiam non agnoscit, nec potest ferre examen Dei, nec hominum recte judicantium, quasi enim vos Domini estis vitae vestrae, & virium veltrarum, & successus laborum veltrorum, ita loquimini, non audetis hunc morem coram Deo defendere. Ergo propter hujusmodi loquendi formulas a vobis usurpatas, profanitatis rei tenemini.
units.tr: The first argument: the formula of summons to God's tribunal is contained in Come now, etc. As if he said: this profane and impious manner of deliberating, which does not acknowledge divine providence, cannot bear the examination of God or of men who judge rightly. For you speak as if you were lords of your own life, of your own strength, and of the success of your labours, and you do not dare to defend this custom before God. Therefore, on account of these forms of speech used by you, you are held guilty of profanity.

units.la: Versi. 14. Qui ignoratis quid futurum sit postero die, quae est enim vita vestra? vapor enim est qui ad exiguum tempus apparet, & deinde evanescit.
units.tr: Verse 14. Whereas you know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appears for a little time, and then vanishes away.

units.la: Arg. 2. Stolide statuitis de futuro, cum ignoremus omnes quid die crastino futurum sit: Profanitatis ergo arguendi hic estis.
units.tr: The second argument: you foolishly determine concerning the future, when we all know not what the next day will bring. Therefore you are convicted here of profanity.

units.la: Quid enim ] Arg. 3. Oblivisci mini vestrae mortalitatis, & fragilitatis vitae vestrae, quae est instar vaporis, qui ad modicum tempus apparet, mox vento dilectus evanescit: Profanitatis ergo merito hic arguendi estis.
units.tr: For what is: The third argument: you forget your mortality and the frailty of your life, which is like a vapour that appears for a short time and soon vanishes, carried off by the wind. Therefore you are rightly convicted here of profanity.

units.la: Vers. 15. Pro eo quod dicere debuistis, Si Dominus voluerit, & vivamus, faciemus hoc aut illud.
units.tr: Verse 15. For that you ought to say, If the Lord will, and we shall live, we shall do this or that.

units.la: Arg. 4. Non consideratis vobis pendendum esse a Divina voluntate, quae rerum omnium est fons, regula & mensura: In quo Argumento simul remedium praescribit adversus hoc malum, ut scilicet semper non tantum Dei voluntatem imperantem, seu revelatam (quae, quid, & quomodo agendum sit nobis praescribit) sed etiam voluntatem Dei arcanam, gubernantem, & efficaciter operantem in nobis, & per nos, quid, & quantum, & quandiu vitum est ipsi serio agnoscamus: cujus voluntati nos actiones nostras, & earum successum, & vitam ipsam nostram submittere debemus, in corde semper considerantes nos sine Dei voluntate efficaci nihil posse: & ut formulis hujusmodi assuefacamus. (Si Deus voluerit, Si vitam, reliquaque ad actionem necessaria suppeditaverit) Quantum ad Dei gloriam satis est: Nam non injicit Apostolus religionem externorum verborum, quasi nunquam has formulas omittere fas esset, sed continuam Divinae providentiae in corde agnitionem requirit, & externam in verbis professionem talem, quae a profanis nos distinguat.
units.tr: The fourth argument: you do not consider that we must depend on the divine will, which is the source, rule and measure of all things. In this argument he at the same time prescribes a remedy against this evil, namely that we should always seriously acknowledge not only the commanding or revealed will of God (which prescribes to us what, and how, we must act), but also the hidden will of God, which governs and effectually works in us and through us, what, and how much, and how long it is pleasing to him that we live. To this will we ought to submit our actions, their success, and life itself, always considering in our hearts that we can do nothing without the effectual will of God; and that we should accustom ourselves to such formulas (If God wills, if he grants life and the rest needed for action). As far as the glory of God is concerned, this is enough. For the Apostle does not impose a religion of outward words, as if it were never lawful to omit these formulas; rather he requires a continual acknowledgment of divine providence in the heart, and an outward profession in words of such a kind as distinguishes us from the profane.

units.la: Vers. 16. Nunc autem gloriamini de arrogantia vestra: omnis ejusmodi gloriatio, mala est. Arg. 5. Admoniti defenditis hunc profanum loquendi modum, & quasi gloriamini in vana veltra jactantia, per quam stuporem cordis impium proditis aperte.
units.tr: Verse 16. But now you glory in your arrogance: all such glorying is evil. The fifth argument: though admonished, you defend this profane manner of speaking, and as it were glory in your vain boasting, by which you openly reveal the impious stupor of your heart.

units.la: Verf. 17. Igitur qui noverit recte facere, nec facit, hic peccato tenetur.
units.tr: Verse 17. Therefore he who knows how to do good, and does not do it, to him it is sin.

units.la: Arg. 6. Per occupationem objectionis, Si omnia vestra negotia Divinæ providentiæ committenda esse scitis, & tamen non tantum contra facitis, sed etiam ne sanctis quidem loquendi formulis in externo sermone providentiam Dei agnoscitis, nonne quanto magis officium vestrum scitis, tanto graviorem reatum, & pœnam vobis accersitis?
units.tr: The sixth argument, by anticipating an objection: if you know that all your business must be committed to divine providence, and yet not only act against this, but also, in your outward speech, do not acknowledge the providence of God even by holy forms of speaking, do you not, the more you know your duty, bring upon yourselves a heavier guilt and punishment?

units.la: Caput Quintum.
units.tr: Chapter 5.

units.la: Vinque hoc capite continentur admonitiones: Prima, ad divites dirigitur, de imminente in illos Dei ira, ad verf. 7. Altera admonitio est pauperum ad patientiam, ad verf. 11. Tertia admonitio est omnium, ne temere jurent, ad verf. 13. Quarta est ad afflictos & ægrotos, ad verf. 19. Ultima est ad omnes, ut errantes in viam revocent, verf. 19, 20.
units.tr: Five admonitions are contained in this chapter. The first, addressed to the rich, concerns the wrath of God hanging over them, to verse 7. The second is an admonition to the poor to patience, to verse 11. The third is an admonition to all not to swear rashly, to verse 13. The fourth is to the afflicted and the sick, to verse 19. The last is to all, that they should call back those who have gone astray, verses 19, 20.

units.la: Verf. 1. Agite nunc divites, flete, ululantes super miseriis vestris superventuris.
units.tr: Verse 1. Come now, you rich, weep and wail over the miseries that are coming upon you.

units.la: Admonitio prima ad divites abutentes divitiis suis, qua excitat eos ad seriam conditionis suæ considerationem, iisque luctus & lachrymarum causas exponit novem. Prima, Quia miseriæ multæ vobis imminent, & brevi supervenient.
units.tr: The first admonition, addressed to the rich who abuse their riches, by which he stirs them to a serious consideration of their condition, and sets before them nine causes for grief and tears. The first: because many miseries hang over you and will soon come upon you.

units.la: Verf. 2. Divitiæ vestræ putrefactæ sunt, vestimenta vestra obnoxia tineis facta sunt.
units.tr: Verse 2. Your riches have rotted, and your garments have become moth-eaten.

units.la: Causa 2. Perditè avari estis, qui nec divitiarum usum fructum ipsi habetis, nec aliis conceditis, sed malletis corrumpi apud vos divitias vestras, quam de iis in pauperum usus quicquam erogare.
units.tr: Cause 2. You are utterly greedy: you neither enjoy the use and fruit of your riches yourselves nor allow others to have them, but would rather let your riches rot among you than spend any of them for the use of the poor.

units.la: Vestimenta ] Causa 3. Jam incipit Dei vindicta quasi lepra depascere vestrum idolum mammona, ut apparet in putredine, tineis, ærugine, quæ tanquam lictores à Deo missi jam invaserunt inutiles vestras opes.
units.tr: Garments] Cause 3. Now God's vengeance has begun to eat away, like a leprosy, at your idol Mammon, as is evident in the rot, the moths and the rust, which, like lictors sent by God, have already invaded your useless wealth.

units.la: Verf. 3. Aurum & argentum vestrum ærugine vitiatum est; & ærugo eorum testabitur adversus vos, & exedet carnes vestras velut ignis: thesaurum congessistis in ultimos dies.
units.tr: Verse 3. Your gold and silver is corroded by rust; and their rust will testify against you and will eat your flesh like fire. You have stored up treasure for the last days.

units.la: Causa 4. Jam parantur adversus vos testes, ærugo, tineæ, & putredo, quæ vobis convincendis & condemnandis, de abusu divitiarum in die judicii sufficient.
units.tr: Cause 4. Now witnesses are being readied against you: rust, moths and rot, which will be enough to convict and condemn you on the day of judgment for the abuse of your riches.

units.la: Causa 5. Vertendi sunt hi testes in tortores post Judicium extremum, quando cremandi estis in inferno, in quo animæ vestræ, infelices, & corpora cruciatibus exedenda erunt, tanquam igne.
units.tr: Cause 5. These witnesses are to be turned into torturers after the final judgment, when you will be burned in hell, where your wretched souls and bodies will be consumed by torments as by fire.

units.la: Causa 6. Cum putatis vos in senectam & posterorum usus thesauros congessisse, iræ thesauros congessistis in ultimum diem, quando revelanda est DEI vindicta in omnes injustos.
units.tr: Cause 6. Since you think you have stored up treasures for your old age and for the use of posterity, you have stored up treasures of wrath for the last day, when God's vengeance is to be revealed against all the unrighteous.

units.la: Verf. 4. Ecce merces operariorum qui messuerunt regiones vestras, à vobis intercepta, clamat: & clamores eorum qui messuerunt, in aures Domini Sabaoth introierunt.
units.tr: Verse 4. Behold, the wages of the workers who reaped your fields, which you have kept back, cry out; and the cries of those who reaped have entered the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth.

units.la: Causa 7. Crudeliter defraudastis operarios mercede suâ, quarum injuriarum vox ascendit ad DEUM Judicem, qui exercitus Cœli & Terræ in vindictam paratos habet, & pro meritis vos tractaturus est.
units.tr: Cause 7. You have cruelly defrauded the workers of their wages, and the voice of these injuries rises up to God the Judge, who has the armies of heaven and earth prepared for vengeance, and he will deal with you according to your deserts.

units.la: Verf. 5. In deliciis vixistis super terram, & lascivistis: enutriistis corda vestra ut in die mactationis.
units.tr: Verse 5. You have lived in luxury upon the earth and wantoned; you have nourished your hearts as on a day of slaughter.

units.la: Causa 8. Luxuriosi estis epulones, voluptatibus securè indulgentes, quasi dies singulì essent dies festivitatis, seu mactationis, quibus ad convivia mactari solent pecudes.
units.tr: Cause 8. You are luxurious feasters, indulging your pleasures without care, as if each day were a day of festivity or of slaughter, on which animals are customarily slaughtered for banquets.

units.la: Verf. 6. Condemnastis, occidistis justum: non resistit vobis.
units.tr: Verse 6. You have condemned, you have killed the just man; he does not resist you.

units.la: Causa 9. Quia injustè & crudeliter curatis condemnandos in judiciis, & occidendos innocentes & impotentes, qui vobis resistere non potuerunt. Ergo justas causas habetis flendi & ejulandi super ærumnis in vos propediem venturis.
units.tr: Cause 9. Because you unjustly and cruelly arrange for the condemnation of men in judgments, and the killing of the innocent and the powerless, who could not resist you. Therefore you have just cause to weep and wail over the calamities that are soon to come upon you.

units.la: Verf. 7. Patientes igitur estote, fratres, usque ad Domini adventum. Ecce, agricola expectat pretiosum fructum terræ, patienter eum expectans, dum accipiat pluviam matutinam & serotinam.
units.tr: Verse 7. Be patient therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. Behold, the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, patiently awaiting it until he receives the early and the late rain.

units.la: Admonitio 2. ad pios oppressos, ut patienter tolerent injurias Divitum improborum. Argumenta hortationis sunt octo. Vsque ad Argumentum primum, Adventus DOMINI terminus erit afflictionum, offerens vindictam in adversarios, & consolationem afflictis. Patientes ergo estote.
units.tr: Admonition 2, to the pious who are oppressed, that they should patiently bear the injuries of the wicked rich. There are eight arguments for this exhortation. "Until": the first argument, the coming of the Lord will be the end of afflictions, bringing vengeance on the adversaries and comfort to the afflicted. Therefore be patient.

units.la: Agricola] Arg. 2. Agricola moram longam inter sementem & messem; inter pluviam matutinam, quæ cadit post semen jactum, & serotinam, quæ cadit sub tempus messis, patienter tolerat ipse messis seu pretiosi fructus terræ. Ergo vos decet patienter tolerare moram, usque in adventum DOMINI sub spe fructus patientiæ, seu liberationis è cœlo venturæ.
units.tr: "Farmer"] Argument 2. The farmer patiently bears the long delay between sowing and harvest, between the early rain, which falls after the seed is sown, and the late rain, which falls near harvest time, that he may have the precious fruit of the earth. Therefore it becomes you to bear patiently the delay until the coming of the Lord, in hope of the fruit of patience, or of deliverance to come from heaven.

units.la: Vers. 8 'Patientes estote & vos, & stabilite corda vestra, quoniam adventus Domini appropinquat'.
units.tr: Verse 8. Be patient you also, and establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord draws near.

units.la: Arg. 3. Propinquus est Domini adventus, ad uniuscujusque solutionem ex hoc tabernaculo: & breve est tempus ad ultimum judicium si comparetur vel cum tempore elapso, vel cum vitâ æternâ futurâ. Obfirmanda ergo vobis sunt corda, & per fidem stabilienda, ut patienter moram feratis.
units.tr: Argument 3. The coming of the Lord is near, for the release of each one from this tabernacle; and the time until the final judgment is short, whether it is compared with the time that has passed or with the future eternal life. Your hearts must therefore be strengthened and established by faith, that you may bear the delay patiently.

units.la: Vers. 9. Ne ingemiscite alius adversus alium, fratres: ut ne condemnemini: ecce, judex ante januam adstat.
units.tr: Verse 9. Do not groan against one another, brothers, that you may not be condemned; behold, the judge stands before the door.

units.la: Arg. 4. per modum hortationis propositum, Patienter ferendæ vobis sunt injuriæ, etiam ab iis qui intra Ecclesiam sunt, sine murmuratione, alius adversus alium. Ergo multò magis ferendæ sunt patienter injuriæ ab impiis Diuitibus vobis illatæ.
units.tr: Argument 4, put by way of exhortation: injuries must be patiently borne, even those from people within the Church, without murmuring against one another. Therefore injuries inflicted by the wicked rich must all the more be patiently borne.

units.la: Vt non ] Confirmat hoc argumentum, Quia alioqui metuendum, ne & vos ipsi culpæ alicujus rei condemnemini à Deo Judice, qui præ foribus stat, paratus ad judicandum, si vel accusatoriè quidem ingemiscatis, alius adversùs alium.
units.tr: "Lest"] This argument is confirmed, because otherwise there is reason to fear that you yourselves may be condemned for some fault by God the Judge, who stands before the doors, ready to judge, if you groan even in accusation against one another.

units.la: Vers. 10. Sumite, fratres mei, pro exemplari afflictionis ac patientiæ, Prophetas, qui locuti sunt in nomine Domini.
units.tr: Verse 10. Take, my brothers, the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord as an example of affliction and patience.

units.la: Arg. 5. Etiam Prophetæ, Dei legati ad Ecclesiam, injurias ab impiis patienter passi sunt. Ergo & vos patienter decet pati.
units.tr: Argument 5. Even the prophets, God's messengers to the Church, patiently suffered injuries from the wicked. Therefore you too should patiently suffer.

units.la: Vers. 11. Ecce, beatos pronuntiamus eos qui afflictionem sustinent. Tolerantiam Job audistis, & finem Domini vidistis; nam valdè misericors est Dominus ac commiserans.
units.tr: Verse 11. Behold, we call blessed those who endure. You have heard of the patience of Job and have seen the end the Lord gave him; for the Lord is very merciful and compassionate.

units.la: Arg. 6 Patienter ferentes injurias beatos prædicamus. Ergo & vos patientes estote. Job ] Arg. 7. Sicut Job non tantùm afflictiones ab hostibus patienter tulit, sed etiam amicorum injurias summas, & tandem lætum exitum ex malis invenit, Sic vobis patienter ferentibus injuriam lætus expectandus est exitus.
units.tr: Argument 6. We call blessed those who patiently bear injuries. Therefore you too should be patient. "Job"] Argument 7. Just as Job not only bore afflictions from enemies patiently, but also endured the greatest injuries from his friends, and at last found a happy outcome from his evils, so for you, who bear injury patiently, a happy outcome is to be expected.

units.la: Abundat ] Arg. 8. confirmans superius, Deus erga afflictos, potissimum injurie vexatos ab hominibus est valde misericors, & ad dandam veniam pro sua misericordia propensus, propterea quod ipsorum malis afficiatur: Ergo patienter ferendæ vobis sunt injuriæ.
units.tr: "Abounds"] Argument 8, confirming what was said above: God is very merciful toward the afflicted, especially those vexed by injuries from men, and is inclined to grant pardon out of his mercy, because he is moved by their evils. Therefore injuries must be patiently borne by you.

units.la: Verl. 12. Ante omnia autem, fratres mei. ne jurate neque per cælum, neque per terram, neque aliud ullud jusjurandum; sit autem vestrum est, est, & non, non, ne in condemnationem incidatis.
units.tr: Verse 12. Above all, my brothers, do not swear, neither by heaven, nor by earth, nor by any other oath; but let your yes be yes, and your no be no, lest you fall into condemnation.

units.la: Admonitio 3. De non temere jurando, à quo vitio specialiter, & ante omnia cavere jubet, quia specialiter in decalogo vetitum est: & Hebraeis videtur nimis familiare fuisse; & ne ambagibus se deluderent, vetat per creaturas jurare, quæ vel in Cælo vel in Terra sunt. Rationes addit duas.
units.tr: Admonition 3. Concerning not swearing rashly, a vice from which he especially, and above all, bids them beware, because it is specifically forbidden in the Decalogue; and it seems to have been too familiar among the Hebrews. And lest they deceive themselves with evasions, he forbids swearing by creatures, whether in heaven or on earth. He adds two reasons.

units.la: Ratio prima, Quia sufficit vera affirmatio, & vera negatio in quotidiano sermone: si quid supra sit, nisi vobis caveatis, peccabitis.
units.tr: The first reason: because a plain affirmation and a plain negation suffice in everyday speech; if you go beyond this, you will sin, unless you take care.

units.la: Ratio 2. Quia alioqui incidetis in Dei judicium, & condemnationem, sicut in lege comminatur Deus.
units.tr: Reason 2: because otherwise you will fall under God's judgment and condemnation, as God threatens in the law.

units.la: Vers 13. Affligitur aliquis inter vos? oret, æquo animo est aliquis? psallat.
units.tr: Verse 13. Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing psalms.

units.la: Admonitio 4. De ratione recte gerendi se in adversis & prosperis; specialiter vero in morbo. Hujus quatuor sunt membra: 1. De ægris animo, ob aliquam afflictionem, ut Deum orent, hoc est, ut in Deum suam solicitudinem exonerent: 2. Membrum de hilaribus animo, ne securitate diffluant, & Dei oblivisccantur, sed hilaritatem animi convertant in laudes Dei, & gratiarum actionem, hoc est, ut spirituali aliquo exercitio foveant ευθυμίαν, ne lætitia ipsorum degeneret in carnalem laicviam.
units.tr: Admonition 4. Concerning the right way to conduct oneself in adversity and prosperity, and especially in sickness. It has four parts: 1. Concerning those who are troubled in spirit because of some affliction, that they pray to God, that is, that they unburden their anxiety upon God. 2. A part concerning those cheerful in spirit, that they not dissolve in security and forget God, but turn the cheerfulness of their spirit into praise of God and thanksgiving, that is, that they foster by some spiritual exercise a sense of well-being [εὐθυμίαν], lest their joy degenerate into carnal levity.

units.la: Verl. 14. Infirmatur quis inter vos? accersat presbyteros Ecclesiæ, & orent pro eo, ungentes eum oleo in nomine Domini.
units.tr: Verse 14. Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord.

units.la: Tertium membrum de ægris corpore, ut antequam ad medicos confugiant, convertant se ad Deum, & Ministros Ecclesiæ advocent, qui in ipsis resipiscentiam, fidem & consolationem excitare & fovere poterint: Deinde ut Presbyteri orent Deum pro ægroto. Tertio, ut si quis inter Presbyteros cujuscunque ordinis, donum sanationis habeat, (quod in Ecclesia temporibus Apostolorum vigebat,) nomine & auctoritate Domini Iesu Christi, qui hoc donum dedit, utatur dono, & exemplo discipulorum Christi, qui Marc. 6. 13. potestate à Christo accepta
units.tr: The third member concerns the sick in body: that before they resort to physicians, they turn to God and call for the ministers of the Church, who can arouse and foster in them repentance, faith and consolation. Then, that the elders pray to God for the sick person. Thirdly, that if anyone among the elders of whatever rank has the gift of healing (which flourished in the Church in the times of the Apostles), he should use the gift in the name and authority of the Lord Jesus Christ, who gave this gift, and following the example of the disciples of Christ, who (Mark 6:13), having received power from Christ,

units.la: accepta acceptâ, unxerunt oleo multos ægrotos, & sanarunt eos) ungat ægrotum illum, de cujus sanitate restituenda Spiritus Sanctus certiorem eum reddiderit: Nam certum est Presbyteros qui dono sanationis præditi erant, non unxisse quoslibet ægrotos, sed eos tantùm, de quorum sanitate restituenda certiores reddebantur à Spiritu Sancto.
units.tr: having received power, anointed many sick people with oil and healed them, let him anoint that sick person about whose restoration to health the Holy Spirit has assured him. For it is certain that the elders who were endowed with the gift of healing did not anoint just any sick people, but only those about whose restoration to health they were assured by the Holy Spirit.
